They might use several of these animals, as they still do in some parts of the world, for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> of burdens and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>: for we may take it for granted that the first inventions for eating men of labour, would be of the simplest kind, and such as came easiest to hand. But keeping flocks of sheep, goats, and such like, would be of great utility, by affording quantities of milk, which is found to be the most nourishing diet both to the young and the old: and their carcasses, though not used as food, might answer some useful purposes perhaps in manuring the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. The Antediluvian world was, in all probability, stocked with a much greater number of inhabitants than the present earth either actually does, or perhaps is capable of containing or supplying. This seems naturally to follow from the great length of their lives, which exceeding the present standard of life in the proportion, at least, of ten to one, the Antediluvians must accordingly in any long space of time double themselves, at least in about the tenth part of the time in which mankind do now double themselves. It has been supposed that they began to beget children as early, and left off as late, in proportion, as men do now; and that the several children of the same father succeeded as quickly one after another as they usually do at this day: and as many generations, which are but successive with us, were contemporary before the flood, the number of people living on the earth at once would be by that means sufficiently increased to answer any defect which might arise from other circumstances not considered. So that, if we make a computation on these principles, we shall find, that there was a considerable number of people in the world at the death of Abel, though their father Adam was not then 130 years old; and that the number of mankind before the deluge would easily amount to above one hundred thousand millions (even according to the Samaritan chronology), that is, to twenty times as many as our present earth has, in all probability, now upon it, or can well be supposed capable of maintaining in its present condition. The following table, made upon the above-mentioned principles by Mr Whiston, shows at least what a number of people might have been in the Antediluvian world. | Number of mankind | Year of the world | Year of doubling | Series | |-------------------|------------------|-----------------|--------| | 4 | 2 | 2 | 1 | | 8 | 6 | 4 | 2 | | 16 | 12 | 6 | 3 | | 32 | 20 | 8 | 4 | | 64 | 30 | 10 | 5 | | 128 | 42 | 12 | 6 | | 256 | 56 | 14 | 7 | | 512 | 72 | 16 | 8 | | 1024 | 90 | 18 | 9 | | 2048 | 110 | 20 | 10 | | 4096 | 132 | 22 | 11 | | 8192 | 156 | 24 | 12 | | 16,384 | 182 | 26 | 13 | | 32,768 | 210 | 28 | 14 | | 65,536 | 240 | 30 | 15 | | 131,072 | 272 | 32 | 16 | | 262,144 | 306 | 34 | 17 | | 524,288 | 342 | 36 | 18 | | 1,048,576 | 380 | 38 | 19 | | 2,077,152 | 420 | 40 | 20 | | 4,143,304 | 462 | 42 | 21 | | 8,388,608 | 506 | 44 | 22 | | 16,777,216 | 552 | 46 | 23 | | 33,554,432 | 600 | 48 | 24 | | 67,108,864 | 650 | 50 | 25 | | 134,217,728 | 702 | 52 | 26 | | 268,435,456 | 756 | 54 | 27 | | 536,870,912 | 812 | 56 | 28 | | 1,073,741,824 | 870 | 58 | 29 | | 2,147,483,648 | 930 | 60 | 30 | | 4,294,967,296 | 992 | 62 | 31 | | 8,589,934,592 | 1056 | 64 | 32 | | 17,179,869,184 | 1122 | 66 | 33 | | 34,359,738,368 | 1190 | 68 | 34 | | 68,719,476,736 | 1260 | 70 | 35 | | 137,438,953,472 | 1332 | 72 | 36 | | 274,877,926,944 | 1406 | 74 | 37 | | 549,755,813,888 | 1482 | 76 | 38 | But But according to a later writer upon the subject, the above table, though the numbers there may be thought sufficient for the peopling of the earth, we could by no means depend upon, for several reasons; particularly, 1. It is laid down there as a foundation, that the Antediluvians would double themselves every forty years; as indeed they would, and in less time, after there came to be 100 marriages. Now, had the author observed this regular progression in his computation, by adding 40 years to every former period of the age of the world, the amount, instead of two millions of millions, &c., would have been above five millions of millions at the year 1656, the age of the world at the deluge, according to the Hebrew numbers, which he contends for. What would the sum then have been, had we carried on the computation for 600 years more, according to the Septuagint? 2. He supposes the period of doubling must have been much shorter in the earliest ages, and much longer in the latter, contrary to reason and fact. For mankind being sprung from one pair only, the increase at first must have been very slow, but come on very fast when a considerable number were married. His table therefore is made not regularly, but according to fancy, by unequal starts or chains, at great intervals in the latter part, where it should have been most regular; it would seem with no other view than to raise such a number, upon the whole, as might be thought sufficient to people the earth. 3. In that calculation the two material <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, the time of nursing and the age of puberty, are quite overlooked, by which all computations of the numbers in the Antediluvian world must be regulated. What unavoidable mistakes this omission must occasion, will be seen by examining the first ten numbers of the said table. | Years of the world and intervals of doublings | Number of increase according to the intervals | |---------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------| | 1 | 2 Adam and Eve. | | 2 | 4 Cain and Abel. | | 6 | 8 | | 12 | 16 | | 20 | 32 | | 30 | 64 | | 42 | 128 | | 50 | 256 | | 72 | 512 | | 90 | 1024 | | 110 | 2048 | On this table it may be observed, 1. That though there were but two persons created at first, this computation makes four persons in the second year of the world. This could not possibly be, except Cain had been born within 12 months after the creation, which is highly improbable, and Abel in the second year, yet far more improbable; for in that case Eve could not have suckled Cain. 2. In the fifth year of the world we have eight persons, that is, six children of Eve's in five years. "But (our author adds) what shall Eve do with six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> in five years? Where could she find so many wet nurses for them? Or would the mother of all living deny her children that nourishment which the Creator had appointed for their first food, the milk in her breasts?" Do they consider that there was but one woman in the Antediluvian world to do for herself, her husband, and her children, what belongs to women to do? We should surely have more respect and compassion for the mother of all mankind, than to lay such an intolerable burden upon her, whose sorrow for her own deception, and thereby ruining both herself and her husband, must have been very great for many years. In punishment of which, though God had said he would greatly multiply her sorrow and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>, the meaning was not, that she should have a child every year, which could not be, because the nature of that food and nourishment appointed by himself for her children would not permit it. Nor yet when he commanded them to increase and multiply and replenish the earth, could the command be obeyed in such a manner as was contrary to the order of nature and providence. But the method intended to answer the design of the command was to prolong their lives to above 800 and 900 years, and their prolific powers for 340 and 360 years of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of life, that by slow and sure and long continuance of increase they might people the earth in due time." 3. The same exception lies to all the following periods of doubling, where the number far exceeds what it could possibly be in fact; but we shall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> them over, and come to the last of them in the year 110, in which the number of mankind is made 2048. Now in the year 110 not one of Adam's children was married, because not yet come to the age of puberty. In that year of the world there could be no more than 18 or 20 persons, at single births, besides Adam and Eve. It is a great mistake therefore to imagine, that the periods of doubling were much shorter in the earlier times than in the latter; the contrary of which is evident to reason. According to our author, two errors have been fallen into in treating of this point; namely, 1. That in the 1st p. 87, first ages of the world, both before and after the Flood, men began to propagate their kind as early as they commonly do at present. 2. That the children of the same father succeeded one after another as fast as they do now, that is, that the women brought forth children every year. The first of these errors he confutes. Of the ages by shewing that the several periods or stages of man's among the life bear a just proportion to one another, and to the Antediluvian whole term of life; and that the period of puberty or maturity has not been the same at all times, but is according to the length or brevity of life in the different ages of the world, according to that remark of St Augustine, *Tanto servior fuit proportione pubertatis, quanto vitae totius <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> annos.* Moses, he observes, gives the age of the world from the creation to the deluge, and from that period to his own time chiefly by generations. A generation is the interval of years between the births of father and son. This the Latins call *etas,* and the Greeks *γενεα.* Now, a generation, or the interval of years between father and son, has not been, neither possibly could be, the same in all ages from the beginning, as Vossius justly observes; but has varied greatly according to the length or brevity of man's life in the several periods of the world. Since the ordinary term of man's life has been reduced to 70 and 80 years, the time of puberty is in proportion to this brevity of life, and reckoned at 20 or 21, which is the fourth part of a life of four score. The several stages Antediluvian stages of human life are infancy, childhood, youth, manhood, full age, declension, old or decrepit age; all which commonly bear a proportion to the whole term of life. Now the bounds and limits of these several stages cannot be precisely the same in all, but vary in respect of the disposition of men's bodies, their course of life, and also the places and ages in which they live. In the Antediluvian world then, when men lived to upwards of 800 and 900 years, can it be thought that they passed through the several stages of life in as short time as men do now, who seldom exceed 80, and not one in ten arrives at that age? But if the Antediluvians arrived at puberty or manhood as soon as men do now, then would the several stages of human life have been lost or confounded, and men would have started from childhood to manhood at once, without any due or regular intervals, contrary to the order of nature. But if, according to the present economy of nature, man is but a youth at 20, which is a fourth part of our term of life, we may reasonably conclude, there would be a suitable proportion of years in a much longer term of life, since nature is constant and uniform in her operations. And though in so long a life as the Antediluvians enjoyed, the time of puberty might be a fifth or a sixth part of their term of life, yet would they be but youths at 150 or 160; which bears much the same proportion to the whole of their life as 20 is to that of ours. The other is an error, he thinks, which could never have been fallen into, had it been considered, that every mother suckled her own children in those early days; and indeed where could she have found another to have done it for her? Taking it for granted, then, that it was an universal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> for women to suckle their children as well before as after the flood, the next question is, for how long time they continued nurses? He shows various influences, that when man's life was reduced to 130 or 140 years, the ordinary time of nursing was two years; he thence infers, that for three or four generations after the flood, when men lived to about 400 years, the time would be so much longer in proportion, and would not be less than three or four years; and consequently, that before the flood, when life was protracted to 800 or 900 years, it would be still longer in proportion to their longevity; so that five years might be the ordinary time of nursing in the old world; and therefore that we cannot reckon less than five years between the births. For man's life being prolonged to many hundred years at first for the more speedy peopling of the earth, he came by slow degrees to mature age, there being a long time required to rear up a body that was to last near 1000 years. The intervals therefore of infancy, childhood, youth, and mature age, were so much longer in proportion to ours as the difference is between our term of life and theirs: and 150 or 160 years, with respect to their longevity, was no more in proportion than 20 is to the brevity of our life. As the Antediluvians therefore were so very long in growing up to mature age, he concludes that the time of nursing could not be shorter than five years, and that the distance between the births in a regular way must be set at five years. Upon the whole, he thinks it evident that there could be no such speedy increase of mankind at the beginning as is imagined; that the time of nursing above specified was no more than necessary for that strength of constitution which was to last for 800 and 900 years; and that women who were to continue bearing children for 340 or 360 years of their life, should have them but slowly, and at the distance of several years, that their strength might hold out, and that they might not be overburthened with too many cares at once; and therefore, when Eve's first child was six years old, it was time enough for her to have another, and so on, though possibly sometimes twins. These points being discussed, he proceeds, 1. To calculate what number upon the whole might be born into the world from the creation to near the time of the deluge; and then, 2. To state the needful deductions for deaths and other deficiencies. 1. How long the parents of mankind continued in paradise, we know not; though longer perhaps than is commonly imagined. We shall even suppose two or three years, in which time there was no child born, nor any attempt towards it. We shall allow them two or three years more to lament their fall, and the miserable estate their want of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and disobedience had brought them to, from a most happy condition; and suppose Cain to be born six years after the creation (in which supposition few, probably, will be apt to think us too hasty), and Abel again six years after him, and so every fifth year Eve to have had a child, the first seven, eight, or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> whereof were probably all males (the males being longer in coming to maturity than the females); and this distance between the births will also be thought a sufficient allowance. At this rate of increase Adam would have in 100 years 16 children, in 200 years 32, and in 400 years 64 children; when we will suppose Eve to have left off child-bearing. Nor need this number of Adam's children be thought too great, when there are instances in these later ages, and this short period of man's life, of those who have had 40 children at single births by two successive wives, and of many others who have had 20, 25, and 30, by one wife; though in such <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> it is not to be supposed that the women suckled their children. 2. Though it is reasonable to think that the Antediluvians, notwithstanding their longevity, came to mature age at 150; yet as we are not sure that they all married so soon as they were ripe for <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, and that the earliest in the genealogies is born in the 162nd year of his father, who might probably be a first born, our author does not suppose Cain, Abel, or any of the succeeding children or grandchildren of Adam to have married till they were 160, but to have had children from 161 or 162 till they were of the age of 500, at the fore-named distance or interval between the births; though Noah we know had three sons after he was 500, at the due intervals. And to all the Antediluvians we may allow, without fear of exceeding, 50 or 54 children in general, according to the course of nature, and the longevity of those first ages of the world. 3. Let us next inquire in what number of years the men of that world might double themselves, notwithstanding the long intervals between the births. The increase indeed will be found very small for the first 300 or 400 years, as they were late in coming to maturity; but the succeeding ages will swell the account exceedingly. Let us suppose at present (what shall be proved afterwards) that in the year of the world 500, there were 200 persons only, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, of full age to marry, the men at 160, the women at 120 or thereabout. The first or second year after the marriage will probably produce 100 births from 100 couples, and every fifth year after 100 more. At this slow progression the 200 married persons will, in 19 or 20 years, be increased to 600; so that the number of mankind would be trebled in 20 years, after there came 100 pair to be married. And in this manner they would increase and multiply every 20 years, or in that space treble themselves. It may perhaps be objected, that though it appears that such an increase might be at first from the first 100 marriages, yet they could not continue thus to multiply at such periods; because, according to the rule we have laid down, none of the issue of these 100 first marriages could increase the number of mankind till the men had attained the age of 160. It is true they could not; but then it must be remembered, that the first 100 pair are still adding every fifth year 100 more to the number of mankind, even till after the 400 born in the first 20 years are married, and begin a new stock for increase; so that when there came to be some hundred couples married, the increase and multiplication would come on very fast, and in 1000 years mankind would be prodigiously increased. But though there be nothing in this supposition contrary to reason, viz. That after the year of the world 500, they might treble themselves in 20 years; yet we will not reckon upon so short an interval, but will allow a much longer time even to their doubling themselves, and shall exhibit two tables of doubling; the first at the interval of 50 years (much too long indeed), the other at the interval of 40 years, and both beginning at the year 500, when there could not be fewer (whatever more there might be) than 100 married or marriageable persons descended from Adam and Eve. | Years of the World | Number of Mankind | |-------------------|------------------| | 500 | 200 | | 550 | 400 | | 600 | 800 | | 650 | 1,600 | | 700 | 3,200 | | 750 | 6,400 | | 800 | 12,800 | | 850 | 25,600 | | 900 | 51,200 | | 950 | 102,400 | | 1000 | 204,800 | | 1050 | 409,600 | | 1100 | 819,200 | | 1150 | 1,638,400 | | 1200 | 3,276,800 | | 1250 | 6,553,600 | | 1300 | 13,107,200 | | 1350 | 26,214,400 | | 1400 | 52,428,800 | | 1450 | 104,857,600 | | 1500 | 209,715,200 | | 1550 | 419,430,400 | | 1600 | 838,860,800 | | 1650 | 1,677,721,600 | This table is calculated at the long interval of 50 years, that it may appear that even by under-rating the number of mankind, there would be so many millions born into the world before the deluge came, that they would be obliged to spread themselves over the face of the earth, though but one half of the sum total of 429,496 millions had been alive at the time of the deluge; but as the interval here allowed may appear to be too long for the time of doubling, the second is calculated at the interval of 40 years, which comes nearer to the truth of the case, though even this may exceed the time of doubling. | Years of the World | Number of Mankind | |-------------------|------------------| | 1700 | 3,355,443,200 | | 1750 | 6,710,886,400 | | 1800 | 13,421,772,800 | | 1850 | 26,843,545,600 | | 1900 | 53,687,091,200 | | 1950 | 107,374,182,400 | | 2000 | 214,748,364,800 | | 2050 | 429,496,729,600 | The first table is brought down no lower than to the year 2050, and the second to the year 2020, though... Antediluvians though there remain by the first 206, and by the second 236 years to the flood: the reason is, that in those last 200 years of the world, mankind would not increase in any measure equal to what they had done in the preceding years (though regularly the increase should have been much greater); because that violence was then great in the earth, and thousands, yea millions, might have been cut off by untimely deaths; for which cause the world's destruction was determined 120 years before the flood came. II. But now against this immense number of mankind that might in a regular and ordinary way have been born into the world between the creation and the deluge in 2056 years, it will no doubt be objected by some (as it has been done to far less numbers), that all such calculations are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> guesswork, the product of fruitful imaginations. But it should be considered, that in calculations of this nature some regular order or method must be observed; and though, according to the course of nature, such an increase and multiplication of mankind there might have been periodically, especially at the beginning, when the command was to increase and multiply and replenish the earth; yet we will not suppose that all things went on thus regularly, without difference or interruption. We do not know what extraordinary obstructions or interruptions there might be to such a regular increase. Though every married pair might by the course of nature have had such a number of children as has been mentioned, yet the Divine Providence might order it otherwise in manifold instances, and it might possibly be in the old world, as it has been since the flood, viz. that some marriages have produced many children, others few, and some none at all. Allowing, therefore, for all such obstructions and deficiencies, and likewise for all casualties and accidents (to which men might be liable in that world as well as in the present), in as ample a manner as can be desired, let the former number be reduced to one half, viz. to $27 \times 87,792,694,400$, that is, 27 billions, or millions of millions, four hundred and eighty-seven thousand seven hundred and ninety millions, six hundred and ninety-four thousand and four hundred. And this we shall now suppose to be the whole number of those who were born into the world before the deluge. But from this sum is to be subtracted the number of those who died before that time. Of those in the genealogies from Adam by Seth, Enoch was translated at the age of 365, Lamech the father of Noah died just before the flood at 753, Mahalaleel at 805. Adam and the other five patriarchs lived to above 900. Before the year 900, therefore, we may suppose there were no deaths except that of Abel, who was slain, a young man, but that all born within that period were alive together. But in the tenth century death began to reign, and Adam and Eve, we may presume, were the first over whom death had power in a natural way, as their disobedience was the cause of it. The children also born of them in the first hundred years would also die in this 10th century, those born in the second hundred would die in the 11th, those born in the third century would die in the 12th, and so on. But though we are far from thinking that after the beginning of the 10th century (till which time few or none died), the deaths would be equal to the births; yet as we have made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> concessions all Antediluvians along, we shall do the same in this case, and suppose them upon the whole to have been equal, especially since we cannot precisely say how long that violence or bloodshed, which was their crying sin, came to prevail; and therefore will reduce the last sum mentioned to one half again, to allow for the deaths and prevailing violence, and suppose the total number of mankind alive upon earth at the time of the deluge to have been no more than $13,743,895,347,200$, that is, 13 billions or millions of millions, seven hundred and forty-three thousand eight hundred and ninety-five millions, three hundred and forty-seven thousand and two hundred; a number vastly exceeding that of the present inhabitants of the whole earth. Notwithstanding the very large allowances and abate-Probabilityments made to reduce the number of mankind, yet even of the last <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> to 13 billions, or millions of millions, &c. seems to vastly great, that it will hardly be thought possible that such a number of men could ever be at one time upon the earth. Now, though we pretend to no certainty in this point (which made it the more requisite to allow largely for deaths and deficiencies), yet the calculation we have given must appear highly probable, since it is founded upon grounds certain and undeniable: for instance, 1. It cannot be denied but that the Antediluvians were come to the age of puberty and marriage at 160 years, when we find a son born in 162. Nor, 2. Can it be said, that they could not have children at the age of 500, when we have an instance of one that had three sons at due distances after that age. Neither, 3. Can it be alleged that we have not allowed a due distance or interval between the births, viz. six years, when most will be of opinion that it could not be so long. Nor yet, 4. Can it be judged that we have made the period of doubling far too short, when we had before showed that after 100 marriages consummated, they would treble themselves in half the time we have taken for their doubling. Nor, 5. Will any one make a doubt, but that there might be 200 persons of mature age for marriage in the year of the world 500, the men at 160, the women younger. Nevertheless, as this is the foundation of our calculation, we shall now show that there was at least such a number of persons marriageable at that age of the world. It may be observed, that as we take 160 for the year of maturity and marriage, according to that period all married or marriageable in the year 500 must have been born in or before the year 340; the males at least, though the females coming sooner to maturity, might some of them be born later or after the year 380. Now, according to this stated period of marriage, 1. In or before the year 340, Adam might have had 54 children, males and females, or 27 pair married or fit for marriage. 2. Cain, whom we suppose to be but six years younger than Adam (which by the by is more than others allow), and to have married in the year 166, might have in the year 340, 28 children, or 14 pair fit for marriage, which added to the former, makes 41 pair. 3. Abel, married six years later, that is, in the year 172, and whom we shall suppose slain in the year 225 or 226, could in that case have no more than eight or nine children, or four pair, which with the former make 45 pair. 4. Adam's third son, married in the year 178, will afford us in the year 340, 26 children, or 13 pair, which increase the number of marriageable persons to 58 pair. 5. A fourth son of Adam's, married in the year 184, will give us in the year 340, 25 children, or 12 pair; which makes the number of pairs 70. 6. A fifth son of Adam's, married in the year 190, might in the year 340 have 24 children, or 12 pair again, which increase the former number to 82 pair. 7. A sixth son of Adam's, married in the year 196, would have in the year 340, 22 children, or 11 pair; which added to the former make up 93 pair. 8. A seventh son of Adam's, married in the year 202, will, in the year 340, give us 20 children, or 10 pair; which makes in the whole 103 pair, already three pair more than we reckoned upon. I need therefore go no farther on to the eighth or ninth son; but the following eight or nine births I may reasonably take to have been daughters, and married to the brothers that preceded them. Here are now no more than 14 children of Adam's married, who have given us the 100 pair we have reckoned upon, and three over. We might yet have 13 pair to bring into the account, all born before the year 340, and marriageable in the year 500, which would very much increase the number of mankind. And by this the reader may perceive that we have been far from building on uncertain or precarious foundations, since we have omitted 13 pair more, which we might have taken into the account. And if it be considered that the command given to Adam was to increase and multiply and replenish the earth, no doubt can be made, but that his own and his children's marriages were fruitful in the procreation of children, that the earth might be inhabited. ANTEGO. See Antigua.

ANTEJURAMENTUM

Pages 24-24

by our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> called juramentum columnae, an oath which anciently both accuser and accused were to take before any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> purgation.—The accuser was to swear that he would prosecute the criminal; and the accused to make oath, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> he was to undergo the ordeal, that he was innocent of the crime <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> against him.

ANTELUCAN

Pages 24-24

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> Writers, is applied to things done in the night <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> before <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. We find frequent mention of the antelucan assemblies (Catus antelucani) of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> in times of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship.

ANTEMURALE

Pages 24-24

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">Military</a> Art, denotes much the same with what the moderns call an out-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>.

ANTENATI

Pages 24-24

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">Modern</a> English <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, is chiefly understood of the subjects of Scotland, born before <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James the First's accession to the English <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and alive after it. In relation to these, those who were born after the accession were denominated Pophamati. The antenati were considered as aliens in England, whereas the postnati claimed the privilege of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> Antenatia subjects.

ANTENCLEMA

Pages 24-24

in Oratory, is where the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the person accused turns on criminating the accuser. Such is the defence of Orestes, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> for Milo: Occidit eft, fed latro. Exceftus, fed rapto.

ANTENICENE

Pages 24-24

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> Writers, denotes a thing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> person <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Nice. We say the Antenicene <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, Antenicene creeds, Antenicene fathers. ANTENNÆ, in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of insects, slender bodies with which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> has furnished the heads of these creatures, being the same with what in English are called horns or feelers. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ANTENOR

Pages 24-24

a Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, came into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, expelled the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-ETRUSCANS">Etruscans</a> on the river Po, and built the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, where his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> is said to be still extant.

ANTEPAGMENTA

Pages 24-24

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, the jambs of a door. They are also ornaments, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> garnishments, in carved <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, of men, animals, &c., made either of wood or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and set on the architrave.

ANTEPENULTIMA

Pages 24-24

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, the third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a> of a word from the end, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the last syllable but two.

ANTEPILANI

Pages 24-24

in the Roman armies, a name given to the halfti and principes, because they marched next before the triarii, who were called pilani.

ANTEPOSITION

Pages 24-24

a grammatical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, whereby a word, which by the ordinary rules of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNTAX">syntax</a> ought to follow another, comes before it. As when, in the Latin, the adjective is put before the substantive, the verb before the nominative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, &c.

ANTEPREDICAMENTS

Pages 24-24

among Logicians, certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRELIMINARY">preliminary</a> questions which illustrate the doctrine of predicaments and categories.

ANTEQUIERA

Pages 24-24

a handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, divided into two parts, the upper and lower. The upper is seated on a hill, and has a castle: the lower stands in a fertile plain, and is watered with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of brooks. There is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> in the mountain; and five miles from the town, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> famous for the cure of the gravel. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 40. N. Lat. 36. 51.

ANTERIOR

Pages 24-24

denotes something placed before another, either with respect to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>.

ANTEROS

Pages 24-24

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, one of the two Cupids who were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. They are placed at the foot of the Venus of Medicis; this is represented with a heavy and full look, agreeably to the poetical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of him, as the cause of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>'s ceasing. The other was called Eros.

ANTESIGNANI

Pages 24-24

in the Roman armies, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> placed before the standards, in order to defend them, according to Livius; but Caesar and Livy mention the antesignani as the first line, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> first body, of heavy-armed troops. The velites, who used to skirmish before the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, were likewise called antesignani.

ANTESTARI

Pages 24-25

in Roman Antiquity, signifies to bear witness against any one who refused to make his appearance in the Roman courts of judicature, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> appointed, and according to the tenor of his bail. The plaintiff, finding the defendant after such a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of his engagement, was allowed to carry him into <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> by force, having first asked any of the persons present to bear witness. The person asked to bear witness in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, expressed his consent by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, which was instantly taken hold of by the plaintiff, and this was to answer the end of a subpoena. The ear was touched upon this occasion, says Pliny, as being the seat of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, and therefore the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> was a sort of caution to the party to remember his engagement. ANTHELION. See CORONA and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARHELION">PARHELION</a>.

ANTHELIX

Pages 25-25

in Anatomy, the inward protuberance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a> within, and almost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the helix. See ANATOMY.

ANTHEM

Pages 25-25

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> song performed in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> by choristers, who sing alternately. It was used to denote both psalms and hymns, when performed in this manner. But, at present, anthem is used in a more confined <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, being applied to certain psalms taken out of the scriptures, and adapted to a particular solemnity. Anthems were first introduced in the reformed service of the English church, in the beginning of the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>.

ANTHERA

Pages 25-25

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the stamen which is fixed on the top of the filamentum, within the corolla: it contains the pollen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fine dust, which, when mature, it emits for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPREGNATION">impregnation</a> of the plant, according to Linnaeus. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APEX">Apex</a> of Ray, Tournefort, and Rivin.; Capsula flaminis, of Malpighi.

ANTHESPHORIA

Pages 25-25

in Antiquity, a Sicilian festival instituted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Proserpine. The word is derived from the Greek ἀνθεσφορία, flower, and ἀναπορεύομαι, I carry; because that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> was forced away by Pluto when she was gathering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> in the fields. Yet Festus does not ascribe the feast to Proserpine; but says it was thus called by reason ears of corn were carried on this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>.—Anthesphoria seems to be the same thing with the florifertum of the Latins, and answers to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>-home among us.

ANTHESTERIA

Pages 25-25

in Antiquity, was a feast celebrated by the Athenians in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>. The most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> derivation of the word is from the Greek ἀνθεσφορία (flower), a flower, it being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> at this feast to offer garlands of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> to Bacchus. The anthesteria lasted three days, the 11th, 12th, and 13th of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>; each of which had a name suited to the proper office of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. The first day of the feast was called μετάστησις, i.e. opening of the vessels, because on this day they tapped the vessels, and tasted the wine. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> day they called ξυλοκόμη, congiis, the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> containing the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of 10 pounds; on this they drank the wine prepared the day before. Anthesterion. The third day they called κύπελλαι, kettles: on this day they boiled all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> in kettles; which however they were not allowed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, as being offered to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>.

ANTHESTERION

Pages 25-25

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>, the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the Athenian year. It contained 29 days; and answered to the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of our November and beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>. The Macedonians called it δεξιον <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> δεξιον. It had its name from the festival anthesteria kept in it.

ANTHOLOGION

Pages 25-25

the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> book used in the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. It is divided into 12 months, containing the offices sung throughout the year, on the festivals of our Saviour, the Virgin, and other remarkable saints.

ANTHOLOGY

Pages 25-25

a discourse of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of beautiful psalms from any authors.—It is also the name given to a collection of epigrams taken from several Greeks poets.

ANTHONY

Pages 25-26

SAINT, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> in 251, and inherited a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fortune, which he distributed among his neighbours and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, retired into solitude, founded a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> order, built many monasteries, and died anno 356. Many ridiculous stories are told of his conflicts with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> and of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>. There are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> epistles extant attributed to him. St Anthony is sometimes represented with a fire by his side, signifying that he relieves persons from the inflammation called after his name; but always accompanied by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOG">hog</a>, on account of his having been a swineherd, and curing all disorders in that animal. To do him the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> in several places keep at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> charges a hog denominated St Anthony's hog, for which they have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> veneration. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have St Anthony's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> on the walls of their houses, hoping by that to be preserved from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>; and the Italians, who do not know the true signification of the fire painted at the side of their faint, concluding that he preserves houses from being burnt, invoke him on such occasions. Both painters and poets have made very free with this saint and his followers: the former, by the many ludicrous pictures of his temptation; and the latter, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> epigrams on his disciples <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> friars; one of which is the following, printed in Stephen's World of Wonders: Once fed'dst thou, Anthony, an herd of swine, And now an herd of monks thou feedest still. For <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and gut alike both charges bin; Both loven filth alike; both like to fill Their greedy paunch alike: nor was that kind More beafty, fottish, twinish, than this laft. All else agrees: one fault I only find, Thou feedest not thy monks with oaken maft. ANTHONY or Knights of St Anthony, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> order, instituted by Albert <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, when he designed to make <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against the Turks in 1382. The knights wore a collar of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. ANTHONY gold made in form of a hermit's girdle, from which hung a stick cut like a crutch, with a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a>, as they are represented in St Anthony's pictures. St Anthony also gives the denomination to an order of religious founded in France about the year 1295, to take care of those afflicted with St Anthony's fire; (see the next article.)—It is said, that, in some places, these monks assume to themselves a power of giving, as well as removing, the ignis fever, or crypsipelas; a power which stands them in great stead for keeping the poor people in subjection, and extorting alms. To avoid the menaces of these monks, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> people present them every year with a fat hog a piece. Some prelates endeavoured to persuade Pope Paul III. to abolish the order; questuarium illorum sancti Antonii, qui deplentant religionem simplices, quique innumeris superstitionibus implicati, de medio tollendos esse. But they failed, notwithstanding, to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, in several places. St Anthony's Fire, a name properly given to the crypsipelas. Apparently it took this denomination, as those afflicted with it made their peculiar application to St Anthony of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a> for a cure. It is known, that anciently particular diseases had their peculiar saints: thus, in the ophthalmia, persons had recourse to St Lucia; in the toothache, to St <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLONIA">Apollonia</a>; in the hydrophobia, to St Hubert, &c.

ANTHORA

Pages 26-26

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of acornutum. See ACONITUM, BOTANY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ANTHORISMUS

Pages 26-26

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, denotes a contrary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of a thing from that given by the adverse party.—Thus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the plaintiff urge, that to take any thing away from another without his knowledge or consent, is a theft; this is called eges, or definition. If the defendant reply, that to take a thing away from another without his knowledge or consent, provided it be done with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to return it to him again, is not theft; this is an Archegetes.

ANTHRACIS

Pages 26-26

ANTHRACIAS, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ANTHRACITIS, names promiscuously used by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> naturalists for very different fossils, viz. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARBUNCLE">carbuncle</a>, haematites, and a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a>. See CARBUNCLE, &c.

ANTHRACOSIS

Pages 26-26

in Medicine, a corrosive fealy ulcer either in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BULB">bulb</a> of the eye <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the eyelids.

ANTHRAX

Pages 26-26

a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, literally signifying a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> coal, used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> to denote a gem, as well as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, more generally known by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARBUNCLE">carbuncle</a>. ANTHRAX is sometimes also used for lithanthrax <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pit coal.

ANTHROPOGLOTTUS

Pages 26-26

among Zoologists, an appellation given to such animals as have tongues resembling that of mankind, particularly to the parrot kind.

ANTHROPOGRAPHY

Pages 26-26

denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body, its parts, structure, &c. See ANATOMY.

ANTHROPOLATRAE

Pages 26-26

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, an appellation given to the Neotrians, on account of their worshipping Christ, notwithstanding that they believed him to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>.

ANTHROPOLATRIA

Pages 26-26

the paying divine honours to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; supposed to be the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kind Anthropo-

ANTHROPOLITES

Pages 26-27

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> denoting petrifications of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body, as those of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> are called zooliths. It has been doubted whether any real human petrifications ever occur, and whether those which have been supposed such were not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> lufus naturee. But the generality of naturalists best versed in this branch assure us of real anthropolites being sometimes found. And indeed, as it is universally admitted that the zooliths are frequently seen, what <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> argument therefore can be brought against the existence of the others? Are not the component parts of the human body nearly similar to those of the brute <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>? Consequently, correspondent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> may be subject to, and acquire, the like accidental changes, wherever the same power <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cause concur to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> upon either object. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the former are not so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, it may be accounted for, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, by reflecting that human bodies are generally deposited in select and appropriated places; whereas the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of animals are dispersed everywhere, and falling into various beds of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, at a greater or less depth, there is more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> of their encountering the petrifying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>. Could we <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> some authors who have treated on this subject, they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> tell us of entire bodies and skeletons that were found petrified. One in particular, discovered at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a> in Provence anno 1583, in a rocky cliff, the cerebrum whereof, when struck against a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, produced sparks, the bones being at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> friable. The reports of Happel and Kircher are too absurd for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>. Van Helmont's strange relations, together with those of Jean'a Coisa, must also be rejected as fabulous. Scheuchzer has published an engraved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, which he calls the Antediluvian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>: how far it is authentic, it would be rash to say. It is, however, asserted by many respectable writers on <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, that whole skeletons petrified have been brought to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> from certain old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, which remained closed up and disfigured for several centuries. These indeed are acknowledged to be very rare. Yet it is a known fact, that detached parts, osseous, are sometimes found, especially in situations where either the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, or both, have been observed to possess a strong putrefactive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. The human vertebrae, fragments or portions of the tibia, and even the whole cranium itself, have been seen in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETRIFICATION">petrification</a>. Some of these are said to appear vitrified or mineralized. As to the petrified bones of pretended giants, they are more probably real zooliths, the bones of the larger animals. All these bones are found in various states, and under different appearances. Some are only indurated; others calcined, vitrified, or mineralized; some, again, are simply incrusted; whilst others have been proved completely petrified. Notwithstanding what is here advanced, it may be granted that a positive lufus naturee, in some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, is repeatedly mistaken for a real petrification. They are, however, distinguishable at all times by an experienced naturalist; particularly by the two following rules: First, We may determine that fossil a lufus naturee which, on a strict <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, is observed to deviate in any material <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> from the true res analogicae existens. Secondly, By the same parity of reasoning, those fossil shells Anthropo-Phagi are to be esteemed certain petrifications, and genuine Antediluvian reliquiae, in which, on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with their analogues collected from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, there appears an exact conformity in size and figure. This comparative observation will hold good for all fossils; that is, such as present themselves either under the animal or vegetable form. It is nevertheless worthy of notice, that all terebraceous fossils are not petrified; since some kinds of them have been found in beds of sand, which retained their original perfect shape and quality, but at the same time they proved very brittle, indeed scarcely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the most gentle touch. Shells of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> are always dissoluble by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to the petrified or calcareous fossil shells, whose <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> it is to resist the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of such like menstrua. See further the article Petrification.

ANTHROPOLOGY

Pages 27-27

among Divines, denotes that manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> by which the inspired writers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> parts and passions to God.

ANTHROPOMANCY

Pages 27-27

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a>, performed by inspecting the entrails of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> creature.

ANTHROPOMORPHA

Pages 27-27

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> formerly given to the primates of that class of animals which have the greatest resemblance to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> kind.

ANTHROPOMORPHISM

Pages 27-27

among <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> Writers, denotes the hereby <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of the Anthropomorphites. See the next article.

ANTHROPOMORPHITES

Pages 27-27

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> heretics, who, taking every thing spoken of God in Scripture in a literal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, particularly that passage of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a> in which it is said God made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> after his own image, maintained that God had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> shape. They are likewise called Audians, from Audens their leader.

ANTHROPOMORPHOUS

Pages 27-27

something that bears the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> resemblance of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. Naturalists give instances of anthropomorphic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, anthropomorphic minerals, &c. These generally come under the class of what they call lyssa <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, or monitors.

ANTHROPOPATHY

Pages 27-27

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> by which some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> is ascribed to God, which properly belongs only to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>.

ANTHROPOPHAGI

Pages 27-28

(of ἀνθρώπος a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and φάγει to eat, Men-eaters.) That there have been, in almost all ages of the world, nations who have followed this barbarous practice, we have abundance of testimonies. The Cyclops, the Leitrygons, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCYLLA">Scylla</a>, are all represented in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> as Anthrophagai, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> man-eaters; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> phantoms, Circe and the Sirens, first bewitched with a flow of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and then destroyed. This, like the other parts of Homer's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, had a foundation in the manners of the times preceding his own. It was still, in many places, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> spoken of by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, When men devour'd each other like the beasts, Gorging on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>. According to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, among the Etesian Scythians, when a man's father died, the neighbours brought several beasts, which they killed, mixed up their flesh with that of the deceased, and made a feast. Among the Malagasy when any person grew old, they killed him and ate his flesh; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he died of sickness, they buried him, esteeming him unhappy. The same author also affirms us, that several nations in the Indies killed all their old people and their sick, to feed on their flesh; he adds, that persons in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> were sometimes accused of being sick, to afford a pretence for devouring them. According to Sextus Empiricus, the first laws that were made, were for the prevention of this barbarous practice, which the Greek writers represent as universal before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Orpheus. Of the practice of anthropophagy in later times, we have the testimonies of all the Roman millionaries who have visited the internal parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and even some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. Herrera speaks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, furnished wholly with human flesh, for the better sort of people. Marcus Paulus speaks of the like in his time, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Concha towards Quinay, and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Zapengi; others, of the great <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>; Barbofa, of the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a> and island of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a>; others, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Samogitians, &c. The philosophers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a>, Chrysippus, and Zeno, followed by the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Stoics, affirmed, that there was nothing unnatural in the eating of human flesh; and that it was very reasonable to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> dead bodies for food, rather than to give them a prey to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>. In order to make the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, however, whether there was any real repugnancy in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> to the feeding of an animal with the flesh of its own <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, Leonardus Floroventius fed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOG">hog</a> with hog's flesh, and a dog with dog's flesh; upon which he found the bristles of the hog to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> off, and the dog to become full of ulcers. When <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> was discovered, this practice was found to be almost universal, inasmuch that several authors have supposed it to be occasioned through a want of other food, or through the indolence of the people to seek for it; though others ascribe its origin to a spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>. It appears pretty certain from Dr Hawkesworth's account of the Voyages to the South Seas, that the inhabitants of the island of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NEW_ZEALAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, a country unfurnished with the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, eat the bodies of their enemies. It appears also to be very probable, that both the wars and anthropophagy of these savages take their rise and owe their continuance to irresistible <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, and the dreadful alternative of destroying each other by violence, or of perishing by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>. See vol. iii. p. 447, et seq. and vol. ii. p. 389, &c. Mr Marden also informs us, that this horrible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> is practised by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTAS">Battas</a>, a people in the island of Sumatra. "They do not eat human flesh (says he) as a means of satisfying the cravings of nature, owing to a deficiency of other food; nor is it sought after as a gluttonous delicacy, as it would seem among the New Zealanders. The Battas eat it as a species of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>; as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of showing their detestation of crimes, by an ignominious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>; and as a horrid indication of revenge and insult to their unfortunate enemies. The objects of this barbarous repast are the prisoners taken in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and offenders convicted and condemned for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> crimes. Persons of the former former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> may be ramomed or exchanged, for which they often wait a considerable time; and the latter suffer only when their friends cannot redeem them by the customary fine of twenty beehenches, or eighty dollars. These are tried by the people of the tribe where the fact was committed, but cannot be executed till their own particular raja or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> has been acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>; who, when he acknowledges the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the intended punishment, sends a cloth to cover the delinquent's head, together with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISH">dish</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and lemons. The unhappy object, whether prisoner of war or malefactor, is then tied to a stake: the people assembled throw their lances at him from a certain distance; and when mortally wounded, they run up to him, as if in a transport of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>; cut pieces from the body with their knives; dip them in the dish of salt and lemon juice; slightly broil them over a fire prepared for the purpose; and swallow the morsels with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> enthusiasm. Sometimes (I presume according to the degree of their animosity and resentment) the whole is devoured; and instances have been known, where, with barbarity still aggravated, they tear the flesh from the carcass with their mouths. To such a depth of depravity may man be plunged, when neither <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> nor <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> enlighten his steps! All that can be said in extenuation of the horror of this diabolical ceremony is, that no view appears to be entertained of torturing the sufferers; of increasing or lengthening out the pangs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; the whole fury is directed against the corpse, warm indeed with the remains of life, but past the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> of pain. I have found a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> in regard to their eating the bodies of their enemies slain in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. Some persons <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> resident there, and acquainted with their proceedings, assert that it is not customary; but as one or two particular instances have been given by other people, it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> to conclude, that it sometimes takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, though not generally. It was supposed to be with this intent, that Raja Neabir maintained a long conflict for the body of Mr Nairne, a most respectable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> and valuable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>, who fell in an attack upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> of that chief, in the year 1775. It may be said, that whether the dead body of an enemy be eaten or buried, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> perfectly indifferent. But whatever the practice of eating human flesh may be in itself, it certainly is relatively, and in its consequences, most pernicious. It manifestly tends to eradicate a principle, which is the chief security of human life, and more frequently restrains the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of the murderer, than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of duty or the dread of punishment. Even if this horrid practice originates from hunger, still it must be perpetuated from revenge. Death must lose much of its horror among those who are accustomed to eat the dead; and where there is little horror at the sight of death, there must be less repugnance to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>. See some further observations on this subject, equally just and ingenious, by Dr Hawkeworth, ut supra.

ANTHROPOPHAGIA

Pages 28-28

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of eating <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>. This is pretended by some to be the effect of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, which leads people affected with it to eat every thing alike. Some choose only to consider it as a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICA">Pica</a>. The annals of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a> furnish an extraordinary instance of anthropophagy. A Milanese woman named <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, from a depraved appetite, like what women with child, and those whose meninges are obstructed, frequently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, had an invincible inclination to human flesh, of which she made provision by enticing children into her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, where she killed and salted them; a discovery of which having been made, she was broken on the wheel and burnt in 1519.

ANTHROPOSCOPIA

Pages 28-28

from anthrope, and scopos, I consider, the art of judging <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> discovering a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s character, disposition, passions, and inclinations, from the lineaments of his body. In which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, anthroposcopy seems of somewhat greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> than physiognomy or metoposcopy. Otto has published an Anthroposcopy, sive judicium hominis de homine ex lineamentis externis.

ANTHRUM

Pages 54-54

among Anatomists, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to de- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> several cavities of the body: as the antrum bigh- morianum, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that in the maxillary or jaw bone; an- trum pylori, or that at the bottom of the pylorus, &c.

ANTHUS

Pages 28-28

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a>, a synonyme of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of loxia. See Loxia, Ornithology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ANTHYPOPHORA

Pages 28-28

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of speech; being the counterpart of an hypophora. See Hypophora.

ANTI

Pages 28-28

in matters of Literature, is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> given to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> pieces written by way of answer to others, whose names are usually annexed to the anti. See the Anti of M. Baillet; and the Anti-Baillet of M. Menage: there are also Anti-Menagiani, &c. Cæsar the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a> wrote two books by way of answer to what had been objected to him by Cato, which he called Anti-Catores; these are mentioned by Juvenal, Cicero, &c. Vives affirms us, he had seen Cæsar's Anti-Catores in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> library.

ANTIBACCHIUS

Pages 28-28

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, a foot consisting of three syllables, the two first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and the last one short; such is the word ambrie.

ANTIBES

Pages 28-28

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of Provence in France, with a strong castle. Its territory produces excellent fruit; and the town stands opposite to Nice, in the Mediterranean. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 9'. N. Lat. 43° 50'.

ANTICAMBER

Pages 28-28

an outer chamber for strangers to wait in, till the person to be spoken with is at leisure.

ANTICHRIST

Pages 28-29

among <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> Writers, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> adversary of Christianity, who is to appear upon the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> towards the end of the world. We have demonstrations, disputations, and proofs, in great order and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, both that the pope is, and that he is not, Antichrist. F. Calmet is very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> in describing the father and mother of Antichrist, his tribe and pedigree, his wars and conquests, his achievements against Gog, Magog, &c. Some <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> at Constantinople, others at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, others at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a>, and some few at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; but the generality at Rome, though these last are divided. Antichrist vided. Grotius and some others suppose Rome Pagan to have been the seat of Antichrist; most of the Lutheran and reformed doctors contend earnestly for Rome Christian under the papal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIERARCHY">hierarchy</a>. In fact, the point having been maturely debated at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAP">Gap</a>, held in 1653, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> was taken thereupon, to insert an article in the Confession of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">Faith</a>, whereby the pope is formally declared to be Antichrist.—Pope Clement VIII. was stung to the quick with this decision; and even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry IV. of France was not a little mortified, to be thus declared, as he said, an imp of Antichrist. M. le Clerc holds, that the rebel Jews and their leader Simon, whose <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is given by Josephus, are to be reputed as the true Antichrist. Lightfoot and Wandelhart rather apply this character to the Jewish Sanhedrim.
