Hippolitus and others held that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> himself was the true Antichrist; that he was to be incarnate, and make his appearance in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> shape before the consummation of all things. Others among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> held that Antichrist was to be born of a virgin by some prolific power imparted to her by the devil. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> writer of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, whom many hold for a saint, has improved on this sentiment; maintaining that Antichrist is to be begotten by the devil on the body of a witch by means of the semen of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> caught in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of a certain crime, and conveyed, &c. Hunnius and some others, to secure Antichrist to the pope (notwithstanding that this latter seemed excluded by not being of the tribe of Dan), have broke in upon the unity of Antichrist, and assert that there is to be both an eastern and a western Antichrist. Father Malvenda, a Jesuit, hath published a large <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> entitled Antichrist, in which this subject is amply discussed. It consists of thirteen books. In the first he relates all the opinions of the fathers with regard to Antichrist. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, he speaks of the times when he shall appear; and shows, that all the fathers who supposed Antichrist to be near at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, judged the world was near its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. In the third, he discourses of his origin and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; and shows that he is to be a Jew, of the tribe of Dan: this he finds on the authority of the fathers; on the passage in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a> xlix. 17. Dan shall be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> by the way, &c.; on that of Jeremiah viii. 16. where it is said, The armies of Dan shall devour the earth; and on Rev. vii. where St John, enumerating all the tribes of Israel, makes no mention of that of Dan. In the fourth and fifth books he treats of the signs of Antichrist. In the sixth, of his reign and wars. In the seventh, of his vices. In the eighth, of his doctrine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>. In the ninth, of his persecutions: and in the tenth, of the coming of Enoch and Elias, the conversion of the Jews, the reign of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Antichrist, after he has reigned three years and a half. See also Lowman on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">Revelation</a>. How endless are conjectures? Some of the Jews, we are told, actually took Cromwell for the Christ; while some others have laboured to prove him Antichrist himself. Plutarch affords us he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a folio book in the Bodleian library, written on purpose to demonstrate this latter <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. Upon the whole, the Antichrist mentioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> John, 1 Ep. ii. 18. and more particularly described in the book of Revelation, seems evidently to be the same with the Man of Sin, &c., characterized by St Paul in his Second Epistle to the Thessalonians, ch. ii. And the entire <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> literally applies to the excesses of papal power. Had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of private judgment, says an excellent writer, been always adopted and maintained, Antichrist could never have been; and when the sacred right comes to be universally asserted, and men follow the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of their own reason and consciences, Antichrist can be no more.

ANTICHRISTIANISM

Pages 29-29

a state <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> in persons or principles, which denominates them antichristian, or opposite to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Christ. M. Jurieu takes the idea of the unity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> to have been the source of Antichristianism. Had not mankind been infatuated with this, they would never have stood in such awe of the anathemas of Rome. It is on this the popes erected their monarchical power. ANTICHRISTIANS properly denote the followers or worshippers of Antichrist. ANTICHRISTIANS are more particularly understood of those who set up or believe a false Christ or Messiah.

ANTICHTHONES

Pages 29-29

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an appellation given to the inhabitants of opposite hemispheres.

ANTICITY

Pages 45-45

Y signifies times <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ages past <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> ago. Thus, we say, the heroes of antiquity, &c. Antiquity is also used to denote the works or monuments of antiquity. See Antiquities.

ANTICOR

Pages 29-29
or ANTICOEUR, among Farriers, an inflammation in a horse's throat, being the same with the quinsy in mankind. See FARRIERY.

ANTICOSTE

Pages 29-29

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARREN_ISLAND">barren <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> lying in the mouth of the river St Lawrence, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 64. 16. N. Lat. from 49. to 53.

ANTICYRA

Pages 29-30

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHOCIS">Phocis</a>, on the Corinthian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, opposite to Cirrha, lying to the west on the same bay. The Phoceans seizing the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, called the Sacred, commenced, and lasted ten years; when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, father of Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, avenged the god by destroying many of the cities of the pillagers. Anticyra was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. It was again taken and subverted by Attilius a Roman general in the war with the Macedonians. It afterwards became famous for its heliobore. That drug was the root of a plant, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> produce of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROCKY_MOUNTAINS">rocky <a class=</a>"xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and of two kinds; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, which had a purgative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, which was an emetic. Sick persons resorted to Anticyra to take the medicine, which was prepared there by a peculiar and very excellent recipe: Hence the adage, Naviget Anticgram, (Horace). By the port in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century was a temple of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, built with selected <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and the inside white-washed: the statue of brons. The agora <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> market-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was adorned with images of the same metal; and above it was a well with a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, sheltered from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> supported by columns. A little higher was a monument formed with such stones as occurred, and designed, it was said, for the sons of Iphitus. One of these, Schedius, was killed by Hector, while fighting for the body of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATROCLUS">Patroclus</a>, but his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> were transported to Anticyra; where his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> died after his return from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>. About two stadia or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> distant was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> rock, a portion of the mountain, on which a temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, the image bigger than a large woman, and made Antigonea by Praxicles. The walls and other edifices at Anticyra were probably erected, like the temple of Neptune, with stones or pebbles. The site is now called Alprospita, or The White Houses; and some traces of the buildings from which it was so named remain. The port is landlocked, and frequented by vessels for corn. Some paces up from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> is a fountain.

ANTIDICOMARIANITES

Pages 30-30
ancient heretics who pretended that the Holy Virgin did not preserve a perpetual virginity, but that she had several children by Joseph after our Saviour's birth. Their opinion was grounded on some expressions of our Saviour, wherein he mentions his brothers and his sisters; and of St Matthew, where he says, that Joseph knew not Mary till she had brought forth her first born son. The Antidicomarianites were the disciples of Helvidius and Jo-vian, who appeared in Rome toward the close of the fourth century.

ANTIDORON

Pages 30-30

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> Writers, a name given by the Greeks to the consecrated <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, out of which the middle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, marked with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, wherein the consecration resides, being taken away by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, the remainder is distributed after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. On the sides of the antidoron are impressed the words "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christus vict." The word is formed from δόρον, donum, "a gift," as being given away loco muneris, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>. The antidoron is also called panis praesanctificatus. Some suppose the antidoron to be distributed in lieu of the sacrament, to such as were prevented from attending in person at the celebration; and thence derive the origin of the word, the eucharist being denominated dorus, "gift," by way of eminence.

ANTIDOSIS

Pages 30-30

in Antiquity, denotes an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> of estates, practised by the Greeks on certain occasions with peculiar ceremonies, and first instituted by Solon. When a person was nominated to an office, the expense of which he was not able to support, he had recourse to the antidosis: that is, he was to seek some other citizen of better substance than himself, who was free from this, and other offices; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the former was excused. In case the person thus substituted denied himself to be the richest, they were to exchange estates, after this manner; the doors of their houses were closed shut up and sealed, that nothing might be conveyed away; then both took an oath to make a faithful discovery of all their effects, except what lay in the silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, which by the laws was excused from all imposts; accordingly, within three days, a full discovery and exchange of estates was made.

ANTIDOTE

Pages 30-30

among Physicians, a remedy taken to prevent, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to cure, the effects of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, &c. ANTIEN. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a>.

ANTIGONEA

Pages 30-31
or Anticonia, in Ancient Geography, a town of Bithynia, so called from Antigonus, the son of Philip, and afterwards called Nicaea (Strabo, Stephanus). Another of Epirus, to the north of the Montes Ceraunii, opposite to the city of Oriscum (Polybius, Ptolemy). A third of Arcadia, namely Maniinea, so called in honour of King Antigonus, (Plutarch, Panoplias.) A fourth in Macedonia, in the territory of Mygdonia (Pliny, Ptolemy). A fifth in the territory of Chalcidice, in Macedonia, on the east side of the Sinus Thermaicus (Livy). A sixth of Antigonus, Syria, built by Antigonus, not far from Antioch, on the Orontes (Stephanus); but soon after destroyed by Seleucus, who removed the inhabitants to Seleucia, a town built by him (Diodorus Siculus). A seventh of Troas, called Alexandria in Pliny's time. ANTIGONUS I, one of the captains of Alexander the Great, was the son of Philip a Macedonian nobleman. After Alexander's death, a division of the provinces taking place, Pamphylia, Lycia, and Phrygia Major fell to his share. But Perdiccas, well acquainted with his ambitious spirit, and great abilities, determined to divest him of his government, and laid plans for his life, by bringing various accusations against him. Antigonus, aware of the danger, retired with his son Demetrius into Greece, where he obtained the favour and protection of Antipater; and in a short time Perdiccas dying, a new division taking place, he was invested not only with the government of the former provinces, but also with that of Laconia. He was likewise entrusted with the command of the Macedonian household troops, and upon Eumenes being declared a public enemy, he received orders to prosecute the war against him with the utmost vigour. On the commencement of this war, Eumenes suffered a total overthrow, and was obliged to retire with only 600 brave followers to a castle situated on an inaccessible rock, where he might rest in safety from all the assaults of Antigonus. In the interval, his friends assembling a new army for his relief, were routed by Antigonus, who now began to exhibit the great projects of his ambition. Polyperchon succeeding to the tutelage of the young king of Macedon after Antipater's death, Antigonus resolved to set himself up as lord of all Asia. On account of the great power of Eumenes, he greatly desired to gain him over to his interest, but that faithful commander effecting his escape from the fortress where he was closely blockaded, raised an army, and was appointed the royal general in Asia. The governors of Upper Asia cooperating with him, he succeeded in several engagements against Antigonus, but was at last delivered up to him through treachery, and put to death. Upon this, the governors of Upper Asia yielded to Antigonus. Those whom he suspected, he either sacrificed to his resentment or displaced them from their offices. Then seizing upon all the treasures at Sula, he directed his march towards Babylon, of which city Seleucus was governor. Seleucus fled to Ptolemy, and entered into a league with him, together with Lydimachus and Cassander, with the intention of giving a check to the exorbitant power of Antigonus, who, notwithstanding this, made a successful attempt upon the provinces of Syria and Phoenicia. Yet these provinces were soon after recovered by Ptolemy, who defeated his son Demetrius, while he himself was employed in repelling Cassander, who had made rapid progress in Lesser Asia. They were again taken by Antigonus, and he being flushed with his success, planned an expedition against the Nabataean Arabs, dwelling in the deserts adjacent to Judea; but on the first enterprise against the town of Petra, his general Athenaeus, with almost all his troops, was cut to pieces by the Arabs. Antigonus then sent his son against them, who returned after forcing them to reasonable terms. Demetrius then Antigonus then expelled Seleucus from Babylon, and success attending his arms wherever he went, the confederates were obliged to make a treaty with Antigonus, in which it was stipulated, that he should remain in possession of all Asia, but that the Greek cities should continue in possession of their liberty. This agreement was soon violated, under the pretence that garrisons had been placed in some of these cities by Antigonus. At first Ptolemy made a successful descent in Lesser Asia and on several of the islands of the Archipelago; but he was at length defeated by the successful arms of Demetrius in a sea-fight, who also took the island of Cyprus, with many prisoners. On this victory Antigonus was so elated that he assumed the title of king, and bestowed the same upon his son; and from that time, B.C. 306, his reign in Asia, and that of Ptolemy in Egypt, and of the other captains of Alexander in their respective governments, properly commence. Irritated at the hostile conduct of Ptolemy, Antigonus prepared a numerous army and a formidable fleet, and having taken the command of the army, he gave the command of the fleet to Demetrius, and hastened to attack him in his own dominions. After enduring the severest hardships, they met in the vicinity of Mount Cassius; but Ptolemy acted with such valour and address that Demetrius could gain no advantage over him; and after several fruitless attempts, he abandoned the undertaking. He next attempted the reduction of Rhodes, but meeting with obstinate resistance, he was obliged to make a treaty upon the best terms that he could, having been called to join Antigonus against Callander, who at this time had formed a confederacy with Seleucus and Lysimachus. When Demetrius united his forces with those of Antigonus, they advanced to Phrygia, and having met the enemy at Ipsus, a decisive battle was fought, in which Antigonus fell, in the 84th year of his age, B.C. 301. Ardent in his passions, Antigonus frequently used improper means for their gratification; but as a folder he was sagacious, active, brave, and fortunate. An insatiable ambition, however, the general passion of great men, proved a strong stimulus to all his actions; but with these blemishes better qualities were blended in his character. The violence and temerity of youth were tempered by the clemency and moderation of advanced life, and he endeavoured to conciliate the affections of those whom force had subjected to his power. In matters of private concern he was strictly just; for when his brother wished him to listen to a cause in private where he was concerned, he exclaimed, "No, my dear brother, I will hear it in the open court of justice, because I mean to do justice." When flattered with the title of god, he replied, "My chamberlain well knows the contrary;" and similar philosophical sentiments would frequently drop from his lips. He apologized for the rigour of his taxes by saying, "Alexander reaped Asia, but I only glean it." He shone with peculiar lustre in domestic retirement. Notwithstanding the strong ambition of his son Demetrius, he continued in perfect harmony both with him and all his family. The son had a full share of the authority of the father; and one day saluting his son upon his return from hunting in the presence of some ambassadors, he desired them to tell their masters upon what terms he lived with his son. (Gen. Biog.) Antigonus Gonatus, son of Demetrius Poliorcetes, was the grandson of the former Antigonus. His character was eminently distinguished by humanity and mildness of disposition. When he besieged Thebes under the command of his father, he strongly remonstrated against the loss of so many lives for such an insignificant object. Filial affection was so powerful in his mind, that when his father was taken prisoner by Seleucus, he generously offered himself in his stead, and being rejected, he wore deep mourning, and refrained from all festivals and amusements during his father's imprisonment. Informed of his death, all the floods of sorrow burst from his tender heart, and failing with a fleet to meet his ashes, he received them with all the demonstrations of filial sentibility and dutiful respect. By the death of his father he became master of all the European dominions of Demetrius, together with the kingdom of Macedon and various other cities in Greece. The Gauls invading his country, he defeated and expelled them, but was soon after routed by Pyrrhus king of Epirus. Some time after, however, Pyrrhus was slain at Argos, and when his head was brought him by his son, he expressed the highest displeasure, and throwing his robe over it, he gave orders to search for his body, and to inter the same with all funeral honours. With singular kindness, also, he treated Helenus, the son of that unfortunate king, who fell into his hands by the fortune of war. In the evening of his reign, he so cultivated the arts of peace, and so conciliated the minds of his subjects, that he secured their affections both to himself and his descendants. The taking of the citadel of Corinth by intrigue was the meanest action of his reign, but he improved that event in maintaining the freedom of the small states of Greece, and in increasing his own dominions. The Achaeans, and Aratus, their famous chief, vigorously opposed his measures, and at length recovered Corinth; but Antigonus was so inclined to peace, that notwithstanding this event, he pursued his wonted plan, and left his kingdom in peace about the 90th year of his life, and the 34th of his reign, B.C. 243; and Demetrius II., his son, next ascended the throne. (Gen. Biog.) Antigraphus, in antiquity, an officer of Athens, who kept a counterpart of the apodecti, or chief treasurer's accounts, to prevent mistakes, and keep them from being falsified. Antigraphus is also used, in middle-age writers, for a secretary or chancellor. He is thus called, according to the old glossarists, on account of his writing answers to the letters sent to his master. The antigraphus is sometimes also called archigraphus; and his dignity antigraphia, or archigraphia. Antigraphus is also used in Hidorus for one of the notes of sentences which is placed with a dot to denote a diversity of sense in translations. Antigraphus is also applied in ecclesiastical writers to an abbreviator of the papal letters. In which sense the word is used by Pope Gregory the Great in his register. Of late days the office of antigraphus consists in making minutes of bulls from the petitions agreed to by his holiness, and renewing the bulls after engraving. Antigua, one of the Antilles or Caribbean islands, situated 20 leagues east of St Christopher's, in

ANTILOGARITHM

Pages 32-32

the complement of the logarithm of a sine, tangent, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECANT">secant</a>; or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of that logarithm from the logarithm of 90 degrees.

ANTILOGY

Pages 32-32

in matters of literature, an insufficiency between two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a> of the same book. ANTILOPE. See Capra.

ANTIMENSIUM

Pages 32-32

in the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, answers to the altare portatile, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> portable altar in the Latin church. They are both only of late <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, though Habertus would have them as old as St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>. But Durant and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONA">Bona</a> do not pretend to find them in any author before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Bede and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>. ANTIMENIA is also applied to other tables, used in offices of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, besides those wherein the eucharist is administered: such, e.g., are those wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOST">host</a> is exposed, &c. The origin of the antimensia is described by Meurinus: when the bishop had consecrated a church, the cloth which had been spread on the ground and over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, was torn in pieces, and distributed among the priests, who carried each a fragment away, to serve to cover the tables in their churches and chapels. Not that it was necessary that such cloths should be laid on all tables; but only on those which either were not consecrated, or at least whose consecration was doubted of.

ANTIMERIA

Pages 32-32

in a more restrained <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> where the noun is repeated instead of the pronoun. The antimeria is frequent in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, and is sometimes retained in our version of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> accordingly: e.g., Hear my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, ye wives of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMECH">Lamech</a>, for my voice, Gen. iv. 23.

ANTIMETABOLE

Pages 32-32

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> which sets two things in opposition to each other. The word is Greek, compounded of ἀντί against, and μεταβολή from μεταβάλλω, I shift <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> transfer, i.e., shifting, or letting two things over-against each other. This figure is twice exemplified in an apophthegm of Musonius; which, on account of its excellence, is called aureum monitum, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> maxim or precept. In English thus: "Allowing the performance of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> to be attended with labour; the labour is soon over, but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> immortal: whereas, should even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> wait on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of what is dishonourable, the pleasure is soon gone, but the dishonour eternal."

ANTIMETATHESIS

Pages 32-33

ANTIMETATHESIS, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, is the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERSION">inversion</a> of the parts <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> members of an antithesis. Such is that of Cicero in Verrem, lib. iv. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 52. "Compare this peace with that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; the arrival of this governor with the victory of that general; his profligate troops with the invincible <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of the other; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> of the former with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> of the latter: you <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> say, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a> was founded by him who took it; and taken by him, who held it when founded."

ANTIMONY

Pages 33-34

a blackish mineral substance, staining the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, shining, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>-like striae, hard, brittle, and considerably heavy. It is found in different parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, Transylvania, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, France, and England; <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> by itself, intermixed with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> and stony matters. Sometimes it is blended with the richer ores of silver, and renders the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a> of that metal difficult by volatilizing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the silver; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the miners, robbing the ore. See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METALLURGY">METALLURGY</a>, for the different operations. Antimony is the fibrium of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; by the Greeks called σικυών. The reason of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> denomination, antimony, is usually referred to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> Valentine, a German monk, who, as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> relates, having thrown some of it to the hogs, observed, that after purging them violently, they immediately grew fat upon it. This made him think, that by giving his fellow monks a like dose, they would be the better for it. The experiment, however, succeeded so ill, that they all died of it; and the medicine thenceforward was called antimony, q. d. anti-monk. Uses. Antimony at first was of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> only in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of paint. Scripture describes it to us as a sort of paint, with which the women blackened their eyebrows. Jezebel, understanding that Jehu was to enter <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>, painted her eyes with antimony; or, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, "put her eyes in antimony." As <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> eyes were thought the finest, they of both sexes, who were careful of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, rubbed their eyes, eyelids, and round the eyes, with a needle dipped in a box of paint made of antimony, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of blackening them.—At this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, the women of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a>, anoint and blacken themselves about the eyes; and both men and women put black upon their eyes in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, to preserve them from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and the piercing of its rays. M. Darvieux tells us, that the Arabian women border their eyes with a black <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> made of tatty, which the Arabians call rebel. They draw a line of this kind of blacking without the corner of their eyes, to make them appear larger. Isaiah, in his enumeration of the several ornaments belonging to the daughters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SION">Sion</a>, has not forgot the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a> which they made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> their eyes and eyelids. Nor has this practice escaped the lash of Juvenal: Ille supercilium madida fuligine tinetum Obliqua producit acu, pingitque trementes Attollens oculos. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a>, discovering the irregularities of the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> under the idea of a debauched woman, says, Antimony, that she bathed and perfumed herself, and that she anointed her eyes with antimony. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a> shows sufficiently how much antimony was in esteem, by calling one of his daughters a vessel of antimony, or a box to put paint in, cornu fibiti. The author of the book of Enoch says, that before the deluge the angel Azazel taught young women the art of painting themselves. Tertullian and St Cyprian have declaimed very warmly against this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of painting the eyes and eyebrows, which was much practised in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> even by the men: Inuign oculos tuos non filio diaboli, fed collyrio Chrifi, says St Cyprian. Pliny, speaking of the Roman ladies, says, that they painted their very eyes: Tanta eff decoris affectatio, ut ingantur oculi quoque. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDANAPALUS">Sardanapalus</a> painted his eyes and eyebrows. Josephus reproaches the feditious with the same, who assumed the name of zealots, and made themselves masters of the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. The modern uses of antimony are very numerous and important. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> ingredient in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECTACLES">spectacles</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> concretes, serving to give the composition a finer texture. It makes a part in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a> metal, and renders the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> more clear. It is mingled with tin, to make it more hard, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and founding; and with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, in the casting of printers letters, to render them more smooth and firm. It is also a general help in the melting of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, and especially in casting of cannon-balls. It is likewise made use of for purifying and heightening the colour of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">CHEMISTRY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. For a long <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> this mineral was esteemed poisonous. In 1566, its use was prohibited in France by an edict of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and in 1609, one Befnier was expelled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> for having given it. The edict was repealed in 1652; antimony having a few years before been received into the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of purgatives. In 1668, a new edict came forth, forbidding its use by any but doctors of the faculty. It is now universally allowed, that pure antimony in its crude state has no noxious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, and that though many of its preparations are most virulently emetic and cathartic, yet, by a slight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> or addition, they lose their virulence, and become mild in their operation. The virtues of antimony in the diseases of animals are greatly extolled. Pigs that have the measles are at all times recovered by it, which proves it a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> purifier of the blood. Horses who have running heels that cannot be cured by the common methods used by the farriers, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> generally be cured by this medicine in a little time. The manner of using it is this: Mix one drachm with every feeding of oats which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> has in a morning. It is best put together in one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, buried under a few oats; and the horse's head being withheld a little, and then let go <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> against that place, he will take it all in at a mouthful. Some horses do not dislike it; others obstinately refuse it, but to these it may be easily given in balls. The virtues of this drug in fattening cattle have been thought imaginary, but experiment proves it to be a real <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. A horse that is lean and scabby, and not to be fattened by any other means, will become fat on taking a dose of antimony every morning for two months together. A boar fed for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, and having an ounce of antimony mony given him every morning, will become fat a fortnight sooner than others put into the flye at the same time, and fed in the same manner, but without the antimony. ANTINOE. See ENFINE.

ANTINOLIA

Pages 34-34

in Antiquity, annual sacrifices, and quinquennial games, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Antinous the Bithynian. They were instituted at the command of Adrian, the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, at Mantinea, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>, where Antinous was honoured with a temple and divine worship.

ANTINOMIANS

Pages 34-34

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, certain heretics who maintain the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> obligation under the gospel-dispensation, or who hold doctrines that clearly supercede the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of good works and a virtuous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. The Antinomians took their origin from John Agricola about the year 1538; who taught that the law is no ways necessary under the gospel; that good works do not promote our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a>, nor ill ones hinder it; that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a> is not to be preached from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECALOGUE">decalogue</a>, but only from the gospel. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> sprung up in England during the protectorate of Oliver Cromwell, and extended their system of libertinism much farther than Agricola the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>. Some of their teachers expressly maintained, that as the elect cannot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, nor forfeit the Divine favor, the wicked actions they commit are not really sinful, nor are to be considered as instances of their violation of the divine law; and that consequently they have no occasion either to confess their sins, or to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> them off by repentance. According to them, it is one of the essential and distinctive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the elect, that they cannot do anything which is either displeasing to God or prohibited by the law.—Luther, Rutherford, Schluffelburg, Sedgwick, Gataker, Witius, Bull, Williams, &c. have written refutations; Crip, Richardson, Saltmarsh, &c. defences, of the Antinomians; Wigandus, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Antinomians. The doctrine of Agricola was in itself obscure, and perhaps represented worse than it really was by Luther, who wrote with acrimony against him, and first styled him and his followers Antinomians. Agricola stood on his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, and complained that opinions were imputed to him which he did not hold. Nicholas Amidorf fell under the same odious name and imputation, and seems to have been treated more unfairly than even Agricola himself. It is rather hard to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> all the opinions that may be inferred from things that have haphazard dropped from him, when he himself disavows such inferences.

ANTINOUS

Pages 34-34

the favourite of Adrian, was born at Bithynus in Bithynia. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> engaged the heart of Adrian in such a manner, that there never was a more boundless and extravagant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> than that of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> towards this youth. After his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, the emperor ordered divine honours to be paid him; and he also erected a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of his name. See ENFINE.

ANTIOCH

Pages 34-36

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, situated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORONTES">Orontes</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 37° 5' N. Lat. 36° 20'. It was built by Seleucus Nicator, founder of the Syro-Macedonian empire, who made it his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. It stood on the above-mentioned river, about 20 miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it empties itself into the Mediterranean; being equally distant from Constantinople and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, that is, about 700 miles from each. Seleucus called it Antioch, from his father's name, according to some; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> from that of his son, according to others. He built 16 other cities <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the same name; of which one, situated in Paphia, is probably that where the name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> was first given to the followers of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ. But that founded on the Orontes by far eclipsed, not only all the others of this name, but all the cities built by Seleucus. Antigonus, not long before, had founded a city in that neighbourhood, which from his own name he had called Antigonia, and designed it for the capital of his empire; but it was razed to the ground by Seleucus, who employed the materials in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, and also transplanted the inhabitants thither. The city of Antioch was afterwards known by the name of Tetrapolis, being divided as it were into four cities, each of them being surrounded with its proper wall, besides a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> one which enclosed them all. The first of these cities was built by Seleucus Nicator, as already mentioned; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> by those who flocked thither on its being made the capital of the Syro-Macedonian empire; the third by Seleucus Callinicus; and the fourth by Antiochus Epiphanes.—About four or five miles distant, stood a place called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAPHNE">Daphne</a>, which was nevertheless reckoned a suburb of Antioch. Here Seleucus planted a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>, and in the middle of it built a temple which he consecrated to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, making the whole an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a>. To this place the inhabitants of Antioch resorted for their pleasures and diversions; whereby it became at last so infamous, that "to live after the manner of Daphne" was used as a proverb to express the most voluptuous and dissolute way of living. Here Lucius Verus, the colleague of M. Aurelius, chose to take up his residence, instead of marching against the Parthians; while his general Cassius forbade by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> any of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to enter or even go near the place. In short, to remarkable was Daphne of old, that the metropolis itself was distinguished by it, and called Antioch near Daphne. Though Antioch <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be, as Pliny calls it, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of the East, for near 1600 years; yet scarce any city mentioned in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> hath undergone such calamities, both from the attacks of its enemies, and its being naturally subject to earthquakes. The first disaster mentioned in history which befell the Antiochians happened about 145 years before Christ. Being at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> very much disaffected to the person and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Demetrius their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, they were continually raising tumults and seditions; insomuch that he found himself at last obliged to solicit assistance from the Jews; and was furnished by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JONATHAN">Jonathan</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACCABEES">Maccabees</a>, with 3000 men; by which reinforcement, believing himself sufficiently strong to reduce the mutineers by force, he ordered them immediately to deliver up their arms. This unexpected order caused a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> uproar in the city. The inhabitants ran to arms, and invested the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 120,000, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to put him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. All the Jews hastened to his relief, fell upon the rebels, killed 100,000 of them, and set fire to the city. On the destruction of the Syrian empire by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, Antioch submitted to them as well as the other cities of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and continued for a long time under their dominion. About the year 115, in the reign of the Antioch, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Trajan, it was almost entirely ruined by one of the most dreadful earthquakes mentioned in history. Trajan himself happened to be there at that time, being returned from an expedition against the Parthians; so that the city was then full of troops, and strangers came from all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> either out of curiosity or upon business and embassies: the calamity was by this means felt almost in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the Roman empire. The earthquake was preceded by violent claps of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>, unusual winds, and a dreadful noise under ground. The shock was so terrible, that great numbers of houses were overturned, and others tottered to and fro like a ship at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Those who happened to be in their houses were for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> buried under their ruins: those who were walking in the streets or in the squares, were, by the violence of the shock, dashed against each other, and most of them either killed or dangerously wounded. This earthquake continued, with some small intermission, for many days and nights; so that vast numbers perished. The most violent shock, according to the Acts of St Ignatius, was on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 23. By this Trajan was much hurt, but escaped through a window. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DION">Dion</a> Cassius pretends, that he was taken out of the window by one who exceeded the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> size in tallness. The same historian adds, that Mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LICON">Licon</a>, which stood at a small distance from the city, bowed its head and threatened to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> upon it: that other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> fell; that new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> appeared, and others that had flowed before forsook their course and vanished. When the earthquake ceased, a woman was heard crying under the ruins; which being immediately removed, she was found with a living child in her arms. Search was made for others; but none was found alive, except one child which continued sucking its dead mother. No doubt, Trajan, who was an eye-witness of this terrible calamity, would contribute largely towards the re-establishment of Antioch in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> splendour. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>, however, did not continue long; for in 155, it was almost entirely burnt by accidental fire; when it was again restored by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTONINUS_PIUS">Antoninus Pius</a>. In 176 or 177, the inhabitants having sided with Cassius, the above-mentioned Roman general, who had revolted from M. Aurelius, that emperor published a severe edict against them, deprived them of all their privileges, suppressed their public assemblies, and took from them the shows and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECTACLES">spectacles</a> to which they were greatly addicted: but his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> being soon appeased, he restored them to their former condition, and even condescended to visit their city. In 194, having sided with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NIGER">Niger</a> against Severus, the latter deprived them of all their privileges, and subjected Antioch as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> village to Laodicea; but, however, pardoned them the next year, at the entreaties of his eldest son, then a child. When the power of the Roman empire began to decline, Antioch became the bone of contention between them and the eastern nations; and accordingly, on the breaking out of a Persian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, it was almost always sure to suffer. In 242, it was taken and plundered by Sapor; and, though he was defeated by Gordian, it underwent the same misfortune in the time of Valerian, about 18 years after; and after the defeat and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> of Valerian, being taken by the Persian monarch a third time, he not only plundered it, but levelled all the public buildings with the ground. The Persians, however, being soon driven out, this unfortunate Antioch city continued free from any remarkable calamity till about the time of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the Roman empire by Constantine in 331. It was then afflicted with so grievous a famine, that a bushel of wheat was sold for 400 pieces of silver. During this grievous distress, Constantine sent to the bishop 30,000 bushels of corn; besides an incredible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, to be distributed among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, widows, orphans, &c. In the year 347, Constantine II. caused a harbour to be made at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SELEUCIA">Seleucia</a>, for the convenience of Antioch. This was effected at an immense expense; the mouth of the Orontes, where the port was made, being full of sands and rocks. When the emperor Julian set out on his expedition against the Persians, he made a long stay at Antioch; during which time, many of the Roman provinces were afflicted with a famine, but which raged more violently at Antioch than in other places. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers of those times say, that this famine followed Julian from place to place; and as he continued longer at Antioch than any other city, it raged more violently there than anywhere else. To remedy this evil, Julian fixed the price of corn; by which means the famine was greatly increased, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> conveying their corn privately to other places, so that this metropolis was reduced to a most deplorable situation. In 381, in the reign of Theodosius the Great, Antioch was again visited by a famine, accompanied by a grievous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>. The latter soon ceased; but, the famine still continuing, the bishop, Libanius, applied to Icarius, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of the East, requesting him by some means or other to relieve the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, who had flocked from all parts to the metropolis, and were daily perishing in great numbers; but to this Icarius gave no other answer, than that they were abhorred and justly punished by the gods. This inhuman answer raised great disturbances; which, however, were terminated without bloodshed. In 387, Theodosius finding his exchequer quite drained, and being obliged to be at an extraordinary expense in celebrating the fifth year of the reign of his son Arcadius, and the tenth of his own, an extraordinary tax was laid upon all the people in the empire. Most of the cities submitted willingly to this; but the people of Antioch, complaining of it as an unreasonable oppression, crowded to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Flavianus, their bishop, as soon as the edict was published, to implore his protection. Being unable to find him, they returned to the forum; and would have torn the governor in pieces, had not the officers who attended him kept back with great difficulty the enraged multitude, till he made his escape. Upon this, they broke some of the emperor's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, and dragged others through the city, uttering the most injurious and abusive expressions against him and his whole family. They were, however, dispersed by a body of archers, who, by wounding only two of the rabble, struck terror into all the rest. The governor proceeded against the offenders with the utmost cruelty; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> some to wild beasts in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> others alive. He did not spare even the children, who had insulted the emperor's statues; and caused several persons to be executed, who had been only spectators of the disorder. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time a report was spread, that a body of troops was at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, with orders to plunder the city. Antioch city, and put all to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, without distinction of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; upon which the citizens abandoned their dwellings in the utmost terror and confusion, retiring to the neighbouring mountains with their wives and families. As the report proved groundless, some of them returned; but the greater part dreading the cruelty of the governor, and the displeasure of the emperor, continued in their retreats. To those who returned, St Chrysostom preached some homilies, which have reached our times, and are greatly admired; and which are said by St Chrysostom himself, as well as some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> writers, to have had a considerable effect in reforming the lives of this licentious and dissolute people. On hearing the news of this tumult, Theodosius was so much enraged, that he commanded the city to be destroyed, and its inhabitants to be put to the sword without distinction; but this order was revoked before it could be put into execution, and he contented himself with a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> similar to that inflicted by Severus above mentioned. He appointed judges to punish the offenders; who proceeded with such severity, and condemned such numbers, that the city was thrown into the utmost consternation. On this occasion, St Chrysostom and the hermits, who were very numerous in the neighbourhood, exerted all their eloquence in behalf of the unhappy people, and obtained a respite for those who had been condemned. They next proceeded to draw up a memorial to the emperor in favour of the citizens in general; and being joined by Flavianus, at last obtained a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>, and had the city restored to all its former privileges. In the year 458, Antioch was almost entirely ruined by an earthquake, which happened on the 14th of September; scarce a single house being left standing in the most beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the city. The like misfortune it experienced in 525, during the reign of the emperor Justin; and in 15 years after, being taken by Cosroes king of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, that infatuated and haughty monarch gave it up to his soldiers, who put all they met to the sword. The king himself seized on all the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver vessels belonging to the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; and caused all the valuable statues, pictures, &c., to be taken down and conveyed to Persia, while his soldiers carried off everything else. The city being thus completely plundered, Cosroes ordered his men to set fire to it; which was accordingly done so effectually, that none of the buildings even without the walls escaped. Such of the inhabitants as escaped slaughter were carried into Persia, and sold as slaves. Notwithstanding so many and so great calamities, the city of Antioch soon recovered its wonted splendour; but in a short time underwent its usual fate, being almost entirely destroyed by an earthquake in 587, by which 30,000 persons lost their lives. In 624, it fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Saracens, who kept possession of it till the year 838, when it was surprized by one Burtzas, and again annexed to the Roman empire. The Romans continued masters of it for some time, till the civil dissensions in the empire gave the Turks an opportunity of seizing upon it as well as the whole kingdom of Syria. From then it was again taken by the Crusaders in 1098. In 1262, it was again taken by Bibars <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> of Egypt, who put a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>. Antioch is now no more than a ruinous town, whose houses, built with mud and straw, and narrow and miry streets, exhibit every appearance of misery and wretchedness. These houses are situated on the southern <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Orontes, at the extremity of an old decayed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>: they are covered to the south by a mountain; upon the slope of which is a wall, built by the Crusaders. The distance between the present town and this mountain may be about 400 yards, which space is occupied by gardens and heaps of rubbish, but prevents nothing interesting. Notwithstanding the unpolished manners of its inhabitants, Antioch was better calculated than <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a> to be the emporium of the Europeans. By clearing the mouth of the Orontes, which is six leagues lower down, boats might have been towed up that river, though they could not have sailed up, as Pococke has asserted; its current being too rapid. The natives, who never knew the name Orontes, call it, on account of the swiftness of its stream, El-aghi, that is, the rebel. Its breadth, at Antioch, is about forty paces. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> leagues above that town it passes by a lake abounding in fish, and especially in eels. A great quantity of these are fished every year, but not sufficient for the numerous faults of the Greek Christians. It is to be remembered, we no longer hear at Antioch, either of the Grove, or Daphne, or of the voluptuous scenes of which it was the theatre. The plain of Antioch, though the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of it is excellent, is uncultivated, and abandoned to the Turcomans; but the hills on the side of the Orontes, particularly opposite Serkin, abound in plantations of figs and olives, vines, and mulberry trees, which, a thing uncommon in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, are planted in quincunx, and exhibit a landscape worthy our finest provinces. Seleucus Nicator, who founded Antioch, built also at the mouth of the Orontes, on the northern bank, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and well fortified city, which bore his name, but of which at present not a single habitation remains; nothing is to be seen but heaps of rubbish, and works in the adjacent rock, which prove that this was once a place of very considerable importance. In the sea also may be perceived the traces of two piers, which are indications of an ancient port, now choked up. The inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> go thither to fish, and call the name of the place Souaidia.

ANTIOCHETTA

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARAMANIA">Caramania</a>, with a bishop's see, over against the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Cyprus. ANTIOCHIA

Pages 36-37

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, situated between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Tigris and Tigradotus (Pliny).—Another of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, on the Meander; called also Pythopolis, Athymbra, and Nyfa, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Nyfa (Stephanus): but Strabo says, that Nyfa was near Tralles.—A third of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a> Trachea, on Mount Craigus (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>).—A fourth, called Epiphanes, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, distinguished from cities of the same name, either by its situation on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORONTES">Orontes</a>, by which it was divided, or by its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROXIMITY">proximity</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAPHNE">Daphne</a> (See Antioch).—A fifth Antiochia, a town of Comagene, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> (Pliny).—A sixth of Lydia Tralles, so called (Pliny).—A seventh of Margiana (Strabo, Pliny, Ptolemy), on the river Margus, taking its name from Antiochus, son of Seleucus, who rebuilt it, and walled it round, being before called <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, from Antiochian from Alexander the founder, and surnamed Syria; in compass seventy stadia; whither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORODES">Orodes</a> carried the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, after the defeat of Crassus (Pliny).—An eighth, in Melopotamia, on the lake Calirrhoes, the old name of Edeleia (Pliny).—A ninth Antiochia, on the river Mygdonius, in Melopotamia, situated at the foot of Mount Marsus, and is the same with Nifibis (Strabo, Plutarch). It was the bulwark and frontier town of the Romans against the Parthians and Persians, till given up to the Persians, by Jovinian, by an ignominious peace (Amnian, Eutropius).—A tenth Antiochia, was that situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Pisidia (Luke, Ptolemy, Strabo): it was a Roman colony, with the appellation Caesarea. There is an Antiochia at Mount Taurus, mentioned by Ptolemy, but by no other author. ANTIOCHIAN <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> or Academy, a name given to the fifth academy, or branch of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">Academies</a>. It took the denomination from its being founded by Antiochus, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Cicero.—The Antiochian academy succeeded the Philonian. As to point of doctrine, the philosophers of this sect appear to have restored that of the ancient academy, except that in the article of the criterion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. Antiochus was really a Stoic, and only nominally an Academic. ANTIOCHIAN Epoch, a method of computing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> granted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Antioch about the time of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARSALIA">Pharsalia</a>.

ANTIOCHUS

Pages 37-37

the name of several kings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>. See that article. Antiochus of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASCALON">Ascalon</a>, a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Philo of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARISSA">Larissa</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Cicero, and the friend of Lucullus and Brutus. He was founder of a fifth academy: but, instead of attacking other sects, he set himself <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to reconcile them together, particularly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the Stoics with that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> academy.

ANTIOPE

Pages 37-37

in Fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, the wife of Licus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Thebes, who, being deflowered by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> in the form of a satyr, brought forth Amphion and Zethus.—Another Antiope was <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMAZONS">Amazons</a>; and, with the assistance of the Scythians, invaded the Athenians; but was vanquished by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a>. ANTIPÆDOBAPTISTS, (derived from ἀπὸ, again, παιδός, child, and βαπτίζω, baptize, whence βαπτιστής), is a distinguishing denomination given to those who object to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a>; because they say infants are incapable of being instructed, and of making that profession of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> which entitles them to this ordinance, and an admission into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANABAPTISTS">Anabaptists</a> and Baptists.

ANTIPAROS

Pages 37-40

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Archipelago, opposite to Paros, from which it is separated by a strait about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles over. It is the Olearos <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Oliaros, mentioned by Strabo, Pliny, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Ovid, &c.; and was, according to Heracles Ponticus as quoted by Stephanus, first peopled by a Phoenician colony from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIDON">Sidon</a>.—According to Mr Tournefort's account, it is about 16 miles in circumference, produces a little wine and cotton, with as much corn as is necessary for the maintenance of 60 or 70 families, who live together in a village at one end of the island, and are mostly Maltese and French corsairs. This island is remarkable for a subterraneous cavern or grotto, accounted one of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> curiosities in the world. It was first discovered in the last century by one Magni an Italian traveller, who has given us the following account: "Having been informed (says he) by the natives of Paros, that in the little island of Antiparos, which lies about two miles from the former, of a gigantic statue that was to be seen at the mouth of a cavern in that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, it was resolved that we (the French <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> and himself) should pay it a visit. In pursuance of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, after we had landed on the island, and walked about four miles through the midst of beautiful plains and sloping woodlands, we at length came to a little hill, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of which yawned a most horrid cavern, that, with its gloom, at first struck us with terror, and almost repressed curiosity. Recovering the first surprise, however, we entered boldly; and had not proceeded above 20 paces, when the supposed statue of the giant presented itself to our view. We quickly perceived, that what the ignorant natives had been terrified at as a giant, was nothing more than a spartry concretion, formed by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> dropping from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of the cave, and by degrees hardening into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> that their fears had formed into a monster. Incited by this extraordinary appearance, we were induced to proceed still further, in quest of new adventures in this subterranean abode. As we proceeded, new wonders offered themselves; the spars, formed into trees and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, presented a kind of petrified <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>; some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, some green; and all receding in due <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>. They struck us with the more amazement, as we knew them to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> productions of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a>, who, hitherto in solitude, had, in her playful moments, dressed the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> for her own amusement. "But we had as yet seen but a few of the wonders of the place, and we were introduced as yet only into the portico of this amazing temple. In one corner of this half illuminated recess, there appeared an opening of about three feet wide, which seemed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to a place totally dark, and that one of the natives assured us contained nothing more than a reservoir of water. Upon this we tried, by throwing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> some <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, which rumbling along the sides of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> seemed at last quashed in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of water. In order, however, to be more certain, we sent a Levantine mariner, who, by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of a good reward, with a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAMBEAU">flambeau</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, ventured into this narrow aperture. After continuing within it for about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, he returned, carrying some beautiful pieces of white <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAR">spar</a> in his hand, which art could neither imitate nor equal. Upon being informed by him that the place was full of these beautiful incrustations, I ventured in once more with him, for about 50 paces, anxiously and cautiously descending by a steep and dangerous way. Finding, however, that we came to a precipice which led into a spacious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>, if I may so call it, full deeper than any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, we returned; and being provided with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LADDER">ladder</a>, flambeaux, and other things, to expedite our descent, our whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> by man, ventured into the same opening, and, descending one after another, we at last <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> ourselves all together in the most magnificent part of the cavern. "Our candles being now all lighted up, and the whole place completely illuminated, never could the eye be presented with a more glittering or a more magnifi- Antiparos cent scene. The roof all hung with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> icicles, transparent as glass, yet solid as marble. The eye could scarce reach the lofty and noble ceiling; the sides were regularly formed with spars; and the whole presented the idea of a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, illuminated with an immense profusion of lights. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> consisted of solid marble; and in several places, magnificent columns, thrones, altars, and other objects, appeared, as if nature had designed to mock the curiosities of art. Our voices, upon speaking or singing, were redoubled to an astonishing loudness; and, upon the firing of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a>, the noise and reverberations were almost deafening. In the midst of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> amphitheatre rose a concretion of about 15 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, that, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, resembled an altar; from which, taking the hint, we caused mats to be celebrated there. The beautiful columns that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> up round the altar, appeared like candlesticks; and many other natural objects represented the customary ornaments of this sacrament. "Below even this spacious grotto, there seemed another cavern; down which I ventured with my former mariner, and descended about 50 paces by means of a rope. I at last arrived at a small spot of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> ground, where the bottom appeared different from that of the amphitheatre, being composed of soft clay, yielding to the pressure, and in which I thrust a stick to about six feet deep. In this, however, as above, numbers of the most beautiful crystals were formed; one of which, particularly resembled a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. Upon our escape from this amazing cavern, we perceived a Greek inscription upon a rock at the mouth; but so obliterated by time, that we could not read it. It seemed to import, that one Antipater, in the time of Alexander, had come thither; but whether he penetrated into the depths of the cavern, he does not think fit to inform us." From this account Mr Tournefort's differs considerably.
