Mr Magni mentions only one descent or precipice from the entry of the cave to the grotto, or most magnificent part; Mr Tournefort says that there were many very dangerous precipices and rugged ways, through which they were obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> sometimes on their back, and sometimes on their belly; but gives no particular account of his journey till he came to the grand cavern. This indeed he describes very pompously; but as by it he evidently wants to support a favorite <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, namely, the vegetation of stones, perhaps the particulars are not altogether to be depended upon. He, informs us, that, at the entry into the cavern, he met with a Greek inscription almost effaced, containing a good <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of proper names; and that there was a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> among the inhabitants, that these were the names of some who had conspired against Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, and having missed their aim, had taken refuge in this grotto. The most particular account, however, of this famous grotto that hath hitherto been published, appeared in the British <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> signed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Saunders, and dated Feb. 24, 1746-7; which, as it is very particular, and seems to bear sufficient marks of authenticity, we shall here insert. "Its entrance lies in the side of a rock, about two miles from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-shore; and is a spacious and very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, formed of rough craggy rocks, overhung with brambles and a great many climbing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, that give it a gloomy aspect which is very awful and agreeable. Our surgeon, myself, and four passengers, attended by six guides Antiparos, with lighted torches, entered this cavern about eight o'clock in the morning, in the middle of August last. We had not gone 20 yards in this cavity when we lost all sight of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>: but our guides going before us with lights, we entered into a low narrow kind of alley, surrounded ever way with stones all glittering like diamonds by the light of our torches; the whole being covered and lined throughout with small crystals, which gave a thousand various colours by their different reflections. This alley grows lower and narrower as one goes on, till at length one can scarce get along it. At the end of this passage we were each of us prefaced with a rope, to tie about our middles; which when we had done, our guides led us to the brink of a most horrible precipice. The descent into this was quite steep, and the place all dark and gloomy. We could see nothing, in short, but some of our guides with torches in a miserable dark place, at a vast distance below us. The dreadful depth of this place, and the horror of the descent through a miserable darkness into it, made me look back to the lane of diamonds, if I may so call it, through which we had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> passed; and I could not but think I was leaving heaven, to descend into the infernal regions. The hope of something fine at my journey's end tempted me, however, to trust myself to the rope and my guides at the top, to let myself down. After about two minutes dangling in this posture, not without much pain as well as terror, I found myself safe, however, at the bottom; and our friends all soon followed the example. When we had congratulated here with one another on our safe descent; I was inquiring where the grotto, as they called it, was. Our guides, shaking their heads, told us, we had a great way to that yet; and led us forward about 30 yards under a roof of rugged rocks, in a scene of terrible darkness, and at a vast depth from the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, to the brink of another precipice much deeper and more terrible than the former. Two of the guides went down here with their torches first; and by their light we could see, that this passage was not so perpendicular indeed as the other, but lay in a very steep slant, with a very slippery rock for the bottom; vast pieces of rough rugged rocks jutting out in many places on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> hand, in the descent, and forcing the guides sometimes to climb over, sometimes to creep under them, and sometimes to round them; and on the left, a thousand dark caverns, like so many monstrous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, ready, if a foot should slip, to swallow them up for ever. We stood on the edge to see these people with their lights descend before us; and were amazed and terrified to see them continue descending till they seemed at a monstrous and most frightful depth. When they were at the bottom, however, they hollered to us; and we, trembling and quaking, began to descend after them. We had not gone 30 feet down, when we came to a place where the rock was perfectly perpendicular; and a vast cavern seemed to open its mouth to swallow us up on one side, while a wall of rugged rock threatened to tear us to pieces on the other. I was quite disheartened at this terrible prospect, and declared I would go back; but our guides assured us there was no danger; and the rest of the company resolving to see the bottom now they were come so far, I would not leave them: so on we went to a corner where Antigonus there was placed an old slippery and rotten ladder, which hung down <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the rock; and down this, one after another, we at length all descended. When we had got to the bottom of this we found ourselves at the entrance of another passage, which was terrible enough indeed; but in this there was not wanting something of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. This was a wide and gradual descent; at the entrance of which one of our guides steadied himself on his breech, and began to slide down, telling us we must do the same. We could discover, by the light of his torch, that this passage was one of the noblest vaults in the world. It is about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> feet high, seven wide, and as for its bottom a fine green glossy marble. The walls and arch of the roof of this being as smooth and even in most places as if wrought by art, and made of a fine glittering <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> and white <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>, supported here and there with columns of a deep blood-red shining porphyry, made, with the reflection of the lights, an appearance not to be conceived. This passage is at least 40 yards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; and of so steep a descent, that one has enough to do, when seated on one's breech, not to descend too quickly. Our guides, that we kept with us, could here keep on each side of us; and, what with the prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and beauty of the place, our easy travelling through it, and the diversion of our now and then running over one another whether we would or not; this was much the pleasantest part of our journey. When we had entered this passage, I imagined we should at the bottom join the two guides we had first set down; but alas! when we were got there we found ourselves only at the mouth of another precipice, down which we descended by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> ladder not much better than the former. I could have admired this place also, would my terror have suffered me; but the dread of falling, kept all my thoughts employed during my descent. I could not but observe, however, as my companions were coming down after me, that the wall, if I may so call it, which the ladder hung by, was one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of blood-red marble, covered with white sprigs of rock crystal as long as my finger, and making, with the glow of the purple from behind, one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> immense sheet of amethysts. From the foot of this ladder we slid on our bellies through another hollow vault of polished green and white marble, about 20 feet; and at the bottom of this joined our guides. Here we all got together once again, and drank some rum, to give us courage before we proceeded any farther. After this short refreshment, we proceeded by a strait, but somewhat flanking passage, of a rough, hard, and somewhat coarse <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, full of a thousand strange figures of snakes rolled round, and looking as if alive; but in reality as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and hard as the rest of the stone, and nothing but some of the stone itself in that shape. We walked pretty easily along this descent for near 200 yards; where we saw two pillars seemingly made to support the roof from falling in; but in reality it was no such thing; for they were very brittle, and made of a fine glittering <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> marble. When we had passed these about 200 yards, we found ourselves at the brink of another very terrible precipice; but this our guides assured us was the last; and there being a very good ladder to go down by, we readily ventured. At the bottom of this steep wall, as I may call it, we found ourselves for some way upon plain even ground; but, after about 40 yards walking, were presented by our guides with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> again; which Antigonus we fastened about our middles, though not to be swung down by, but only for fear of danger, as there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and deep waters all the way from hence on the left hand. With this caution, however, we entered the last alley; and horrible <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> it was indeed to get through it. All was perfectly horrid and dismal here. The sides and roof of the passage were all of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> stone; and the rocks in our way were in some places so steep, that we were forced to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> all along on our backs, and slide down; and so rough, that they cut our clothes, and bruised us miserably in passing. Over our heads, there was nothing but ragged black rocks, some of them looking as if they were every moment ready to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in upon us; and, on our left <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, the light of our guides' torches showed us continually the surfaces of dirty and miserably looking lakes of water. If I had heartily repented of my expedition often before, here I assure you I was all in a cold sweat, and fairly gave myself over for lost; heartily cursing all the travellers that had written of this place, that they had described it so as to tempt people to see it, and never told us of the horrors that lay in the way. In the midst of all these reflections, and in the very dismallest part of all the cavern, on a sudden we had lost four of our six guides. What was my terror on this sight! The place was a thousand times darker and more terrible for want of their torches; and I expected no other but every moment to follow them into some of these lakes, into which I doubted not but they were fallen. The remaining two guides said all they could indeed, to cheer us up; and told us we should see the other four again soon, and that we were near the end of our journey. I do not know what effect this might have upon the rest of my companions; but I assure you I believed no part of the speech but the last, which I expected every moment to find fulfilled in some pond or precipice. Our passage was by this time become very narrow, and we were obliged to crawl on all-fours over rugged rocks; when in an instant, and in the midst of these melancholy apprehensions, I heard a little hissing noise, and saw myself in utter, and not to be described, darkness. Our guides called indeed cheerfully to us, and told us that they had accidentally dropped their torches into a puddle of water, but we should soon come to the rest of them, and they would light them again; and told us there was no danger, and we had nothing to do but to crawl forward. I cannot say but I was amazed at the courage of these people; who were in a place where, I thought, four of them had already perished, and from whence we could none of us ever escape; and determined to lie down and die where I was. Words cannot describe the horror, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> darkness of the place. One of our guides, however, perceiving that I did not advance, came up to me, and clapping his hand firmly over my eyes, dragged me a few paces forward. While I was in this strange condition, expecting every moment <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in a thousand shapes, and trembling to think what the guide meant by this rough proceeding, he lifted me at once over a great stone, let me down on my feet, and took his hand from before my eyes. What words can describe at that instant my astonishment and transport! Instead of darkness and despair, all was splendour and magnificence before me: our guides all appeared about us: the place was illuminated by 50 torches, Antiparos, torches, and the guides all welcomed me into the gro- to of Antiparos. The four that were first missing, I now found had only given us the slip, to get the torches lighted up before we came; and the other two had put out their lights on purpose, to make us enter out of utter darkness into this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVILION">pavilion</a> of splendour and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>. I am now come to the proper business of this letter: which was to describe this grotto. But I must confess to you that words cannot do it. The amazing beauties of the place, the eye that sees them only can conceive. The best account I can give you, however, pray accept of. "The people told us, the depth of this place was 485 yards, the grotto, in which we now were, is a cavern of 120 yards wide, and 13 long, and seems about 60 yards high in most places. These <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> differ something from the accounts travellers in general give us; but you may depend upon them as exact, for I took them with my own hand. Imagine then yourself, an immense arch like this, almost all over lined with fine and bright crystallized white marble, and illuminated with so torches; and you <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> then have some faint idea of the place I had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> to spend three hours in. This, however, is but a faint <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of its beauties. The roof, which is a fine vaulted arch, is hung all over with icicles of white shining marble, some of them ten feet long, and as thick as one's middle at the root; and among these hang a thousand festoons of leaves and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, of the same substance; but so very glittering, that there is no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> to look up at them. The sides of the arch are planted with seeming trees of the same white marble, rising in rows one above another, and often enclosing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the icicles. From these trees there are also hung festoons, tied as it were from one to another in vast quantities; and in some places among them there seem <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of marble winding through them in a thousand meanders. All these things are only made, in a long course of years, from the dropping of water, but really look like trees and brooks turned to marble. The floor we trod upon was rough and uneven, with crystals of all colours growing irregularly out of it, red, blue, green, and some of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> yellow. These were all shaped like pieces of falkpetre; but so hard, that they cut our shoes: among these, here and there, are placed icicles of the same white shining marble with those above, and seeming to have fallen down from the roof and fixed there; only the big end of these is to the floor. To all these our guides had tied torches, two or three to a pillar, and kept continually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> them to make them burn bright. You may guess what a glare of splendour and beauty must be the effect of this illumination, among such rocks and columns of marble. All round the lower part of the sides of the arch are a thousand white masses of marble, in the shape of oak trees. Mr Tournefort compares them to cauliflowers, but I should as soon compare them to toadstools. In short, they are large enough to enclose, in many places, a piece of ground big enough for a bedchamber. One of these chambers has a fair white curtain, whiter than satin, of the same marble, stretched all over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of it. In this we all cut our names, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> of the year, as a great many people have done before us. In a course of years afterwards, the stone blisters out like this white marble over the letters. Mr Tourne- fort thinks the rock grows like oaks or apple trees for this reason; but I remember I saw some of the finest cockle and mulete shells, in the rock thereabouts, that ever I saw in my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. I wonder whether he thinks they grow there too. Besides, if this rock grows so fast, the cavern ought to be all grown up by this time; and yet, according to his measures and mine, the cavern seems on the other hand to be turned larger since. Indeed, all that I can gather from his account of this glorious place is, that he had drank a little or two too much before he went down into it."

ANTIPAS HEROD

Pages 40-42
or HEROD ANTIPAS, the son of Herod the Great, by one of his wives called Cleopatra, a native of Jerusalem. Herod the Great, in his first will, appointed Antipas his successor in the kingdom; but afterwards, altering that will, he named his son Archelaus his successor, giving to Antipas the title only of tetrarch of Galilee and Perea. Antipas took a great deal of pains in adorning and fortifying the principal places of his dominions. He married the daughter of Aretas king of Arabia; whom he divorced about the year of Christ 33, to marry his sister-in-law Herodias, wife to his brother Philip, who was still living. St John the Baptist claiming continually against this incest, was taken into custody by order of Antipas, and imprisoned in the castle of Macherus, (Mat. xiv. 3, 4. Mark i. 14. vi. 17, 18. Luke iii. 19, 20.) Josephus says, that Antipas caused St John to be laid hold of, because he drew too great a concourse of people after him; and that he was afraid lest he should make use of the authority which he had acquired over the minds and affections of the people, to induce them to revolt. But the evangelists, who were better informed than Josephus, as being eye-witnesses of what passed, and acquainted in a particular manner with St John and his disciples, assures us that the true reason of imprisoning St John was, the aversion which Herod and Herodias had conceived against him for the liberty he had used in censuring their scandalous marriage. The virtue and holiness of St John were such that even Herod feared and respected him; but his passion for Herodias had prevailed with him to have killed that prophet, had he not been restrained by his apprehensions of the people, who esteemed John the Baptist as a prophet. (Mat. xiv. 5, 6.) One day, however, while the king was celebrating the festival of his birth, with the principal persons of his court, the daughter of Herodias danced before him; and pleaded him so well, that he promised with an oath to give her whatever she should ask of him. By her mother's advice she asked the head of John the Baptist: upon which the king commanded John to be beheaded in prison, and the head to be given her. Aretas, king of Arabia, to revenge the affront which Herod had offered to his daughter, declared war against him, and overcame him in a very obstinate engagement. Herod being afterwards detected as a party in Sejanus's conspiracy, was banished by the emperor Caius to Lyons in Gaul; whither Herodias accompanied him. This Antipas is the Herod who, being at Jerusalem at the time of our Saviour's passion (Luke xxiii. 11.), ridiculed him, by dressing him in a white robe, and directing him to be conducted back to Pilate, as a mock king, whose ambition gave him no umbrage. The time when Antipas died is not known: however, it is certain Antipater, certain he died in exile, as well as Herodias. Josephus says, that he died in Spain, whither Caius upon his coming to Gaul, the first year of his banishment, might order him to be sent. Antipater, the disciple of Aristotle, and one of Alexander the Great's generals, was a man of great abilities, and a lover of the sciences; but was accused of poisoning Alexander. He subdued the revolted Thracians, relieved Megalopolis, and overthrew the Spartans there. He died 321 years before the Christian era. Antipater, an Idumean of illustrious birth, and possessed of great riches and abilities, taking advantage of the confusion into which the two brothers Hyrcanus and Aristobulus plunged Judea by their contest for the office of high priest, took such measures as to gain Hyrcanus that office, and under his government to obtain the absolute direction of all affairs; while his great abilities and application to business made him so considerable, that he was honoured as much as if he had been invested with the royal authority in form: but he was at last poisoned by a Jew, named Malachus, 43 years before the Christian era. He left among his other children, the famous Herod king of the Jews. Antipater, Caelius, a Roman historian, who wrote a history of the Punic war, much valued by Cicero. The emperor Adrian preferred him to Sallust. Antipater of Sidon, a Stoic philosopher, and likewise a poet, commended by Cicero and Seneca: he flourished about the 171st Olympiad. We have several of his epigrams in the Anthologia. Antipathy, in Philosophy, is formed from the two Greek words ἀντί contrary, and πάθος passion. Literally taken, the word signifies incompatibility: but for the most part the term antipathy is not used to signify such incompatibilities as are merely phyletic; it is reserved to express the aversion which an animated or sensitive being feels at the real or ideal presence of particular objects. In this point of view, which is the light in which we at present consider the term, antipathy, in common language, signifies "a natural horror and detestation, an insuperable hatred, an involuntary aversion, which a sensitive being feels for some other object, whatever it is, though the person who feels this abhorrence is entirely ignorant of its cause, and can by no means account for it. Such is, they say, the natural and reciprocal hostility between the salamander and the tortoise; between the toad and the weasel; or between sheep and wolves. Such is the invincible aversion of particular persons against cats, mice, spiders, &c.; a prepossession which is sometimes so violent, as to make them faint at the sight of these animals. Of these and a thousand other antipathies the ancient naturalists, the schoolmen, and the vulgar, form so many legends; and relate them as certain facts, that they may demand an explication of them from the philosophers. But these fables begin with investigating whether such antipathies actually exist or not. To explore the matter without prejudice, we shall find it necessary to abstract from the subjects of this dilapidation, 1. All such antipathies as are not after-mentioned; as that which is supposed to be felt by hens at the sound of an harp whose strings are made of a fox's bowels, between the salamander and tortoise, and Antipathies between the weasel and the toad. Nothing is less confirmed, or rather nothing is more false, than these facts, with which vulgar credulity and astonishment are amused and actuated: and though some of these antipathies should be ascertained, this would be no proof that the animals which feel them are not acquainted with their causes, according to their mode and proportion of knowledge; in which case it will be no longer the antipathy which we have defined. 2. We must abstract those antipathies which can be extinguished or removed at pleasure; those fictitious aversions, which certain persons feel, or pretend to feel, with affected airs, that they may appear more precise and fixed, or singularly and prodigiously elegant; that they may seem to have qualities so exquisitely fine, as require to be treated with peculiar delicacy. One who bestows any attention on the subject, would be astonished to find how many of these chimerical aversions there are, which are pretended, and passed upon the world by those who affect them as natural and unconquerable. 3. When we abstract those aversions the causes of which are known and evident; we shall be surprized after our deduction of these pretended antipathies from the general sum, how small, how inconsiderable, is the quantity of those which are conformable to our definition. Will any one pretend to call by the name of antipathy, those real, innate, and incontestable aversions which prevail between sheep and wolves? Their cause is obvious; the wolf devours the sheep, and subsists upon its victims; and every animal naturally flies with terror from pain or destruction; sheep ought therefore to regard wolves with horror, which for their nutrition tear and mangle the unresisting prey. From principles similar to this, arises that aversion which numbers of people feel against serpents; against small animals, such as reptiles in general, and the greatest number of insects. During the credulous and susceptible period of infancy, pains have been taken to impress on our minds the frightful idea that they are venomous; that their bite is mortal; that their sting is dangerous, productive of tormenting inflammations or tumours, and sometimes fatal: they have been represented to us as ugly and loathsome; as being, for that reason, pernicious to those who touch them; as poisoning those who have the misfortune to swallow them. These horrible prepossessions are industriously inculcated from our infancy; they are sometimes attended and supported by dismal tales, which are greedily imbibed, and indelibly engraven on our memories. It has been taught us both by precept and example, when others at their approach have assumed in our view the appearance of detestation and even of terror, that we should fly from them, that we should not touch them. Is it then wonderful (if our false impressions as to this subject have been corrected neither by future reflections nor experiments), that we should entertain, during our whole lives, an aversion for these objects, even when we have forgot the admonitions, the conversations, and examples, which have taught us to believe and apprehend them as noxious beings? and in proportion to the sensibility of our frame, in proportion as our nerves are irritable, our emotions at the sight of what we fear will be more violent, especially if they anticipate our Antipathy, our expectation, and seize us unprepared, though our ideas of what we have to fear from them are the most confused and indistinct imaginable. To explain these facts, is it necessary to fly to the exploded subterfuge of occult qualities inherent in bodies, to latent relations productive of antipathies, of which no person could ever form an idea? It is often sufficient to influence a person who had formerly no aversion for an object, if he lives with some other associate who gives himself up to such capricious panics; the habit is insensibly contracted to be agitated with disagreeable emotions at the presence of an object which had been formerly beheld with indifference and cold blood. I was acquainted (says the author of the article Antipathy in the French Encyclopédie) with a person of a very sound understanding, whom thunder and lightning by no means terrified; nay, to whom the spectacle appeared magnificent and the sound majestic: yet to a mind thus feebly fortified against the infectious terror, no more was necessary than spending the summer with a friend in whom the appearance of lightning excited the strongest emotions, and whom the remotest clap of thunder affected with extravagant paroxysms, to become timid in excess at the approach of thunder; nor could he ever afterwards surmount the fear which it inspired. The frightful stories of dogs and cats, which have killed their masters, or which have given them mortal wounds, are more than sufficient to inspire a timorous person with aversion against these animals; and if the olfactory nerves of such a person be delicate, he will immediately discover the smell of them in a chamber: disturbed by the apprehension which these effluvia excite in his mind, he gives himself up to the most violent uneasiness, which is tranquillized when he is assured that the animal is no longer in the room. If by chance, in the search which is made to calm the uneasiness of this timorous person, one of these creatures should at last be discovered, every one presently exclaims, A miracle! and admits the reality of antipathies into his creed; whilst all this is nothing but the effect of a childish fear, founded on certain confused and exaggerated ideas of the hazard which one may run with these animals. The antipathy which some people entertain against cats, though they are eaten by others with pleasure, arises from nothing but the fear of serpents, to which these fishes are in some degree similar. There are likewise other antipathies which do not originate in the imagination, but arise from some natural incongruity; such as we often remark in children, for particular kinds of victuals, with which their taste is not offended, but which their stomachs cannot digest, and which are therefore digested as soon as swallowed. To what then are those antipathies, of which we have heard so much, reducible? Either to legendary tales; or to aversions against objects which we believe dangerous; or to a childish terror of imaginary perils; or to a delirium, of which the cause is dilated; or to a ridiculous affectation of delicacy; or to an infirmity of the stomach; in a word, to a real or pretended reluctance for things which are either invited, or supposed to be inveterate, with qualities hurtful to us. Too much care cannot be taken in preventing, or regulating, the antipathies of children; in familiarizing them with objects of every kind; in discovering to them, without emotion, such as are dangerous; in teaching them the Antipathy means of defence and security, or the methods of clearing their noxious influence; and, when the rational Antipathy powers are matured by age, in reflecting on the nature of those objects which we fear, in ascertaining what has been told concerning their qualities, or in vigorously operating upon our own dispositions to overcome those vain repugnancies which we may feel. See Sympathy, which is the opposite of Antipathy. Antipathy, in Ethics, hatred, aversion, repugnancy. Hatred is entertained against persons; aversion, and antipathy, indiscriminately against persons or things; and repugnancy, against actions alone. Hatred is more voluntary than aversion, antipathy, or repugnancy. These last have greater affinity with the animal constitution. The causes of antipathy are less known than those of aversion. Repugnancy is less permanent than either the one or the other. We hate a vicious character, we feel aversion to its exertions: we are affected with antipathy for certain persons at first sight; there are some affairs which we transact with repugnancy—Hatred calumniates; aversion keeps us at a distance from certain persons: antipathy makes us detest them; repugnancy hinders us from imitating them.

ANTIPATRIS

Pages 42-42

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, anciently called Caphtor Saba, according to Josephus, but named Antipatris by Herod the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of his father Antipater. It was situated in a pleasant valley near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, in the way from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> to Caesarea. Josephus places it at about the distance of nineteen miles from Joppa.

ANTIPELARGIA

Pages 42-42

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, whereby children are obliged to furnish necessaries to their aged parents. The ciconia, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stork, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> famous for the care it takes of its parents when grown old. Hence, in some Latin writers, this is rendered lex eiconioria, or the stork's law.

ANTIPHONARY

Pages 42-42

antiphonarium, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> book, which contained all the invitatories, responsories, collects, and whatever else was sung <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> said in the choir, except the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a>. This is otherwise called responsorium, from the responses therein contained. The author of the Roman antiphonary was Pope Gregory the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>. We also find mention of nocturnal and diurnal antiphonaries, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the daily and nightly offices; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> and winter antiphonaries; also antiphonaries for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> churches, &c. By the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> constitutions of Archbishop Winchelsey, made at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERTON">Merton</a>, A.D. 1205, it is required that one of these should be found in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>. The use of these, and many other popish books, was forbidden by the 3rd and 4th of Edward VI. c. 10.

ANTIPHONY

Pages 42-42

the answer made by one choir to another, when the psalm <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> anthem is sung between two.

ANTIPHONY SOMETIMES

Pages 42-44

y sometimes denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of psalmody, wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a>, being divided into two parts, repeat the psalms, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> for verse, alternately. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, antiphony stands contradistinguished from symphony, where the whole congregation sings together. Antiphony differs from responsorium, because in this latter the verse is only spoken by one person, whereas Antiphony as in the former, the verses are sung by the two choirs alternately. The original of antiphonal fingering in the western churches is referred to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a>, about the year 374. That father is said to have first introduced it into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the eastern church, where it appears to be of greater antiquity, though as to the time of its <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, authors are not agreed; it was most probably introduced at Antioch, between the year of Christ 347 and 356. Antiphony is also used to denote the words given out at the beginning of the psalm, to which both the choirs are to accommodate their singing. Antiphony, in a more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> sense, denotes a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> made of several verses extracted out of different psalms, adapted to express the mystery solemnized on the occasion. Antipodes, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a name given to those inhabitants of the globe that live diametrically opposite to each other. The word is Greek, and compounded of ὁπή, opposite, and πόδας, a foot; because their feet are opposite to each other. The antipodes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> under opposite meridians and opposite parallels; in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of latitude, but of opposite denominations, one being <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and the other south. They have nearly the same degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, days and nights of equal length, but in opposite seasons. It is noon to one, when midnight to the other; and the longest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> with the one, is the shortest with the other. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> is esteemed the first who thought it possible that the antipodes subsisted, and is looked upon as the inventor of the word. As this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> apprehended the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> to be spherical, he had only one step to make to conclude the existence of the antipodes. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, in general, treated this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> with the highest contempt; never being able to conceive how men and trees could subsist suspended in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> with their feet upwards, for so they apprehended they must be in the other hemisphere. They never reflected that these terms upwards and downwards are merely relative; and signify only nearer to, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> farther from, the centre of the earth, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> centre to which all heavy bodies gravitate; and that, therefore, our antipodes have not their feet upwards and head downwards any more than ourselves; because they, like us, have their feet nearer the centre of the earth, and their heads farther from it. To have the head downwards and feet upwards, is to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the body in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of gravity tending from the feet to the head; but this cannot be supposed with regard to the antipodes; for they, like us, tend toward the centre of the earth, in a direction from head to foot. Antipolis, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> Geography, now Antigone, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Provence, a colony of the Massilians, near the river Verus, in Gallia Narbonensis (Livy), three leagues to the west of Nice. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° N. Lat. 43° 42'. Antiquare, among Roman Lawyers, properly denotes the rejecting of a new <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, or refusing to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> it. In which sense, antiquating differs from abrogating; as the latter imports the annulling an old law, the former the rejecting a new one. Antiquare is also used for a law's growing obsolete, or into disuse, either by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> or non-observance. Antiquarii, a name given to copiers of old Antiquarian books. After the decline of learning amongst the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and when many <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses were erected, learning was chiefly in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the clergy; the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of whom were regulars, and lived in monasteries. In these houses were many industrious men who were continually employed in making new copies of old books, either for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> or for their own emolument. These <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> monks were distinguished by the name of Antiquarii. They deprived the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> librarians, or common scriptores, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of their business, so that these found it difficult to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> a subsistence for themselves and families. This put them upon finding out more expeditious methods of transcribing books. They formed the letters smaller, and made use of more jugsations and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBREVIATIONS">abbreviations</a> than had been usual. They proceeded in this manner till the letters became exceedingly small; the abbreviations were very numerous, and extremely difficult to be read. This in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> accounts for the great variety of hands in the species of writing called Modern Gothic. When a number of copies were to be made of the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, it was usual to employ several persons at the same time in writing it; each person, except him who wrote the first skin, began where his fellow was to leave off. Antiquary, a person who studies and searches after monuments and remains of antiquity; as old medals, books, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, sculptures, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>; and, in general, all curious pieces that may afford any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> into antiquity. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> cities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, there were persons of distinction called antiquaries, whose business it was to show strangers the antiquities of the place, to explain the ancient inscriptions, and to give them all the assistance they could in this way of learning.—Pausanias calls these antiquaries ἐκτενοῦσι. The Sicilians call them μυστικοῖ. There was an ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of antiquaries erected in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> by Ollamh Fodhla, 700 years before Christ, for composing a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>: And to this, say the Irish historians, it is owing that the history and antiquities of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> may be traced back beyond those of most other nations. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of antiquaries in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and another in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, incorporated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>. See Society. Antiquary is also used by ancient writers for the keeper of the antiquarium or cabinet of antiquities. This officer is otherwise called archivota, or antiquary of a king, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, a state, or the like. Henry VIII. gave John Leland the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of his antiquary; a title which, says the author of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, nobody ever enjoyed besides himself. But the restriction, we suppose, was only intended to the understanding in respect of the kings of England. M. Schott, we find, had the title of antiquary to the king of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>; P. Pedruzzi, that of antiquary of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Parma; M. Galland resided some time in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> under the title of antiquary of the king of France.—The university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> have still their antiquary under the denomination of cyfus archivorum.—The kings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> have been at great expenses in order to illustrate the antiquity of their country, having established an academy of antiquaries with this single view.—The office Antiquated of the ancient Irish antiquaries was to preserve the genealogies of the kings of Ireland, to correct the regal tables of succession, and deliver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the pedigree of every collateral branch of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family.

ANTIQUE

Pages 44-44

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, something that is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is chiefly used by sculptors, painters, and architects, to denote such pieces of their different arts as were made by the ancient Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. Thus we say, an antique butt, an antique statue, &c. Antique is sometimes contradistinguished from ancient, which signifies a less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of antiquity. Thus, antique <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> is frequently distinguished from ancient architecture.

ANTIQUITIES

Pages 44-45

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> implying all testimonies, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> authentic accounts, that have come <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to us, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> nations. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a> calls antiquities the wrecks of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, or such particulars as industrious and learned persons have collected from genealogies, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>, monuments, coins, names, etymologies, archives, instruments, fragments of history, &c. Antiquities form a very extensive science, including "an historical knowledge of the edifices, magistrates, offices, habiliments, manners, customs, ceremonies, worship, and other objects worthy of curiosity, of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> ancient nations of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>." This science is not a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> curiosity, but is indispensable to the theologian who ought to be thoroughly acquainted with the antiquities of the Jews, to enable him properly to explain numberless <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in the Old and New Testaments; to the lawyer who, without the knowledge of the antiquities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> and Rome, can never well understand and properly apply the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Roman laws; to the physician and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, that they may have a complete knowledge of the history and principles of the physic and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; to the critic, that he may be able to understand and interpret ancient authors; to the orator and poet who <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be thereby enabled to ornament their writings with numberless images, allusions, comparisons, &c. Antiquities are divided into sacred and profane, into public and private, universal and particular, &c. It is true, that the antiquaries (especially such as are infected with a spirit of pedantry, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of these is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>) frequently carry their inquiries too far, and employ themselves in laborious researches after learned trifles; but the abuse of a science ought never to make us neglect the applying it to rational and useful purposes. Many antiquaries also restrain their learned labours to the elucidation of the antiquities of Greece and Rome; but this field is far too confined, and by no means contains the whole of this science, seeing it properly includes the antiquities of the Jews, Egyptians, Persians, Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Hetruscans, Germans, and, in general, all those principal nations mentioned in ancient history: so far as any accounts of them are come down to us. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> to the general subjects above mentioned we add the particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of antiques, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, bas-reliefs, and the precious relics of medals, coins, paintings, cameos, medals, &c., we shall perceive how Antiquities form a science very extensive and very complicated, and with which only a very small acquaintance could have been attainable by any one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, if our predecessors had not prepared the way for us; if they had not left us such inestimable works as those of Gronovius, Gravius, Montfaucon, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Caylus, Winckelmann, the Hebraic antiquities of D. Iken of Bremen, the Grecian antiquities of Brunings, the Roman antiquities of Nieuport, and especially that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which is entitled Bibliographia Antiquaria <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a>. Alberti Fabricii, professor at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMBURG">Hamburg</a>; &c. &c. Nor must we here forget that very valuable work, with which our countryman Mr Robert Wood has lately enriched this science, and which is so well known, and to justly esteemed by all true connoisseurs, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the Ruins of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALMYRA">Palmyra</a>, and those of Baalbec. It is by this work that we are fully convinced of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and magnificence, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and elegance, of the buildings of the ancients. We here see that the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of these matters is not all owing to the Greeks, but that there were other nations who served them as models. For though many of the edifices of Palmyra are to be attributed to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Aurelian, and to Odenatus and his wife Zenobia, who reigned there about the year 264, yet there are found at the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> ruins of buildings that appear to be of far greater antiquity, and that are not less beautiful. The ancient Persepolis is sufficient to prove this assertion. When we duly reflect on all these matters, and especially if we attempt to acquire any knowledge of this science, we shall soon be convinced that it but ill becomes a petit-maitre to laugh at a learned antiquary. The knowledge of those monuments of the ancients, the works of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, statuary, graving, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, &c., which they call antiquities, requires a strict <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> with regard to the matter itself on which the art has been exercised; as the wax, clay, wood, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of every kind, marble, flint, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a>, and every sort of metal. We should begin by learning on what matter each ancient <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> principally worked, and in which of the fine arts they excelled: For the matter itself, as the different sorts of marble, compositions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of precious stones, serve frequently to characterize the true antique, and to discover the counterfeit. The connoisseurs pretend also to know, by certain distinct <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> and execution of a work of art, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> and nation where it was made. They find, moreover, in the invention and execution, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of excellence which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> artists are not able to imitate. Now, though we ought to allow, in general, the great merit of the ancients in the polite arts, we should not, however, suffer our admiration to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>. There are pieces of antiquity of every sort, which have come down to us; some that are perfectly excellent; and others so wretched, that the meanest among modern artists would not acknowledge them. The mixture of the good and bad has taken place in all subjects, at all times and in all nations. The misfortune is, that most of our great antiquaries have been so little skilled in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> as scarcely to know how to draw a circle with a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPASSES">compasses</a>. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>, therefore, which frequently directs them to give the palm to the ancients, rather than a judgment founded by a knowledge of the art. That character Antiquity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> which they find so marvellous in the works of antiquity, is often nothing more than a mere chimera. They pretend that the artists of our days constantly exaggerate their expressions; that a modern <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a> has the appearance of a man distracted with intoxication; that a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> seems to be animated with the spirit of a fury; and so of the rest. But let them not decide too hastily. Almost all the antique figures are totally void of all spirit of expression; we are forced to guess at their characters. Every <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> expression requires, moreover, to be somewhat exaggerated. A statue or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> is an inanimate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; and must therefore have a very different effect from one which, being endowed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, has the muscles constantly in play, and where the continual change of the features, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the eyes, and the looks more or less lively, easily and clearly express the passions and sentiments. Whereas, in a figure, that is the produce of art, the delicate touches, that should express the passions, are lost to the eyes of the spectators: they must therefore be struck by strong bold characters, which can affect them at the first glance of the eye. A very moderate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> is sensible, at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, that he is not to give his figures extravagant expressions, nor to place them in distorted attitudes.

ANTIQUITY LIKEWISE

Pages 45-45

y likewise expresses the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of a thing; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we say, the antiquity of a family, the antiquity of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>.

ANTIRRHINIUM

Pages 45-45

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a promontory at the mouth of the Corinthian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, where it is scarce a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and where it separates Aetolia from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>; so called from its opposite situation to Rhium in Peloponnesus (Pliny): both are now called the Dardanelles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEPANTO">Lepanto</a>.

ANTISABBATARIANS

Pages 45-45

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> who oppose the observance of the Christian Sabbath. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> principle of the Antisabbatarians is, that the Jewish Sabbath was only of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONIAL">ceremonial</a>, not moral obligation; and consequently was abolished by the coming of Christ.

ANTISAGOGUE

Pages 45-45

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> differing little from that called concession. The following passage from Cicero is an instance of it: Difficilis ratio belli gerendi; at plena fidei, plena pietatis: et si dicas, magnus labor, multa pericula proponuntur; at gloria ex his immortalis est consecutura. See Concession.

ANTISCII

Pages 45-45

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, people who live on different sides of the equator, whose shadows at noon are projected opposite ways. Thus the people of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> are Antisci to those of the south; the one projecting their shadows at noon towards the north pole, and the other toward the south pole.

ANTISEPTICS

Pages 45-46

an appellation given to such substances as resist <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>. We have some curious experiments in relation to antiseptic substances by Dr Pringle, who has ascertained their several virtues. Thus, in order to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the antiseptic virtue of salts, he compared it with that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; which being one of the weakest, he supposes equal to unity, and expresses the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> strength of the rest by higher numbers, as in the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. | Salts, their antiseptic virtue | |-------------------------------| | Sea salt | 1 | | Sal geminae | 1+ | | Tartar vitriolated | 2 | | Spiritus Mindereri | 2 | | Tartarus solubilis | 2 | | Salt diureticus | 2+ | | Crude sal ammoniac | 3 | | Saline mixture | 3 | | Nitre | 4+ | | Salt of hawthorn | 4+ | | Salt of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMWOOD">wormwood</a> | 4+ | | <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">Borax</a> | 12+ | | Salt of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a> | 20+ | | <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">Alum</a> | 30+ | In this table the proportions are marked in integral numbers: only to some there is added the sign +, to show, that those salts are possessed of a stronger antiseptic virtue than the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> in the table expresses, by some fractions: unless in the three last, where the same sign imports that the salt may be stronger by some units. Some resinous and other substances even exceed the antiseptic virtues of the neutral salts; thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MYRRH">myrrh</a>, afaetida, terra japonica, and aloes, are at least 12 times more antiseptic than sea salt. Two grains of camphor are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to 60 grains of that salt. An infusion of a few grains of Virginian snake-root, in powder, exceeds 12 times its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of sea salt. Chamomile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> have nearly the same extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. The Jesuits bark has it also. Besides these, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, ginger, saffron, contravera root, are 12 times more antiseptic than sea salt. Dried sage, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-RHUBARB">rhubarb</a>, the root of the wild valerian, mint, angelica, ground ivy, fennel, green <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> roses, wormwood, mustard, and horseradish, were likewise found more antiseptic than the standard. To the class of antiseptic medicines may likewise be added fermented liquors, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, spirits, and even those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> called anti-acids, and erroneously supposed hasteners of putrefaction, particularly horseradish. Now vegetables, possessing this virtue, are the more valuable, in that being usually free of acrimony, they may be taken in much greater quantities than either spirits, acids, resins, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even the neutral salts. Antiseptics are prescribed in all putrid, malignant, and pellitential <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. It is to be remarked, however, that different kinds of them are to be given in different cases, and even in different stages of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. Thus, the bark is a specific in gangrene, when the vessels are relaxed, and the blood resolved or disposed to putrefaction; but <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> fail, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the vessels are too full, or the blood be too thick. With the same caution is the bark to be used in wounds, viz. chiefly in cases of absorbed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, when it infects the humours, and brings on a hectic fever. By the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiseptic virtue of alum, the bark, and other astringents, it should seem, that attrition had no small share in the cure of putrid disorders; and, indeed, the very <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of putrefaction consists in a separation or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> of the parts. But as astringents are improper to be administered in many cases, contrary- Antitasis va root, snake root, camphor, &c. may supply their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; which, though highly antifeptic, have very little, or any, of an astringent quality.

ANTISPASMODICS

Pages 46-46

are medicines proper for the cure of palpms and convulsions. Opium, balsam of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, and the essential oils of many vegetables, are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> in this class of medicines. Opium excels, for its immediate effects. Peruvian balsam, in many instances, produces more lasting benefit than opium, and sometimes succeeds where opium fails. As antispasmodics, the essential oils differ in this from opium, that they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> more on a particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> than on the system in general, and have no soporific effect. Some medicines remove palpms by immediate contact, as ashes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, cream, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of almonds; others by repelling <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAS">gas</a>, sulphur, nitre, sal ammoniac, &c. And where the affections are produced by inanition and defect of vital heat, palpms are removed by those medicines that restore the vis vitae, such as valerian, caltrop, mulk, &c.

ANTISTASIS

Pages 46-46

in Oratory, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> from the consideration that had it been omitted worse would have ensued. This is called by Latin writers comparativum argumentum; such, e.g. would be the general's defence who had made an inglorious <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>, That, without it, the whole <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> must have perished.

ANTISTHENES

Pages 46-46

a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, and founder of the Cynics. He was born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, and passed the former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> as a soldier. Having afterwards been an attendant at the lectures of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, he was principally charmed with those exhortations of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> philosopher, which persuaded to frugality, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>, and to moderation; these Antisthenes was resolved to practice by carrying every precept to its utmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. Permitting therefore his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> to grow, he went about the streets in a threadbare coat, scarcely to be distinguished from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> beggar. He prided himself upon the most rigid virtue, and thought himself obliged to attack the vicious wherever he found them. This gave him some reputation in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>; but it may be supposed, that, in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> so very luxurious as Athens, he had more enemies than disciples. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> consisted rather in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> than in speculation: it was therefore his constant maxim, That to be virtuous was to be happy, and that all virtue consisted in action; that the wise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> should live for himself, contented in all situations, and happy alone in the consciousness of his own virtue. He acknowledged nothing to be good but what was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a>; and affirmed, that virtue might be acquired by practice. Laertius tells us there were ten times of his works; and he has given us many of his apophthegms.

ANTISTOECHON

Pages 46-46

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, the using one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> instead of another: as oll for ill.

ANTISTROPHE

Pages 46-46

among Lyric Poets, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a song and dance in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, which was performed before the altar, in returning from west to east; in opposition to strophe. See Strophe and Ode. ANTITACTÆ, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a branch of Gnostics, who held, that God was good and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a>, but antithesis that a creature had created evil; and consequently that it is our duty to oppose this author of evil, in order to avenge God of his adversary.

ANTITHENAR

Pages 46-46

in Anatomy, a name given to the adductor indicis. See Anatomy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles.

ANTITHESIS

Pages 46-46

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> opposition of words or sentiments. Such is that of Cicero, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Catilinarian: "On one side stands <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, on the other impudence; on one fidelity, on the other deceit; here piety, there sacrilege; here continency, there lust, &c." Such also is that of Augustus to some factitious young men, Audite, juvenes, Jovenem, quem juvenem fenes audirete. Such again is that of Seneca: Curae leviores loquuntur, ingenies fluebent. And that of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>: Fleclere si nequeo superos, Acheronta movebo. St Augustine, Seneca, Salvian, and many other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, seem greatly to affect antitheses; but among the moderns they are generally decried. Defmaretz represents them as the favourites of young writers. The following is an example of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> antithesis. Though gentle, yet not dull; Strong, without rage; without overflowing, full. Antithesis is sometimes used for controversy. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, we meet with antithetic method, antithetic discourses, &c. Marcion composed a volume of Antitheses, or contrarieties and oppositions between the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> and the gospel.

ANTITRAGUS MUSCULUS

Pages 46-46

in Anatomy, a muscle of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. See Anatomy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles.

ANTITRINITARIANS

Pages 46-46

those who deny the trinity, and teach that there are not three persons in the Godhead. Thus the Samotatenians who do not believe the distinction of persons in God; the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>, who deny the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> of the Word, and the Macedonians who deny that of the Holy Spirit, are all properly Antitrinitarians. Among the moderns, Antitrinitarians are particularly underflowed of Socinians, called also Unitarians. The Bibliotheca Antitrinitariae:um, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Antitrinitarian Library, is a posthumous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of Christopher Sandius, an eminent Antitrinitarian; wherein he gives a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a>, digested in order of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCINIAN">Socinian</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Antitrinitarian authors, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> account of their lives, and a catalogue of their works. See Unitarian.

ANTITYPE

Pages 46-47

a Greek word, properly signifying a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYPE">type</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> corresponding to some other type. The word antitype occurs twice in the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>; viz. in the epistle to the Hebrews, ix. 24. and in St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, i Eph. iii. 21. where its genuine import has been much controverted. The former says, that "Christ is not entered into the holy places made with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, which are, antitypes, the figures or antitypes of the true—now to appear in the presence of God for us." Now τύπος signifies the pattern by which another thing is made; and as Moses was obliged to make the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABERNACLE">tabernacle</a>, and all things in it, according to the pattern shown him in the mount; the tabernacle so formed was the antitype of what was shown to Moses: any thing, therefore, formed according to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> or pattern, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANT">ANT</a> Antium, is an antitype. In the latter passage, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> speaking of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, and the deliverance only of eight persons in the ark from it, says, οὐκ ἦσαν αὐτοὶ ἀπὸ τῶν ἐν τῷ κιβώτῳ, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">Baptism</a> being an antitype to that, now saves us; not putting away the filth of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, but the answer of a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> towards God, etc. The meaning is, that righteousmen, or the answer of a good conscience towards God, now saves us by means of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> of Christ, as formerly righteousmen saved these eight persons by means of the ark, during the flood. The word antitype, therefore, here signifies a general similitude of circumstances; and the particle ὁ, ὑπερέκεινος, refers, not to the immediate antecedent, ὕδωρ, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, but to all that precedes. Antitype, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> Greek Fathers, and in the Greek liturgy, is also applied to the symbols of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and wine in the sacrament. Hence it hath been argued, by many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, that the Greeks do not really believe the doctrine of transubstantiation; because they call the bread and wine antitypes, ὑπερέκεινος, q.d. figures, similitudes; and this even after the consecration.

ANTIUM

Pages 47-47

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Volsci, (Livy); situated on the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, yet without a harbour, because they had a neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMLET">hamlet</a> called Ceno, with a harbour, (Strabo). The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> gained their first reputation in naval affairs against the Antiates; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of whose ships they conveyed into the arsenal of Rome, and part they burnt; and with their beaks <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rostrum adorned the pulpit erected in the forum, thence called Rostra, (Livy, Florus.) Here stood a famous temple of Fortune, (Horace). Addison says, there were two Fortunes worshipped at Antium.—It is now extinct, but the name still remains in the Capo d'Anno.

ANTIVARI

Pages 47-47

a strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, a Greek archbishop's see, and subject to the Turks. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 29. 15. N. Lat. 43. 0. ANTIVIRGILIAN husbandry, an appellation given to Mr Tull's new method of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-hoeing husbandry. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a>.

ANTLER

Pages 47-47

among Sportsmen, a start <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> branch of a deer's antler. Brow-Antler, denotes the branch next the head; and, Bes-Antler, the branch next above the brow-antler.

ANTLIA

Pages 47-47

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> machine, supposed to be the same with our <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>. Hence the phrase in antlum condemnari, according to the critics, denotes a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> whereby criminals were condemned to drain ponds, ditches, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like.

ANTOEICI

Pages 47-47
