in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, those inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> who live under the same meridian, and at the same distance from the equator: the one toward the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and the other toward the south. Hence they have the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>; and their latitude is also the same, but of a different denomination. They are in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a> of the meridian, but opposite in parallels. They have precisely the same hours of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> and night, but opposite seasons; and the night of the one is always equal to the day of the other.

ANTOINE

Pages 47-47

a town of France, in Dauphiny, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VIENNE">Vienne</a>, with a celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>. It is seated among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, 13 miles east of Lyons. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 20. N. Lat. 43. 43.

ANTONA

Pages 47-47

(Tacitus); a river of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, which Camden supposes to be a faulty <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> for Avona <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Aulona, (the Avon).

ANTONACUM

Pages 47-47

Antonnacum, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Antunnacum, a town of the Treviri; now Andernach, below Coblentz. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 5. N. Lat. 50. 25.

ANTONIA

Pages 47-47

Saint, a town of France, in Rouergue, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Rhodez, whose fortifications are demolished. It is seated on the river Aveyron. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 55. N. Lat. 44. 10. ANTONIAN waters, medicinal waters of Germany, very pleasant to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and esteemed good in many chronic and hypochondriac <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. See Tonstein.

ANTONIANO

Pages 47-48

Silvio, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning, who raised himself from a low condition by his merit, was born at Rome in the year 1540. When he was but ten years old, he could make verses upon any subject propounded to him; and these so excellent, though pronounced extempore, that even a man of genius could not compose the like without a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and pains. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a> coming to Rome, to congratulate Marcellus II. upon his being raised to the pontificate, was so charmed with the genius of Antoniano, that he carried him to Ferrara, where he provided able matters to instruct him in all the sciences. From thence he was sent for by Pius IV. who made him professor of the belles lettres in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> at Rome. Antoniano filled this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> with so much reputation, that, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> when he began to explain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> pro Marco Marcellio, he had a vast crowd of auditors, and among them no less than 25 cardinals. He was afterwards chosen rector of the college; and after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Pius IV., being seized with a spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, he joined himself to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Neri, and accepted the office of secretary to the sacred college, offered him by Pius V. which he executed for 25 years with the reputation of an honest and able man. He refused a bishopric which Gregory XIV. would have given him; but he accepted the office of secretary to the briefs, offered him by Clement VIII. who made him his chamberlain, and afterwards a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>. Antoniano killed himself by too great fatigue: for he spent whole nights in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> letters; which brought on a sickness, whereof he died, in the 63rd year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He wrote with such ease, and fluency, that he never almost made any blot <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rasure; and it is said of him, that he preserved the flower of his virginity during his whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. ANTONIDES Vander Goes, John, an eminent Dutch poet, born at Goes in Zeeland, the 3d of April 1647. His parents were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANABAPTISTS">Anabaptists</a>, people of good character, but of low circumstances. They went to live at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> when Antonides was about four years old; Antonides, old; and, in the ninth year of his age, he began his studies, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HADRIAN">Hadrian</a> Junius and James Cocceius. Antonides took great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> the Latin poets, and carefully compared them with Grotius, Heinsius, &c. By this means he acquired a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and enriched his mind with noble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>. He first attempted to translate some pieces of Ovid, Horace, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; and, having formed his taste on these excellent models, he at length undertook one of the most difficult tasks in poetry, to write a tragedy: this was entitled Traxil, or The Invasion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. Antonides, however, was so modest, as not to permit it to be published. Vondel, who was then engaged in a dramatic piece, which was taken also from some event that happened in China, read Antonides's tragedy; and was so well pleased with it, that he declared, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the author would not print it, he would take some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> out of it, and make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of them in his own tragedy. He accordingly did so; and it was reckoned much to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Antonides, to have written what might be adopted by so great a poet as Vondel was acknowledged to be by all good judges. Upon the conclusion of the peace between Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, in the year 1674, Antonides wrote a piece, entitled Bellona aan band, i.e., "Bellona chained;" a very elegant poem, consisting of several hundred verses. He next wrote an ingenious heroic poem, which he entitled The River I (the river on which Amsterdam is built). Antonides's parents had bred him up an apothecary; but his remarkable genius for poetry soon gained him the esteem and friendship of several persons of distinction; and particularly of Mr Buïero, one of the lords of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a> at Amsterdam, and a great lover of poetry, who sent him at his expense to pursue his studies at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, where he remained till he took his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of physic, and then his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> gave him a place in the admiralty. In 1678, Antonides married Sufanna Bermans, a minister's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, who had also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for poetry. His <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> was celebrated by several eminent poets, particularly by the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Francius, professor of eloquence, who composed some Latin verses on the occasion. After marriage, he did not much indulge his poetic genius; and within a few years he fell into a consumption, of which he died on the 18th September 1684, being then but thirty-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years and a few months old. He is esteemed the most eminent Dutch poet after Vondel. His works have been printed several times, having been collected by Father Anthony Taniz. The last edition was printed by Nicholas Ten Hoom, at Amsterdam, in the year 1714, in 4to, under the direction of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Van Hoogstraaten, one of the masters of the Latin school of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, who added to it also the life of the poet.

ANTONINUS PIUS

Pages 48-52

a celebrated Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, was born A.D. 85, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAVINIUM">Lavinium</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Distinguished for eminence of character, his family had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> maintained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Nimes in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, from whence they had descended. Both his father and grandfather had held the office of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>. Aris Antoninus his maternal grandfather by his amiable disposition, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of literature, had acquired an eminent character, and was very intimate with Pliny the younger. Under him the young Titus after his father's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> completed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. His Antoninus character on arriving at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of maturity, manifested itself in the most promising manner. To an improved understanding, a virtuous heart, a mild and dignified character, and a noble eloquence, he joined a happy physiognomy. Simple in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and guided by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> in all his actions and sentiments, he was entirely free from all affectation and pomposity. In the year 120, among the many public honours which his birth and connexions gave him a claim to, he was elevated to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of consul, and was afterwards appointed by Adrian to be one of the four consuls, betwixt whom the supreme power of Italy was divided. Becoming in his turn proconsul of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, he acquitted himself with such reputation, that he even excelled his grandfather Aris who had formerly enjoyed that high trust. Returning from Asia he was not only received into the favour, but likewise the confidence and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Adrian, and was always disposed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> with lenity. He married Annia Faustina, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Annius Verus, whose character was far from being untaxed with reproach, but his lenient disposition induced him to avoid public scandal, and he behaved towards his aged father-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> with the most becoming respect. Two sons and two daughters were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. The sons died when they were young, and the eldest daughter, who was married to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMIA">Lamia</a> Sylvanus, died when Titus proceeded towards his Asiatic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Faustina the youngest married Marcus Aurelius, who was afterwards emperor. After the death of Verus, Adrian resolving to adopt Antoninus, he was induced to accept of the succession to so important a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> as the Roman empire, although with a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of reluctance, and was accordingly nominated by Adrian in February 25, A.D. 138, in the presence of a council of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> senators, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> created him his colleague in performing the proconsular and tribunitial duties. Extending his plans of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADOPTION">adoption</a> still farther, Adrian caused Antoninus adopt the son of Verus, then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years of age, and Marcus Annius, afterwards named Aurelius, then seventeen years of age, a relation of Adrian's, and nephew to his own wife. The dutiful and merited <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> which Antoninus bestowed on Adrian during the last months of his illness, gives a very high idea of his character. On <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 10, A.D. 138, he succeeded to the empire amidst the universal acclamations of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> and people, who anticipated in his well tried virtues that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> which a good and wise sovereign is able to bestow upon his subjects. The Roman world enjoyed such tranquillity under his reign that it affords few materials for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; yet it is to be regretted that Capitolinus is the only historian from whom any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> information can be received concerning this peaceful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, and he is none of the most perspicuous. It however appears that the usual honours and titles, together with the addition of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Pius, which both his conduct and zeal in defending and honouring the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of his predecessor united to suggest, were willingly conferred upon him by the senate. In the beginning of his reign there were several conspiracies formed against him, but this only afforded him an instance of finalizing his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a>, which he did in the most striking manner. Although he was unable to prevent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> from taking its due course... Antoninus' course against the ringleaders, he prohibited all <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> after their accomplices, and took the son of Attius, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> conspirators, under his protection. Various commotions were raised in several parts of the empire; but by the vigilance of his lieutenants, these were easily quelled. The incursions of the Brigantes in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> were restrained, and a new wall which was built to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of that of Adrian, from the mouth of the Esk to that of Tweed, and which was called the Wall of Antoninus, was fixed as the boundary of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> in Britain. The reign of Antoninus upon the whole was singularly peaceful, and realized a saying of Scipio, "That he preferred saving the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of one citizen, to destroying a thousand enemies." A desire of promoting the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of his people, of protecting them from oppression, of administering justice through every corner of his realm, and of being instrumental to the happiness and peace of his government, influenced all his proceedings. He delighted greatly in laying before the senate the motives of all his actions, and in his manner of living and conversing he employed the same prudential economy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of equality, which had so distinguished his predecessors Trajan and Adrian. On account of the sweetness of his temper he bore with firmness many indignities offered him; and under his reign the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of informers were entirely extinguished, and condemnations and confiscations were very rare. The various public calamities which occurred in his time were all relieved by him with the greatest benevolence. He avoided as much as possible laying any burdens upon his people, and on this account made few journeys through his dominions. He was frugal in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the public revenues, but profuse in his own patrimony, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> economist, devoid of avarice, and very liberal towards works of ornament and utility, and even towards gratifying the pleasures of his people. A temple in honour of Adrian in Rome, and perhaps the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a> and aqueduct at Nîmes, were his chief buildings. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">Jurisprudence</a> was to this emperor, like that of his predecessor, an interesting subject for improvement, and several decrees which he issued, display his commendable spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this equity was, that Antoninus acquired a reputation and fame which no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> achievements could have conferred; and his friendship was courted by the neighbouring princes. There is scarcely a blot to be found to tarnish his character; and frugality, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, and harmless amusement <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to employ his private hours. It may perhaps be admitted that he was too indulgent towards an unworthy wife, and that the divine honours he bestowed on her memory were not merited by her conduct. In the management of his complicated business, he was exact to such a degree that it was even ridiculed by some; but he found the daily advantage of this accuracy. The growing virtues of Marcus Aurelius soon drew his attention after he ascended the throne, and having given him his daughter in marriage, he declared him Caesar. Nor was he mistaken in his choice; for Aurelius acted with the utmost fidelity and affection amid all the honours Antoninus that he continued to confer upon him. Enjoying this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> share of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> bliss, in the 74th year of his life he was seized with a fever at his favourite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> seat of Lori. Convinced of his approaching fate, he convened the principal officers of the state, and confirmed his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of Aurelius, and gave him the imperial ensigns. A delirium ensued, in an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of which he gave the watchword Aquanimitas, and calmly resigned his breath in the 23rd year of his reign. His ashes were consigned to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of Adrian, and divine honours paid to his memory. He was universally regretted, and succeeding emperors bore his name as a badge of honour. The senate and his successor erected a sculptured pillar to his memory, which is still shown to strangers as one of the chief ornaments of Rome. (Gen. Biog.) Antoninus Philosophus, Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor, born at Rome, the 26th of April, in the 121st year of the Christian era. He was called by several names till he was admitted into the Aurelian family, when he took that of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HADRIAN">Hadrian</a>, upon the death of Ceionius Commodus, turned his eyes upon Marcus Aurelius; but, as he was not then 18 years of age, and consequently too young for so important a station, he fixed upon Antoninus Pius, whom he adopted, upon condition that he should likewise adopt Marcus Aurelius. The year after this adoption, Hadrian appointed him quaestor, though he had not yet attained the age prescribed by the law. Upon the death of Hadrian, Aurelius married Faustina, the daughter of Antoninus Pius, by whom he had several children. In the year 139, he was invested with new honours by the emperor Pius, in which he behaved in such a manner as endeared him to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> and the whole people. Upon the death of Pius, which happened in the year 161, he was obliged by the senate to take upon him the government; in the management of which he took Lucius Verus as his colleague. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DION">Dion</a> Cassius says, that the reason of doing this was, that he might have leisure to pursue his studies, and on account of his ill state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>; Lucius being of a strong vigorous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, and consequently more fit for the fatigues of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> he took upon him the name of Antoninus, which he gave likewise to Verus his colleague, and betrothed his daughter Lucilla to him. The two emperors went afterwards to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>; where, after having performed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNERAL_RITES">funeral <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of Pius, they pronounced each of them a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> to his memory. They discharged the government in a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMICABLE">amicable</a> manner. It is said that, soon after Antoninus had performed the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOTHEOSIS">apotheosis</a> of Pius, petitions were presented to him by the Pagan priests, philosophers, and governors of provinces, in order to excite him to persecute the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; which he rejected with indignation, and interposed his authority for their protection, by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of Asia, then held at Ephesus (a). The happiness which the empire began to enjoy under these two emperors was interrupted, in the year 162, by a dreadful inundation of the Tiber, which (a) Eusebius has preserved this letter, Hist. Ecclel. lib. iv. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 13, but he falsely ascribes it to Antoninus Pius, whereas it was wrote by Marcus Antoninus, as Valerius makes it appear in his annotations on Eusebius. Antoninus, which destroyed a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cattle, and occasioned a famine at Rome. This calamity was followed by the Parthian war; and at the same time the Catti ravaged Germany and Rhaetia. Lucius Verus went in person to oppose the Parthians; and Antoninus continued at Rome, where his presence was necessary. During this war with the Parthians, about the year 163 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 164, Antoninus sent his daughter Lucilla to Verus, having been betrothed to him in marriage, and attended her as far as Brundisium: he intended to have conducted her to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>; but it having been intimated by some persons, that his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of going into the east was to claim the honour of having finished the Parthian war, he returned to Rome. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> having gained a victory over the Parthians, who were obliged to abandon Mesopotamia, the two emperors triumphed over them at Rome in the year 166; and were honoured with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Fathers of their country. This year was fatal, on account of a terrible pestilence which spread itself over the whole world, and a famine under which Rome laboured: it was likewise in this year that the Marcomanni, and many other people of Germany, took up arms against the Romans; but the two emperors having marched in person against them, obliged the Germans to sue for peace. The war, however, was renewed the year following, and the two emperors marched again in person; but Lucius Verus was seized with an apoplectic fit, and died at Altinum. The Romans were now defeated with great slaughter; and the emperor, not choosing to burden his subjects with new taxes, exposed to public <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> the furniture of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver plate belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and his wife's rich garments embroidered with gold, and a curious collection of pearls, which Adrian had purchased during his long progress through the provinces of the empire, and was called Adrian's cabinet. In the year 170, Antoninus made vast preparations against the Germans, and carried on the war with great vigour. During this war, in 174, a very extraordinary event is said to have happened, which, according to Dion Cassius, was as follows: Antoninus's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> being blocked up by the Quadi, in a very disadvantageous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, where there was no possibility of procuring <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; in this situation, being worn out with fatigue and wounds, oppressed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and thirst, and incapable of retiring or engaging the enemy, in an instant the sky was covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, and there fell a vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>; the Roman army were about to quench their thirst, when the enemy came upon them with such fury, that they must certainly have been defeated, had it not been for a shower of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>, accompanied with a storm of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, which fell upon the enemy, without the least annoyance to the Antonines. Romans, who by this means gained the victory (b). In 175, Antoninus made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> with several nations of Germany. Soon after, Avidius Cassius, governor of Syria, revolted from the emperor: this insurrection, however, was put an end to by the death of Cassius, who was killed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CENTURION">centurion</a> named Anthony. Antoninus behaved with great lenity towards those who had been engaged in Cassius's party; he would not put to death, nor imprison, nor even fit in judgment himself upon any of the senators engaged in this revolt; but he referred them to the senate, fixing a day for their appearance, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it had been only a civil affair. He wrote also to the senate, desiring them to act with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> rather than severity; not to shed the blood of any senator or person of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, or of any other person whatsoever; but to allow this honour to his reign, that, even under the misfortune of a rebellion, none had lost their lives, except in the first heat of the tumult. In 176, Antoninus visited Syria and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>: the kings of those countries, and ambassadors also from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTHIA">Parthia</a>, came to visit him. He laid several days at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>; and, after he had settled the affairs of the east, went to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, on which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> he conferred several honours, and appointed public professors there. From thence he returned to Rome with his son Commodus, whom he chose consul for the year following, though he was then but 16 years of age, having obtained a dispensation for that purpose. On the 27th of September, the same year, he gave him the title of Imperator; and on the 23rd of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, he entered Rome in triumph, with Commodus, on account of the victories gained over the Germans. Dion Cassius tells us, that he remitted all the debts which were due to himself and the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> during 46 years, from the time that Hadrian had granted the same favour, and burnt all the writings relating to those debts. He applied himself likewise to correct many enormities, and introduced several excellent regulations. In the year 179, he left Rome with his son Commodus, in order to go against the Marcomanni, and other barbarous nations; and the year following gained a considerable victory over them, and would, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, have entirely subdued them in a very short time, had he not been taken with an illness, which carried him off on the 17th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 180, in the 59th year of his age, and 19th of his reign. The whole empire regretted the loss of so valuable a prince, and paid the greatest regard to his memory: he was ranked amongst the gods, and almost every person had a statue of him in their houses. His book of meditations has been much admired by the best judges. (b) The Pagans, as well as Christians, according to Mr Tillemont (p. 621, art. xvi.), have acknowledged the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of this prodigy, but have greatly differed as to the cause of such a miraculous event; the former alleging it, some to one magician and some to another: In Antoninus's pillar, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> is ascribed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, the god of rain and thunder. But the Christians affirmed, that God granted this favour at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> in the Roman army, who are said to have composed the twelfth or Melitene legion; and, as a mark of distinction, we are told that they received the title of the Thundering Legion, from Antoninus (Euseb. Eccle. Hist. lib. v. cap. 5.) Mr Moyles, in the letters published in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> volume of his works, has endeavoured to explain this story of the Thundering Legion; which occasioned Mr Whilton to publish an answer, in 1726, entitled, Of the Thundering Legion; or, Of the miraculous deliverance of Marcus Antoninus and his army, upon the prayers of the Christians. Antoninus's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">Column</a>. See Column. Antoninus's Wall, the name of the third rampart or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> that had been built or repaired by the Romans against the incursions of the North Britons. It is called by the people in the neighbourhood, Graham's Dyke; from the notion that one Graham, or Grimus, first made a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> in it after the retreat of the Romans out of Britain. The first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> erected by the Romans was the chain of forts made by Agricola* from the frith of Forth to that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a>, in the year 81, to protect his conquests from the inroads of the Caledonians. * See Agricola—see the chain of forts made by Agricola* from the frith of Forth to that of Clyde, in the year 81, to protect his conquests from the inroads of the Caledonians. * See Adri—second was the vallum, or dyke, flung up by Adrian† in the year 121. It terminated on the western side of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> at Aelodunum, or Brugh, on the Solway firths, and was supposed to have reached no further than Pons Aelii, or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, on the eastern. But from an inscription lately discovered, it appears to have extended as far as the wall of Severus‡. This rampart of Adrian's was situated much farther south than Agricola's chain; the country to the north having been either, according to some authors, recovered by the native Britons after the departure of Agricola; or, according to others, voluntarily slighted by Adrian. However, this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of Adrian's did not long continue to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> boundary of the Roman territories to the north in Britain. For Antoninus Pius, the adopted son and immediate successor of Adrian, having, by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> Lollius Urbicus, recovered the country once conquered by Agricola, commanded another rampart to be erected between the friths of Forth and Clyde, in the track where Agricola had formerly built his chain of forts. The great number of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> which have been found in or near the ruins of this wall, or rampart, to the honour of Antoninus Pius, leave us no room to doubt its having been built by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> and command. If the fragment of a Roman pillar with an inscription, now in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> library of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, belonged to this work, as it is generally supposed to have done, it fixes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> of its execution to the third consulship of Antoninus, which was A.D. 140, only 20 years after that of Adrian, of which this seems to have been an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>. This wall or rampart, as some imagine, reached from Caer-ridden on the frith of Forth to Old Kirkpatrick on the Clyde; or, as others think, from Kinniel on the east to Dunglass on the west. These different suppositions hardly make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in the length of this work, which, from several actual mensurations, appears to have been 37 English or 49 Roman miles. Capitolinus, in his life of Antoninus Pius, directly affirms, that the wall which that emperor built in Britain was of turf. This in the main is unquestionably true; though it is evident (from the vestiges of it still remaining, which not very many years ago were dug up and examined for near a mile together) that the foundation was of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. Mr Camden also tells us, from the papers of one Mr Anthony Pont, that the principal rampart was faced with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> stone, to prevent the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> from falling into the ditch. The chief parts of this work were as follows: 1. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and deep ditch, whose dimensions cannot now be discovered with certainty and exactness, though Mr Pont says, it was 12 feet wide. 2. The principal wall or rampart was about 12 feet thick at the foundation, but its original height cannot now be determined. This wall was situated on the south brink of the ditch. 3. A military way on Antoninus's fourth side of the principal wall, well paved, and raised a little above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the ground. This work, as well as that of Adrian, was defended by garrisons placed in forts and stations along the line of it. The number of these forts or stations, whose vestiges were visible in Mr Pont's time, was 18, situated at about the distance of two miles from each other. In the intervals between the forts, there were turrets or watch towers. But the number of these, and their distance from each other, cannot now be discovered. It is not a little surprising, that though it is now more than 1600 years since this work was finished, and more than 1500 since it was slighted, we can yet discover, from authentic monuments, which are still remaining, by what particular bodies of Roman troops almost every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it was executed. This discovery is made from inscriptions upon <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, which were originally built into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the wall, and have been found in or near its ruins, and are carefully preserved. The number of stones with inscriptions of this kind now extant, is 11; of which six may be seen at one view in the college of Glasgow, one in the college of Aberdeen, one in the college of Edinburgh, one in the collection of Baron Clerk, one at Cochmoch house, and one at Calder house. From these inscriptions it appears in general, that this great work was executed by the second legion, the vexillation of the fifth legion and of the twentieth legion, and one cohort of auxiliaries. If these corps were all complete, they would make in all a body of 7800 men. Some of these inscriptions have suffered greatly by the injuries of time and other accidents; so that we cannot discover from them, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> certainty, how many paces of this work were executed by each of these bodies of troops. The sum of the certain and probable information contained in these inscriptions, as it is collected by the learned and illustrious Mr Horley, stands thus: | Legion/Corps | Paces | |-------------------------------------|-------| | The second legion | 11,603| | The vexillation of the fifth legion | 7411 | | The vexillation of the twentieth legion | 7801 | | All certain | 26,815| | The vexillation of the twentieth legion, the monument certain, and the number probable | 3411 | | The same vexillation, on a plain monument, no number visible, supposed | 3500 | | The fifth legion, a monument, but no number, supposed | 3000 | | Cohors prima Cugernorum | 3000 | Total 39,726 or 39 miles 726 paces, nearly the whole length of the wall. It would have been both useful and agreeable to have known how long time these troops were employed in the execution of this great work. But of this we have no information. Neither do we know what particular bodies of troops were in garrison in the several forts and stations along the line of this wall, because these garrisons were withdrawn before the Notitia Imperial was written. Though we cannot discover exactly how many years this this wall of the emperor Antoninus continued to be the boundary of the Roman territories in Britain, yet we know with certainty that it was not very long. For we are told by an author of undoubted <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, that, in the reign of Commodus, A.D. 180, "he had wars with several foreign nations, but none so dangerous as that of Britain. For the people of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, having palled the wall which divided them from the Romans, attacked them, and cut them to pieces."

ANTONIO

Pages 52-52

St., a Dutch fort in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AXIM">Axim</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. It stands on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> rock, which projects into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>; and is so environed by rocks and dangerous shoals, as to be inaccessible to an enemy but by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, where it is fortified by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a>, drawbridge, and two batteries of heavy cannon. Besides this it has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> towards the sea. The three batteries consist of 24 cannon. Its form is triangular; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> is neat, strong, and commodious for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, that being but small, on account of the narrowness of the rock on which it is built. The garrison is usually composed of 25 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> men, and an equal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>, under the command of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERGEANT">sergeant</a>. It is maintained at the expense of the West <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>; and when well stored with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, is capable of making a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> against any number of negroes. It is, however, as well as all other forts on this coast, liable to inconveniences from the heavy and continual rains, which damage the walls, and render frequent reparations necessary. This obliges the Dutch always to keep ready a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of lime <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cement made of calcined oyster shells, of which the coast produces <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers. This settlement was first founded by the Portuguese during the reign of Emmanuel. They fixed it first upon a small point; where, finding themselves insecure, they built the fort where it now stands. They were driven out by the Dutch in 1642; and, upon the conclusion of a peace with the States General, the fort remained by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Dutch West India Company, who have kept possession of it ever since.

ANTONIUS MARCUS

Pages 52-53

a famous Roman orator. While he filled the office of praetor, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> fell to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>, and he cleared the seas of the pirates which infested that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. He was made <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> with A. Posthumius <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBINUS">Albinus</a>, in the year of Rome 653; when he opposed the turbulent designs of Sextus Titus, tribune of the people, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> and success. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, he was made governor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of proconsul; where he performed so many great exploits, that he obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of a triumph. We cannot omit observing, that, in order to improve his great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for eloquence, he became a scholar to the greatest men at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, in his way to Cilicia, and when on his return to Rome. Soon after, he was appointed censor; which office he discharged with great reputation, having carried his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> before the people, against Marcus Duronius, who had preferred an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> of bribery against him, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> for Antonius's having erased his name out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of senators, which this wise censor had done, because Duronius, when tribune of the people, had abrogated a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> Antonius, law which restrained immoderate expense in feasts. He was one of the greatest orators ever known at Rome; and it was owing to him, according to the testimony of Cicero, that Rome might boast herself a rival even to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> itself in the art of eloquence. He defended, amongst many others, Marcus Aquilius; and moved the judges in so sensible a manner, by the tears he shed, and the scars he showed upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> of his client, that he carried his cause. He never would publish any of his pleadings, that he might not, as he said, be proved to say in one cause, what might be contrary to what he should advance in another. He affected to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of no learning. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, and many other qualifications, rendered him no less dear to many persons of distinction, than his eloquence made him universally admired. He was unfortunately killed during those bloody confusions raised at Rome by Marius and Cinna. He was discovered in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where he had hid himself, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> were sent to despatch him; but his manner of addressing them had such an effect, that none but he who commanded them, and had not heard his discourse, had the cruelty to kill him. His head was exposed before the rostra, a place which he had adorned with his triumphal spoils. This happened 90 years before the Christian era. Antonius, Marcus, the triumvir, grandson to the former, was very handsome in his youth; for which reason he was greatly beloved by Curio, a senator, who, by carrying him about in all his debaucheries, made him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> such heavy debts, that his own father forbade him his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. Curio, however, was so generous as to bail him for 250 talents. When the civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> broke out, Curio took Caesar's party, and prevailed with Antonius to do the same; for which he was made a tribune of the people, and in that office did Caesar great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. Caesar having made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Rome, gave Antonius the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARSALIA">Pharsalia</a>, Caesar confided so much in him, that he gave him the command of the left wing of his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, whilst he himself led the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>. After Caesar was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a> he made Antonius general of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, though he had never been praetor; in which command he exerted his power with the utmost violence. He was made consul, when Caesar enjoyed that honour for the fifth time, the last year of that usurper's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. On Caesar's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he harangued the populace with great art, and raised their fury against his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDERERS">murderers</a>; flattering himself that he should easily get into the place which Caesar had filled; but his haughty behaviour made him lose all the advantages his affected concern for Caesar had gained him. His ill treatment of Octavius, and quarrel with him, produced another civil war; which ended in an accommodation between him, Octavius, and Lepidus, fatal to the peace of Rome. They agreed to share the supreme power among them; and many of the most illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> were sacrificed by proscription to cement this bloody <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>, which is known by the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">Second</a> Triumvirate. But the triumvirs were too ambitious, and hated one another too much, to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> united. Antonius went into <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> to raise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> for his soldiers; during his absence, Fulvia his wife quarrelled with Octavius. When Antonius was in Asia, indulging himself in all manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>, the famous Cleopatra inspired him with the most violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. Hearing of the quarrel between Fulvia and Octavius, and finding Octavius was become publicly his enemy, Antonius entered into a confederacy with Sextus Pompeius, who was still master of Sicily. He then went into Italy, in order to fight Octavius; but Fulvia, who had been the author and promoter of this war, dying, Octavius and Antonius came to an agreement. One of the conditions of this new peace was, that they should together attack Pompey, though the former had lately make an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with him. Antonius then married <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCTAVIA">Octavia</a>, sister to Octavius, as a pledge of their renewed friendship; but returned soon after to his beloved Cleopatra, and again lived with her in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>. Octavius took hold of this pretence to inveigh against him, and begin the war again. At last they engaged in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> fight at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIUM">Actium</a>, in which Octavius gained a complete victory; which was followed by the deaths both of Antonius and Cleopatra. The infatuated Antonius fell upon his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; and Cleopatra flung herself to death with an asp, as was supposed, to avoid gracing the victor's triumph at Rome.

ANTONOMASIA

Pages 53-53

a form of speech, in which, for a proper name, is put the name of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, office, profession, science, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> trade; or when a proper name is put in the room of an appellative. Thus a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> is called his majesty; a nobleman, his lordship. We say the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> instead of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, and the orator for Cicero: Thus a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is called by the name of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, a German, an Italian; and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> man is called a Cato, and a wise man a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>.

ANTOSANDRIANS

Pages 53-53

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of rigid Lutherans, who oppose the doctrine of Oftander relating to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTIFICATION">justification</a>. These are otherwise denominated Oftandromagites.—The Antosandrians deny that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a>, with that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> wherewith God himself is just; that is, they assert, that he is not made essentially, but only imputatively, just; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, that he is not really made just, but only pronounced so.

ANTRIM

Pages 54-54

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of An- <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRIM">trim</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, seated at the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> end of the lake Lough Neagh, about six miles from the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, having a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> before it, with a pier near the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, within which vessels <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> dry at low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It was anciently a borough of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, as appears from the mayor's being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> of a consider- able <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, as well in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">Down</a> as in this coun- try; the corporation enjoying the customs paid by all vessels within those bounds, the creeks of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANGOR">Bangor</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELFAST">Belfast</a> only excepted. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>, however, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> repurchased, and thereupon transferred the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>- <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> to Belfast, to which town it is now much inferi- <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> as well in size as in trade. It is, however, still a place of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, and sends two members to the house of commons. It gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the noble fa- mily of M'Donnel.—At Antrim is a seat, with noble demesnes, and beautiful and highly cultivated lands, of the earl of Maflareene. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 26. N. Lat. 54° 45'.

ANTWERP

Pages 54-56

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Brabant, in the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the marquisate of Antwerp, otherwise called the marquisate of the holy Roman empire, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 15. N. Lat. 51. 12. It lies in a low marshy ground on the Scheld, 24 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. It is the third city in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in Brabant, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and well built, contain- ing 22 squares, and above 200 streets, all straight and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, especially that called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">Mere</a>, in which six coaches can go abreast. Most of the houses are of freestone, and have an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of antiquity, being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, with courts before and gardens behind. At the head of the Mere is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRUCIFIX">crucifix</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> thirty-three feet high. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> dedicated to the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, the stadthoufe, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, are magnificent struc- tures: the latter is the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of that kind in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and on its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> the exchanges of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> are built. Its pillars are all of blue marble, and carved, but all in a different manner. The exchange cost the city 300,000 crowns. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANT">Ant</a>- werp, towards the end of the fifteenth century, was one of the most celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> that ever existed. The Scheld, on which it stands, being 20 feet deep at low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and rising 20 feet more at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, ships of the greatest burden came up to the quays, as in the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> at London; but when the United Provinces formed themselves into a free state, after having shaken off the yoke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, they got the entire command of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> of the Scheld; which ruined the trade of Antwerp, and transferred it to Amsterdam. This made the inhabitants turn their heads to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, jewelling, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANKING">banking</a>, which they have <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success and reputation; for at Ant- werp bills of exchange may be negotiated for any sum to any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Europe; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, two brothers of the name of De Konings, paid the one the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of France, and the other that of the confederates. Besides, here is a fine manufacture of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACE">lace</a>; and, for the promoting of trade, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSURANCE">insurance</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> has been erected. This city is the see of a bishop, who, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of St Bernard, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> prelate in Brabant. The bishopric is of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and the cathedral a most noble pile, with one of the finest steeples in the world. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. when he made his entry into Antwerp, said it ought to be put in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, and showed only once a year for a rarity. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANSE">hanse</a> towns, built when the city was in its flourishing condition, is a flatly building, with magazines above for dry goods, and cellars below for wet, and in the middle story were 300 lodging rooms for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>; but now it is turned to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> barrack. There is a market here called the Friday's market, because it is held every Friday, where all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> goods, pictures, and jewels, are sold by auction. No city in the Ne- therlands has so many and so fine churches as this. Many of them, particularly the cathedral and Jesuits <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, are adorned with paintings, by Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Paul Rubens, who was a native of this city; and by Quin- tin Massys, who is said to have been a blacksmith; but having fallen in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with a painter's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, and been told by her father, when he asked her of him in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, that he would have none but a paint- er for his son-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> paint- ing, and, in a few years, returned to eminent in his new profession, that he found no difficulty in obtaining the father's consent. He is interred at the entry of the cathedral, where his effigy is put up, with an inscription, signifying, that conjugal love made an A- pelles of a blacksmith. The above-mentioned Jesuits church is extremely magnificent, and the chapel of the Virgin, joining to it, still more so. Among the cloisters the most remarkable are, the noble and rich <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of St Michael, on the banks of the Scheld, the apartments of which are truly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>, and in which all sovereign princes that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> this way actually lodge; and the English nunnery, of the order of St Teresa, the nuns of which never wear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, nor eat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> upon straw: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATES">grates</a> of the convent are so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIS">dis</a>- mal, that it looks like a prison. As to the fortifica- tions of the city, it is environed with a fine wall, plant- ed with rows of trees on each side, with walks between, broad enough for two coaches to go abreast, being also defended by a very strong, large, regular citadel, in form of a pentagon, erected by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Alva in 1568, which commands the town and the neighbour- ing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The magistracy of this city is chosen only out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> patrician families; and consists of two burgomasters and 18 echevins, besides inferior magistrates. Among the privileges granted to it by its princes, there is one by which every person born in it is a citizen, though both his father and mother were foreigners. In 1585, Antwerp underwent a remarkable siege by the duke of Parma. It was then the most wealthy city in the Netherlands, and had long been the object of his designs; but the difficulties attending the enter- prise obliged him to postpone it for a considerable time. In order to succeed, it was necessary to cut off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a>. Antwerp communication of the city with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, Ghent, and all places above and below Antwerp on the Scheld. To effect this, he laid siege to Liefenhousk and Tillo, places of the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to the security and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of the city: both were obstinately defended; and the siege of the latter was raised, after it had been carried on for three months; however, the duke gained several other posts on the river, where he built forts, and greatly annoyed the shipping and trade of the city. He next laid siege to Dendermonde, in order to cut off the communication with Ghent, in which he succeeded by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of the town. His next attempt was on Vilvorde: this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> he took by assault, and thereby cut off the communication with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUGES">Bruges</a>. Finding, however, this method of hemming in the city tedious, and ineffectual while an opening to the mouth of the river remained, he formed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of building a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> across the Scheld, the extremities of which were to be defended by strong forts and outworks. He began with collecting great quantities of wood at Callo and Fort St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, where he intended the bridge should be built; but his project was for some time retarded by the Antwerpers, who broke <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the dykes, overflowed the whole country, and carried off his magazines by the inundation. Not discouraged by this loss, he applied himself diligently to repair it, and with incredible expedition cut a canal from Steken to Callo, by which he carried off the waters. He then set to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> upon the bridge, and finished it in seven months, without any interruption from the Zealanders. During the building of this bridge, Aldegonde, governor of Antwerp, proposed to build a fort on Couvensteyn dyke, in order to secure that important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>, and then breaking down the dyke when the bridge was near finished; but he was violently opposed by certain citizens, who apprehended that their lands and villas would be destroyed by the inundation. This unseasonable opposition, with the negligence of the magistrates, who, because the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> were high, had not laid in a sufficient stock of corn, occasioned the loss of the city. However, in despite of all the duke of Parma's precautions, the Zealanders found means to throw in a convoy of corn; but the citizens, knowing they would not run the risk of carrying it back again, so cheapened the price, that these bold traders refused ever to bring their goods again to so bad a market. The Antwerpers, having thus through avarice brought on their ruin, began in a short time to suffer by famine; they then pressed the Zealanders to attempt something for their relief, but it was now too late. While the magistrates were deliberating on some means for destroying the bridge, which they might have prevented from being ever completed, one Ginebelli, a Mantuan engineer, offered his services, undertaking at a certain expense to blow it into the air. Even in this extremity the expense was grudged; but <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> at last overcame this obstacle; Ginebelli was furnished with two large vessels, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small boats, and every thing necessary. He formed the two large vessels into fire ships, which he set adrift with the stream, deceiving the enemy by means of false fires lighted up in the fleet of small boats. The train of one of the fire ships was expended before the time expected, and she blew up with a terrible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a>, but with little damage to the bridge. The other was more successful, carrying off all the outworks, setting fire to the whole bridge, and burying above 500 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> in the ruins it made. The fire, however, was soon extinguished, and the bridge repaired by the duke of Parma, while the Antwerpers were prevented by avarice from repeating the experiment; so that they were soon reduced to the greatest straits, and obliged to surrender. It is said that the city of Amsterdam had obstructed every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> for the relief of Antwerp, hoping to profit by its destruction. It was not doubted but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> would forsake it as soon as it fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of an arbitrary Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; and this conjecture was soon fulfilled by the removal of many families with their effects to Amsterdam.—After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAMILLIES">Ramillies</a>, the city of Antwerp surrendered to the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>. It was taken by the French in 1746, but restored to the house of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANUBIS">Anubis</a>, a symbolical deity of the Egyptians, was regarded as the faithful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a> and of Isis. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">Temples</a> and priests were consecrated to him, and his image was borne in all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ceremonies. Cynopolis, the present Minieh, situated in the Lower Thebais, was built in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Anubis. The temple wherein he was worshipped no longer subsists. The priests celebrated his festivals there with great pomp, and consecrated the dog to him as his living representation. "Anubis (says Strabo) is the city of dogs, the capital of the Cynopolitan prefecture. These animals are fed there on sacred aliments, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> has decreed them a worship." An event, however, related by Plutarch, brought them into considerable discredit with the people. Cambyses having slain the god <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APIS">Apis</a>, and thrown his body into a field, all animals rejected it except the dogs, which alone ate of his flesh. This <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPURITY">impurity</a> diminished the popular veneration for them. Cynopolis was not the only city which burned incense on the altars of Anubis. He had chapels in almost all the temples. On solemnities, his image always accompanied those of Isis and Osiris. Rome having adopted the ceremonies of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, the emperor Commodus, to celebrate the Iliac feasts, shaved his head, and himself carried the god Anubis. The statue of this god was either of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> gilt, as well as the attributes that accompanied him. Anubis signifies gilded. The denomination was mysterious; and the Egyptian priests, it would seem, had not given it without reason. The signification of this emblematical deity is thus explained by Plutarch: "The circle which touches and separates the two hemispheres, and which is the cause of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, receiving the name of horizon, is called Anubis. He is represented under the form of a dog, because that animal watches day and night." St Clemens of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, who was well informed in the mythic <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> of the Egyptians, favours this explication. The two dogs, says he, (the two Anubes) are the symbols of two hemispheres which environ the terrestrial globe. He adds in another place: Others pretend that these animals, the faithful guardians of men, indicate the tropics, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> on the south and on the north like porters. According to the former of these interpretations, the priests, regarding Anubis as the horizon, gilded his statue; to mark, that this circle, receiving the first rays of the sun, appears sparkling with brightness on its rising, and that at his setting he reflects his last rays upon the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. They said in their sacred fables, that Anubis was the son of Osiris, but illegitimate. In fact, he only gives to the earth a borrowed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; and cannot be effaced, like <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORUS">Horus</a>, as the father of the day, or as the legitimate offspring of Osiris. It may be added, that the visible horizon <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> with the sun, is his inseparable companion. In the latter of these explications, where Anubis represents the tropics, he is also the faithful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> of Isis and Osiris. In fact, the course of the sun and of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> is contained between the circles wherein the festivities are performed. They neither deviate to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> nor left. These limits assigned by the Author of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> might therefore, in hieroglyphic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, be represented by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> with the head of a dog, who seemed to oppose their passage on the side of the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>. The other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, notwithstanding, seems more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, and to be more analogous to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of the priests. Upon the whole, it is reasonable to imagine, that Anubis at first was only a symbolical image, invented by astronomers to give a sensible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of their discoveries; that afterwards, the people, accustomed to see it in their temples, which were the depositories of science, adored it as a deity; and that the priests favoured their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> by connecting it with their religion. The worship of Anubis introduced, that of the dog became its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a>. Almost all the gods of the Gentiles have originated in this manner.

ANVIL

Pages 56-56

a smith's utensil, serving to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> on to be hammered <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> forged. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> or uppermost surface of the anvil, must be very flat and smooth, without flaws, and so hard that a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILE">file</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not touch it. At one end there is sometimes a pike, bickern or beak-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, for the rounding of hollow work. The whole is usually mounted on a firm wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>.—Forged anvils are better than those of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> work, and the best have the upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> made of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>. Locksmiths have a smaller kind of anvil called the flake, which is moveable, and placed ordinarily on their work <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is for setting small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> work straight, or to cut or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNCH">punch</a> on with the cold chisel or cold punch.

ANXUR

Pages 56-56
