in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Volsci, in Latium; called Tarracina, by the Greeks; and Latins: Now Terracina; situated on an eminence (Livy, Horace, Sil. Italicus). Ancura, a citizen of Anxur (Livy). And the epithet Anxurus, a name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, worshipped without a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> at Anxur (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>). Though others read Anxur, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Axyrus, without a razor. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. 5. Lat. 41. 18.

AONIDES

Pages 56-56

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, one of the many appellations of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>; so called from Aonia, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>.

AORASIA

Pages 56-56

in Antiquity, the invisibility of the gods. The word is Greek, ορασις, and derived from οραω, priv. and εγω, to see. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> with regard to the appearance of the gods to men, was that they never showed themselves <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> to face, but were known from their backs as they withdrew. Nep- tum assumed the form of Calchas to speak to the two Ajaxes; but they knew him not till he turned his back to leave them, and discovered the god by his majestic step as he went from them. Venus appeared to Aeneas in the character of a huntress; but her form knew her not till she departed from him; her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> was then betrayed by her radiant head, her flowing robe, and her majestic pace.

AORIST

Pages 56-56

among Grammarians, a tense peculiar to the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, comprehending all the tenses; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather, expressing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDETERMINATE">indeterminate</a> manner, without any regard to past, present, or future.

AORISTIA

Pages 56-56

in the Sceptic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, denotes that state of the mind wherein we neither affirm nor deny anything positively, but only speak of things as seeming <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> appearing to us in such a manner. The aoristia is one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> or terms of scepticism, to which the philosophers of that denomination had continual recourse by way of explication, or subterfuge. Their adversaries, the dogmatists, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> them with dogmatizing, and afflicting the principles and positions of their feet to be true and certain.

AORNUS

Pages 56-57

a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> rock of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, having its name from its extraordinary height, as being above the flight of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>. Its circuit was about 25 miles, its height 11 furlongs, and the way leading up to the top <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> and narrow. At the bottom, on one side, ran the river <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDUS">Indus</a>; on the top was a fine plain, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of which was covered with a thick wood; the rest arable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, with a fountain furnishing abundance of excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. This rock was taken by Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, in whose <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> there was a report that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> had attempted it in vain; however, according to Ari- stan, this report was without foundation. It is probable indeed, that it was raised after the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was taken, in order to magnify Alexander's exploit. While the Macedonian monarch was preparing all things necessary for the siege, an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> with his two sons, who had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> lived in a cave near the summit, came and offered to show him a private way of ascending. This being readily accepted, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, with a considerable body of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-armed troops, was despatched with them, with orders, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> they succeeded, to intrench themselves strongly upon the rock, in the wood to which the old man was to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> them, before they ventured to attack the Indians. Ptolemy exactly executed his orders; and gave notice, by a lighted torch set upon a pole, that he had got safely up. Upon this, Alexander gave immediate orders for a body of troops to attempt the passage by which the rock was <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> ascended; but they were repulsed with great slaughter. He then sent an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> with letters to Ptolemy, desiring him, the next time an attack was made by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> way, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> upon the enemy behind. But in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, those who defended the rock attacked Ptolemy with great vigour; but were at last repulsed, though with much difficulty: but the next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, when Alexander renewed the attack, though Ptolemy attacked the Indians in the rear, the Macedonians were repulsed on both sides. At last, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> perceiving that the strength of the Indians lay in the straitness and declivity of the way by which they were attacked, caused a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of trees to be felled, and with them filled the cavities between the plain on which which the Indians were encamped and the highest of his own advanced posts. The Indians at first derided his undertaking; but at length perceiving the ardour with which the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was carried on, and having felt the effects of the missile weapons of the Macedonians, they sent deputies to propose terms of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>. Alexander, suspecting that their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> was only to amuse him till they made their escape, withdrew his guards from the avenues. As soon as he knew the Indians were descended, he, with 700 of Ptolemy's light-armed foot, took possession of the deserted rock, and then made a signal for his forces to fall upon the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> Indians. They, setting up a loud shout, so terrified the fugitives, that numbers of them fell from the rocks and precipices, and were dashed to pieces, while the greatest part of the remainder were cut off in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>.

AORTA

Pages 57-57

in Anatomy, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> artery which rises immediately from the left ventricle of the heart, and is from thence distributed to all parts of the body. It is divided into two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> trunks, distinguished by the epithets ascending and descending. See ANATOMY.

AOSTA

Pages 57-57
or Aost, a town of Italy, in Piedmont, and capital of the duchy of the same name, a bishop's see, and subject to the king of Sardinia. It is remarkable for several monuments of the Romans, and for the birth of Anselm archbishop of Canterbury. It is seated at the foot of the Alps, on the river Doria. E. Long. 7° 33'. N. Lat. 47° 38'. Aosta, a territory of Piedmont, with the title of a duchy. It is a valley 30 miles in length, and extends from the pass of St Martin's, near the frontiers of Yvre, to St Bernard. It abounds in pastures, and all sorts of fruits. The capital is of the same name.

APACHES

Pages 57-57

a people of New <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. They are brave, resolute, and warlike, fond of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and the inveterate enemies of tyranny and oppression. Of this disposition the Spaniards had fatal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> towards the end of the last century, when they revolted against the Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, massacred several of his officers, and committed the greatest devastations. Ever since, they have remained the allies, not the subjects of the Spaniards; and the viceroy of Mexico has been obliged to maintain a more formidable garrison, and a greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of troops. APÆDUSIA, denotes <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> unskillfulness in what relates to learning and the sciences. Hence also persons uninstructed and illiterate are called apædeute. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> apædeute was particularly used among the French in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Huet; when the men of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> were divided into two factions, one called by way of reproach apædeute, and the others eruditi. The apædeute are represented by Huet as persons who, finding themselves either incapable or unwilling to undergo a severe course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> in order to become truly learned, conspire to decry learning, and turn the knowledge of antiquity into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>, thus making a merit of their own incapacity. The apædeute in effect were the men of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; the eruditi the men of study. The apædeute in everything pre- ferred the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> writers to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, to supercede Apagoge the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of studying the latter. The eruditi derided the moderns, and valued themselves wholly on their acquaintance with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>.

APAGOGE

Pages 57-57

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a>, is sometimes used to denote a progress <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> passage from one proposition to another; when the first having been once demonstrated, is afterwards employed in the proving of others.

APAGOGICAL DEMONSTRATION

Pages 57-57

an indirect way of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, by showing the absurdity of the contrary.

APALACHIAN MOUNTAINS

Pages 57-57

more properly called the Alleghany <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a>, have their southern beginning near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, in the latitude of 32°, extending northerly on the back of the British colonies, and running <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> to the latitude of 40° <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; but their distance from the sea, on the west, is not exactly known, though it is generally thought to be above 200 miles. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of these mountains is covered with rocks, some of which are of a stupendous height and bulk; the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> between them is generally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, but in some places differently coloured, composed of pieces of broken rock and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAR">spar</a>, of a glittering appearance, which seem to be indications of minerals and ores, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> proper search was made for them. Chestnuts and small oaks are the trees that principally grow on these mountains, with some chinkapin* and other small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>. The grass is *Fagus thin, mixed with vetch and small pease; and in some places there is very little vegetable appearance. The rocks of the Appalachian mountains seem to engross one half of the surface. They are mostly of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> grey <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; some are of a coarse grained marble like alabaster; others of a metallic lustre; some pieces are in the form of flate, and brittle; others in lumps, and hard; and some appear with spangles, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> covered over with innumerable small shining specks, like silver. These frequently appear at the roots of trees when torn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. The different spars are found mostly on the highest and steepest parts of the hills, where there is little grass and few trees; but the greatest part of the soil between the rocks is generally a dark sandy-coloured kind of mould, and shallow; yet fertile, and productive of good corn, which encourages the Tallapoosa, a clan of the Cherokee Indians, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> among them in latitude 34°: and they are the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> that has a constant residence upon these mountains.

APAMEA

Pages 57-58
or APAMIA, the name of several ancient cities. 1. One of Bithynia, formerly called Myrlea, from Myrlius, general of the Colophonians: destroyed by Philip, father of Perseus; and given to his ally Prusias, who rebuilt it, and called it Apamea, from the name of his queen Apama (Strabo). Stephanus says, that Nicomedes Epiphanes, son of Prusias, called it after his mother; and that it had its ancient name from Myrlea, an Amazon. The Romans led a colony thither (Strabo); Apamea bo); called Colonia Apamena (Pliny, Appian). The gentilic name is Apamaeus and Apamenus (Trajan in a letter to Pliny). 2. Another Apamea, called Cibotus, of Phrygia, at some distance from the Meander (Agathodemon); but by a coin of Tiberius, on the Meander. The name is from Apame, mother of Antiochus Soter, the founder, and the daughter of Artabazus (Strabo). The rise, or at least the increase, of Apamea, was owing to the ruins of Celene. The inhabitants were called Apamenses; and, though inland, were worshippers of Neptune. The reason, it has been conjectured, was, that they had suffered often from earthquakes, of which he was supposed the author. Mithridates gave a hundred talents towards the restoration of the city; which, it is said, had likewise been overthrown in the time of Alexander. Their tribute money was remitted to them for five years on the same account under the emperor Tiberius. The subterraneous passage of the Lycus and other streams showed that the ground had many cavities; and these, it has been furnished, rendered the region very liable to be shaken. 3. A third, on the confines of Parthia and Media, named Raphene (Strabo, Pliny). 4. A fourth Apamea, a town of Mesene, an island in the Tigris (Pliny, Ammianus); where a branch of the Euphrates, called the Royal River, falls into the Tigris (Ptolemy). 5. A fifth in Mesopotamia, on the other side the Euphrates, opposite to Zeugma on this side, both founded by Seleucus, and joined by a bridge, from which the latter takes its name (Pliny, Isidor, Characenus). 6. A sixth Apamea, now Famia, also in Syria, below the confluence of the Orontes and Mariyas; a strong city, and situated in a peninsula, formed by the Orontes and a lake. "It is here (says Strabo) that the Seleucidae had established the school and nursery of their cavalry." The soil of the neighbourhood, abounding in pasturage, fed no less than 30,000 mares, 300 stallions, and 500 elephants; instead of which, the marshes of Famia at present scarcely afford a few buffaloes and sheep. To the veteran soldiers of Alexander, who here repented after their victories, have succeeded wretched peasants, who live in perpetual dread of the oppressions of the Turks and the inroads of the Arabs. Apamea was also the ancient name of Pella, in the Decapolis.

APANAGE

Pages 58-58
or APPENAGE, in the French customs, lands assigned by a sovereign for the subsistence of his younger sons, which revert to the crown upon the failure of male issue in that branch to which the lands are granted.

APANOMIA

Pages 58-58

a town of Santorin, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, called in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> by some the sea of Candia. It has a spacious harbour, in the form of a half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>; but the bottom is so deep, that ships cannot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> there. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 25° 59'. N. Lat. 36° 18'.

APANTHROPY

Pages 58-58

in Medicine, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of solitude, and aversion for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of mankind. Apanthropy is by some reckoned among the symptoms, by others among the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> degrees of melancholy; and also passes for an ill indication in lexicographic <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>.

APARINE

Pages 58-58

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a synonyme of the urticaria and several other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>.

APARITHMESIS

Pages 58-58

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, denotes the answer to the protasis <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> proposition itself. Thus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the protasis be, Appellandi tempus non erat.—The aparithmesis is, At tunc anno plus visi.

APARTISMENU

Pages 58-58

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, an appellation given to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, which comprehended an entire <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sentence in itself. This is sometimes also written apartimentum, i.e., suspended, as not needing any following verse.

APATHY

Pages 58-58

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophers, implied an utter privation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, and an insensibility of pain. The word is compounded of priv. and affectio, affection. The Stoics affected an entire apathy; they considered it as the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> to enjoy a perfect calmness <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tranquillity of mind, incapable of being ruffled by either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> or pain. In the first ages of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> adopted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> apathy, to express a contempt of all earthly concerns; a state of mortification, such as the gospel prescribes. Clemens Alexandrinus, in particular, brought it exceedingly in vogue; thinking hereby to draw the philosophers to Christianity, who aspired after such a sublime pitch of virtue. Quietism is only apathy disguised under the appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>.

APATURIA

Pages 58-58

in Antiquity, a solemn feast celebrated by the Athenians in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>. The word is usually derived from amar, fraud. It is said to have been instituted in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of a fraudulent victory obtained by Melanthus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, over Xanthus, king of Beotia, in a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, which they agreed upon, to put an end to a debate between them relating to the frontiers of their countries. Hence Budaeus calls it festum deceptionis, "the feast of deceit." Other authors give a different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> of this feast: They tell us, that the young Athenians were not admitted into the tribes on the third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the asturia; till their fathers had first sworn that they were their own children; and that, till that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, they were supposed, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, to be without fathers, ἀπατεῖναι; wherefore the feast, say they, took its name. Xenophon, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, informs us, that the relations and friends met on this occasion, and joined with the fathers of the young people who were to be received into the tribes; and that from this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> the feast took its name: that in asturēs, the α, far from being a privative, being here a conjunctive, signifies the same thing with ἀπατεῖναι, together. This feast lasted four days: the first day, those of the same tribe made merry together; and this they called ἀστυρία. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> day, which they called ἀστυριασμός, they sacrificed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>. The third day, which they called ἀστυριασμός, such of their young men and maids as were of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> were admitted into their tribes. The fourth day they called ἀστυριασμός.

APAUMEE

Pages 80-80

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, denotes one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> extended, with the full palm appearing, and the thumb and fingers at full length.

APAVLIA

Pages 58-59

in Antiquity, the third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> solemnity. It was thus called, because the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a>, returning to her father's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, did ἀστυριασμός, lodge apart from the bridegroom. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have the apavlia to have been the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> day of the marriage, viz., that wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> was performed; thus called by way of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> from the first day, which was called ἀστυριασμός. On APE the day called ἀπαλία (whenever that was), the bride presented her bridegroom with a garment called ἀπαλία.

APE

Pages 59-59

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the general English name of a very numerous <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of animals, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of which is given at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> under the article SIMIA; comprehending Apes, properly so called, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> such as want tails; and Monkeys and Baboons, or such as have tails, the former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and the other short, ones. See SIMIA. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> Ape, a name given by Steller to a marine animal which he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and is thus described*. "The head appeared like that of a dog, with sharp and upright ears, large eyes, and with both lips bearded; the body round and conoid; the thickest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> near the head; the tail forked; the upper lobe the longest; the body covered with thick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, gray on the back, reddish on the belly. It seemed destitute of feet. It was extremely wanton, and played a multitude of monkey tricks. It sometimes swam on one side, sometimes on the other side of the ship, and gazed at it with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> admiration. It made so near an approach to the vessel, as almost to be touched with a pole; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> anybody moved, it instantly retired. It would often stand erect for a considerable space, with one-third of its body above <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; then dart beneath the ship, and appear on the other side; and repeat the same thirty times together. It would frequently arise with a sea plant, not unlike the bottle gourd, toss it up, and catch it in its mouth, playing with it numberless fantastic tricks.

APELLA

Pages 59-59

among Physicians, a name given to those whose prepuce is either wanting <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> shrunk, so that it can no longer cover the glans. Many authors have supposed this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the word Apella warranted from the passage in Horace, credat judaeus Apella non ego. But, according to Salmahus and others, Apella is the proper name of a certain Jew, and not an adjective signifying circumcised.

APELYTES

Pages 59-59

Christian heretics in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century, who affirmed that Christ received a body from the four elements, which at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> he rendered back to the world, and so ascended into heaven without a body.

APENE

Pages 60-60

in Antiquity, a kind of chariot wherein the images of the gods were carried in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> on certain days, attended with a solemn pomp, songs, hymns, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, &c. It was very rich, made sometimes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of silver itself, and variously decorated.

APENNINUS

Pages 60-60

now the Apennine; a mountain, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ridge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, running through the middle of Apennine <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west to south-west for 700 miles, in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a> (Pliny); beginning at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a> in Liguria, or the Riviera di <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>; and terminating at the strait of Messina, or at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGGIO">Reggio</a>, and the promontory Leucopetra; and separating, as by a back or ridge, the Adriatic from the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> (Pliny, Strabo, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, Polybius, Vitruvius). This mountain, though <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, is greatly short of the height of the Alps. Its name is Celtic, signifying a high mountain.

APENRADE

Pages 60-60

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Sleiwick, seated at the bottom of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> in the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, between Flensbourg and Hadschleben. It is 25 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> from Sleiwick. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 28'. N. Lat. 55° 4'.

APENZEL

Pages 60-60

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of the same name, seated on the river Chus. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 1'. N. Lat. 47° 31'. The canton itself, which was allied to the others in 1513, consists only of three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four valleys; having the town and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALL">Gall</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Toggenburg on the west; the lordship of Sax in the canton of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZURICH">Zurich</a>, and that of Gambs in the canton of Schwyz, on the south; and the Rheinthal, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>-valley, on the east; its greatest length is about thirty miles, and its breadth about twenty. It yields good pasturage, and consequently is not deficient of cattle, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, or cheese. Considerable quantities also of wheat, rye, barley, oats, beans, pease, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, and wine, are produced in it; besides a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of fruit, wood, and turf; with mineral waters, and warm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. There are many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in the canton, the highest of which is that called the Hohefantis, or the Hohe Mefmer, which commands a prospect of a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. There are also several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. The inhabitants, who are partly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, and partly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>, subsist chiefly by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, crape, fustian, and thread, or by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLEACHING">bleaching</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of their cattle, butter, cheese, horses, wood, and coal. Of the twenty-three parishes in the canton, four are Papists, and nineteen Protestant. Before the Reformation, the inhabitants were subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of St Gall; but they then shook off his yoke, and united themselves with the other cantons; after that, however, there were violent animosities between the Papists and Protestants, the former continually persecuting the latter, till at last, in 1587, by the mediation of the other cantons, the two parties came to an accommodation, by which certain districts were assigned to each party, whereas before they lived promiscuously together; and though these two divisions now constitute but one canton, yet each forms a distinct <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> or free state, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FENCING">fencing</a> its particular representatives to the diets of the confederacy, and having its separate councils and officers. In spirituals the Papists are subject to the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a>, but the Protestants to their own consistory. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a> of the former does not exceed 3000, whereas those of the latter amount to 10,000.

APEPSIA

Pages 60-61

(from a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, and πνεύμα, to digest) Indigestion. Abstemiousness and excess are alike causes of indigestion. An over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> of the stomach may in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> injure its proper tone; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> fasting, by inducing a bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> in the juices secreted into the stomach, renders it feeble, and generates <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. Hard drinking, and any of the causes of an anorexia, also injure digestion. The columbo root is said to be particularly useful when the stomach is languid, the appetite defective, digestion with difficulty carried on, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> when a nausea with flatulence attends. It is prescribed in substance, with any grateful aromatic, or infused in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADEIRA">Madeira</a> wine, now and then interposing gentle doses of the tincture of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-RHUBARB">rhubarb</a>. A mixture of mustard seed with the columbo root is of admirable utility in complaints of this kind; particularly where acidity and flatulence prevail much in the prime vae.

APERIENTS

Pages 61-61

in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, an appellation given to such medicines as facilitate the circulation of the humours by removing obstructions. The five aperient roots of the shops are, mallage, fennel, asparagus, parsley, and butchers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROOM">broom</a>.

APERTURE

Pages 61-61

the opening of any thing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a hole or cleft in any continuous subject. Aperture, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, the space between two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> which meet in a point and form an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>. Aperture, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, a round hole in a turned bit of wood or plate of tin, placed within the side of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TELESCOPE">telescope</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>, near to the object glass, by means of which more rays are admitted, and a more distinct appearance of the object is obtained. Apertures, or Apertions, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, are used to signify doors, windows, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIMNEYS">chimneys</a>, &c.

APETALOSE

Pages 61-61
or APETALOUS, among Botanists, an appellation given to such plants as have no flower leaves.

APHACA

Pages 61-61

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, situated between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELIOPOLIS">Heliopolis</a> and Byblus, near Lebanon; infamous for a temple of Venus, called Aphacitis, near which was a lake, round which fire usually burst forth, and its waters were so heavy, that bodies floated on them. The temple was destroyed by Constantine, as being a school of incontinence, (Eusebius.) The name is of Syriac origin, signifying emaciation. APHÆRESIS, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> by which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a> is cut off from the beginning of a word. Thus riconia, by apharesis, is written <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONIA">conia</a>; contemnere, temere; omittere, mittere, &c. A like retrenchment at the end of a word is called apocope. APHÆRESIS, in Medicine, denotes a necessary taking away or removal of something that is noxious.—In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, it signifies an operation whereby something superfluous is taken away. APHANES. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

APHASIA

Pages 61-61

(from α, and φαίνω, "I speak,") in the sceptic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, denotes a state of doubt, wherein a person not knowing what to determine on, it is best for him to be silent. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, ἀφάσις stands opposed to πληθύς, under which are included both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFIRMATION">affirmation</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATION">negation</a>. APHÉK, the name of several cities mentioned in Scripture. 1. Aphek in the tribe of Judah, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILISTINES">Philistines</a> encamped when the ark was brought from Shiloh, which was taken by them in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, 1 Sam. iv. 1, 2, &c. It is thought to be the same with Aphekah mentioned in Joth. xv. 53. 2. Aphek in the valley of Jezreel, where the Philistines encamped while <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a> and his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> were near Jezreel, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Gilboa, 1 Sam. xxix. 7, &c. 3. Aphek a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> belonging to the tribe of Asher, near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Sidonians; (Joth. xix. 35. and xiii. 4.) 4. Aphek a city of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> in Benhadad's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, near which the battle was fought between Ahad and Benhadad, wherein the Syrians were worsted; and whereof, as they retreated with precipitation into the city, the walls fell upon them, and crushed in pieces 27,000, (1 Kings xx. 26, et seq.) This city lay between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELIOPOLIS">Heliopolis</a> and Byblus. APHÉLIUM, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> APHELION, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, is that point in any planet's orbit, in which it is farthest distant from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, being that end of the greater axis of the elliptical orbit of the planet most remote from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> where the sun is.

APHIOUM

Pages 61-61

KARAHISSART, a town of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATOLIA">Natolia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>; it is named Aphium, because it produces a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of opium, called aphium by the Turks. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 32. 18. N. Lat. 38. 35.

APOSTATA CAPIENDO

Pages 75-75

in the English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a writ that formerly lay against a person who, having entered into some order of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, broke out again, and wandered up and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>.

APOSTATE

Pages 75-75

one who deserts his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. Among the Romanists, it signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who, without a legal dispensation, forsakes a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> order of which he had made profession. A POSTERIORI, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> demonstration à posteriori. See DEMONSTRATION.

APOSTIL

Pages 75-75

in matters of Literature, the same with a marginal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>.

APOSTLE PROPERLY

Pages 75-77

E properly signifies a messenger <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> person sent by another upon some business; and hence, by way of eminence, denotes one of the disciples commissioned by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ to preach the gospel. Our blest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> selected twelve out of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his disciples to be invested with the apostleship. Their names were Simon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, Andrew, James the greater, John, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, Bartholomew, Thomas, Matthew, James the less, Jude named Lebbeus or Thaddeus, Simon the Canaanite, and Judas Iscariot. Of these Simon, Andrew, James the greater, and John, were fishermen; and Matthew a publican, or receiver of the public revenues; of what profession the rest were, we are not told in Scripture; though it is probable they were fishermen. There are various conjectures as to the reason of our Saviour's making choice of twelve apostles. The most probable is, that it might be in allusion to the twelve patriarchs, as the founders of their several tribes; or to the twelve <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> heads or rulers of those tribes, of which the body of the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> consisted. This <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> seems to be countenanced by what our Saviour tells his apostles, that "when the Son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> shall sit on the throne of his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, they also shall sit upon twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel." Our Lord's first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> to his apostles was in the third year of his public ministry, about eight months after their solemn <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>; at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he sent them out by two and two. They were to make no provision of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> for their subsistence in their journey, but to expect it from those to whom they preached. They were to declare, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of heaven, or the Messiah, was at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; and to confirm their doctrine by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>. They were to avoid going either to the Gentiles or to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SAMARITANS">Samaritans</a>, and to confine their preaching to the people of Israel. In obedience to their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a>, the apostles went into all the parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a> inhabited by the Jews, preaching the gospel, and working miracles. The evangelical <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is silent as to the particular circumstances attending this first preaching of the apostles; and only informs us, that they returned, and told their Master of all that they had done. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> commission, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> before our Lord's ascension into heaven, was of a more extensive and particular <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. They were now not to confine their preaching to the Jews, but to "go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." Accordingly they began publicly, after our Lord's ascension, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> the office of their ministry, working miracles daily in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of their mission, and making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of converts to the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. This alarmed the Jewish Sanhedrim; whereupon the apostles were apprehended, and, being examined before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> and elders, were commanded not to preach any more in the name of Christ. But this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJUNCTION">injunction</a> did not terrify them from performing in the duty of their calling; for they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> daily, in the temple, and in private houses, teaching and preaching the gospel. After the apostles had exercised their ministry for twelve years in Palestine, they resolved to disperse themselves in different parts of the world, and agreed to determine by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> what parts each should take. According to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, St Peter went into Pontus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALATIA">Galatia</a>, and those other provinces of the Lesser <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. St Andrew had the vast northern countries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCYTHIA">Scythia</a> and Sogdiana allotted to his portion. St John's was partly the same with Peter's, namely the Lesser Asia. St Philip had the Upper Asia assigned to him, with some parts of Scythia and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLCHIS">Colchis</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Felix fell to St Bartholomew's share. St Matthew preached in Chaldea, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTHIA">Parthia</a>; St Thomas preached likewise in Parthia; as also to the Hyrcanians, Bactrians, and Indians. St James the less continued in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> he was bishop. St Simon had for his portion <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRENE">Cyrene</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a>; St Jude, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> and Mesopotamia; and St Matthias, who was chosen in the room of the traitor Judas, Cappadocia and Colchis. Thus, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a> of the apostles, Christianity was very early planted in a great many parts of the world. We have but very short and imperfect accounts of their travels and actions. In order to qualify the apostles for the arduous task of converting the world to the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, they were, in the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, miraculously enabled to speak the languages of the several nations to whom they were to preach; and, in the second place, were endowed with the power of working miracles, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of the doctrines they taught; gifts which were unnecessary, and therefore ceased, in the after ages of the church, when Christianity came to be established by the civil power. St Paul is frequently called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a>, by way of eminence; and the apostle of the Gentiles, because his ministry was chiefly made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of for the conversion of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENTILE">Gentile</a> world, as that of St Peter was for the Jews, who is therefore styled the apostle of the circumcision. The several apostles are usually represented with their respective badges or attributes; St Peter with the keys; St Paul with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; St Andrew with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> or saltier; St James <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> with a fuller's pole; St John with a cup, and winged <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> rising from it; St Bartholomew with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>; St Philip with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, whose upper end is formed into a cross; St Thomas with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCE">lance</a>; St Matthew with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HATCHET">hatchet</a>; St Matthias with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>-axe; St James <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> with a pilgrim's staff and a gourd bottle; St Simon with a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>; and St Jude with a club. This appellation was also given to the ordinary travelling ministers of the church.—Thus St Paul, in the Epistle to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, xvii. 7, says, "Salute Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and fellow prisoners, who are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> among the apostles." It was likewise a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> given to those sent by the churches to carry their alms to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> of other churches. This usage they borrowed from the synagogues, who called those whom they sent on this message by the same name; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a> or office itself ἀπόστολος, ἀπόστολος, q.d. mission. Thus St Paul, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> to the Philippians, tells them that Epaphroditus their apostle had ministered to his wants, ch. ii. 25. The appellation is given in like manner to those persons who first planted the Christian faith in any place. Thus Dionysius of Corinth is called the apostle of France; Xavier, the apostle of the Indies, &c. In the East Indies the Jesuit missionaries are also called apostles. Apostle is also used among the Jews for a kind of officer anciently sent into the several parts and provinces in their jurisdiction, by way of visitor or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a>, to see that the laws were duly observed, and to receive the monies collected for the reparation of the temple, and the tribute payable to the Romans. The Theodosian code, lib. 14. De jure, calls those apostoli, qui <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> exigendum aurum aquae argentum, a patriarcha certo tempore dirigantur. Julian the apostate remitted the Jews the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLOS">apollos</a>, ἀπόστολοι; that is, as he himself explains it, the tribute they had been accustomed to send him. These apostles were a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> below the officers of the synagogue called patriarchs, and received their commissions from them. Some authors observe, that St Paul had borne this office; and that it is this he alludes to in the beginning of the epistle to the Galatians: as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had said, Paul, no longer an apostle of the synagogue, nor sent thereby to maintain the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of Moses, but now an apostle and envoy of Jesus Christ, &c. St Jerome, though he does not believe that St Paul had been an apostle of this kind, yet imagines that he alludes to it in the passage just cited. Apostle, in the Greek liturgy, is particularly used for a book containing the epistles of St Paul, printed in the order wherein they are to be read in churches, through the course of the year. Another book of the like kind, containing the Gospels, is called Εὐαγγέλιον, Gospel.—The apostle, of late days, has also contained the other canonical epistles, the acts of the Apostles, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">Revelation</a>. Hence it is also called Acts of the Apostles, Πράξεις Ἀποστόλων; that being the first book in it. Apostle is also thought by many to have been the original name for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, before the denomination bishop was appropriated to their order. Thus Theodoret says expressly, the same persons were anciently called promiscuously both bishops and prebys ters, whilst those who are now called bishops were called apostles. In the arsenal of Bremen, there are twelve pieces of cannon called the Twelve Apostles, on a supposition that the whole world must be convinced, and acquiesce in the preaching of such apostles. Apostles' Creed: a formula, or summary of the Christian faith, drawn up, according to Rufinus, by the apostles themselves: who, during their stay at Jerusalem, soon after our Lord's ascension, agreed upon this creed, as a rule of faith, and as a word of distinction by which they were to know friends from foes. Baronius, and some other authors, conjecture, that they did not compose it till the second year of the reign of Claudius, a little before their dispersion. As to their manner of composing it, some fancy, that each apostle pronounced his article, which is the reason of its being called symbolum <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-APOSTOLICUM">apostolicum</a>, it being made up of sentences jointly contributed, after the manner of persons paying each their club (symbolum) or share of a reckoning. But there are reasons which may induce us to question whether the apostles composed any such creed as this. For, first, Neither St Luke in the Acts, nor any other <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writer before the fifth century, make any mention of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the apostles in order to the composing of a creed. Secondly, The fathers of the three first centuries, in disputing against the heretics, endeavoured to prove that the doctrine contained in this creed was the same which the apostles composed; but they never pretend that the apostles composed it. Thirdly, If the apostles had made this creed, it would have been the same in all churches, and in all ages; Apostolare and all authors would have cited it after the same manner. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is quite otherwise. In the second and third ages of the church, there were as many creeds as authors, and one and the same author sets <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the creed after a different manner in several places of his works; which is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> that there was not at that time any creed which was reputed to be the apostles. In the 4th century, Rufinus compares together the three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> creeds of the churches of Aquileia, Rome, and the East, which differ very considerably in the terms. Besides, these creeds differed not only in the terms and expressions, but even in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, some of which were omitted in one or other of them; such as those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> of the saints, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> everlasting. From these reasons it may be gathered, that though this creed may be said to be that of the apostles in regard to the doctrines contained therein, yet it is not to be referred to them as the authors and first composers of it. Who was the true author of it, is not so easy to determine; though its great antiquity may be inferred from hence, that the whole form, as it now stands in the English liturgy, is to be found in the works of St <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a> and Rufinus, the former of whom flourished in the 3rd century, and the latter in the 4th century. The primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, in regard they always concealed this and their other <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a>, did not publicly recite the creed, except at the times of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>; which, unless in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, were only at Easter and Whitsuntide. The constant repeating it was not introduced into the church till the end of the 5th century; about which time Petrus Gnapheus, bishop of Antioch, prescribed the recital of it every time divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> was performed.

APOSTOLARE

Pages 77-77

APOSTOLICARE, apostolizing, in some middle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> writers, denotes the being preferred to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of pope.

APOSTOLATE

Pages 77-77

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is used for mission. In this sense, Olearius has a discourse concerning the apostolate of Christ.

APOSTOLATE MORE PROPERLY

Pages 77-77

E more properly denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> office of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> of Christ; but it is also used, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, for the office of a bishop. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we meet with several letters, petitions, requests, &c. directed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of your apostolate, or apostolatus vester. But as the title <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTOLICUS">apostolicus</a> had been appropriated to the pope, so that of apostolate became at length restrained to the sole dignity of the popedom. Every bishop's see was anciently dignified with the title of fides apostolica, an apostolical see, which is now the peculiar denomination of the see of Rome.

APOSTOLI

Pages 77-77

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, denote those letters missive which are demanded in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>.

APOSTOLIANS

Pages 77-77

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the Mennonites, which first sprung up in the year 1664, and derived its name from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLOS">Apollos</a>, one of the Mennonite ministers at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>. They concurred with them in doctrine, and admitted to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> those only who professed to believe all the sentiments which are contained in their public confession of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>.

APOSTOLIC

Pages 77-77

in the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, was an appellation given to all such churches as were founded by the apostles; and even to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of those churches, as being the reputed successors of the apostles.—These were confined to four, viz., Rome, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, Antioch, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. In after times, other churches assumed the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, on account, principally, of apostolical conformity of their doctrine with that of the churches which were apostolical by foundation, and apostolic, because all bishops held themselves successors of the apostles, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> acted in their dioceses with the authority of apostles. The first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> apostolical is attributed to bishops, as such, is in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of Clovis to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, held in 511, though that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> does not there expressly denominate them apostolical but (apostolicae fidei dignitatis) highly worthy of the apostolical see. In 581, Guntram calls the bishops, met at the council of Magon, apostolical pontiffs, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOSTOLICI">apostolici</a> pontifices. In progress of time, the bishop of Rome growing in power above the rest, and the three patriarchates of Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem, falling into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Saracens, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> apostolical was restrained to the pope and his church alone. Though some of the popes, and St Gregory the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, not contented to hold the title by this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a>, began, at length, to insist, that it belonged to them by another and peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, as being the successors of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a> in 1049 declared that the pope was the sole apostolical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> of the universal church. And hence a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of apostolicals; apostolical see, apostolical nuncio, apostolical notary, apostolical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a>, apostolical chamber, apostolical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>, &c. APOSTOLICAL Constitutions. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">Constitution</a>. APOSTOLICAL Traditions. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">Tradition</a>. APOSTOLICAL Fathers is an appellation usually given to the writers of the first century who employed their pens in the cause of Christianity. Of these writers, Cotelarius, and after him Le Clere, have published a collection in two volumes, accompanied both with their own annotations and the remarks of other learned men.

APOSTOLICI

Pages 77-78
or APOSTOLICS, was a name assumed by three different sects, on account of their pretending to imitate the manner and practice of the apostles. The first apostolici, otherwise called Apotactici and Apotacticii, rose out of the Encratites, and Cathari, in the third century. They made profession of abstaining from marriage, and the use of wine, flesh, money, &c. Gerhard Sagarelli was the founder of the second sect; he obliged his followers to go from place to place as the apostles did, to wander about clothed in white, with long beards, dishevelled hair, and bare heads, accompanied with women, whom they called their spiritual sisters. They likewise renounced all kinds of property and possessions, inveighed against the growing corruption of the church of Rome, predicted its overthrow, and the establishment of a purer church on its ruins. Sagarelli was burnt alive at Pavia in the year 1302, and was afterwards succeeded by Dulcinus, who added to the character of an apostle those of a prophet and a general, and carried on a bloody and dreadful war for the space of more than two years against Reynerius, bishop of Vercelli; he was at length defeated, and put to death in a barbarous manner in the year 1307. Nevertheless, this fact subsisted in France, Germany, and in other countries, till the beginning of the fifteenth century, when it was totally extirpated under the pontificate of Boniface IX. The other branch of apolitici was of the twelfth century. These also condemned marriage, preferring celibacy, and calling themselves the chaste brethren and sisters; though each was allowed a spiritual sister, with whom he lived in a domestic relation; and on this account they have been charged with concubinage: they held it unlawful to take an oath; they set aside the use of baptism; and in many things imitated the Manichees. Bernard wrote against this fact of apolitici. APOSTOLICUM is a peculiar name given to a kind of song or hymn, anciently used in churches. The apoliticum is mentioned by Greg. Thaumaturgus as used in his time. Vossius understands it as spoken of the apostles' creed: Suicer thinks this impossible, for that this creed was then unknown in the churches of the east.

APOSTROPHE

Pages 78-78

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of a word by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMA">comma</a>: as call'd for called, tho' for though. APOTACTITÆ, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> APOTACTICI, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, who affecting to follow the evangelical counsels of poverty, and the examples of the apostles and primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, renounced all their effects and possessions. It does not appear that they gave into any errors during their first state; some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers assure us they had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> holy virgins and martyrs under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> of Diocletian in the fourth century; but they afterwards fell into the opinions of the Encratites, and taught that the renouncing of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> was not only a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of counsel and advice, but of precept and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>. And hence the sixth <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> in the Theodosian code joins the Apotactite with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUNOMIANS">Eunomians</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>.

APOTEICHISMUS

Pages 78-78

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">Military</a> Art, a kind of line of circumvallation drawn round a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in order to besiege it. This was also called peri-teichismus. The first thing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> went about, when they designed to lay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> siege to a place, was the apoteichismus; which sometimes consisted of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> wall <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rampart, raised of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; the innermost to prevent sudden fallies from the town, the outermost to keep off foreign enemies from coming to the relief of the beleaguered. This answered to what are called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of con- Apothecary and circumvallation among the moderns.

APOTHECARIES

Pages 78-78

Apothecarius, in writers of the middle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, denotes a shop-keeper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> warehouse-keeper. APOTHECARIES is also used to denote a store-keeper, or officer appointed to have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANARY">granary</a>, &c. In which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> apothecarii is sometimes rendered by horaei and rationarii.

APOTHECARY

Pages 78-78

one who practises the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, the apothecaries are one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> companies. They were incorporated by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. procured at the solicitation of Dr Mayne and Dr Aitkins; till that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they only made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the grocers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; plums, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, spice, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> treacle, mithridate, &c. were sold in the same shop and by the same person. The reason of separating them was, that medicines might be better prepared, and in opposition to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> persons who imposed unwholesome remedies on the people. By an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> which was made perpetual in the ninth year of George I. they are exempted from serving upon juries, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> offices. They are obliged to make up their medicines according to the formulas prescribed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> dispensatory; and are liable to have their shops visited by the censors of the college, who are empowered to destroy such medicines as they think not good. They have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Friars, where there are two fine laboratories, out of which all the surgeons' chests are supplied with medicines for the British <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>. To his majesty belong two apothecaries: the salary to the first, £200.; to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, £75l.—To the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> belong also two. The charitable dispensation of medicines by the Chinese is well deserving notice. They have a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which is ten cubits <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, erected in the public squares of their cities; on this stone are engraved the names of all sorts of medicines, with the price of each; and when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> stand in need of any relief from physic, they go to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, where they receive the price each medicine is rated at.

APOTHEOSIS

Pages 78-78

in Antiquity, a heathen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, whereby their emperors and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men were placed among the gods. The word is derived from ἀπό, and θεός, God. After the apotheosis, which they also called deification and consecration, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, altars, and images were erected to the new deity; sacrifices, &c. were offered, and colleges of priests instituted. It was one of the doctrines of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, which he had borrowed from the Chaldees, that virtuous persons after their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> were raised into the order of the gods. And hence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> deified all the inventors of things useful to mankind; and those who had done any important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the commonwealth.—Tiberius proposed to the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> the apotheosis of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, as is related by Eusebius, Tertullian, and Chrysostom. Juvenal rallying the frequent apotheoses, introduces <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, complaining that he was ready to sink under the burden of so many new gods as were every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> added to the heavens. Seneca ridicules the apotheosis of Claudius with admirable humour. The ceremony, according to Herodian's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>,

APPARENT

Pages 79-79

among Mathematicians and Astronomers, denotes things as they appear to us, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> from real <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> true; thus we say, the apparent diameter, distance, magnitude, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, &c. of bodies. APPARENT Heir, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>. No inheritance can vest, nor can any person be the actual complete heir of another, till the ancestor is previously dead. Nemo est heres viventis. Before that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the person who is next in the line of succession is called an heir apparent, or heir presumptive. Heirs apparent are such, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of inheritance is indefeasible, provided they outlive the ancestor; as the eldest son or his issue, who must by the course of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law be heirs to the father whenever he happens to die. Heirs presumptive are such, who, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the ancestor should die immediately, would in the present circumstances of things be his heirs; but whose right of inheritance may be defeated by the contingency of some nearer heir being born; as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, or nephew, whose presumptive succession may be destroyed by the birth of a child; or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, whose present hopes may be hereafter cut off by the birth of a son. Nay, even if the estate hath descended, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the owner, to such brother, or nephew, or daughter, in the former <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, the estate shall be divested and taken away by the birth of a posthumous child; and, in the latter, it shall also be totally divested by the birth of a posthumous son.

APPARITION

Pages 79-80

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes simply the appearance of a thing. In a more limited sense, it is used for a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECTRE">spectre</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ghost. Several instances of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARITIONS">apparitions</a> occur in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>; that of Samuel, raised by the witch of Endor, has occasioned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> disputes. We find great controversies among authors, in relation to the reality, the existence or non-existence, the possibility or impossibility, of apparitions.
