Her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> was then changed into perpetual imprisonment, but this punishment did not afflange the fury of her barbarous enemies. They craftily laid a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s dress in her chamber, and she, induced by the sight of an apparel in which she had gained so much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, put it on; and, upon being discovered, her enemies condemned her to the stake, interpreting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> into a relapse of heresy. She suffered her punishment in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1431, at the market-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Rouen, with great firmness; and even the English themselves beheld the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> with tears. Her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> forever cast an indelible stigma on the character of her cruel prosecutors. Charles did nothing towards avenging her cause; but ten years afterwards, contented himself with procuring the restoration of her <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> by the pope, and a reverence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>. She was styled in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, a "<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a> to her <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, her country, and her king." In their enthusiastic admiration, her countrymen were not slow in honouring her memory. Many marvellous stories were related by them concerning her death. Some supposed that she was not actually dead, and continually expected, that, as formerly, she would come, and at their head <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> them on to victory. A confis- ent and uniform judgment respecting the actions and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> of this personage cannot be made by posterity. That she gave herself up to the influence of a heated fancy, and that she was confident in the idea of her divine inspiration, and that this notion was so improved by certain favourites of Charles, as to excite the emotions of the public, seems to be the most probable supposition. That the appearance of the Maid of Orleans tended to give a decisive turn to the contest between the English and the French, has never in the least been questioned. The praise and exploits of this noble heroine have formed the subject of various works both in prose and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. In verse, that of Voltaire is very licentious and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLESQUE">burlesque</a>, and is an injury to her memory; but it has in a great degree been repaired by that most spirited and sublime poem of Southey, in English, which represents her in the most lively and striking colours of heroism and virtue; and by that of Chapelain, although it did not meet with such success. (Gen. Biog.)

ARCADE

Pages 145-145

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, is used to denote any opening in the wall of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> formed by an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>.

ARCADI

Pages 145-145
or Arcadians, the name of a learned society at Rome. See Academy.

ARCADIA

Pages 145-145

an inland district in the heart of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a> (Strabo). It is mountainous, and fitter for pasture than corn; and therefore chiefly celebrated by bucolic <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pastoral poets, who feign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">Pan</a>, the god of shepherds, to be the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> of it (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>). It has to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> Achaea, to the east <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACONIA">Laconia</a>, Messenia to the south, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIS">Elis</a> to the west. According to Pliny, the wine of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> cured barrenness in women, and inspired the men with rage; and the berries of the yew gathered there were so strong a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, that whoever slept or took refreshment under that tree was sure to die. In Strabo's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> there were few cities remaining in it, most of them being destroyed in the Grecian wars. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUSTATHIUS">Eustathius</a> says, that the country was anciently called Pelafragia, from Pelafragos, who brought the people, from roots, herbs, and leaves of trees, to feed on acorns, especially beech mast; as Artemidorus observes, that the Arcadians usually lived on acorns. It was also called Lycaonia, Gigantia, and Parrhasia (Stephanus). The Arcadians are greatly commended for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of, and skill in, music (Virgil, Polybius). To imitate the Arcadians, is to labour and toil for the benefit of others, never conquering their own, but the enemies of others (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HESYCHIUS">Hesychius</a>). This probably took its rise from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Arcadians being accustomed to hire themselves out as mercenaries to foreign nations. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> commends their martial prowess, their pastures, their sheep, and their country well watered. The gentilious name is Arcades; who boasted of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity, and that they were older than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> (Apollonius Rhodius, Nonnius, Plutarch, Ovid, Statius). They were the first who had a year of three months, and therefore called Proceleni, because their year was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to that adjusted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> to the course of the moon (Censorinus).

ARCANGIS

Pages 145-145

in the Turkish armies, an inferior kind of infantry, which serve as ensigns perdus, and to harass and pillage the enemy's frontiers. The Arcangis are an order inferior to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANIZARIES">Janizaries</a>; and when any of them distinguish themselves, are usually preferred into the Janizaries order. They have no pay, but are Arcanum to subsist on their plunder.

ARCANUM

Pages 145-145

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a villa of Q. Cicero, Tully's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, in Latium, (Cicero). Now Arce, in the Terra di Lavora, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, on the borders of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAGNA">Campagna</a> di Roma, on the river Melpis, between Arpinum and Aquinum.

ARCESILAUS

Pages 145-145

a celebrated Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, about 300 years before the Christian era, was born at Pitane, in Eolis. He founded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> academy, which is called the second school. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> erudition, and well versed in the writings of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. He was remarkable for the severity of his criticisms; but nevertheless he knew how to accommodate himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and pursue the allurements of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. He had a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of disciples. His doctrines were different in several respects from those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> school: and perhaps he was led into this diversity of opinions by many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> errors in the ancient school, such as the incredible arrogance of the dogmatists, who pretended to assign causes for all things; the mysterious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> they had thrown upon the doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>; the entirely discarding the testimony of the senses; the objections of the Pyrrhonists, who now began to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROACH">broach</a> their opinions; the powerful opposition of the Stoics and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIPATETICS">Peripatetics</a>, who discarded the feeble parts of the Academic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. These might have given cause to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> the ancient school, and to found a new one. The middle school, therefore, laid it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> as a principle, that we could know nothing, nor even assure ourselves of the certainty of this position; from whence they inferred, that we should affirm nothing, but always suspend our judgement. They advanced, that a philosopher was able to dispute upon every subject, and bring conviction with him, even upon contrary sides of the same question; for there are always reasons of equal force both in the affirmative and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> of every argument. According to this doctrine, neither our senses, nor even our reason, are to have any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>: and therefore, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> affairs, we are to conform ourselves to received opinions. Arcesilaus was succeeded by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACYDES">Lacydes</a>.

ARCH

Pages 145-146

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the circumference of a circle <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> curved line, lying from one point to another, by which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the whole circle or line, or some other thing sought after, may be gathered. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">Bridge</a>. Arch, a concave or hollowed piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, constructed in such a manner that the several <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of which it is composed keep one another in their places. The terms arch and vault properly differ only in this, that the arch expresses a narrower, and the vault a broader, piece of the same kind. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in the form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> is, that some are circular, and others elliptical; the former having a larger or smaller part of a circle, the other of an ellipse. What are called flat arches, are those frequently used over doors and windows, the upper and under edges of which are straight and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a>, and the ends and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> joints all pointing toward a centre. The space between two piers of a bridge is called an arch, because usually arched over. Triumphal Arches are magnificent entries into cities, erected to adorn a triumph, and perpetuate the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. The arches of Titus and Constantine make at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> among the ruins of old Rome. Arch, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">Composition</a>, signifies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>; or of the first class; as archangel, archbishop, &c. ARCHÆUS, or Archeus. See Archeus.

ARCHANGEL

Pages 146-146

an angel occupying the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in the celestial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIERARCHY">hierarchy</a>. See Angel and Hierarchy. Archangel, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Russia, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Dwina, situated on the east side of the river Dwina, about six miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">White</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 40° 21'. N. Lat. 64° 30'. The city extends about three miles in length and one in breadth. It is rich, populous, built in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and is a metropolitan see. It rose from a castle built on the spot by Bafilowitz II. to protect the increasing trade brought there by the discovery of the White sea by the English, and took its name from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> built in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the archangel Michael. Before this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the commercial intercourse between Russia and the northern parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> had been long carried on by the Hanseatic <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>; which usually failed to Revel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARVA">Narva</a>, and from thence passed through Dorpt to Plescot and Novgorod, where their factories were established. The accidental discovery of Archangel, in 1553, deprived the Hanseatic towns of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of this lucrative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, and transferred it to the English. On the 11th of May, in the above-mentioned year, three ships sailed from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPTFORD">Deptford</a>, in order to explore the northern seas, under the command of Sir Hugh Willoughby. Two of these vessels penetrated as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as the 72nd <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of latitude, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Spitzbergen; and being afterwards forced by fires of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the river Arzina in Russian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>, both their crews were frozen to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Richard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">Chancellor</a>, who commanded the other ship, called the Bonaventure, discovering the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> bordering upon the White sea, landed near the mouth of the Dwina, in a bay, which he denominated the Bay of St Nicholas, from a convent of that name near the present port of Archangel. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CZAR">czar</a> Iwan Bafilowitz, being informed of his arrival, invited him to his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, where he was hospitably entertained, and the czar indulged the English with a free trade in his dominions; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this permission, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> was incorporated in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; and being encouraged by particular privileges from the czar, let on foot a considerable commerce, to the mutual advantage of both nations. This traffic the English for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> enjoyed without competition. The Dutch, however, and other nations, gradually infatuated themselves into this commerce; which they carried on to a very great disadvantage, as not being favoured with those privileges which the czar had granted to the English company. These were at last suddenly annihilated by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXIS">Alexis</a> Michaelovich; who in 1648 banished the English merchants from all his dominions. The cause of this expulsion is generally imputed to the resentment which the czar conceived against the English for the execution of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I., with whom he was closely connected by leagues of amity and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>; but in effect he abolished the company's privileges in the year before that event; and his indignation against the English for their rebellion, Mr Coxe affirms, was only a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a>; the real <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> being derived from the offers made by the Dutch to pay duties of export and import to the amount of 15 per cent, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were indulged with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of carrying on as free a trade as the English throughout his dominions. For not long afterwards, the czar suffered William Prideaux, Cromwell's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>, to reside at Archangel; and permitted the English to renew their commerce in that port upon the same footing with other foreigners. And upon this footing alone our merchants ever after <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to trade. The commodities chiefly imported into Archangel, were <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver stuffs and laces, gold wire, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COCHINEAL">cochineal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, and other drugs for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>; wine, brandy, and other distilled spirits. The customs arising to the czar were computed at 200,000 rubles a-year, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of foreign ships at 400 annually. But upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of Petersburg, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the Great abolished the immunities of Archangel, and removed the commerce of the White sea to the havens of the Baltic. Still, however, its exports of tar were considerable; in 1730, to the amount of 40,000 lasts, of 11 barrels each. It sends, during winter, great quantities of the rawaga, a small <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of three-finned cod, to Petersburg frozen. In 1752 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> again restored the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> immunities of Archangel; and its present trade is not inconsiderable. It supplies the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Archangel, part of those of Nifinie-Novgorod and Cafan, with European commodities; and draws in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> from those parts corn, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, cordage, sails, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, and tallow, which are mostly conveyed by the Dwina; it forms also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the northern and western parts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, from whence the merchants procure furs, skins, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. The houses of Archangel are generally of wood, but well contrived; and every chamber is provided with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOVE">stove</a>, as a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, which is here excessive in the winter. The streets are paved with broken pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> and rubbish, disposed so unskillfully, that one cannot walk over it without running the risk of falling, except when the streets are rendered smooth and equal by the snow that falls and freezes in the winter. Notwithstanding the severity of the cold in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, there is always plenty of good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>; butchers meat, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, wild fowl, and fish, in a great variety, are sold surprisingly cheap. The most remarkable edifice in Archangel is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> townhouse, built of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> in the Italian manner, and divided into three parts. One of these consists of large commodious apartments, for the accommodation of merchants, strangers as well as natives: here they are permitted to reside with their merchandise till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of October, when all the foreign ships set sail for the respective countries to which they belong. Then the traders are obliged to remove their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> from the townhouse, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, which hath a spacious court, that reaches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the river.

ARCHBISHOP

Pages 146-147

the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIGNITARY">dignitary</a> Archbishops were not known in the first class till about the year 320; and though there were some soon after who had the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, yet that was only a personal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, by which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of considerable cities were distinguished. It was not till of late that archbishops became metropolitans, and had suffragans under them. Athanasius appears to be the first who used the title Archbishop, which he gave occasionally to his predecessor; Gregory Nazianzen, in like manner, gave it to Athanasius; not that either of them were entitled to any jurisdiction, nor even any precedence in virtue of it. Among the Latins, Theodore Hilpalensis is the first that speaks of archbishops. He distinguishes four orders <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> degrees in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIERARCHY">hierarchy</a>, viz. patriarchs, archbishops, metropolitans, and bishops. The archbishop, beside the inspection of the bishops and inferior clergy in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> over which he presides, exercises episcopal jurisdiction in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>. He is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> of the spiritualities of any vacant see in his province, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> is of the temporalities; and exercises ecclesiastical jurisdiction in it. He is entitled to present by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPSE">lapse</a> to all the ecclesiastical livings in the disposal of his diocesan bishop, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not filled within six months. He has likewise a customary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>, upon consecrating a bishop, to name a clerk or chaplain to be provided for by such bishop; in lieu of which it is now usual to accept an option. He is said to be enthroned when vested in the archbishopric; whereas bishops are said to be installed. The ecclesiastical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of England is divided into two provinces, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>. Canterbury hath the following suffragan bishoprics appertaining to it, St. Asaph, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANGOR">Bangor</a>, Bath and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHICHESTER">Chichester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LITCHFIELD">Litchfield</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVENTRY">Coventry</a>, St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>'s, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a>, Landaff, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, Peterborough, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>. To York appertaineth the bishoprics of Carlisle, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>; to which may be added the bishopric of Sodor and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, whose bishop is not a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. See Canterbury and York. The archbishop of Canterbury had anciently, viz. till the year 1152, jurisdiction over <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> as well as England, and was styled a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>, and sometimes alterius orbis <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPA">papa</a>, and orbis Britannici pontifex. Matters were done and recorded in his name thus, Anno pontificatus nostrae primo, &c. The first archbishop of Canterbury was Auffin, appointed by King <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ETHELBERT">Ethelbert</a>, on his conversion to Christianity, about the year 598. He was also regatus natus. He even enjoyed some special marks of royalty; as, to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of a bishopric, which he was of Rochester; and to make knights, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> moneys, &c. He is still the first peer of England, and the next to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family; having precedence of all dukes and all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. It is his privilege, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, to crown the kings and queens of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. He may retain and qualify eight chaplains; whereas a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> is allowed by statute only five. He has, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, the power of probate of wills and testaments, and granting letters of administration. He has also a power to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> licenses and dispensations in all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> formerly used for in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Rome, and not repugnant to the law of God. He accordingly issues special licenses to marry, to hold two livings, &c. and he exercises the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of conferring degrees. He also holds several courts of jurisdiction: as, court of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, court of audience, prerogative court, and court of peculiars. The archbishop of York has the like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> in his province as the archbishop of Canterbury. He has precedence of all dukes not of the royal blood; and of all officers of state, except the lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>. He has also the rights of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> palatine over Hexhamshire. The first archbishop of York was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAULINUS">Paulinus</a>, appointed by Pope Gregory about the year 622. He had formerly jurisdiction over all the bishops of Scotland; but in the year 1470, Pope Sextus IV. created the bishop of St Andrew's archbishop and metropolitan of all Scotland. Scotland, whilst episcopacy prevailed in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, had two archbishops, of St Andrew's and Glasgow; of which the former was accounted the metropolitan; and, even before it arrived at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of an archbishopric, resisted with great spirit all the attempts of the archbishops of York in England to become the metropolitans of Scotland. The fees of Argyll, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a>, and the Isles, were suffragans to Glasgow; all the others in the kingdom to St Andrew's. Ireland has four archbishops; of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMAGH">Armagh</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, Cashel, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-TUAM">Tuam</a>; of whom the former is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> of all Ireland.

ARCHBISHOPRIC

Pages 147-147

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> subject to the jurisdiction of an archbishop.

ARCHBUTLER

Pages 147-147

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> officers of the German empire, who presents the cup to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> on solemn occasions. This office belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>.

ARCHCHAMBERLAIN

Pages 147-147

an officer of the empire, much the same with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> chamberlain in England. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a> was appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> bull archchamberlain of the empire.

ARCHCHANCELLOR

Pages 147-147

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> officer who, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times, presided over the secretaries of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. Under the two first races of the kings of France, when their territories were divided into Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARLES">Arles</a>, there were three archchancellors: and hence the three archchancellors still subsisting in Germany; the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a> being archchancellor of Germany, the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a>, and the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREVES">Treves</a>.

ARCHCOUNT

Pages 147-147

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> formerly given to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, on account of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> power and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>.

ARCHDEACON

Pages 147-147

an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIGNITARY">dignitary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> officer next to a bishop, whose jurisdiction extends either over the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> or only a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it. He is usually appointed by the bishop himself; and hath a kind of episcopal authority, originally derived from the bishop, but now independent and distinct from his. He therefore visits the clergy; and has his separate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of offenders by spiritual censures, and for hearing all other causes of ecclesiastical cognizance. There are 60 archdeacons in England.

ARCHDEACON'S COURT

Pages 147-148

is the most inferior <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> in the whole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> polity. It is held in the archdeacon's absence, before a judge appointed by himself and called his official; and its jurisdiction is sometimes Archdruid in concurrence with, sometimes in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of, the bishop's court of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>. From hence, however, by statute 24 Hen. VIII. c. 12, there lies an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to that of the bishop.

ARCHDRUID

Pages 148-148

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pontiff of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRUIDS">druids</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. See Druid.

ARCHDUKE

Pages 148-148

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> peculiar to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>; all the sons of which are archdukes, and the daughters archduchesses. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a>.

ARCHELAUS

Pages 148-148

the son of Apollonius, one of the greatest sculptors of antiquity, was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, and is thought to have lived in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Claudius. He executed, in marble, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOTHEOSIS">apotheosis</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>. This masterpiece in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> was found in 1568, in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> named Fratocchia, belonging to the princes of Colonna, where, it is said, the emperor Claudius had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. Father Kircher, Cupertino, Spanheim, and several other learned antiquaries, have given a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> and explication of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>.

ARCHERS

Pages 148-148

a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> soldiery armed with bows and arrows. The word is formed of arcus, "a bow;" whence arcarius, and even argus, and arquites, as they are also denominated in the corrupt state of the Latin tongue. Archers were much employed in former times; but they are now laid aside, excepting in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> and some of the eastern countries; where there are companies of archers still subsisting in their armies, and with which they did terrible execution at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEPANTO">Lepanto</a>.—As an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, the practice of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHERY">archery</a> is still kept up in many places. See the article Archery. In France, the officers who attend the lieutenants de <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a> and provosts to make captures, seizures, arrests, &c., are called archers; though their arms be only halberds or carbines. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> they say, the archers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> prévôt de l'hôtel; of the prévôt des marchands; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> archers; the archers du guet, or of the watch, &c.—Small parties of archers, called allo-gens de marechauffe, are continually patrolling on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, to secure them against robbers.—The Archery, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> of Lyons, &c., are always escorted by a party of archers. To the diligence of these archers, or marshal's men, it is partly owing, that persons now travel in all parts of France in the utmost security; there being fewer robberies on the highway in that whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> in a year than about <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>.

ARCHERY

Pages 148-153

the art <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> with a bow and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a>. In most nations, the bow was anciently the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> implement of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and by the expertness of the archers alone was often decided the fate of battles and of empires.—In this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> archery was greatly encouraged in former times, and many statutes were made for the regulation thereof; whence it was that the English archers in particular became the best in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and procured them many signal victories. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">Artillery</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, though they have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> disused the weapon, are the remains of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> fraternity of bowmen or archers. Artillery gia, vol. vii. (artillerie) is a French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> signifying archery; as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s bowyer is in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> styled artilleur du roy: And from that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> the English seem to have learnt at least the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-bow archery. We therefore find that William the Conqueror had a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of bowmen in his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HASTINGS">Hastings</a>, when no mention is made of such troops on the side of Harold: And it is supposed that these Norman archers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> with the arbalest (or cross-bow), in which formerly the arrow was placed in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a>, being termed in French a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADREL">quadrel</a>, and in English a bolt. Of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when shooting with the long bow first began among the English, at which exercise they afterwards became so expert, there appear no certain accounts. Their chroniclers do not mention the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of archery as expressly applied to the cross bow, or the long bow, till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Richard I., who was killed by an arrow at the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMOGES">Limoges</a> in Guienne, which Hemingford mentions to have issued from a cross bow.—After this, which happened in 1199, there appear not upon record any notices of archery for nearly 150 years, when an order was issued by Edward III., in the 15th year of his reign, to the sheriffs of most of the English counties for providing 500 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> bows and 300 bundles of arrows, for the then intended war against France. Similar orders are repeated in the following years; with this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> only, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a> is directed to furnish 500 painted bows as well as the same number of white. The famous battle of Crecy was fought four years afterwards, in which our chroniclers state that we had 2000 archers, who were opposed to about the same number of the French, together with a circumstance which seems to prove, that by this time we used the long bow, whilst the French archers shot with the arbalest. The circumstance alluded to is as follows: Previously to the engagement there fell a very heavy <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, which is said to have much damaged the bows of the French, or perhaps rather the strings of them. Now the long bow (when unstrung) may be most conveniently covered, so as to prevent the rain's injuring it; nor is there scarcely any addition to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>; whereas the arbalest is of a most inconvenient form to be sheltered from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. As therefore, in the year 1342, orders were issued to the sheriffs of each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> county to provide 500 bows, with a proper proportion of arrows, it seems probable that these were long bows, and not the arbalest. At the above-mentioned battle, the English ascribed their victory chiefly to the archers.—The battle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POITIERS">Poitiers</a> was fought A.D. 1356, and gained by the same means. Sometimes the archers gained <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> victories without even the least assistance from the men at arms; as particularly, the decisive victory over the Scots at Homildon, A.D. 1402. In that bloody battle, the men-at-arms did not strike a stroke, but were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> spectators of the valour and victory of the archers. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Douglas, who commanded the Scotch army in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, enraged to see his men falling thick around him by showers of arrows, and trusting to the goodness of his armour (which had been three years in making), accompanied by about eighty lords, knights, and gentlemen, in complete armour, rushed forward, and attacked the English archers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. But he soon had reason to repent his rashness. The English arrows were so sharp and strong, and discharged with so much force, that no armour could repel them. The earl of Douglas, after receiving five wounds, was made prisoner; and all his brave companions were either killed or taken. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> de Comines acknowledges, what our own writers assert, that the English archers excelled those of every other nation; and Sir John Fortescue says again and again,—"that the might of the realm of England standeth upon archers." The superior dexterity of their archers gave the English a great advantage over their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> enemies the French and Scots. The French depended chiefly on their men-at-arms, and the Scots on their pikemen; but the ranks of both were often thinned and thrown into disorder by flights of arrows before they could reach their enemies. James I. of Scotland, who had seen and admired the dexterity of the English archers, and who was himself an excellent archer, endeavoured to revive the exercise of archery among his own subjects, by whom it had been too much neglected. With this view, he ridiculed their awkward manner of handling their bows, in his humorous poem, of Christ's Kirk on the Green; and procured the following <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> to be made in his first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, A.D. 1424, immediately after his return to Scotland: "That all men might 'bulk <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THAME">thame</a> to be archers fra the be 12 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and that ilk ten pounds worth of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> thair be made bow markes, and speciallie near paroche kirks, quhairin upon halfe dayis men may cum, and at the leist schute thrice about, and have usage of archarie; and whaif usis not archarie, the laird of the land sal rais of him a wedder; and gif the laird raisis not the said pane, the king's thirf, or his minsters, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> rais it to the king." But the untimely death of that excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> prevented the effectual execution of this law. There is not found any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament of Henry V. in relation to archery, and all the orders in Rymer till the battle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGINCOURT">Agincourt</a> relate to great guns, from which he seems at first to have expected more considerable advantage than from the training of bowmen. It should seem, however, that this fort of artillery, from its unwieldiness, bad and narrow <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, together with other defects, was as yet but of little use in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> operations. In the year 1417 this king therefore attributes his victory at Agincourt to the archers, and directs the sheriffs of many counties to pluck from every goose six wing-feathers for the purpose of improving arrows, which are to be paid for by the king. In 1421, though the French had been defeated both at Crely, Poitiers, and Agincourt, by the English archers, yet they still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the use of the crossbow; for which reason, Henry V., as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Normandy, confirms the charters and privileges of the bailiwick, who had been long established as a fraternity in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a>. In the fifth of Edward IV., an act passed, that every Englishman, and Irishman dwelling with Englishmen, shall have an English bow of his own height, which is directed to be made of yew, wych, hazel, ash, or awburne, or any other reasonable tree according to their power. The next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> also directs that butts shall be made in every township, which the inhabitants are obliged to shoot up and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> every feast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, under the penalty of a halfpenny when they shall omit this exercise. In the 14th year, however, of this same king, it appears by Rymer's Fadera, that 1000 archers were to be sent to the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, whose pay is settled at sixpence a day, which was a considerable sum in these times, when the value of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> was so much higher than it is at present. This circumstance seems to prove, very strongly, the great estimation in which archers were still held. In the same year, Edward, preparing for a war with France, directs the sheriffs to procure bows and arrows, "as most specially requisite." On the war taking <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> with Scotland, eight years after this, Edward provides both ordnance and archers; so that though the use of artillery (as we now term it) was then gaining ground, yet that of the bow and arrow was not neglected. Richard III., by his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to archery, was able to send 1000 bowmen to the duke of Bretagne, and he availed himself of the same troops at the battle of Bolwolth. During the reign of Henry VII., however, there appears no order relative to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a> or artillery; whilst on the other hand, in 1488, he directs a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> levy of archers to be sent to Brittany, and that they shall be reviewed before they embark. In the 19th year of his reign, this same king forbids the use of the crossbow, because "the long bow had been much used in this realm, whereby <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and victory had been gotten against outward enemies, the realm greatly defended, and much more the dread of all Christian princes by reason of the fame." During the reign of Henry VIII., several statutes were made for the promotion of archery. The 8th Eliz. c. 10, regulates the price of bows, and the 13th Eliz. c. 14, enacts, that bow flaves shall be brought into the realm from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANSE">Hanse</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and the Eastward; so that archery still continued to be an object of attention in the legislature. In Rymer's Fadera there is neither statute or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> of James I. on this head; but it appears by Dr. Birch's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of his son (Prince Henry), that at eight years of age, he learned to shoot both with the bow. bow and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a>, whilst at the same time this prince had in his establishment an officer who was styled bowbearer. The king granted a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> to the Artillery Company, by which the powers they had received from Henry VIII. were considerably extended. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. appears, from the dedication of a treatise entitled *The Bowman's <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">Glory</a>*, to have been himself an archer; and in the eighth year of his reign he issued a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> mayor, and several of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, to prevent the fields near London being enclosed as "to interrupt the necessary and profitable exercise of shooting," as also to lower the mounds where they prevented the view from one mark to another. Catherine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> to Charles II.) seems to have been much pleased with the sight at least of this exercise; for in 1676, by the contributions of Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGERFORD">Hungerford</a> and others, a silver badge for the marshal of the fraternity was made, weighing 25 ounces, and representing an archer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> the long bow (in the proper manner) to his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, with the following inscription: *Reginae Catherine Sagittariae*. The supporters are two bowmen, with the arms of England and Portugal. In 1682 there was a most magnificent cavalcade and entertainment given by the Finsbury archers, when they bestowed the titles of "duke of Shoreditch," "marquis of Ilfording," &c., upon the most deserving. Charles II. was present upon this occasion; but the day being rainy, he was obliged soon to leave the field. So lately as the year 1753 targets were erected in the Finsbury fields, during the Easter and Whitsun holidays; when the best shooter was styled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> for the ensuing year, and the second <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">Lieutenant</a>. Why this military weapon was so decisive in the battles of former days, the following reasons may be suggested. Before the introduction of fire arms the enemy could only be struck at a distance by slings, the bow used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, or the crossbow; to all which the English long bow was infinitely superior. As for slings, they never have been used in the more northern parts of Europe by armies in the field; nor does their use indeed seem to have been at all convenient or extensively practicable, for two principal reasons: In the first place, slingers cannot advance in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> body, on account of the space to be occupied by this weapon in its rotatory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; in the next place, the weight of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> to be carried must necessarily impede the slingers greatly in their movements. The bow of the ancients again, as represented in all their reliefs, was a mere toy compared with that of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>; it was therefore chiefly used by the Parthians, whose attacks (like those of the present Arabs) were deftly executed. As for the crossbow, it is of a most inconvenient form for carriage, even with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> improvements; and, in case of rain, could not be easily secured from the weather. After the first shot, moreover, it could not be recharged under a considerable time, whilst the bolts were also heavy and cumbersome. The English long bow, on the other hand, together with the quiver of arrows, was easily carried by the archer, as easily secured from the rain, and recharged almost instantaneously. It is not therefore extraordinary, that troops, who solely used this most effectual weapon, should generally obtain the victory, even when opposed to much more numerous armies. It may be urged, that these losses having been experienced by our enemies, must have induced them to practise the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of warfare.—But it is thought that the long bow was not <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used even in England till the time of Edward III., when the victory at Crecy sufficiently proclaimed the superiority of that weapon. It required, however, so much training before the archer could be expert, that we must not be surprised <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> soon afterwards this military exercise was much neglected, as appears by the preambles of several ancient statutes. Whilst the military tenures subsisted, the sovereign could only call upon his tenants during war, who therefore attended with the weapons they had been used to, and which required no previous practice. On the other hand, the English archers were obliged by acts of parliament, even in time of peace, to erect butts in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>, and to shoot on every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> and holiday, after repairing perhaps to these butts from a considerable distance, whilst the expense of at least a new bow is represented as being a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> which they were scarcely equal to. The king and parliaments of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> having thus compelled the inhabitants to such training, the English armies had (it should seem) the same advantage over their enemies as the exclusive use of fire-arms would give us at present. It appears also, by what hath been already stated, that the long bow continued to be in estimation for more than two centuries after gunpowder was introduced, which probably arose from muskets being very cumbersome and unwieldy. It is well known that rapid movements are generally decisive of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>; and for such the archers were particularly adapted, because, as they could not be annoyed at the same distance by the weapons of the enemy, they had scarcely any occasion for armour. The flower of ancient armies likewise was the cavalry, against which the long bow never failed to prevail, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> were too large objects to be missed; and hence the great number of French <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> who were prisoners at Crecy, Poitiers, and Agincourt; for being dismounted (if not wounded) whilst they were also clad in heavy armour, they could not make their escape. The same reason accounts for the English obtaining these signal victories with so inferior numbers; for the nobility and gentry thus becoming prisoners, the other parts of the French army made little or no resistance. No wonder, therefore, that in England the greatest anxiety was shown to promote the exercise of this most important weapon, and that so many statutes were made for that purpose. In Scotland, also, little less attention, though apparently not with equal success, was shown to the encouragement of the art. In both kingdoms, it was provided, that the importers of merchandise should be obliged, along with their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, to import a certain proportion of bows, bow flares, and shafts for arrows. In both, every person was enjoined to hold himself provided in bows and arrows, and was prohibited the frequent use of archery. In both, a restraint was imposed upon the exercise of other games and sports, lest they should interfere with the use of the bow; for it was intended, that people should Archery be made expert in the use of it as a military weapon, by habituating them to the familiar exercise of it as an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of amusement. As there was no material difference between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> and bodily strength of the two people, it might be supposed that the English and Scots wielded the bow with no unequal vigour and dexterity; but from undoubted historical monuments it appears that the former had the superiority; of which one instance has been already narrated. By the regulations prescribed in their statute book for the practice of archery, we find that the English shot a very long bow, those who were arrived at their full growth and maturity being prohibited from shooting at any mark that was not distant upwards of 220 yards. In the use of the bow, great dexterity as well as strength seems to have been requisite. Though we hear of arrows at Cheviot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHASE">Chase</a> which were a yard long, yet it is by no means to be supposed that the whole band made use of such, or could draw them to the head. The regulation of the Irish statute of Edward IV. viz. that the bow shall not exceed the height of the man, is allowed by archers to have been well considered; and as the arrow should be half the length of the bow, this would give an arrow of a yard in length to those only who were six feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. A strong man of this size in the present times cannot easily draw above 27 inches, if the bow is of a proper strength to do execution at a considerable distance. At the same time it must be admitted, that as our ancestors were obliged by some of the old statutes to begin shooting with the long bow at the age of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>, they might have acquired a greater flight in this exercise than their descendants, though the latter should be allowed to be of equal strength. As the shooting with the long bow was first introduced in England, and practised almost exclusively for nearly two centuries, so it hath occasioned a peculiar method of drawing the arrow to the ear and not to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>. That this is contrary to the usage of the ancients is very clear from their reliefs, and from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMAZONS">Amazons</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off one of their paps as it occasioned an impediment to their shooting. The Finshbury archer is therefore represented in this attitude of drawing to the ear, both in the Bowman's Glory, and in the silver badge given by Catherine to the Artillery Company. Not many years ago there was a man named Topham, who exhibited surprising feats of strength, and who happened to be at a public <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> near Illington, to which the Finshbury archers resorted after their exercise. Topham considered the long bow as a plaything, only fit for a child; upon which one of the archers laid him a bowl of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNCH">punch</a>, that he could not draw the arrow two-thirds of its length. Topham accepted this bet with the greatest confidence of winning; but bringing the arrow to his breast instead of his ear, he was greatly mortified by paying the wager, after many fruitless efforts. As to the distance to which an arrow can be shot from a long bow with the best elevation of 45 degrees, that must necessarily depend much both upon the strength and flight of the archer; but in general the distance was reckoned from eleven to twelve score yards. The butts for exercise, as above noticed, were directed to be distant upwards of 220 yards. There is indeed a tradition, that an attorney of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WIGAN">Wigan</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a> (named <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEIGH">Leigh</a>) shot a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in three flights; but the same tradition states, that he placed himself in a very particular attitude, which cannot be used commonly in this exercise. According to Neade, an archer might shoot six arrows in the time of charging and discharging one musket. The archers consider an arrow of from 20 to 24 drop weight to be the best for flight or hitting a mark at a considerable distance, and that yew is the best material of which they can be made. As to the feathers, that of a goose is preferred; it is also wished, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> should be two or three years old, and that the feather may drop of itself. Two out of three feathers in an arrow are commonly white, being plucked from the gander; but the third is generally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> or gray, being taken from the goose; and, from this difference in point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, informs the archer when the arrow is properly placed. From this most distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> therefore the whole arrow sometimes receives its name: And this, by-the-by, affords an explanation of the gray goose wing in the ballad of Cheviot Chase. Arrows were armed anciently with flint or metal heads, latterly with heads of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; of these there were various forms and denominations. By an act of parliament made the 7th of Henry IV. it was enacted, That for the future all the heads for arrows and quarrels should be well boiled or braided, and hardened at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>; and that every arrow head or quarrel should have the mark of the maker; workmen disobeying this order, were to be fined and imprisoned at the king's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, and the arrow heads or quarrels to be forfeited to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. Arrows were reckoned by sheaves, a sheaf consisting of 24 arrows. They were carried in a quiver, called Ancient Arms also an arrow case, which served for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a>; arrows for immediate use were worn in the girdle. In ancient times phials of quicklime, or rather combustible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> houses or ships, were fixed on the heads of arrows, and shot from long bows. This has been also practised since the use of gunpowder. Neade says, he has known by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, that an archer may shoot an ounce of firework upon an arrow 12 score yards. Arrows with wildfire, and arrows for fireworks, are mentioned among the stores at Newhaven and Berwick, in the 1st of Edward VI. The force with which an arrow strikes an object at a moderate distance, may be conceived from the account given by King Edward VI. in his journal; wherein he says, that 100 archers of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> shot before him two arrows each, and afterwards all together; and that they shot at an inch board, which some pierced quite through and struck into the other board; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> pierced it quite through with the heads of their arrows, the boards being well-fastened <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>; their distance from the mark is not mentioned. To protect our archers from the attacks of the enemy's horse, they carried long stakes pointed at both ends: these they planted in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, sloping before them. In the 1st of Edward VI. 350 of these were in the stores of the town of Berwick, under the article of archers stakes; there were also at the same time eight bundles of archers stakes in Pontefract castle. To prevent the bowstring from striking the left arm, Archery. The arm, the arm is covered with a piece of smooth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, fastened on the outside of the arm; this is called a bracer; and to guard the fingers from being cut by the bowstring, archers wore shooting gloves. Chaucer in his prologue to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> Tales, thus describes an archer of his day: And he was clad in cote and hode of grene, A fleas of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a> arwes bright and keen, Under his belt he bare full thriftily; Wel coude he drewe his takel yewmanly, His arwes droued not with fetheres lowe, And in his hand he bare a mighty bowe, A not hed hadde he, with broune vifage, Of wood craft coude he wel all the ufege; Upon his arms he had a gai bracer, And by his side a fverd and a bockeler, And on the other side a gaie daggere Hamefied wel, and sharp as pointe of sperre: A cristofre on his breast of silver thene, A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a> he bare, the baudrik was of grene, A forester was he foethey as I gelle. Though archery continued to be encouraged by the king and legislature for more than two centuries after the first knowledge of the effects of gunpowder, yet by the latter end of the reign of Henry VIII, it seems to have been partly considered as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASTIME">pastime</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a>, the elder <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Henry, is said to have been fond of this exercise, inasmuch that a good shooter was styled Prince Arthur. We are also informed, that he pitched his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENT">tent</a> at Mile End in order to be present at this recreation, and that Henry his brother also attended. When the latter afterwards became king, he gave a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a> to those who should excel in this exercise; and a capital shot having been made, Henry said to Barlow (one of his guards), "If you kill win, you shall be duke over all archers." Barlow therefore having succeeded, and living in Shoreditch, was created duke thereof. Upon another occasion, Henry and the queen were met by 200 archers on Shooter's hill, which probably took its name from their assembling near it to shoot at marks. This king likewise gave the first charter to the Artillery Company in the 29th year of his reign, by which they are permitted to wear dresses of any colour except purple and scarlet, to shoot not only at marks but birds, if not pheasants or herons, and within two miles of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> palaces. They are also enjoined by the same charter not to wear furs of a greater price than those of the martin. The most material privilege, however, is, that of indemnification from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, if any person passing between the shooter and the mark is killed, provided the archers have first called out fuff. The following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of an archer, his bow, and accoutrements, is given in a MS. written in the time of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. "Captains and officers should be skilful of that most noble weapon, and to see that their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> according to their draught and strength have good bows, well nocked, well stringed, everie stringe whippe in their nocke, and in the myddes rubbed with wax, braier and thuring glove, some spare stringes trymed as aforeaid, every man one sheaf of arrows, with a case of leather defendible against the rayne, and in the same fower and twentie arrowes, whereof eight of them should be <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than the residue, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALL">gall</a> or affoyne the enemye with the hailshot of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> arrows, before they shall come within the danger of their harque-bus shot. Let every man have a brigandine, or a little cote of plate, a skull or hufkyne, a mawle of leade of five foot in lengthe, and a pike, and the same hanging by his girdle, with a hook and a dagger; being thus furnished, teach them by mutters to marche, thoote, and retire, keepeinge their faces upon the enemy's. Sumtyme put them into great numbers, as to battell appertayneth, and thus use them often times practised, till they be perfecte; for those men in battell ne skirmith can not be spared. None other weapone maye compare with the same noble weapon." The long bow, as already observed, maintained its place in our armies long after the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of firearms. Nor have there been wanting experienced soldiers who were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> for its continuance, and who in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> even preferred it to the harquebus or musket. King Charles I. twice granted special commissions under the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> for enforcing the use of the long bow. The first was in the 4th year of his reign: but this was revoked by proclamation four years afterwards, on account of divers extortions and abuses committed under sanction thereof. The second, anno 1633, in the 9th year of his reign, to William Neade and his son, also named William, wherein the former is styled an ancient archer, who had presented to the king a warlike invention for uniting the use of the pike and bow, seen and approved by him and his council of war; wherefore his majesty had granted them a commission to teach and exercise his loving subjects in the said invention, which he particularly recommended the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> officers of his trained bands to learn and practice; and the justices and other chief magistrates throughout England, are therein enjoined to use every means in their power to assist Neade, his son, and all persons authorized by them in the furtherance, propagation, and practice of this useful invention. Both the commissions and proclamation are printed at large in Rymer. At the breaking out of the civil war, the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a> issued a precept, dated in November 1643, for stirring up all well affected people by benevolence, towards raising a company of archers for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the king and parliament. Archery with the long bow continues to be used as a manly exercise by the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, and in many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>; nor is it totally neglected in Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. There are several <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of archers in England; the chief of which are, the Woodmen of Arden, and the Toxophilite. But the most noted <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of this kind, now existing, is The Royal Company of Archers in Scotland.—The ancient records of this Company having been destroyed by fire about the beginning of the present century, no authentic traces of their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> now remain. It is said that they owe their origin to the commissioners appointed in the reign of James I. of Scotland for enforcing and overseeing the exercise of archery in different counties. Those commissioners, who were in general men of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and power, picking out amongst the better sort of people under their cognizance the most expert archers, formed them into a company, and upon perilous occasions made a pretence of their services to the king as his chief body guards; in which situation Archery, they often distinguished themselves for their loyalty, their courage, and skill in archery. This rank of the king's principal body guards the Royal Company still claim, within seven miles of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of Scotland. Certain it is, that by an act of the privy council of Scotland, in 1677, this Company was recognized under the name and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of "His Majesty's Company of Archers;" and by the same act a piece of plate of the value of 25l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> was ordered to be given to be shot for by them at their annual parades, called Weapons-showings, and to be called The King's Prize. At this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the Royal Company consisted, as it does at present, of the principal nobility and gentry of Scotland. But their unfortunate <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to anti-revolution principles, upon that event's taking place, put almost a period to their existence: Their public parades or marches were discontinued, and the royal prize was withheld.
