In these, the first thing to be considered is the situation; which may be some large creek or haven of water, in or near the place where the harbour is intended to be made, or at the entrance of a large river, or near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>: for a harbour should never be dug entirely out of dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, unless upon some extraordinary occasions, where it is impossible to do otherwise, and yet a harbour is absolutely necessary. When a proper place is found, before it is fixed upon, it must be considered whether ships can lie there safe in stormy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, especially when those winds blow which are most dangerous upon that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>; whether there be any hills, rising ground, or high buildings, that will cover it; in these cases, the situation is very proper: but if there be nothing already that will cover the ships, it must be observed whether any covering can be made at a moderate expense, otherwise it would be useless to build a harbour there. The next thing to be considered is, whether there be a sufficient depth of water for large ships to enter with safety, and lie there without touching the ground; and if not, whether the entrance and inside might not be made deeper at a moderate expense: or, in case a sufficient depth of water is not to be had for large ships, whether the harbour would not be useful for small merchantmen; for such a one is often of great advantage, when situated upon a coast much frequented by small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COASTING">coasting</a> vessels. The form of the harbour must be determined in such a manner, that the ships which come in when it is stormy weather may lie safe, and so as there may be sufficient room for as many as pass that way: the depths of water where the piers are to be built must be taken at every 10, 15, or 20 feet distance, and marked upon piles driven here and there, in order that the workmen may be directed in laying the foundation. This being done, it must be considered what kind of materials are to be used, whether stone, brick, or wood. When stones are to be had at a moderate price, they ought to be preferred, because the work will be much stronger, more lasting, and need fewer repairs, than if made with any other materials; but when stones are scarce, and the expense becomes greater than what is allowed for building the harbour, the foundation may be made of stone as high as low water mark, and the rest finished with brick. If this manner of building should still be too expensive, wood must be used; that is, piles are driven as close as is thought necessary; which being fastened together by cross bars, and covered with strong oaken planks, form a kind of coffer, which is filled with all kinds of stones, chalk, and shingles. The manner of laying the foundation in different French methods of water, and in various soils, requires particular methods to be followed. When the water is very deep, the French throw in a great quantity of stones at random, so as to form a much larger base than would be required upon dry land; this they continue to within 3 or 4 feet of the surface of the water, where they lay the stones in a regular manner, till the foundation is raised above the water: they then lay a great weight of stones upon it, and let it stand during the winter to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a>; as likewise to see whether it is firm, and resists the force of the waves and winds: after that, they finish the superstructure with large stones in the usual manner. As this method requires a great quantity of stones, it can be practised only in places where stones are in plenty; and therefore the following one is much preferable. A coffer is made with dove-tail piles, of about 30 yards long, and as wide as the thickness of the foundation is to be; then the ground is dug and levelled, and the wall is built with the best mortar. As soon as the mortar is tolerably dry, those piles at the end of the wall are drawn out, the side rows are continued to about 30 yards farther, and the end enclosed; then the foundation is cleared, and the stones laid as before. But it must be observed, that the end of the foundation finished is left rough, in order that the part next to it may incorporate with it in a proper manner; but if it is not very dry, it will incline that way of itself, and bind with the mortar that is thrown in next to it: this method is continued till the whole pier is entirely finished. It must likewise be observed, that the piers are not made of one continued solid wall; because in deep water it would be too expensive: for which reason, two walls are built parallel to each other, and the interval between them is filled up with flint, chalk, and stone. As these walls are in danger of being thrust out or overflown by the corps in the middle, together with the great weight laid at times on the pier, they are tied or bound together by cross walls at every 30 or 40 yards distance, by which they support each other in a firm and strong manner. In a country where there is great plenty of stones, piles may be driven in as deep as they will go, at about two or three feet distance; and when the foundation is sunk and levelled, large stones may be let down, which will bed themselves: but care must be taken to lay them close, and so as to have no two joints over each other; and when the wall is come within reach, the stones must be cramped together. Another method practised is to build in coffers much after the same manner as has been done in building the piers of Westminster bridge; but as in this case the ends of the coffers are left in the wall, and prevent their joining... joining so well as to be water tight, the water that penetrates through and enters into the corps may occasion the wall to burst and to tumble down. Another inconvenience arising from this manner of building is, that as there are but few places without <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, which will destroy wood wherever they can find it; by their means the water is let into the pier, and consequently makes the work liable to the same accident as has been mentioned above. To prevent these inconveniences, the best method is to take the wood away, and joggle the ends of the walls together with large stones, pouring terrafirma mortar into the joints; when this is done, the water between the two walls may be pumped out, and the void space filled up with stone and flinting as usual; or if these joggles cannot be made water tight, some dovetail piles must be driven at each end as close to the wall as can be done, and a strong sail cloth put on the outside of them, which, when the water is pumped out, will stick so close to the piles and wall, that no water can come in. This method is commonly used in Russia. The thickness of a pier depends on two considerations: it ought to be both such as may be able to resist the shock of the waves in stormy weather; and also to be of a sufficient breadth above, that ships may be laden or unladen whenever it is thought necessary. Now, because the specific gravity of sea water is about one half that of brick, and as 2 to 5 in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of stone; and since the pressure of stagnated water against any surface is equal to the weight of a prism of water whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a> is the length of that surface, and whose base is a right-angled isosceles triangle, each of the equal sides being equal to the depth of the water; therefore a pier built with bricks, whose thickness is equal to the depth of the water, will weigh about four times as much as the pressure of the water against it; and one of stone of the same breadth, about six times and a quarter as much. Now this is not the force to be considered, since this pressure is the same within as without the pier; but it is that force with which the waves strike against the piers, and that depends on the weight and velocity of the waves, which can hardly be determined; because they vary according to the different depths of water, the distance from the shore, and according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>, winds, and other causes. Consequently the proper thickness of the piers cannot be determined by any other means than by experience. Practitioners suppose, that if the thickness of a pier is equal to the depth of the water, it is sufficient; but for a greater security they allow 2, 3, or 4 feet more. This might probably do, if piers were built with solid stones cramp together; but as this is hardly ever the case, and on the contrary, as the inside is filled up with flinting, chalk, or other loose materials, their rule is not to be depended upon; besides it makes the space above too narrow for lading and unlading the ships, unless in a great depth of water; so that it does not appear that their method can be followed, excepting in a very few cases where the water has but very little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. When stone can be had, no other materials should be used, because they being of a larger bulk than brick, will better resist the waves by their own weight, till such time as the mortar is grown hard; for after this is effected, brick will resist better against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of sea water than soft stones. The wall must be built with terrafirma mortar from the bottom to the height of low water mark, and the rest finished with cinder or tile-dust mortar, which has been found sufficiently good in those places where the wall is wet and dry alternately. The upper part of the pier should be paved with flat hewn stones laid in strong mortar, in order to prevent any water from penetrating into it: iron rings ought also to be fixed here and there at proper distances, to fasten the ships, and prevent them from striking against the pier when agitated by the waves. Wooden fenders or piles should be driven at the inside close to the wall, and cramp to it with iron, to prevent the ships from touching them, and from being worn by the continual motion. Where the sea breaks against the piers with great violence, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAKERS">breakers</a> should be made at proper distances; that is, two rows of piles are driven nearly at right angles to the piers for the length of about 12 or 15 feet, and at about 8 or 10 feet distant from each other; and then another to join the two former: these piles being covered with planks, and the inside being filled with flintings and rubble stones, then the top is paved with stones of about a foot in length, set longwise to prevent the waves from tearing them up. This precaution is absolutely necessary where the water rushes in very strongly. --- **Architecture** **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">Military</a> Architecture**, the same with what is otherwise called fortification. See Fortification. **Naval Architecture**, the art of building ships. See Ship-Building. **Architrave**, in Architecture, that part of a column which lies immediately upon the capital, being the lowest member of the entablature. See Plate XXXIX. Over a chimney, this member is called the mantel-piece; and over doors or windows, the hyperthyron. **Architricleinus**, in Antiquity, the master or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of a feast, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with the order and economy of it, the covering and uncovering of the tables, the command of the servants, and the like. The architricleinus was sometimes called servus tricliniarcha, and by the Greeks προσευχής, i.e., praefactor, or forefather. Potter also takes the architricleinus for the same with the sympostrache. **Archivault**, in Architecture, implies the inner contour of an arch, or a band adorned with mouldings, running over the faces of the arch stones, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> upon the impost. It has only a single face in the Tuscan order, two faces crowned in the Doric and Ionic, and the same mouldings as the architrave in the Corinthian and Composite. The Tuscan Order The Doric Order. The Ionic Order. The Corinthian Order The Composite Order.

ARCHIVE

Pages 211-237
or ARCHIVES, a chamber or apartment wherein the records, charters, and other papers and evidences, of a state, house, or community, are preserved, to be consulted occasionally. We say, the archives of a college, of a monastery, &c. The archives of ancient Rome were in the temple of Saturn; the archives of the court of chancery are in the rolls office.

ARCHIVIST

Pages 237-237

ARCHIVISTA, a keeper of an archive. Under the emperors, the archivist was an officer of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, held equal to the proconsuls, vested with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a>, styled clarissimus, and exempted from all public offices and taxes. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks and Persians, the trust was committed to none but men of the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>; among the Franks, the clergy being the only men of letters, kept the office among themselves. Since the erection of the electoral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a> has had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the archives of the empire.

ARCHMARSHAL

Pages 237-237

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> marshal of the empire, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>.

ARCHONS

Pages 237-237

in Grecian Antiquity, were magistrates appointed after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Codrus*. They were chosen from the most illustrious families till the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Arildides, who got a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> passed, by which it was enacted, that, in electing these magistrates, less regard should be paid to birth than to merit. The tribunal of the archons was composed of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> officers. The first was properly the archon; by whose name the year of his administration was distinguished. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>; that of the third, polemarchus: to these were added five thesmothete. These magistrates, elected by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCRUTINY">scrutiny</a> of beans, were obliged to prove, before their respective tribes, that they had sprung, both in their father's and their mother's side, for three descents, from citizens of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. They were likewise to prove that they were attached to the worship of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, the tutelary god of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; that they had in their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> an altar consecrated to Apollo; and that they had been respectfully obedient to their parents; an important and sacred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of their character, which promised that they would be faithful servants to their country. They were likewise to prove, that they had served in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> capacity the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of years which the republic required of every citizen: and this qualification gave the state experienced officers; for they were not allowed to quit the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> till they were 40 years old. Their fortune too, of which they were to inform those before whom they were examined, was a warrant for their fidelity. After the commissioners, who were appointed to inquire into their character and other requisites, had made a report of them, they were then to swear that they would maintain the laws; which obligation <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they neglected, they engaged to send to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a> a statue of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of their bodies. According to a law of Solon, if an archon got drunk, he was condemned to pay a heavy fine, and sometimes even punished with death. Such magistrates as the Athenian archons were well entitled to respect. Hence it was eternal infamy to insult them; and hence <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEMOSTHENES">Demosthenes</a> observed, that to treat the thesmothete with disrespect, was to show Archon disrespect to the republic. Another qualification indispensably required of the second officer of this tribunal, who was called the king, was that he had married the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of an Athenian citizen, and that he had espoused her a virgin. This was exacted of him, says Demosthenes, because part of his duty was to sacrifice to the gods jointly with his wife, who instead of appealing, would have irritated them, if she had not possessed both these honours. The inquiry into the private title of the nine archons was very severe; and this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> was the more necessary, as they had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to take a seat in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AREOPAGUS">Areopagus</a>, after they had quitted their office, and given an account of their administration. When any obscurity occurred in the laws relative to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and the worship of the gods, the interpretation was submitted to the tribunal of the archons. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> observes, that Solon, whose aim was to make his people happy, and who found their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> in his time aristocratical, by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of the nine archons, who were annual magistrates, tempered their power, by establishing the privilege of appealing from them to the people, called by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> to give their suffrage, after having taken the oath of the Heliaia, in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> near the Panathenaicum, where Hippas had formerly calmed a sedition of the people, and bound them to peace by an oath. The archons were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> officers, not only in civil, but likewise in sacred matters, and especially in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>. The archons, however, who were surnamed eponymi, were chiefly employed in civil affairs; yet they presided at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> feasts, and held the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> there. Hence they are sometimes styled priests. Archon is also applied by some authors to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> officers, both civil and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, under the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Greek empire. Thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> are sometimes called archontes; and the same may be said of the lords of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. We also read of the archons of the antimentia, archon of archons, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> archon, archon of churches, archon of the gospel, archon of the walls, &c.

ARCHONTICI

Pages 237-237

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a branch of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALENTINIANS">Valentinians</a>, who maintained that the world was not created by God, but by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> called Archontes.

ARCHPRIEST

Pages 237-237

ARCHPREBSTER, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESBYTER">presbyter</a> established in some dioceses, with a pre-eminence over the rest. Anciently the archpriest was the first person after the bishop: he was seated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> next after the bishop; and even acted as his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>, in his absence, as to all spiritual concerns. In the sixth century, there were found several archpriests in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>; from which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have them to have been called deans. In the ninth century, they distinguished two kinds of cures or parishes: the smaller governed by simple priests; and the baptismal churches by archpriests; who, besides the immediate concern of the cure, had the inspection of the other inferior priests, and gave an account of them to the bishop, who governed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> church, in person. There are archprebyteries still subsisting in the Greek church; vested with most of the functions and privileges of chorepiscopi or rural deans.

ARCHTREASURER

Pages 237-238

ARCHITREASURER, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of the German empire. This office was created with the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a>, in favour of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> Palatine, who had lost his former electorate, which was given to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Ferdinand II., who took it away from Frederic V., elector Palatine, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a>, where he was defeated in maintaining his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of archtreasurer was contested between the elector of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a>, who claimed it in virtue of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> from the elector Frederic, and the elector Palatine.

ARCIS-SUR-AUBE

Pages 238-238

a small town of France, in Champagne, now the department of Aube, seated on the river Aube. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 15'. N. Lat. 48° 40'.

ARCONA

Pages 238-238

a strong town situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Rugen in the Baltic. It stood on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> promontory, with the east, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and south sides defended by steep and lofty precipices, and the west by a wall 50 feet high, proportionably thick, and secured by a deep and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> ditch. It was, however, taken and ruined, in 1168, by Valdemar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. One of the conditions imposed by the conqueror was, that the inhabitants should destroy a temple they had erected to St Vitus, and deliver up the vast <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> belonging to this tutelary saint. Another was, that they should pay 40 silver yokes for oxen, by way of tribute, and enter as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> in the Danish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> when called upon.

ARCOS

Pages 238-238

a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, seated on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> craggy rock, at the bottom of which runs the Guadalete. Its strength lies not only in its situation, but in the works erected for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, and it is inaccessible on every side but one. The governor resides in an old castle, from whence there is a delightful prospect, which extends very far into the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2° 10'. N. Lat. 36° 40'.

ARCTIC

Pages 238-238

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, an epithet given to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> pole, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the pole raised above our horizon. It is called the arctic pole, on occasion of the constellation of the little bear, in Greek called αρκτος; the last <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> in the tail whereof nearly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> out the north pole. Arctic Circle is a lesser circle of the sphere, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the equator, and 23° 50' distant from the north pole; from whence its name. This, and its opposite, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANTARCTIC">antarctic</a>, are called the two polar circles; and may be conceived to be described by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> of the ecliptic, round the poles of the equator, or of the world.

ARCTURUS

Pages 238-239

ARCTURUS, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a fixed <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a>, of the first magnitude, in the constellation Arctophylax, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Bootes. The word is formed of *aegrez*, bear, and *yez*, tail, q. d. bear's tail, as being very near it. This star was known to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, as in the following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>: *Arcturus, pluviafique Hyades, geminafique Triones.* See also <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a> ix. 9. xxxviii 32.

ARCUCIO

Pages 239-239

Arcutio, a machine made of a board, covered with pieces of hoops, like the tilt of a waggon; used in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> to prevent children from being overlaid and smothered by nurses <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> others. Every nurse in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> is obliged to lay her child in an arcucio, under pain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCOMMUNICATION">excommunication</a>.

ARCULATION

Pages 239-239

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, the method of raising trees by layers, which is done in the following manner: Strong mother <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stools must be planted in a clear border, and in a straight line, about five feet apart. When these have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> five or six main branches from the roots, and as many collateral branches, the former must be bent to the ground, and there fastened. The small branches must be covered three inches deep upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, and have a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> basin of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> made round them to hold the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. About the middle of September they may be opened, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they have taken root, may be immediately removed into the nursery; but if they have not sufficiently extended their roots, they must be suffered to remain till the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, and then transplanted.

ARDAMON

Pages 239-239
or Ardama, in Antiquity, a vessel of water placed at the door of a person deceased, till the time of burial, as a token that the family was in mourning, and to serve to sprinkle and purify persons as they came out of the house.

ARDASSES

Pages 239-239

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, the coarsest of all the silks of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>; and as it were the refuse of each kind. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, they say, the legis, the housetes, the chouft, and the payas ardaflés, to signify the worst of those four sorts of Persian silks.

ARDASSINES

Pages 239-239

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, called in France ablaquers; a very fine sort of Persian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, little inferior <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in fineness to the fourbaïs, or rather charbafis, and yet it is little used in the silk <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of Lyons and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOURS">Tours</a>, because that kind of silk <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not bear hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in the winding.

ARDEA

Pages 239-239

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Latium, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence of Turnus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Rutuli, (Livy); so called, either from the augury of the heron, (Hyginus); <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> from the excessive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, (Martial). It was in a marshy, fleshy situation, (Strabo, Seneca). It was built by Danaë, the mother of Perseus, (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>); above five miles distant from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and 20 from Rome; now a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMLET">hamlet</a>. It was a Roman colony, (Livy); the inhabitants called Ardeates. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17. 49. N. Lat. 41. 30.

ARDEBIL

Pages 239-239
or Ardevil, a town of Persia in the province of Aderbijan. It was taken and burnt by Jenghiz Khan in 1222, when most of the inhabitants were destroyed; but it has been since rebuilt; and is still ranked for dignity among the best cities of the kingdom, on account of its having been the residence and burying-place of some of the Persian kings; particularly the sepulchre of Sheik Sefi is at this place, to which the people resort in pilgrimage. He founded a place, which they call his kitchen, with a revenue sufficient to maintain 1000 poor people, and to feed them three times a day. Three or four of the largest principal streets have shops, and are planted on each side with elms and linden trees, to keep off the excessive heat of the sun; but the houses are poorly built, with bricks dried in the sun; yet most of them, that are not in the bazars or market places, have the pleasure and conveniency of a garden full of trees bearing fruit; and there are large spots in the out parts of the town, where the houses are at a distance from each other, and the spaces between planted with trees, which render the city of a large extent. The meidan, or great square, is 300 paces long, and 150 broad, having shops all round; which, when this place was in a flourishing condition, were stored with all manner of valuable commodities. Through the city there pass two branches of a rivulet, which are sometimes enlarged by the melting of the snow on the mountains, so that they have been forced to make canals to divert the stream. In the reign of Shah Abbas, it broke down the dikes, and carried away a great number of houses. The city is without walls, and is seated in the midst of a large plain encompassed with mountains, the highest of which lies westward, and is always covered with snow. These render the air sometimes extremely hot, and at others intolerably cold, which occasions epidemical distempers, that carry off great numbers of people. The soil produces no fruit near the city but apples, pears, and peaches; and yet is good both for corn and pasture. The sheep are so numerous, that 100,000 have passed over the city bridge in a day. There are here several fountains of mineral waters, which serve both for common bathing, and for the cure of various diseases; one of these is a sulphurous spring, whose exhalations render the circumambient air extremely disagreeable. There are three springs which produce water as hot as if it was boiling; and from which, waters are conveyed to the public baths in the city. About half a league from the city, on the right hand of the public road, there is a pool of standing water, which is covered all over with salt like ice. E. Long. 47. 30. N. Lat. 37. 55.

ARDECHE

Pages 239-239

a department of France, which derives its name from a river, and comprehends <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Dauphiny.

ARDEN

Pages 239-239

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> name of forests among the Celts, from the widely extensive one which ranged for 500 miles across the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that which covered more than half the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and the sites of which still retain the appellation of Arden, to the much smaller one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Manconien, that covered and surrounded the site of the present <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a>. It is written Ardven by Cæsar and Tacitus in speaking of the forest in Gaul, and Arden by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OSSIAN">Ossian</a> in mentioning the woods of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALEDONIA">Caledonia</a>. It cannot (says Mr Whittaker) be compounded of ar the prepositive article in Celtic, and the substantive den, as Baxter and Camden assert it to be; but is formed of ar an adjective, and ven the same as den. The meaning of the name therefore is not, as Mr Baxter renders it, simply the hills, or even, as the ingenious translator

ARDENBURG

Pages 239-240

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, and formerly the most considerable in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; but it has been dismantled by the Dutch. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 30. N. Lat. 51. 16.

ARDENNE

Pages 240-240

a forest in France, formerly of vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; but the trees are in many places grubbed up, and where they stood are built cities, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and abbeys. At present it extends from <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol21.html#article-THIONVILLE">Thionville</a>, near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a>, to Donchery and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEDAN">Sedan</a>, on the confines of Champagne. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> are so narrow in some places, that two waggons cannot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> each other; and therefore the waggons are obliged to provide themselves with bells <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> horns to give one another notice to stop in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>.

ARDENNES

Pages 240-240

a department of France, which comprehends <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Champagne, and takes its name from the forest.

ARDENTES

Pages 240-240

in middle-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> writers, an appellation given to those afflicted with the ignis facer, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> erysipelas. They were thus called, as seeming to be scorched or burned with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. Hence also the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of St Genevieve at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> is called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOMUS">Domus</a> Ardentium, by reason, as it is said, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers were cured of that distemper at the shrine of this saint, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> VI.

ARDES

Pages 240-240

a town of France, in Lower Auvergne, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Mercœur. It serves as a mart for the commodities and trade between Upper and Lower Auvergne. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 10. N. Lat. 45. 22.

ARDFERT

Pages 240-240

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KERRY">Kerry</a>, with an university, which was held in the highest esteem. It is a bishop's see, and borough by ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, and has been held in commendam with the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMERICK">Limerick</a> ever since the Restoration. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> were anciently called Bishops of Kerry. St <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDON">Brandon</a>, to whom the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is dedicated, had his first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, under Bishop Ert; but he finished his studies in Connaught, St Jarlath bishop of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-TUAM">Tuam</a> being his preceptor. The ruins here are very extensive. Near the cathedral was an anchorite tower, the loftiest and finest in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, being 120 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>: it fell suddenly in 1771. In the ruined churches there are several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> round the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDINGS">mouldings</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; and over an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, behind <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Glandore's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, is an inscription in relief done in a masterly manner, but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> unknown.

ARDRAH

Pages 240-240

a small territory <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> properly so called. It lies at the bottom of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of St Thomas, and has a town called Ardres, supposed to be the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. The inhabitants are very licentious, and have neither temple nor any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship. However they are very courageous; and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> till lately that the king of Dahomy made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> upon this and the neighbouring territories, brought them under subjection, and burnt the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, particularly Ardres. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is very unwholesome to Europeans: yet the natives live to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; but the smallpox makes great destruction among them. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is fertile in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> corn, palm wine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, which last all the year; and they make a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>.

ARDRES

Pages 240-240

a town of France, in Lower Picardy, now the department of the Straits of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALAIS">Calais</a>. Here was an interview between Francis I. and Henry VIII., <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of England in 1520. It is seated in the midst of a morass eight miles south of Calais. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 0. N. Lat. 50. 35.

ARDS

Pages 240-240
BARONY OF, in the county of Down in Ireland: it is a narrow strip of land, in some places three and in none above six miles broad; but the soil is for the most part tolerably good. It lies between the lake of Strangford and the sea, and in the south part it is opposite to Lecale. Sir Thomas Smith obtained a patent for this barony from Queen Elizabeth, and sent his natural son with a colony to possess it; but he was intercepted and slain by an Irishman. After Sir Thomas's death, Ards was granted by James I. to some of the Scots nobility.

ARDUBA

Pages 240-240

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Pannonians. It was taken by Germanicus about the 7th year of the Christian era: but its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> was more owing to the disagreement that reigned among the inhabitants than to the valour of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. The greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the citizens were for submitting; but the women more fond of their ancient laws and liberties than the men, joined some Roman deserters, and falling upon their husbands, killed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of them: but being at last overcome by the men, who then submitted to the Romans, the women either threw themselves headlong from the tops of the walls, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, setting fire to their houses burnt themselves and their children to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>.

AREBO

Pages 240-240
or AREBON, a town on the Slave coast of Guinea, in Africa, seated at the mouth of the river Formosa. The English had once a factory there, as the Dutch have still. It is a large oblong place, indifferently well peopled, and furnished with housetops built of reeds and leaves. E. Long. 5. 5. N. Lat. 5. 0.

ARELATE

Pages 240-241
or ARELATUM, is a town of Gallia Narbonensis, situated on the Rhone, denoting a town on, or beyond, a marsh, according to the particular situation. ARE Arenberg situation of the speaker; called Areolate Sextanorum, (Pliny, Mela, Coin), because it had a colony of the sixth legion. Writers of the lower age call it Arelas, -alis, (Prudentius, Aulonius). There was a double Arelas, one on each side of the river, and joined by a bridge, (Aulonius); that on the left side is thought to have been built by Constantine. Tiberius's father was sent by Julius Caesar at the head of the colony, (Suetonius); and hence the appellation Julia Paterna, as appears from an inscription. It was a favorite place of the Romans, and greatly ornamented; and hence called Gallula Roma, (Aulonius). It is now called Arles. E. Long. 5. N. Lat. 43. 40.

AREMBERG

Pages 241-241

a small town of Germany, in the circle of Westphalia, defended by a castle. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name, and was erected into a principality by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Maximilian II. in favor of John de Ligne, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of Barbazon, who took the name of Arenberg. It is seated on the river Aer, E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 3. N. Lat. 50. 27.

AREMORICA

Pages 241-241
or Armorica, a part of Gaul between the Sequana and Ligeris, (Caesar, Hirtius); denoting a country on, or beyond the sea, ar moer, or are moer, Celtic. Pliny indeed says, that Aquitania was formerly called Aremorica; but in this he stands alone. In the lower age, the term Armorica was confined to Bretagne in France.

ARENA

Pages 241-241

in Roman Antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the gladiators fought; so called from its being always strewed with sand, to conceal from the view of the people the blood spilt in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>. Nero is said to have strewed the arena with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> dust.

ARENACUM

Pages 241-241
or Arenacus, one of the four towns or larger villages in the island of the Batavi, (Tacitus). Now Arnhem, in Guelderland. E. Long. 5. 20. N. Lat. 52. 2.

ARENARIUM

Pages 241-241

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> Writers, denotes a cemetery <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> burying ground. The arenas were properly a kind of pits, or holes, under ground, wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> not only buried their dead, but held their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> assemblies in times of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>.

ARENARIUS

Pages 241-241

in Antiquity, gladiators who combated with beasts in the arena <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>. The arenarii were slaves of the lowest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>; so that, though manumitted, they were not capable of being Roman citizens. They were the same with what were otherwise called Befiarrii.

ARENSBERG

Pages 241-241

a small town of Germany, in the circle of Westphalia, upon the river Roer. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 20. N. Lat. 51. 25.

ARENSBURG

Pages 241-241

an episcopal and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, seated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Osel, in the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 22. 40. N. Lat. 58. 15.

AREOLA

Pages 241-241

among Anatomists, the coloured circle surrounding the nipple of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>.

AREOPAGUS

Pages 241-244

a sovereign tribunal at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, famous for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and impartiality of its decrees, to which the gods themselves are said to have submitted their differences. It was in the town, on a rock <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hill opposite to the citadel. The word signifies strictly, rock of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>. Plutarch attributes the establishment of the Areopagus to Solon. Other authors think differently: and Areopagus, with good reason; for it appears undeniable, that this tribunal was instituted before Solon. But the best authorities allow him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of its restoration. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Athens, governed till this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> by tribunals of a circumscribed jurisdiction, which were multiplied by the most trifling accidents and circumstances, took no fixed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> or civil form, however closely united the members of those tribunals were by their general views towards the public good, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. As each of those tribunals could only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> in proportion to the power delegated to it, it was impossible that so many different and unequal imprestions should give to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> machine of the state that uniform and regular movement which, by an impulse always the same, would keep each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> in the situation it should maintain with relation to the whole. To effect this universal and harmonious power, it was necessary to unite the different channels of public authority, which, by being too much distributed, lost its force. This authority Solon collected, and placed it all in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Areopagus, which consequently became the main <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. The judges of this court, who, under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRACO">Draco</a>, decided only in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, now took cognizance of crimes of every kind; and the same tribunal which inflicted <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> on murder, poisoning, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of houses, theft, &c. struck at the roots of those crimes, by arraigning idleness, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>, and debauchery. Equally attentive to stimulate the indolence of the young, and the languor of the old, these sage judges roused in the one the laudable ambition to serve the state, and restored to the others their former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>. Satisfied that extremes produce the same effects, they thought the republic had as much to fear from the excess of wealth as from the gripe of poverty. Hence they exacted a minute account of the effects of every individual. Hence their great severity to those idle citizens, who, instead of being useful members in a state, are its bane and its dishonour. Isocrates draws a most beautiful and striking <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of those venerable and afflicting men, and of the order and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> which flourished in Athens by their wise administration. The judges of the Areopagus, says that authority, were more inducive to prevent crimes, by representing them in an odious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, than to establish modes of punishment. It was their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the enemies of the state were the instruments defined by the gods to punish the wicked; but that it was their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> to correct and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> public and private manners. They were vigilantly attentive to the conduct of all the citizens, but particularly to that of the youth. They well knew that the impetuosity of juvenile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> gave the most violent shocks to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and growing virtue; that it was the duty of inspectors of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> to soften the austerity of moral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> with innocent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; and that no recreations were more eligible than bodily exercises, which enable a young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to give a good education its full play, which improve health, give a pleasurable and agreeable vivacity, and even fortify the mind. The fortunes of the Athenians were too unequal to admit the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of education; and therefore the youth were trained in a manner suitable to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and circumstances of their respective families. Those of the inferior classes were taught <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; from this principle, that idleness is followed by indigence, and that indigence excites to the most daring and atrocious crimes. Having thus endeavoured, by wise precautions, to preclude the entrance of moral evil, they thought they had little to fear. Exercises of the body, such as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORSEMANSHIP">horsemanship</a> and hunting, were objects of education to the youth of liberal fortune. In this sage distribution, their great aim was to prevent the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> from committing crimes, and to facilitate to the rich the acquisition of virtue. Not satisfied with having established good laws, they were extremely careful to see that they were observed. With this view they had divided the city into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, and the country into cantons. Thus every thing passed under their eyes; nothing escaped them; they were acquainted with the private conduct of every citizen. Those who had been guilty of any irregularity were cited before the magistrates, and were reprehended, or punished in proportion to their misdemeanor. The same Areopagites obliged the rich to relieve the poor. They repressed the intemperance of the youth by a severe discipline. Corruption in magistrates was suppressed by the punishments denounced against it; and the old men, at the sight of the employments of the young, felt themselves animated with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of juvenile vigour and activity. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a> came likewise under the cognizance of the Areopagites. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> durst never, as we are told by <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-JUSTIN_MARTYR">Justin <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">Martyr</a>, divulge his private opinion concerning the Deity. He had learned from the Egyptians the doctrine of Moses. It appeared to him the best, and he embraced it with ardour. But his dread of the Areopagites, who were attached to the prevailing system, would not permit him even to name the author of sentiments which opposed the common <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>. The public edifices, the cleanliness of the streets, the pay of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, the distribution of the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; in a word, whatever interested the republic, was under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the Areopagus. The people themselves, jealous as they were of their power, did nothing without consulting this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, and suffered it without a murmur, to amend their precipitate decrees. Yet this authority, however great it may seem, was subject to the laws; by them rewards and punishments were determined; and those respectable judges gave an account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of their trust to public censors, who were placed between them and the people, to prevent the aristocracy from growing too powerful. The most important qualifications were required in those who entered into the Areopagus. Solon made a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, by which they who had not been archons for a year should not be admitted members of the Areopagus. To give more force to his law, he subjected himself to it, and was only admitted on that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>. This was but the first step; those annual magistrates, after having given law to the republic, were interrogated on their administration. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> their conduct was found irreproachable, they were admitted Areopagites with eulogium; but the smallest misconduct excluded them from that honour for ever. What administration was not to be expected from a tribunal so well composed! what veneration was not due to men of such rare talents and virtue! Such respect was paid them, that people professed not to laugh in their presence; and so well established was their reputation for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>, that those whom they condemned, or dismissed without granting their petition, never complained that they had been unjustly treated. The edifice of the Areopagus was extremely simple; and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, which was at first of the most common materials, remained in that state till the time of Augustus. This we learn from Vitruvius. Orestes was the first who thought of embellishing it. He raised in it an altar to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>. He likewise adorned it with two feet of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> silver; on one of which the acyclus sat, and the acyclus on the other. The one seat was consecrated to Injury, and the other to Impudence. This <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> sketch was brought to perfection by Epimenides, who erected altars to those allegorical deities, and soon after a temple, which Cicero mentions in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> book of laws. This temple corresponded with that which Orestes had built to the Furies, who brought him to Athens, and procured him the protection of Minerva. Epimenides dedicated it a second time to the Furies, or severe Goddesses, as they were termed by the Athenians. A man was thought lost without resource, and a victim to every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> ill, if he enforced a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a> by invoking the sacred name of those tremendous divinities. Those who employed their thoughts in solving the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of Paganism, imagined that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUMENIDES">Eumenides</a> had their temple so near the court of Areopagus, that they might enlighten the judges by their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>, and, by their continual assistance, prevent them from committing those errors to which human weakness is liable. To propitiate those terrible deities, and to procure their favour for the Areopagus, they were worshipped with great punctuality and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> itself appointed their priests. Demotthenes had been nominated to preside over their sacrifices; and he thought it very extraordinary, that he, to whom the republic had confided so important an office, should be publicly impeached. It was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to associate with the Eumenides the other deities who shared with them the sovereign empire over the dead. Epimenides placed in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of Pluto, of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, and of Telsus. They were all, according to Pausanias, of an agreeable form. Each of them was placed upon an altar, on which the citizens, or strangers, who had been acquitted by the Areopagus, made their grateful offerings. But it was not to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> alone that these several deities owed all the incense that smoked upon their altars. They who had been accused before the senate, harafted with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, and uncertain how these deities would be affected towards them, were lavish of sacrifices to obtain their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a>, by which they hoped their judges would likewise be influenced. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OEDIPUS">Oedipus</a> was another of the ornaments of the Areopagus. It was in the outward court of the Areopagus, where a barge was likewise placed, which made a part of the pomp at the public games. Whatever homage and implicit obedience the court of Areopagus might derive from all this religious parade, the public good was always dearer to them than... their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> to avail themselves of the abilities of others. Areopagus. What undoubtedly led him into that mistake, was an inviolable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of that tribunal, which prohibited, in pleadings, all that warm and picturesque oratory which seduces the judgment and inflames the passions. When the suffrages were collected, each person gave his in silence. They voted with a small flint, which they held betwixt the thumb and the two next fingers, and which they put into one of the two urns that stood in a corner of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>. One stood before the other. The first was called the urn of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; the second, the urn of compassion. That of death was of brafs, and was termed proper; that of compassion was of wood, and was termed improper. The judges <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> brought their flint to the assembly, and put it into the urn; but, that all the suffrages might be collected, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERALD">herald</a> took the two urns, and presented them, one after another, to every senator, commanding him, in the name of the republic, no longer to defer his acquittal or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a>. From this method of giving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, which was called ἀποφάσις ἄνωθεν, because it kept the vote of each person undiscovered, the Thirty Tyrants, to make themselves masters of the decisions of the Areopagus, substituted another, by means of which they knew exactly the opinion of each of the judges; for they obliged them to bring their flints publicly, and lay them upon two tables placed before them, the situation of which was quite opposite to that of the urns; for the first of those tables was that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and the second that of death. The first substances with which they gave their suffrages were not small pieces of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOG">hog</a>, as some authors assert, but <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> shells, for which pieces of brafs, of the same form, termed ἐπόνδυλα, were afterwards substituted. The substances with which they voted were distinguished by their form and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. Those which condemned were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and perforated in the middle; the others were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and not perforated. The precaution of piercing the black ones tends to prove, what we have already observed, that the court of Areopagus sat in the night: for what end did it serve to pierce the black shells, or flints, if the judges could have seen them and the white ones, and consequently have distinguished their colours by the affluence of the light? But as they passed sentence in the dark, it is evident that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> besides that of colour was necessary, to know the black ones from the white. The judges were likewise permitted to multiply at pleasure the distinctions between signs, which essentially distinguished the fates of men. After the suffrages were collected, they were taken out of the two urns, and put into a third vase of brafs. They were then counted; and as the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of white or of black flints was higher or inferior, one of the judges drew with his nail a shorter or a longer line on a tablet with a waxen surface, on which the result of each cause was marked. The short line expressed acquittal; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, condemnation. With regard to the emoluments of the judges, they were as moderate as those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a>. The length of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> did not enhance its expense; and when the decision of a cause was postponed till the next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, the committee were only paid an obolus on that day. Hence Mercury, in Lucian, is surprized that such sensible ARE Areopagus, sensible old men as the senators of Areopagus were should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> at so low a price the trouble of ascending so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. As to the number of the judges which composed the Areopagus, some authors, attentive only to a part of Solon's regulations, by which he enacted, that for the future, none but the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> archons should be admitted members of the Areopagus, have imagined, that this tribunal was filled anew every year, and that it never consisted of more than nine magistrates. This opinion, and some others, are refuted by the circumstantial account which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> Laertius gives us of the condemnation of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>. This great man wished to substitute a rational <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> for the fabulous and extravagant system of religion which prevailed in his time. His project, however laudable, appeared impious in the eye of superstition. Information was laid against him before the Areopagus, and he had as many accusers as fellow citizens. After the charges and the answers were heard, they proceeded to suffrages. The opinions were divided, but not equally, for the number of those who condemned him exceeded by 281 the number of those who declared him innocent. He made an ironical reply to this iniquitous sentence, by telling his judges, that he took it for granted, they would admit him to a maintenance in the Prytaneum. On this sarcasm, 80 of those who had voted in his favour forsook him, went over to the opposite party, and condemned him to die. Here then we have 361 judges who condemn; to whom if we add those who perished in acquitting him, the number must be very considerable. Of all the judgments of the Areopagus, the most famous one, excepting that of Mars, was the sentence which they passed on Orestes. His <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, which happened under Demophoon the 12th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Athens, in 375 of the Attic era, owed all its fame to a remarkable circumstance, that gave rise to a custom which was observed ever afterwards. Orestes had killed his mother. He was accused before the Areopagus, and cited to appear in that court. He would have lost his life in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the votes, had not Minerva, moved with his misfortunes, declared herself for those who had absolved him, and joined her suffrage to theirs. Thus Orestes was saved. In veneration to this miracle, the Areopagites, whenever the suffrages were equally divided, decided in favour of the accused, by granting him what they termed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a> of Minerva. Cephalus and Daedalus were condemned by the Areopagus long before the time of Orestes. We find in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> authors some decisions of this tribunal, which bear the strongest marks of justice, though their objects are not interesting. We shall here quote an anecdote from Aulus Gellius, and Valerius Maximus, of a woman, who was accused of having poisoned her husband and her son. She was taken and brought before Dolabella, who was then proconsul of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. She was no sooner in his presence than she owned the fact; and added, that she had very good reasons for putting her husband and her son to death.—"I had (said she) to my first husband a son whom I tenderly loved, and whose virtues rendered him worthy of my affection. My second husband, and the son whom I bore to him, murdered my favour- ite child. I thought it would have been unjust if Areopagus, have suffered those two monsters of barbarity to live. If you think, Sir, that I have committed a crime, it is your province to punish it: I certainly shall never repent of it." This affair embarrassed Dolabella. She was afterwards sent to the Areopagus; and that court, when they had examined her a long time, ordered her and her accuser to appear before them again a hundred years after, from the first day of her trial. We must not, however, suppose that the Areopagus always preserved its old reputation; for such is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of human affairs, that perfection, with regard to them, is a violent, and consequently a transitory, state. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERICLES">Pericles</a>, who lived about 100 years after Solon, to flatter the people and win them to his party, used his utmost efforts to weaken the authority of the Areopagus, which was then disliked by the multitude. He took from it the cognizance of many affairs which had before come under its jurisdiction; and to forward his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of humbling it, employed the eloquence of Epilautes, whose talents were formidable, and who was an avowed enemy to the great men of Athens. The Areopagus itself seemed to second the endeavours of a man who projected its ruin, and by its misconduct hastened its fall. The old rules of the court, by which none were admitted its members but those whose unexceptionable conduct would support its majesty, seemed too severe. They grew less delicate in their choice; and presuming that the faults with which they dispensed, would soon be reformed in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of so many good examples, vice imperceptibly crept among them: corruption, at first secret and timid, grew infinitely open and daring, and made such progress, that the most shameful crimes were soon exhibited on the stage; and they were not copied from the low and abandoned multitude, but from these senators, once the venerable and austere censors of idleness and of vice. Demetrius, the comic poet, wrote a piece which he entitled The Areopagite, where he strips the mask off those hypocritical legislators, who were now equally apt to be seduced by wealth and by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. So much had the Athenian senate degenerated in the days of Isocrates, cir. 340 years before the Christian era. Before this tribunal St Paul was called to give an account of his doctrine, and converted Dionysius one of their number. The end of this court of judicature is as obscure as its origin, which was derived from very remote antiquity. It existed, with the other magistracies, in the time of Pausanias, i.e. in the 2nd century. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of its subsequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> is not ascertained; but a writer, who lived under the emperors Theodosius the Elder and Younger, in the 5th century, mentions it as extinct.

AREQUIBA

Pages 244-244

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a> in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 73°. S. Lat. 1°. It is one of the most beautiful cities in all Peru, being delightfully situated in the valley of Quilca, 100 leagues from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMA">Lima</a>, and 20 from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, with which it communicates by a fine river. The entrance into the harbour is rather shallow for ships of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> burden; but when once they are entered, they may ride securely in 18 fathoms <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. This city was founded in 1539, by order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a> Francisco Pizarro, in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> known likewise by the name of Arequipa; but its situation being found disadvantageous,

ARES

Pages 244-245

a word of Paracelsus's, by which he would express that power of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in the whole material world, by which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are divided into individuals. ARETÆUS of Cappadocia, a Greek physician of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the Pneumaticists, lived in the reign of Augustus, according to some; according to others, under Trajan <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Adrian. He wrote several treatises in the Ionian dialect, on acute diseases, and other medicinal subjects; some of which are still extant. The best edition of his works is that of Boerhaave, in Greek and Latin, with notes, printed in 1731; that of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WIGAN">Wigan</a>, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> in 1723, in folio, is also much esteemed.

ARETHUSA

Pages 245-245

a celebrated fountain near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, famous for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of its waters, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fishes it contained. Many fables were invented by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> concerning this fountain. They had also a notion that the river Alpheus ran under <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> through the waters of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, without mixing with them, from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a> to Sicily. Mr Brydone informs us, that it still continues to send forth an immense quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, rising at once to the size of a river, but is entirely abandoned by the fishes it formerly contained in such plenty. At some distance from Arethusa is a fountain of fresh water which boils up very strongly in the sea, inasmuch that, after piercing the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> water, it may be sometimes taken up very little affected by it.
