This fountain Mr Brydone thinks the ancients were ignorant of, or they would not have failed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it as an argument for the submarine journey of Alpheus. Mr Swinburne describes this once famous fountain as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pool of water near the quay, defended from the sea by a wall, and almost hidden by houses on every other side. The water is not salt, but brackish, and fit for no purpose but washing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>. "This (says he) is the celebrated fountain of Arethusa, whose soft poetical name is known to every reader. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a> and her constant lover Alpheus, the excellency of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, and the charms of its situation, are themes on which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> poets have indulged their fancy, and exercised their pens. Alas, how altered! rubbish chokes up its wholesome sources; the waves have found a passage through the rocks, which repeat earthquakes have split; and not a fish is to be seen in it. Sometimes, after an earthquake, it has been left dry; and, at other times, the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of its waters has been tainted by subterranean effluvia. Its fountain head probably lies among the neighbouring hills." ARETHUSA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. ARETIA. See Botany Index.

ARETIN

Pages 245-246

Guido, famous for his musical improvements, lived in the 13th century. He was a native of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-AREZZO">Arezzo</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>; and having been taught the practice of music in his youth, and probably retained as a chorister in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the Benedictine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> founded in that city, he became a monk professed, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of the order of St Benedict. In this retirement he seems to have devoted himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of music, particularly the system of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and, above all, to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> their method of notation. The difficulties that attended the instruction of youth in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> offices were so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, that, as he himself says, ten years were generally consumed barely in acquiring the knowledge of the plain song; and this consideration induced him to labour after some amendment, some method that might facilitate instruction, and enable those employed in the choral office to perform the duties of it in a correct and decent manner. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we may <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> those legendary accounts that are extant in old monastic <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, we should believe he was assisted in his pious intention by immediate communications from heaven: some speak of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the syllables as the effect of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>; and Guido himself seems to have been of the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, by his saying it was revealed to him by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as some interpret his words, in a dream: but graver historians say, that being at vespers in the chapel of his monastery, it happened that one of the offices appointed for that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a> * to St John. UT queant laxis RESonare fibris Mira gestorum FAmuli tuorum SOLve pollutis LABii reatum, Sancte Joanne. During the performance of the hymn, he remarked the iteration of the words, and the frequent returns of UT, RE, MI, FA, SOL, LA: he observed likewise a familiarity between the closeness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a> MI and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> open <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of FA, which he thought could not fail to impress upon the mind a lasting idea of their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGRUITY">congruity</a>; and immediately conceived a thought of applying these six syllables to perfect an improvement either then actually made by him, or under consideration, viz. that of converting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> tetrachords into hexachords. Struck with the discovery, he retired to his study, and having perfected his system, began to introduce it into practice; the persons to whom he communicated it were the brethren of his own monastery, from whom it met with but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> reception, which in the epistle to his friend, he ascribes undoubtedly to its true cause, envy: however his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>, and his employment in the chapel, gave him an opportunity of trying the efficacy of his method on the boys who were training up for the choral service, and it exceeded the most languishing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a>. "To the admiration of all (says <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Baronius) a boy there- The fame of Guido's invention soon spread abroad, and his method of instruction was adopted by the clergy of other countries. We are told by Kircher, that Hermannus, bishop of Hamburgh, and Elviricus bishop of Osnaburg, made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it, and by the authors of the *Histoire Litteraire de la France*, that it was received in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and taught in all the monasteries in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. It is certain that the reputation of his great skill in music had excited in the pope a desire to see and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> with him; of which, and of his going to Rome for that purpose, and the reception he met with from the pontiff, he himself has given a circumstantial account in the epistle hereafter mentioned. The particulars of this relation are very curious; and as we have his own authority, there is no room to doubt the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of it. It seems that John XX., or as some writers compute, the 10th pope of that name, having heard of the fame of Guido's school, and conceiving a desire to see him, sent three messengers to invite him to Rome; upon their arrival, it was resolved by the brethren of the monastery, that he should go thither attended by Grimaldo the abbot, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the canons of the church of Arezzo. Arriving at Rome, he was presented to the holy father, and by him received with great kindness. The pope had several conversations with him, in all which he interrogated him as to his knowledge in music; and upon sight of an antiphoner which Guido had brought with him, marked with the syllables agreeable to his new invention, the pope looked on it as a kind of prodigy; and ruminating on the doctrines delivered by Guido, would not stir from his seat till he had learned perfectly to sing off a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>: upon which he declared, that he could not have believed the efficacy of the method, if he had not been convinced by the experiment he had himself made of it. The pope would have detained him at Rome; but labouring under a bodily disorder, and fearing an injury to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and the heats of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, which was then approaching, Guido left that city upon a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> to revisit it, and explain to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a> the principles of his new system. On his return homewards, he made a visit to the abbot of Pomposa, a town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a>, who was very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> to have Guido <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in the monastery of that place; to which invitation it seems he yielded, being, as he says, desirous of rendering so great a monastery still more famous by his studies there. Here it was that he composed a tract on music, entitled *Micrologus*, i.e., "a short discourse;" which he dedicated to Theodald bishop of Arezzo; and finished, as he himself at the end of it tells us, under the pontificate of John XX. and in the 34th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Vossius speaks also of another musical treatise written by him, and dedicated to the same person. Most of the authors who have taken occasion to mention Guido, speak of the Micrologus as containing the sum of his doctrine: but it is in a small tract, entitled *Argumentum <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVI">novi</a> Cantus inventandi*, that his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of his use of the syllables, with their several mutations, and in short his whole doctrine of formation, is to be found. This tract makes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of an epistle to a very dear and intimate friend of Guido, whom he addresses thus, "Beatissimo atque dulcisissimo fratri Michaeli;" at whose request the tract itself seems to have been composed. Whether Guido was the author of any other tracts, is not easy to determine. It nowhere appears that any of his works were ever printed, except that Baronius, in his *Annales Ecclesiastici*, tom. xi. p. 73, has given at length the epistle from him to his friend Michael of Pomposa, and that to Theodald bishop of Arezzo, prefixed to the Micrologus: and yet the writers on music speak of the Micrologus as of a book in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of every one. Martini cites several manuscripts of Guido; namely, two in the Ambrosian library at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, the one written about the twelfth century, the other less ancient; another among the archives of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of Pistoia, a city in Tuscany; and a third in the Mediceo-Laurenziano library at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, of the 15th century: these are clearly the Micrologus. Of the epistle to Michael of Pomposa, together with the *Argumentum novi Cantus inventandi*, he mentions only one, which he says is somewhere at Ratibon. Of the several tracts above mentioned, the last excepted, a manuscript is extant in the library of Balliol-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. Several fragments of the two first, in one volume, are also among the Harleian manuscripts now in the British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a>, No. 3199; but so very much mutilated, that they afford but small satisfaction to a curious inquirer. Aretin, Leonard, one of the most learned men of the 15th century, was secretary to the republic of Florence, and translated from the Greek into Latin some of the Lives of Plutarch, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s Ethics: he also composed three books of the Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, that may serve as a supplement to those wanting in Livy; the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the transactions in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> during his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; that of ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; that of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>; that of the republic of Florence; and many other books. He died in 1443, aged 74. Aretin, Francis, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of great <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, and well acquainted with the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. He translated into Latin the Commentaries of St Chrysostom upon St John, and about 20 Homilies of the same father: he also translated the Letters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHALARIS">Phalaris</a> into Latin, and wrote a treatise *De balneis Puteolanis*. He studied at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIENNA">Sienna</a>, about the year 1443; and afterwards taught <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> there with such reputation, that they called him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of Subtleties, and his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> became a proverb. He displayed his talents chiefly in disputes, in which nobody could withstand him. He gave his opinions in law with so much confidence, as to assure those who consulted him that they should carry their cause: nor did <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> contradict him; for it was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> saying at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, such a cause has been condemned by Aretin, it must therefore be lost. He taught also in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a>, and in that of Ferrara. He was at Rome under the pontificate of Sixtus IV. but did not stay here <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; for he soon perceived that the great hopes which he had built upon his reputation would come to nothing. This pope, however, declared he would have given him a cardinal's hat, had he not thought he should have done a public injury by depriving the youth of such an excellent professor. When old age would not permit him to go through the duties of his office, they dispensed with his reading.

ARETIUM

Pages 332-332

(Cicero, Caesar); Arrhetium, (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); Urbs Arrhetinorum, (Polybius); one of the twelve <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, near the Arno and Clanis, situated in a pleasant valley. Now <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-AREZZO">Arezzo</a>, 42 miles east of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13. 18. Lat. 43. 15.

AREZIO

Pages 246-247

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, seated in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, on the declivity of a hill that overlooks the neighbouring plain, between the Citta di Castelli and Florence. It is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> city and a bishop's see; and was famous for a kind of earthen <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a> much esteemed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. It was greatly fallen to decay when Cosimo de' Medici took it under his protection; since which it has been recovering gradually. It is famed for being the birthplace of Meccenas. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12. 2. N. Lat. 43. 27.

ARGEA

Pages 247-247
or ARGELI, in Roman Antiquity, thirty human figures, made of rushes, thrown annually by the priests or vestals into the Tiber, on the day of the ides of May.—Plutarch, in his Roman Questions, inquires why they were called Argae. There are two reasons assigned. The first, that the barbarous nations who first inhabited these parts call all the Greeks they could meet with into the Tiber: for Argians was a common name for all Grecians: but that Hercules persuaded them to quit so inhuman a practice, and to purge themselves of the crime by instituting this solemnity. The second, that Evander, an Arcadian, and a sworn enemy of the Argians, to perpetuate that enmity to his posterity, ordered the figures of Argians to be thus cast into the river.

ARGELIA

Pages 247-248
or ARGOLIS, a district of Peloponnesus, situated between Arcadia to the west, the Egean sea to the east, Laconia and the Sinus Argolicus to the south, and to the north the territory of Corinth and the Sinus Saronicus (Livy, Ptolemy); so called from ARGOS, the capital: Now Romania di Morea. By the Greeks the people were called Argelii, from Argi or Argos; by the Romans, Argivi, Argives. They were a colony who migrated, it is said, from Egypt, under the command of Inachus. Polemon and Ptolemy Mendesius, ancient Greek writers, inform us, that Inachus was contemporary with Amosis, who demolished Avaris, and expelled the shepherds out of Egypt. If, with some learned chronologers, we suppose Inachus to have begun to reform the Argives B.C. 1856, and to have died B.C. 1808, he must have been coeval with Amosis, who reigned in Upper Egypt 15 years before the expulsion of the shepherds, and 10 years after that event, which happened B.C. 1866. Inachus was styled the Son of the Ocean, because his origin was not known, or because he had come by sea into Greece. Before his arrival the inhabitants were rude and barbarous. These he united and civilized, and instructed in various arts. His son Phoroneus instituted the laws of government; and, on that account, has been called the first king in Argos, the first of men, and the father of mortals. The family of Inachus, after having kept possession of the throne... ARGENTARIUS is frequently used in Roman writers for a money changer or banker. The argentarii were monied people, who made a profit either by the changing, or lending of money at interest. They had their tabernae, or offices, in the forum Romanum, built there as early as the reign of L. Tarquinius Priscus. The argentarii and feneratores were much hated on account of their covetousness and extortion.

ARGENTATI MILITES

Pages 248-248

in Antiquity. Livy, lib. vi. speaks of argentati milites, as distinguished from aurati. Aquinas supposes these to have been similar to the argyraspides and chrysaepides; but the descriptions do not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRATURE">quadrature</a>. Livy only represents the argentati as clothed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> coats.

ARGENTEUIL

Pages 248-248

a town of the Ille de France, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, five miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. It is a very beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, with fine vineyards. In the environs are quarries of flueco. In the Benedictine priory they pretend to have the seamflefs coat of Christ. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 28. N. Lat. 48. 52.

ARGENTIERE

Pages 248-248

a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Archipelago, near Milo. It is about 18 miles in compass; and is full of barren <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, producing nothing but barley, cotton, and a few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a> fit only for eating. The barley and cotton are grown round the only village there is in the island. The ladies are handsome enough, have no other employment but making cotton stockings, and take up with the sailors who put into the port. The men all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> become good pilots. They have very little <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, are very ignorant, and of very bad morals. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">Justice</a> is administered by an itinerant cadi, who is sometimes the only Musliman in the whole island. The only article relating to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is the terra Cimolia so highly esteemed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; it is a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> chalk, which is very heavy, without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and crumbles easily: they use it in wailing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 23. 10. N. Lat. 36. 50. ARGENTINA. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ARGENTINUS

Pages 248-248

a deity worshipped by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, as the god of silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>; as Aesculapius, whom they made his father, was the god of brafs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, which was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> before silver.

ARGENTON

Pages 248-248

a town and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of France, in the department of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDRE">Indre</a>, divided into two by the river Creule. Here was formerly a castle; but it was demolished by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> XIV. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 38. N. Lat. 40. 30.

ARGENTORA

Pages 248-248

Argentina, (Notitia;) Argentoratum, (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>;) Argentoratus, (Ammian;) a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Tribocci; one of the fifty forts built by Drusus on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, (Florus:) an appellation formed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> from the German, Argen Straffen, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Straten, "unsafe <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> for travellers," from the marauding parties of the garrisons that infested the roads. Now Straßburg, in Lower <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALSACE">Alsace</a>, on the rivulet Ill, near the Rhine. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 35. N. Lat. 48. 38.

ARGENTUM ALBUM

Pages 248-249

in our old customs, silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BULLION">bullion</a> that anciently passed for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. By Doomsday <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a>, some rents to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> were paid in argento albo, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> silver pieces of money; other rents in libris urbis et <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENATES">penates</a>, in metal of full <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and purity: in the next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, that rent which was paid in money, was called blancb fearm, and Argentum and afterwards subite rent; and what was paid in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, was termed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> mail. Argentum Dei, God's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>, anciently signified <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> money, or money given to bind a bargain; in some places called erler, or arler, and by the civilians and canonists, arrhe. Et capit de praedicto Henrico tres denarios de argenti Dei prae manibus. Argentum Mythum is a metal consisting of silver-like flakes, used for the colouring of platter figures, and for other purposes, as pigment. It consists of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMALGAM">amalgam</a> of equal parts of tin, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISMUTH">bismuth</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>. It is to be mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> of eggs, or spirit <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>, and then applied to the intended <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which is afterwards to be burnished. Argentum Vivum, Mercury, or Quicksilver. See Mercury and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ARGESTES

Pages 249-249

is used by Vitruvius for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> which blows from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the horizon, which is 75° from the south and westward. Ricciolus uses the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> to denote the wind which blows at 22° 30' from the west towards the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, coinciding with that which is otherwise called west-north-west.

ARGIL

Pages 249-249

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of ardea. See Ardea, Ornithology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ARGIVI

Pages 249-249
or ARGEII, the people of Argelia or Argolis. See Argelia.

ARGO

Pages 249-249

in Antiquity, a ship <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vessel celebrated among the poets; being that wherein the Argonauts, of whom Jason was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, made their expedition in quest of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEECE">fleece</a>. Jason having happily accomplished his enterprise, consecrated the ship Argo to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>; or, as others say, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, in the isthmus of Corinth; where, they add, it did not remain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before it was translated into heaven, and made a constellation. The generality of authors represent the ship Argo as of a long make, resembling the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> galleys; and furnished with thirty benches of rowers. It could not, however, be of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> bulk, since the Argonauts were able to carry it on their backs from the Danube to the Adriatic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. ARGO Navis, the Ship Argo, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, is a constellation in the southern hemisphere, whose stars, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s catalogue, are 45; in Tycho's 11; in the Britannic catalogue, and Sharp's Appendix, 64.

ARGOB

Pages 249-249

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> lying beyond Jordan, in the half tribe of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Bashan, one of the most fruitful on the other side of Jordan. In the region of Argob there were sixty cities, called Bashan-horoth-joir, which had very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> walls and strong gates, without reckoning many villages and hamlets which were not enclosed, Deut. iii. 4. 14. and 1 Kings iv. 13. But Argob was more particularly the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the region of Argob, which Eusebius says was 15 miles west from Geraa. ARGONAUTA. See <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ARGONAUTIC

Pages 249-249

something belonging to the Argonauts. The Argonautic expedition is one of the greatest epochs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> periods of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> which Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton endeavours to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a>, and from thence to rectify the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>. This he shows, by several authorities, to have been one <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> or about 30 years earlier than the taking of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, and 43 years later than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>. See Chronology. Dr Bryant, however, rejects the history of the Argonautic expedition as a Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, founded indeed on a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> derived from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and ultimately referring to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>'s preservation, &c., in the ark. But although we are not to believe all the romantic stories which poets, and even some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> historians, have told us of those famous adventurers, yet it seems unreasonable to discredit entirely the Argonautic expedition. See Argonauts.

ARGONAUTICA

Pages 249-249

in Literary <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, denotes poems on the subject and expeditions of the Argonauts. We have the Argonautics of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a> in epic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, published by H. Stephens; the Argonauticon of Valerius Flaccus, in eight books of Latin heroics, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of Apollonius, with respect to which Burman observes that the imitator has often surpassed the original; the Argonautics of Apollonius Rhodius, an heroic poem, consisting of four books, opus, as Quintilian calls it, non contemnumendum.

ARGONAUTS

Pages 249-250

in Antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of illustrious Greeks, who embarked along with Jason, in the ship Argo, from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLCHIS">Colchis</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to obtain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEECE">fleece</a>. The occasion of this expedition is thus represented by Greek writers. Phryxus, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> with his sister Helle from the rage of their stepmother Ino, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADMUS">Cadmus</a>, went on board a ship, whose ensign was a golden ram, and sailed to Colchis, (now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINGRELIA">Mingrelia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a>). Helle was drowned by the way, in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> which from her was called the Hellespont, now the Dardanelles. This, according to some, was the ground of the poetical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, that a ram with a golden fleece swam away with them to Colchis; and that the Argonauts undertook their famed expedition, in order to find that fleece. But Strabo and Arrian inform us, that it was a practice of the Colchians to collect <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> on Mount <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a> by extending fleeces across the beds of the torrents; and as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> palled, the metallic particles remained entangled in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>; hence, according to those historians, the adventure was named the expedition of the golden fleece. Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton thinks that this expedition was really an embassy sent by the Greeks, during the intestine divisions of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> in the reign of Amenophis, to persuade the nations upon the coasts of the Euxine and Mediterranean seas, to take that opportunity of shaking off the yoke of Egypt, which Sesostris had laid upon them; and that fetching the golden fleece, was only a pretence to cover their true design. But the most judicious and satisfactory account of the Argonautic expedition seems to be that given by Dr Gillies in his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. "The northern districts of Thrace being peculiarly exposed to the dangerous fury of invaders, the petty princes of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> entered into a confederacy for their mutual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. They assembled in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> and autumn at Thermopylae, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> afterwards so illustrious, and then governed by Amphidryon, a descendant of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEUCALION">Deucalion</a>, whose name is immortalized in the Amphidryonic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. The advantages which the confederates derived from this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, were soon perceived by their neighbours. The central states gradually acceded... Argonauts, ed to their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>; and about the middle of the 14th century before Christ, Acrisius <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>, and other princes of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, were allowed to share the benefits and security of this useful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a>. See Amphictyons. "After this event, the Amphictyons appear to have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> confined themselves to the original purpose of their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>. The states, whose <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> were directed by this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> found sufficient occupation in defending their own territories; and near a century elapsed, before they undertook, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> consent, any distant expedition. But it was not to be expected that their restless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> could be always exhausted in defensive <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The establishment of the Amphictyons brought together the chiefs most distinguished by birth and bravery. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">Glory</a> and emulation prompted them to arms, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> directed those arms against the barbarians. Jason, Admetus, and other chieftains of Thessaly, having equipped a small fleet in the neighbouring harbour of Iolcus, and particularly the ship Argo of superior size and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> to any before known, were animated with a desire to visit foreign lands, to plant colonies in those parts of them that appeared most delightful, and to retort on their inhabitants the injuries which Greece had suffered from strangers. The princes of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> having proclaimed this spirited design over the central and southern provinces, the standard of enterprise and glory was speedily surrounded by the flower of the Grecian youth, who eagerly embraced this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> opportunity to signalize their manly valour. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PELEUS">Peleus</a>, Tydeus, Telamon, and in general the fathers of those heroic chiefs who in the succeeding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> shone with distinguished lustre in the plains of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, are numbered among the leaders of the Argonauts. They were accompanied by the chosen warriors, and by the venerable prophets, of their respective tribes; by an Eucalypus, the admired father of the healing art; and by the divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, whose sublime genius was worthy to celebrate the amazing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of their adventures. "These adventures, however, have been too much adorned by the graces of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, to be the proper subject of historical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. The designs of the Argonauts are veiled under the allegorical, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at least doubtful, phrase, of carrying off the golden fleece; which, though easily explained, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we admit the report that the inhabitants of the eastern banks of the Euxine extended fleeces of wool, in order to collect the golden particles which were carried <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by the torrents from Mount Caucasus, is yet described in such various <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, that almost every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> who examines the subject, thinks himself entitled to offer, by way of explanation, some new conjecture of his own. But in opposition to the most approved of these conjectures, we may venture to affirm, that the voyage to Colchis was not undertaken with a view to establish extensive plans of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, or to search for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of gold, far less to learn the imaginary art of converting other substances into that precious metal; all such motives supposing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of speculation and refinement unknown in that age to the gallant but uninstructed youth of Thessaly. The real object of the expedition may be discovered by its consequences. The Argonauts fought, conquered, and plundered; they settled a colony on the shores of the Euxine; and carried into Greece a daughter of the king of Colchis, the celebrated Medea, a princess of Egyptian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>, whose crimes and enchantments are condemned to eternal infamy in the immortal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a>." Argonauts of St Nicholas, was the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> order instituted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> III, king of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, in the year 1382, for the advancement of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, or, as some say, merely for preserving amity among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>. They wore a collar of shells, enclosed in a silver <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>, whence hung a ship with this device, Non credo temporis, "I do not trust <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>." Hence these Argonaut knights came to be called knights of the shell. They received the order of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, archbishop of Naples; and held their assemblies in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Nicholas, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>.

ARGOPHYLLUM

Pages 250-250
White leaf (Forst. Nov. Gen.): A genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the pentandra clas of plants. The capsule is trilocular; the nectarium is pyramidal, pentagonal, and the length of the corolla. There is but one species, the nitidum or glossy, a native of New Caledonia. This genus has great affinity with the ivy; but differs in the nectarium, and perhaps in the fruit.

ARGOS

Pages 250-251

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>; from Argos, one of the kings, (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, Strabo). Argos, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, and an inland town, of Argolis <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Argelia. It had different surnames; as Achaeum, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, or an ancient people, (Homer); Hippium, from its breed of horses; and Inachium, from the river Inachus, which runs by, or from Inachus the founder of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, whose name was also given to the river. The Argives, related, that this was one of the river gods who adjudged the country to Juno, when he contended for it with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, which deity in return made their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to vanish; the reason why the Inachus flowed only after <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, and was dry in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. The source was a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, not copious, on a mountain in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>, and the river served there as a boundary between the Argives and Mantineaus. Ancient Argos stood chiefly on a flat. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> were near the surface; and it abounded in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, which were said to have been invented by the daughters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANAUS">Danaus</a>. This early personage lived in the acropolis or citadel, which was named <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARISSA">Larissa</a>, and accounted moderately strong. On the ascent was a temple of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> on the ridge, which in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the seat of an oracle. The woman who prophesied was debarred from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>. A lamb was sacrificed in the night monthly; when, on telling of the blood, she became possessed with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. Farther on was a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADIUM">stadium</a>, where the Argives celebrated games in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Nemean <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and of Juno. On the top was a temple of Jupiter, without a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, the statue off the pedestal. In the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> there, among other curious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, was a wooden Jupiter, with an eye more than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, having one in the forehead. This statue, it was said, was once placed in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Priam, who fled as a suppliant to the altar before it, when <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a> was sacked. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> was also the brazen tower in which Danaë, being confined there by her father, was deflowered by Jupiter. Argos retains its original name and situation, stand- ing near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which are the boundary of the plain, with Napoli and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> in view before it. The shining houses are whitened with lime or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>. Churches, mud-built cottages and walls, with gardens and open areas, are interspersed, and the town is of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. Above the other buildings towers a very handsome mosque shaded with solemn cypresses; and behind is a lofty hill, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> and naked, of a conical form, the summit crowned with a neglected castle. The devastations of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> have effaced the old city. We look in vain (says Mr Chandler) for vestiges of its numerous edifices, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, the gymnasium, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, and monuments, which it once boasted, contending even with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> in antiquity and in favours conferred by the gods. **Argos Amphilocheum**, (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a>), a city of Arcadia, (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCYLAX">Scylax</a>, Pliny); its territory Ambrachia: situated on the east side of the Sinus Ambracius, (Thucydides); distant an hundred and eighty stadia to the south-east of Ambracia, (Polybius). Also called Argia Amphilochea, (Mela); Amphiloce and Amphilochei the people, (Stephanus). The name is from Amphilocheus, son of Amphiarus; and from Argos, the name of his country, in Peloponnesus, (Thucydides). **Argos Hippium**. See Argos in Peloponnesus, supra. **Argos Hippium**, the ancient name of Arpi; but Lampe is a still more ancient; afterwards called Argyrippa, and Argyrippa; built by, and the residence of, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOMEDES">Diomedes</a>, on the Ceralus, (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>); afterwards a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and populous city, (Livy): A town of Apulia; now in ruins, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called Arpi. **Argos Pelasgicum**, (Homer); an appellation denoting Thelytia; so called from the Pelagi. **Argos Portus**, a port of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, (Strabo): now Porto Ferraro, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELBA">Elba</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11° 30'. N. Lat. 42° 35'.

ARGUIM

Pages 251-251

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, about sixteen miles distant from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLANCO">Blanco</a>, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16° 30'. N. Lat. 20° 20'. It is scarce two miles in length; notwithstanding which, it was a bone of contention for 87 years between the Portuguese, Dutch, English, and French; and, after a variety of fortune, has at last been totally abandoned. This island was first discovered by the Portuguese in 1444, when a fleet bound to the east touched at Arguim, and from some little trade carried on with the natives, it was imagined that a settlement there might be of some advantage to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, a fort was erected on the island, and the Portuguese enjoyed the peaceable possession of it till 1638. At this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the Dutch having received a minute account of the condition of the island, resolved to attack it; and accordingly landed without molestation from the garrison, which was too weak to oppose them. The Portuguese, however, defended themselves with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> intrepidity, and at last surrendered upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> terms. The Dutch immediately let about repairing the fortifications, and securing it in the best manner they could: however, in 1665, the fort was reduced almost to a heap of rubbish by an English squadron; but as the fortifications were totally destroyed, and only a small garrison left there, it was easily retaken by the Dutch the next year. They now redoubled their diligence in strengthening the island, entering into <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with Moorish chiefs, procuring a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of families to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> under protection of the fort, and giving extravagant prices for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, in order to monopolize the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> trade. By this means the gum trade of the French <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENEGAL">Senegal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> was almost entirely destroyed; upon which they fitted out a squadron, dispossessed the Dutch, and had the island finally ceded to them by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of Nimeguen. Though the Dutch now seemed to be finally expelled, they resolved not to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> so easily with such a valuable settlement. Under pretence of being subjects of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, therefore, they erected one of the forts which had been demolished, and there maintained themselves in spite of the utmost endeavours of the French Company to dispossess them. Numerous were the memorials, protests, recriminations, &c., which were published on this occasion, till a new <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> in 1701 put an end to them. In 1717, however, the French Company having found all their remonstrances ineffectual, fitted out a new squadron; but this armament did not arrive at Arguim before Feb. 26, 1721. The Dutch defended themselves with such intrepidity and conduct as had almost baffled the utmost efforts of the French; but the latter having found means to draw off a Moorish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> from his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>, the Dutch were obliged to evacuate Arguim, and retire to Portendic, where they fortified themselves, determining to watch a favourable opportunity for recovering their settlement at Arguim. This was not long wanting, by means of the weakness of the garrison and the imprudence of Duval the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>; who having quarrelled with the Moors, was surprised, defeated, and killed by them; in consequence of which, the settlement fell again into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Dutch on the 11th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1722. In 1723, the Dutch were attacked by another French squadron under the command of the Sieur Rigaudiere. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> boasted that the fort could not hold out one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; but though he prevailed so far as to get possession of the cisterns which contained the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of the besieged, he was at last shamefully repulsed, and forced to raise the siege with precipitation. The Dutch, however, did not long enjoy the possession which they had so bravely defended; for, in 1725, their fort was entirely demolished by the French under Du Caffe, and has never since been rebuilt by any European <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>.

ARGUMENT

Pages 251-251

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, and Logic, an inference drawn from premises, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of which is indubitable, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at least highly probable. See Logic. **Argument**, in Matters of Literature, denotes also the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">abridgment</a> or heads of a book, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>, &c. See Syllabus.

ARGUMENTATION

Pages 251-251

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of inventing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> framing arguments, of making inductions, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> conclusions. See Induction, &c. Argumentation, according to Cicero, is the delivering or unfolding of an argument.—The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of arguments is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>; the form, their due disposition, with regard to one another, so as a conclusion may be drawn from them. See Enthymeme, Proposition, Ratiocination, Sorites, Syllogism, &c.

ARGUS

Pages 251-252

in Fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, was the son of Ariadne, and had 100 eyes, 50 of which were always open. Juno made choice of him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> Io, whom <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> had <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARGUS_SHELL">Argus-shell</a> had transformed into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> heifer, but Jupiter, pitying Io for being so closely confined, sent <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, who, with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>, charmed Argus to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, sealed up his eyes with his caduceus, and then cut off his head; when Juno, to reward his fidelity, turned him into a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a>, and placed his eyes in his tail. Argus-shell, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> shell, beautifully variegated with spots, resembling in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> those in a peacock's tail. ARGUTIÆ, witty and acute sayings, which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> signify something further than what their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> words at first sight seem to import. Writers on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> speak of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> species of argutiae, viz. ARGUTIAE <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> alieno, when something is said, which seems repugnant either to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of a thing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, the laws, &c., which yet in reality is consistent therewith; or when something is given as a reason of another, which yet is not the reason of it. For instance, Si Cainus nihil didicisset, errasset minus; again, Aureum boe faculum est, quia plurimum jam auro bonos venit. ARGUTIAE ab allusione, those wherein allusion is made to some history, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, proverb, or the like; e.g. Multi umbrae captant et carmen amittunt. ARGUTIAE à comparatione, when two things are compared together, which yet at first sight appear very different from each other, but so as to make a pretty kind of simile or diurnal; e.g. Par est pauper ille cuipiens principi omnia habent. ARGUTIAE à repugnantibus, when two things meet in a subject, which yet regularly cannot be therein; or when two things are opposed to each other, yet the epithet of the one is attributed to the other, e.g. Dum tacent clamant.

ARGYLLSHIRE

Pages 252-253

one of the counties of Scotland, supposed to have formed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Caledonian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, when the eastern provinces of Scotland submitted to the irresistible power of the Roman empire. It is bounded on the east by the shires of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERTH">Perth</a> and Dunbarton; on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>; on the west and south by the Irish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and the frith of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a>, which enter into various bays, sounds, and inlets, round the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, and form both in the mainland and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, many spacious and commodious harbours. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> is subdivided into the districts of Kintyre, Knapdale, Argyll Proper, Cowal, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORN">Lorn</a>. Within the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> are also comprehended several Hebridian islands, of which two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three are of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. Its length from south to north, between the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULL">mull</a> of Kintyre and the point of Ardnamurchan, where it joins the shire of Inverness, is about 114 miles, and its breadth, in several places, including the isles, is 70. The inland part of the county is, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, with an appendent triangle. Similar to the other parts of the Highlands of Scotland, this county presents a very wild and horrid prospect of hills, rocks, and huge <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, piled upon each other in a stupendous and dreadful disorder, bare, bleak, and barren to the view; or, at best covered with shaggy heath, which appears <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and dismal to the eye, except in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, when it is variegated with an agreeable bloom of a purple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. Hence lofty mountains, deep glens, inlets of the sea entering far into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, form the most striking features in Argyllshire, the general aspect of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Cruachan Ben in this country is one of the loftiest mountains in Scotland, and where this county meets the confines of Perth and Dunbarton, the mountains contiguous to Ben-Lomond are but little inferior in height to that mountain. The Loch Fine, Loch Etive, Linne Loch, are inlets of the sea. The district of Kintyre enters into the north channel, and is almost divided from the main land at the narrow isthmus of Tarbat. The district of Cowal is also nearly peninsulated by Loch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a> on one side and Loch Fine on the other. The interior parts of the county are interspersed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small fresh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>. A barrenness of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and scanty vegetation prevail chiefly on the summits of the great mountains, which exhibit great masses of stratified rocks or groups in a columnar form. Even a number of the glens are barren, and afford little pasturage, and are covered in several places with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fragments, which have been separated and precipitated from the impending rocks. On the declivities of the hills and the banks of the lakes there are, however, numerous woods intermixed, which unite with the lofty mountains to form a most romantic <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>. In a run of several miles, fertility, verdure, and cultivation, reign through the valley of Glenurchay. Remains of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> forests are still very extensive in various places, and these consist chiefly of oaks, alces, pines, and birches. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the country, towards the southern parts, descends the nearest to an equality with that of the sea. The elevation of the country is highest towards the interior parts of the counties of Perth and Inverness. The mountains and forests abound with fallow-deer, roes, flags, and all kind of wild <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>; and all over the sea coast the moors, the heaths, and on the lakes the wild fowl are numerous. The mountains feed an innumerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of black cattle, which run wild among the hills in winter as well as summer. The circumambient sea, with its lochs, bays, and harbours, pours forth myriads of fish; and in several places of the country <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> and minerals have been dug out. Yet, notwithstanding these numerous local advantages, Argyllshire, as well as the other parts of the Highlands, struggles with many great obstructions in the way of improvement. The want of long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEASES">leases</a> is one of the most material. What inducement can a person have to manure or cultivate a piece of land which he may have taken, when his first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is to erect a hut for himself; and after all the disagreeable inconveniences attending it, he holds his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>, year by year, dependent on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of his landlord? When he also reflects, that by cultivating his ground in such a manner, the rent which he was this year scarcely able to pay, may be nearly doubled the next year, how can he be able to defray the expense necessarily attending such an improvement, when he is uncertain of a competent return for his labour? It is hoped that proprietors will at length see the manifest advantage that will arise from granting long leases, both to themselves and their tenants; and, by so doing, either to encourage the tenants to build houses, by paying any expense that may remain unpaid at the end of the lease, or build houses for the tenants themselves; and, by these means, they would have surer payment of their rents, which would be augmented; their grounds would be greatly improved, and their vassals would enjoy comfort and ease. Another great obstacle to the general improvement is the rugged <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of this county, which renders the great <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> few in number, and the intersected roads for the purpose of conveying manure to the grounds being still in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> rudeness. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> branch of husbandry followed over the greatest part of this country is the management of sheep, black cattle, and goats. In former times, the ordinary animal stock consisted mostly of black cattle: but within these last 20 years a more skilful method of managing flocks of sheep than was formerly practised, having been introduced by the farmers of the low country; these have been multiplied with great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and affluency. Cows and oxen now form only the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> considerable branch of the animal flock. Barley, oats, and potatoes, are the principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of crop; and, in some places, the proper manner of tillage has been made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, excellent manures have been laid upon the ground, and the most suitable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a> of crops has been adopted. In years of ordinary plenty it would appear, that besides affording a considerable surplus to the breweries and distilleries, the grain <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> produced in this county is a sufficient sustenance for its inhabitants. Besides the great profits arising from the iron works and the salmon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> of woods has brought much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> into Argyll, and still continues to be equally beneficial to the labourer and the landlord. When the projected canal shall be completed, and some villages and harbours erected, the populous county of Argyll (Mr Knox affirms) will become one of the most valuable provinces of the British empire. Wafted on both sides by the sea; deeply indented by navigable lakes and bays; having an easy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> grounds on the north Highlands, with Glasgow and the trading <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> on the Clyde, with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITEHAVEN">Whitehaven</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, and other marts on the west coast of England; we may easily conceive, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> is at no great distance when Argyllshire will become a great commercial county. To corroborate this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> he observes, that after a vessel gets under sail from this coast, she enters at once into the Atlantic, where she meets with no interruption till she makes the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> or the West Indies. The line, therefore, which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> out for the inhabitants is that of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-making, fishing, ship-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, freight, or the carrying trade; <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> and glass-making, by means of the kelp upon their shores, and sand found upon the islands of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURA">Jura</a> and Gigha, which is adapted for the latter. In this district the deeds of the celebrated Fingal, whose invincible arm gave a check to the progress of the conquerors of the world, were mostly achieved. Many of the scenes of the battles of that illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> and his gallant followers, which are so beautifully described by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OSSIAN">Ossian</a>, are still pointed out, and many very ancient monuments still display the warlike spirit of its former inhabitants. In the course of the eighth and ninth centuries, Argyll, along with the neighbouring isles, was conquered by the Danes and Norwegians. For five or six centuries it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> under the dominion of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, and during that period was under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> administration of feudal chieftains, generally of Norwegian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>, who each maintained an almost independent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Along with the Hebridean isles, all the western parts of Argyll became the conquest of the Scottish monarchs in the fourteenth century. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, Macdonald, the representative of this region, obtained leave from the Scottish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> to hold his possessions as a feudatory to that kingdom; but the turbulent spirit of him and his family could not remain in quietude, and therefore their rebellions were punished with forfeiture. Their estates and titles were bestowed on the Campbells; and these have ever since retained them in peace and loyalty, beloved and honoured by their country. The county of Argyll gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the chief of this family. He likewise enjoys several other important posts under the crown, and is the chief of the Scottish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>.* His vassals are so numerous, that in former times he could on occasion bring 3000 or 4000 fighting men into the field. Argyllshire is generally peopled by this clan, and affords a great number of castles and seats belonging to gentlemen who hold of the duke, and boast themselves descended from his family. Argyllshire sends one member to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>: it is also the seat of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a>. It contains 2 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> boroughs and 49 parishes; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of which is as follows. | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">Parish</a> | Population in 1755 | Population in 1790-1798 | |-----------------|-------------------|------------------------| | Ardchattan | 2195 | 2400 | | Ardnamurchan | 5000 | 4542 | | Campbelltown | 4597 | 8700 | | Craignish | 769 | 770 | | Dunoon | 1757 | 1683 | | Glaffary | 2751 | 2568 | | Glenorchy | 1654 | 1869 | | <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERARY">Inverary</a> | 2751 | 1832 | | Invercaolin | 944 | 504 | | Kilbrandon | 1492 | 2060 | | Kilcalmonell | 1925 | 2448 | | Kilcrenman | 1030 | 1124 | | Kilfinan | 1793 | 1417 | | Killeean | 2391 | 1911 | | Kilmadan | 806 | 351 | | Kilmartin | 1150 | 1537 | | Kilmore | 1200 | 1886 | | Kilninver | 1045 | 1178 | | Knapdale, North | 1309 | 1509 | | Knapdale, South | 1292 | 1524 | | Lifmore | 2812 | 3526 | | Lochgoylehead | 1505 | 1012 | | Morven | 1223 | 1764 | | Saddel | 1309 | 1341 | | Southend | 1391 | 1300 | | Strachur | 1193 | 1061 | **ISLANDS** | <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a> | Population in 1790-1798 | |-----------------|-------------------------| | Torofay | 1012 | | Mull | | | Kilfinichen | 1685 | | Kilninian | 2590 | | Ilay | | * This is the Crinan canal, which is now navigable.

ARGYRASPIDES

Pages 253-254
or Argyroaspides, in Antiquity, persons armed with silver bucklers, or bucklers silvered. The argyraspides, according to Quintus Curtius, made the second corps of Alexander's army; the first was the phalanx.—According to Justin's account, lib. xii. cap. 7. Alexander having penetrated into India, and extended his empire as far as the ocean; for a monument of his glory, ordered the armour of his soldiers, and the houfings of his horses, to be adorned with silver. And hence commanded them to be called argyraspides, from the Greek ἀγγύρος, silver, and ἀσπίς, buckler. By this author it should seem, that Alexander's whole army were called argyraspides.—After that prince's death, the argyraspides despised all other chiefs of the army, disdaining to obey any other, having borne arms under Alexander. ARGYRIPÆ. See Argos Hippium.

ARGYRUNTUM

Pages 254-254

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town of Illyria (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, Pliny). Nor Novigrad, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17° 30'. N. Lat. 44° 32'.

ARHUSEN

Pages 254-254

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUTLAND">Jutland</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, to the south of Wilburg, about 60 miles in length and 30 in breadth. It contains two <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> cities, called Arhusen and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANDERS">Randers</a>; besides several market <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, and upwards of 300 villages. Arhusen, one of the capitals, is advantageously situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, at the mouth of the river Guda, which runs through it; and it is surrounded with forests full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10° 0'. N. Lat. 56° 10'.

ARIA

Pages 254-254

and Ariana, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, whether the same <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> distinct countries authors are not agreed. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> has only Aria, and knows nothing about Ariana. Pliny mentions only Ariana, and says nothing about Aria; but distinguishes between the Arii and Ariani: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTHIA">Parthia</a>, he says, has the Arii to the east, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARAMANIA">Caramania</a> and the Ariani to the south; from which it is conjectured, the Ariani extended farther than the Arii, and comprised the Gedrosia and the Drangae. Arrian has only Aria and Arii, and is silent about Ariana.
