But Strabo gives more extensive bounds to Ariana than to Aria, without particularly defining them; only in general he says, that Ariana begins from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, and quotes Eratothenes; according to whom, Ariana is bounded by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDUS">Indus</a> on the east; on the south by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; by Paropamius on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, quite to Portae Caspiae; on the west by the same boundaries by which Parthia is separated from Media, Caramania from Paracene and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>; and thus Ariana is extremely extensive.—Aria has its limits thus described by Ptolemy: On the north, some parts of Margiana and Bactriana; on the east, the Paropamisdae; on the south the Drangiana; and Strabo says, the Arii adjoin to the Paropamisdae on the west.

ARIADNE

Pages 254-254
daughter of Minos king of Crete, Theseus being sent to destroy the Minotaur, Ariadne was so taken with him, that, as a testimony of her love, she gave Theseus a clue of thread to guide him out of the labyrinth. Theseus, having killed the Minotaur, carried off the Athenians he had relieved, together with Ariadne; whom, however, he afterward forsook.

ARIADNEA

Pages 254-254

in Grecian Antiquity, two festivals at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAXOS">Naxos</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of two women named Ariadne. One of them being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a>, they had, in the solemnity dedicated to her, a show of sorrow and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a>; and, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of her being left by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a> near the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of child-birth, it was usual for a young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> and counterfeit all the agonies of a woman in labour. This festival is said to have been first instituted by Theseus, to atone for his ingratitude to that princess.—The other Ariadne was thought to be of a gay and sprightly temper; and therefore her festival was observed with music and other expressions of mirth and joy.

ARIANA

Pages 254-254

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an extensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, comprising Paropamius, Arachosia, Drangiana, and Gedrosia, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we suppose it to reach to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. See Aria.

ARIANNA

Pages 254-254

a small village six miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>. Here is a beautiful range of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Carthaginian aqueduct, 74 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, supported by columns 16 feet <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and which still increased in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> the nearer it approached <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> are all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> cut. Near this spot several ancient magazines, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> subterranean magazines for corn, have been discovered within these few years, capable of containing 100 bushels, strongly arched with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> square stones. The Moors have already begun to demolish them, it being their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> to do so with every thing beautiful as soon as it comes to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>.

ARIANO

Pages 254-254

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, in the Ulterior Principality, with a bishop's see. Mr Swinburne describes it as an ugly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, built upon the uneven summit of a mountain, with an extensive look-out on all sides, but exposed to every blast that blows. It does not appear to be so old as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; therefore may be supposed to owe its rise to the demolition of some neighbouring town, and to the advantages its situation afforded for discovery and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. It is but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, without

ARIANS

Pages 254-255

followers of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIUS">Arius</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESBYTER">presbyter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> about the year 315; who maintained, that the Son of God was totally and essentially distinct from the Father; that he was the first and noblest of those beings whom God had created, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> by whose subordinate operation he formed the universe; and therefore inferior to the Father both in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>; also, that the Holy Ghost was not God, but created by the power of the Son. The Arians owned that the Son was the Word, but denied that Word to have been eternal. They held, that Christ had nothing of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in him but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, to which the ἀνάγκη <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Word was joined, which was the same as the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> in us. See Lardner's Credibility, &c. vol. ix. book i. c. 69. The Arians were first condemned and anathematized by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> at Alexandria in 320, under Alexander, bishop of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>; who accused Arius of impiety, and caused him to be expelled from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> of the church; and afterwards by 380 fathers in the general council of Nice, assembled by Constantine in the year 325. But, notwithstanding that, it was not extinguished; on the contrary, it became the reigning <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, especially in the east, where it obtained much more than in the west. Arius was recalled from banishment by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Constantine in two or three years after the council of Nice, and the laws that had been enacted against him were repealed. In the year 335, Athanasius, his zealous opponent, was deposed and banished into <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, and Arius and his followers were reinstated in their privileges, and received into the communion of the church. In little more than a year after this, he fell a victim to the resentment of his enemies, and died a tragic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, occasioned probably by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, or some other violence. The Arian party found a protector in Constantius, who succeeded his father in the empire of the east; and the zeal with which he abetted them produced many animosities and tumults to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his death in the year 362. They underwent various revolutions, persecuting and oppressing, under succeeding emperors, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> they had in the civil power, till at length Theodosius the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> exerted every possible effort to suppress and dispel them. The Arians were divided into various sects, of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers give an account under the names of Semi-Arians, Eusebians, Aetians, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUNOMIANS">Eunomians</a>, Acacians, Pothiers, and others. But they have been <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> distributed into three classes, viz. the Genuine Arians, Semi-Arians, and Eunomians. Arianism was carried in the fifth century into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> under the Vandals; and into <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, the Gauls, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, were also deeply infected with it; and towards the commencement of the sixth century, it was triumphant in many parts of Asia, Africa, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. But it sunk almost all at once, when the Vandals were driven out of Africa, and the Goths out of Italy, by the arms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>. However, it revived again in Italy under the protection of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOMBARDS">Lombards</a> in the seventh century. Erasmus seems to have aimed in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to restore Arianism at the beginning of the sixteenth century, in his Commentaries on the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. Accordingly, he was reproached by his adversaries with Arian interpretations and glosses, Arian tenets, &c. To which he made little answer, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> that there was no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> more thoroughly extinct than that of the Arians: Nulla heresis magis extincta quam Arianorum. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of things was soon changed. Servetus, a Spaniard by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, published in 1531 a little treatise against the Trinity, which once more revived the opinions of the Arians in the west. Indeed he rather showed himself a Photinian than an Arian; only that he made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of Scripture, and the same arguments against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> of our Saviour, with the proper Arians. It is true, Servetus had not, properly speaking, any disciples; but he gave occasion after his death to the forming of a new system of Arianism in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, much more subtle and artful than his own, and which did not a little perplex Calvin. From Geneva the new Arians removed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, where they gained considerable ground; but at length became Socinians. The appellation Arian has been indiscriminately applied in more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times, to all those who consider <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ as inferior and subordinate to the Father; and whose sentiments cannot be supposed to coincide exactly with those of the ancient Arians. Mr Whitton was one of the first divines who revived this controversy, in the beginning of the 18th century. He was followed by Dr Clarke, who published his famous book, entitled "The Scripture Doctrine of the Trinity," &c. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which, he was reproached with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Semi-Arian. He was also threatened by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a>, and combated by argument. Dr <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATERLAND">Waterland</a>, who has been <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with verging towards Tritheism, was one of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> adversaries. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this controversy during the present century, may be found in a pamphlet, entitled, "An Account of all the considerable Books and Pamphlets that have been wrote on either Side, in the Controversy concerning the Trinity, from the Year 1712; in which is also contained an Account of the Pamphlets written this last Year, on each side, by the Diffenters, to the End of the Year 1719." Published at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> 1720.

ARICA

Pages 256-256

a port town of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Los Charcas, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>. It was formerly a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, but the earthquakes, which are frequent here, have almost entirely ruined it; for there are no more than 150 families, which are most of them blacks, mulattoes, and Indians. Most of the houses are made with canes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> reeds, set upright, and bound together with cords or thongs; and as it never rains here, they are covered only with mats, which makes the place look at a distance like a heap of ruins. The vale of Arica is about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> wide, and five leagues <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, next the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and is all a barren <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, except the spot where the old town stood, which is divided into little meadows of clover grass, and plots for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> canes, with a few olive and cotton trees intermixed. This vale grows narrower as it runs eastward; and a league up there is a village, where they begin to cultivate pimento or Jamaica <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, which is planted throughout all the rest of the vale; and there are several farms, which produce nothing else, that bring in the value of 80,000 crowns yearly. The Spaniards of Peru are so used to this pepper, that they dress no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> without it. W. Long. 70° 15'. S. Lat. 18° 26'.

ARICINA

Pages 255-256

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>; under which appellation she was honoured in the forest Aricine, so called from Aricia a princess of the blood <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. Hippolytus, to whom this princess was married, is said to have erected a temple to Diana in this forest, where he was concealed after his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> by Esculapius, and to have established a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> and festivals.

ARICONIUM

Pages 256-256

a town of the Silures, (Antonine); now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a>, (Camden). W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2° 42'. Lat. 52° 6'.

ARIDAS

Pages 256-256

a kind of taffety, manufactured in the East Indies from a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> thread which is got from certain herbs, whence they are styled aridas of herbs.

ARIDULLAM

Pages 256-256

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a kind of zarchich found in the East Indies. See ZARCHICH.

ARIES

Pages 256-256

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a constellation of fixed stars, drawn on the globe, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a ram. It is the first of the twelve figures of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>, from which a twelfth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ecliptic takes its denomination.

ARILLUS

Pages 256-256

an improper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> invented by Linnaeus, and defined to be the proper exterior coat <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> covering of the feed which falls off spontaneously. All feeds are not furnished with an arillus; in many, a dry covering, or scarf skin, supplies its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. In jasmine; <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HOUND">hound</a>'s tongue, cynoglossum; cucumber; fraxinella, dictamnus; <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> tree, celastrus; spindle tree, euonymus; African spirea, diofma; and the coffee tree, coffee; it is very confusious. In the genus hound's tongue, four of these arilli or proper coats, each enfolding a single seed, are affixed to the stylus; and in this circumstance, says Linnaeus, does the essence of the genus consist. In fraxinella, the arillus is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to two feeds. The staff tree has its seeds only half involved with this cover. The arillus is either baccatus, succulent, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a berry; as in the spindle tree, euonymus. Carilagineus, cartilaginous, or griffly; as in the African spirea, diofma. Coloratus, coloured; as in the staff tree, Elaficus, ended with elasticity, for differing the feeds; as is remarkable in the African spirea, diofma, and fraxinella. Scaber, rough and knotty; as in hound's tongue. Although covered with an arillus or other dry coat, feeds are said to be naked (Jemina nuda) when they are not enclosed in any <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of pericarpium or fruit velvety; as in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, and the labiati or lipped <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of Tournefort, which correspond to the didynamia gymnoferma of Linnaeus. Seeds are said to be covered (Jemina testa) when they are contained in a fruit velvety, whether <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPSULE">capsule</a>, pod, or pulpy pericarpium, of the apple, berry, or cherry kind: (See SEMEN). This exterior coat of the seed is, by some former writers, styled calyptra. See CALYPTRA. The different skins or coverings of the feed, are adapted, lay naturalists, for receiving the nutritive juices, and transmitting them within.

ARIMANIUS

Pages 256-257

the evil god of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Persians. The Persian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGI">Magi</a> held two principles; a good demon, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> god, and an evil one: the first the author of all good, and the other of all evil: the former they supposed to be represented by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and the latter by darkness, as their truest symbols. The good principle they named Yezad or Tefdan, and Ormazd or Hormizda, which the Greeks wrote Oromazdes; and the evil demon they called Abriman, and the Greeks Arimanus. Some of the Magians held both these principles to have been from all eternity; but this fact was reputed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HETERODOX">heterodox</a>: the original doctrine being, that the good principle only was eternal, and the other created. —Plutarch (De Iside et Osiride, p. 369.) gives the following account of the Magian traditions in relation to these gods, and the introduction of evil into the world, viz. That Oromazes consisted of the most pure light, and Arimanus of darkness; and that they were at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with each other: that Oromazes created six gods; the first, the author of benevolence; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>; the third, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> which attends good actions; and that Arimanus made as many, who were the authors of the opposite evils or vices: that then Oromazes, triplicating himself, removed as far from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> as the sun is from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and adorned the heaven with stars, appointing the dog <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> for their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> and leader: that he also created 24 other gods, and enclosed them in an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>; but Arimanus having also made an equal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, these last perforated the egg, by which means evil and good became mixed together. However, the fatal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> come, when Arimanus, the introducer of plagues and famine, must be of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> utterly destroyed by the former, and annihilated; then the earth being made plain and even, mankind shall live in a happy state, in the same manner, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, and using one and the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Theopompos writes, that, according to the Magians, the laid two gods, during the space of 3000 years, alternately conquer, and are conquered; that for other 3000 years, they will ARIASPI will wage mutual war, fight, and destroy the works of each other, till at last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HADES">Hades</a> (or the evil spirit) shall perish, and men become perfectly happy, their bodies needing no food, nor casting any shadow, i.e. being perfectly transparent.

ARIMASPI

Pages 257-257

(Pliny), a people of Sarmatia Europea, to the south of the Montes Ripheei, said by Melo to have but one eye; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> broached by Aristeas Proconnesius, according to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>.

ARIMATHEA

Pages 257-257

a town of Judea, (Evangelists); thought to be the same with Ramatha, 1 Sam. i. and thus in the tribe of Ephraim, (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a>).—This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is now called Ramla; and is in a very ruinous state, containing nothing but rubbish within its boundaries. The aga of Gaza resides here in a Serai, the floors and walls of which are tumbling <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. He maintains about one hundred horsemen, and as many Barbary folderies, who (says Mr Volney) are lodged in an old Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the nave of which is used as a stable, and in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> khan, which is disputed with them by the scorpions. The adjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is planted with lofty olive trees, disposed in quincunces. The greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of them are as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as the walnut trees of France; but they are daily perishing through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, the ravages of contending factions, and even from secret mischief: for, in these countries, when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a> would <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> himself of his enemy, he comes by night, and saws <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cuts his trees <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the ground, and the wound, which he takes care to cover, draining off the sap like an issue, the olive tree languishes and dies. Amid these plantations, we meet, at every step, with dry wells, cisterns fallen in, and vast vaulted reservoirs, which prove that, in ancient times, this town must have been upwards of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> and a half in circumference. At present it scarcely contains two hundred families. The little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> which is cultivated, by a few of them, belongs to the mufti, and two or three persons related to him. The rest content themselves with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> cotton, which is chiefly purchased by two French houses established there. The only remarkable antiquity at Ramla is the minaret of a ruined mosque on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to Yafa, which is very lofty; and by an Arabic inscription appears to have been built by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> Saladin.

ARIMINUM

Pages 257-257

a town of Umbria, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Romagna, at the mouth of the Ariminus, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. The seizing on it by Caesar gave rise to the civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. Now called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIMINI">Rimini</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13. 32. Lat. 44. 8.

ARIOLI

Pages 257-257

in Antiquity, a kind of prophets, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> conjurers, who by abominable prayers, and horrible sacrifices at the altars of idols, procured answers to their questions concerning future events. Ibid. Orig. lib. viii. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 9. These are also called bariolii, and the operation bariolation. Sometimes they were denominated aruspices or haruspices. The ariolii were distinguished by a floventy dress, disorderly and matted beards, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, &c.

ARION

Pages 257-257

an admirable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, much more famous in poetic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> than Bucephalus in that of Alexander. Authors speak variously of his origin, though they agree in giving him a divine one. His production is most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> ascribed to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>. This god, according to some, raised him out of the ground by a stroke of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIDENT">trident</a>; according to others, he begot him upon the body of the fury Erinnyes; according to others, upon that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>, whom he ravished in the form of a horse, having previously assumed the form of a mare to elude his pursuit. This horse was nursed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEREIDS">Nereids</a>; and being sometimes yoked with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> horses of Neptune to the chariot of this god, he drew him with incredible swiftness through the sea. He had this singularity in him, that his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> feet resembled those of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. Neptune gave him to Capreus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Hallartus. Capreus made a present of him to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>; who mounted him when he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIS">Elis</a>, gained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> with him in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> against Cygnus the son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a> near Tracena, and at last made a present of him to Adrafinus. It is under this last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> that Arion has signalized himself the most: he won the prize for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACING">racing</a> at the Nemean games, which the princes who went to behove Thebes instituted in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Archemonus; and was the cause that Adrafinus did not perish in this famous expedition as all the other chiefs did.

ARIOSTO LOROVICO

Pages 257-258

the famous Italian poet, and author of Orlando Furioso, was born at the castle of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGGIO">Reggio</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a> in 1474. His father, who was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> domo to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, lived to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of his fortune, so left but little at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Ariosto, from his childhood, showed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> marks of genius, especially in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>; and wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> on the story of Pyramus and Thisbe, which his brothers and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a> played. His father being utterly unlearned, and rather regarding profit than his son's inclination, compelled him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, in which having plodded some years to no purpose, he quitted it for more pleasing studies; yet often lamented, as Ovid and Petrarch did before him, and our own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> fancied, that his father banished him from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>.* See his At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 24, Ariosto lost his father, and found Latin poem, himself perplexed with family affairs. However, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">Ad</a> Patrem, about five years he was, for his good parts, taken into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a> Hippolito, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol9.html#article-ESTE">Este</a>. At this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he had written nothing but a few sonnets; but now he resolved to make a poem, and chose Bayardo's Orlando Inamorato for a groundwork. However, he was prevented <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> for a great many years, and was chosen as a fit person to go on an embassy to Pope Julio II. where he gave such satisfaction, that he was sent again, underwent many dangers and difficulties, and at his return was highly favoured. Then, at his leisure, he again applied himself to his poem; but, soon after, he incurred the cardinal's displeasure for refusing to accompany him into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>; by which he was so discouraged, that he deferred writing for 14 years, even till the cardinal's death. After that, he finished by degrees, in great perfection, that which he began with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a>. Duke Alfonso offered him great promotions <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he would serve him; but preferring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, he refused this and other great offers from princes and cardinals, particularly from Leo X. from all whom he received notwithstanding great presents. The duke of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a> delighted. Ariosto delighted so much in his comedies, of which he wrote five, that he built a stage on purpose to have them played in his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and enabled our poet to build himself a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in Ferrara, with a pleasant garden, where he used to compose his poems, which were highly esteemed by all the princes in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, who sent him many presents; but he said, "I would not sell his liberty for the best cardinal's hat in Rome." It was but a small, though convenient house: being asked, why he had not built it in a more magnificent manner, since he had given such noble descriptions of sumptuous palaces, beautiful porticos, and pleasant fountains, in his Orlando Furioso? he replied, That words were cheaper laid together than <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Upon the door was the following inscription: Parva, sed opta mihi, sed nulli obnoxia, sed non Sordida, parva meo sed tamen ære, donum. Which Mr <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARRINGTON">Harrington</a> thus translates: This house is small, but fit for me, but hurtful unto none; But yet not fluttilh, as you see, yet paid for with mine own. In his diet he was temperate, and so careless of dainties, that he was fit to have lived in the world when they fed upon acorns. Whether he was ever married, is uncertain. He kept <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with one <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, to whom, it was reported, he was married privately, and a lady Genevera, whom he filly mentions in the 24th book of his Orlando, as poets are apt to intermix with their fictions some real amours of their own. He was urged to go <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to Pope Clement, but would by no means accept this embassy. He translated the Menechmi of Plautus: and all his own comedies were so esteemed, that they were frequently acted by persons of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; and when his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENA">Lena</a> was first represented, Ferdinand of Este, afterwards marquis of Maffa, so far honoured the piece as to speak the prologue. He began one of his comedies in his father's lifetime, when the following incident shows the remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> he had for poetry. His father one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> rebuked him sharply, charging him with some great fault; but all the while he returned him no answer. Soon after, his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> began on the same subject: but he easily refuted him, and, with strong arguments justified his own behaviour. "Why then (said his brother) did you not satisfy my father?" "In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> (said Lodovico) I was thinking of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> in my comedy; and methought my father's speech to me was so suited to the part of an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s chiding his son, that I forgot I was concerned in it myself, and considered it only to make it a part of my play." It is also reported of Ariosto, that coming by a potter's shop, he heard him singing a stanza out of his Orlando, with so bad a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, that, out of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>, he broke with his stick several of his pots. The potter, in a pitiful tone, asking what he meant by wronging a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> man than had never injured him? "You rascal (he replied), I have not done thee half the wrong thou hast done me: for I have broken but two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three pots of thine, nor worth so many halfpence; whereas thou hast broken and mangled a stanza of mine worth a mark of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>." Ariosto was tall, of a melancholy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>, and so absorbed in study and meditation, that he often forgot himself. His <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> was drawn by Titian in a masterly manner. He was honoured with the laurel by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. He was naturally affable, always assuming less than was his due, yet never putting up a known injury, even from his superiors. He was so fearful on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, that, whenever he went out of a ship, he would see others go before him; and, on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, he would alight from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> on the least <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of danger. He was of an amorous disposition, and left two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> sons. He enjoyed the friendship of the most eminent men of learning of his time, most of whom he mentions with great respect in the last <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTO">canto</a> of his Orlando Furioso. His <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> was but weakly, so that he was obliged to have recourse to physicians the greatest part of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He bore his last sicknesses with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> and serenity; and died at Ferrara the 8th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1533, according to Sir John Harrington, being then 59 years of age. He was interred in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the Benedictine monks, who, contrary to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, attended his funeral. He had a bust erected to him, and the following epitaph, written by himself, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> upon his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>: Ludovici Ariosti humantur ossa Sub hoc marmore, seu sub hac humo, seu Sub quidquid voluit benignus hæres, Sive haerede benignior comes, seu Opportunius incidens viator: Nam feire haud potuit futura: sed nec Tanti erat, vacuam fibi cadaver Ut urnam cuperet parare. Vivens ita tamen fibi paravit, Quae scribi voluit fuo sepulchro, Olim si quod haberet id sepulchrum: Ne cum spiritus hoc brevi pereat Prefcripto spatio millesim artus, Quos segre ante reliquerat, repofcat, Hac et hac cinerem huc et huc revellem Dum nocat proprium, diu vagetur.

ARIPO

Pages 258-258

a town on the western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Ceylon, at the mouth of the river Sarunda. To the east of this town is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, where they fish for pearls. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 80. 25. N. Lat. 8. 42.

ARISBA

Pages 258-258

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LESBOS">Lesbos</a> (Herodot.)—Another of Troas on the continent, in the territory and to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABYDOS">Abydos</a> (Polyb.) : the rendezvous of Alexander's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> after the passage of the Hellespont (Arrian); a colony of the Mitylenians (Stephanus); taken and plundered by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a> (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>). The residence of Axylus, celebrated by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> for his hospitality, which gained him the character of Friend of Mankind.

ARISI

Pages 258-258

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> name for the plant which produces the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>. See ORYZA, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ARISTA

Pages 258-258
or AwN, among Botanists, a long needle-like beard, which stands out from the husk of a grain of corn, grass, &c. ARISTÆUS, son of Apollo and Cyrene, whom, for the many services he had rendered to mankind by his knowledge of all profitable arts, the gods placed amongst the stars; so that he is the Aquarius in the zodiac. The resemblance of his history to that of Moles has been curiously discredited by Huetius.

ARISTANDER

Pages 258-259

a famous footsayer under Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, over whom he gained a wonderful ful influence by the good success of his art. He had already had the same employment at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>; and it was he who explained better than his brethren the dream that this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> had after having married Olympias.

ARISTARCHUS

Pages 259-259

a celebrated grammarian, much esteemed by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> Philometor, who committed to him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of his son. He applied himself chiefly to criticism, and made a revival of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>'s poems, but in too magisterial a way; for such verses as he did not like he treated as spurious. He commented on other poets. Cicero and Horace made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his name to express a very rigid critic. ARISTIDA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ARISTIDES

Pages 259-262

surnamed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">Just</a>, one of the most celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> for purity and integrity, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Themistocles, was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LYCURGUS">Lycurgus</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of middle <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, and born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. His dispositions and temper from his youth all conjoined in anticipating that greatness to which he afterwards arose. To a firm, resolute, and placid temper, he likewise added a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> contempt of dissimulation, and an utter abhorrence of every thing dishonourable. He began very early to meditate on subjects of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and applied to his studies with the greatest avidity. He imbibed a strong predilection for oligarchy upon becoming acquainted with the laws of Lycurgus, which excited his admiration, and gave him a distaste of the unlimited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEMOCRACY">democracy</a> then established in his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, Themistocles favoured democracy; and even when at school, he is said to have been his constant antagonist on that point. A perpetual opposition to one another in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, whether just <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> unjust, was the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> when their abilities raised them to several important stations in the state. Although it was deemed absolutely necessary at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> for a party leader to oppose all the acts of his antagonist whatever with the greatest vehemence, yet Aristides did not follow this practice without self-reproach. It is related, that one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> having firmly opposed a proposal of Themistocles in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, which in his own confidence he knew to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, on coming out he exclaimed, "The affairs of the Athenians <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> never prosper, till they throw both of us into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARATHRUM">barathrum</a>" (the dungeon for condemned criminals). Aristides maintained a strict observance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and when in his own opinion a friend was guilty, he would never screen him from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> due to his offence. Neither desirous of profit nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, he served his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> from the purest principles of duty; and his character was so universally known, that once, when the verses of Alcæus, describing Amphiarus, were recited in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, "To be, and not to seem, is this man's maxim; His mind repose on its conscious worth, And wants no other praise." the eyes of the whole assembly were immediately directed towards Aristides, as the true <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of the idea the poet wished to delineate. When in the office of public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, by convicting Themistocles and several others of making free with the public <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, he raised up a party against himself; and when he gave in his own account, they, to retaliate the affront, accused him of embezzling the public stores; and it was only by the interpolation of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AREOPAGUS">Areopagus</a> that he got himself cleared. He was, however, again elected to that office, and then, although he kept a secret account against those people concerned with him, he permitted them to plunder without reprehension. It consequently fell out that he was universally praised, his acquaintance cultivated with the greatest avidity, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> made on all sides to continue him in office: But when the people were about to proceed to elect him again to that trust, he fervently chided them, and said, "that while he had served them with fidelity he was treated with calumny, and incurred their displeasure; now that he had really violated his trust, he met with general applause, and was reckoned an excellent citizen." He then exhibited their deceits, and made all parties ashamed of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> they had acted. Aristides was present at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARATHON">Marathon</a>, fought B.C. 490, and was next in command among the Athenians to Miltiades; and there, upon that general's proposing to come to battle as soon as possible, he seconded his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> with the utmost vigour. In the field he distinguished himself with intrepidity, valour, and generosity; and being left after the battle to secure the spoils, he executed his trust with honour and fidelity, bringing all to the public account, reserving nothing for himself. He was elected to the important office of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> the year following; but by the art of Themistocles, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> authority he had attained by his merits was at length converted into an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> against him; and he was accordingly banished by the ostracism, although a mild, often an unjust <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> in the policy of the Athenian state, for getting a temporary relief from the presence of any political influence by which they thought their independence might be injured. A circumstance which occurred on this occasion gives a very high idea of his character. A rustic citizen coming up to vote against him, although not personally acquainted with Aristides, and being himself unable to write, ordered the first person whom he met, who accidentally happened to be Aristides himself, to inscribe his name upon the shell, signifying his acquiescence in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of the state. The patriot said, "Did Aristides ever injure you?" The rustic replied, "I do not so much as know him, but I am tired with everywhere hearing him called the Just."—Aristides, taking the shell, wrote his own name upon it, and returned it in silence to the voter. Lifting up his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> to heaven, he supplicated that the Athenians might never behold the day which should induce them to remember Aristides; and then quitted the city. As the Persians were meditating a new invasion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, he employed himself in his exile in encouraging the Greeks to defend their liberties against the invaders. The Athenians immediately, upon the approach of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a>, recalled Aristides, whose absence they began sincerely to regret, along with their other exiles, At this critical moment, upon his return, he suspended all political animosities; and upon understanding that it was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of Themistocles to fight the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> in the straits of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMIS">Salamis</a>, he waited on him in private, proposed an oblivion of all past circumstances, extolled his intentions, and gave him his sincere <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> to do the utmost in his power towards effecting their designs. Themistocles, some time after the battle of Salamis, acquainted the Athenians that he had formed a scheme which, although it was of such a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> as forbade his public avowal of it to them, was of inestimable advantage to the state. They immediately ordered that he should communicate it to Aristides. It was a project for confining the whole confederate fleet of Greece by fire, except their own ships; and thus the entire sway of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> would be left to the Athenian navy. Aristides reported that nothing could be more unjust, and at the same time nothing more advantageous than the scheme of Themistocles. Upon this report, the people immediately determined to drop any further thought of it. It was equally to the honour of the Athenians that they made such a determination, and to Aristides that he was made the referee on this occasion. Aristides, before the battle of Platæa, was of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in persuading his countrymen, who were elevated with their former successes, to submit to the superior power of the Spartans, and in preserving peace and amity between the confederate forces. He acquitted himself with great valour and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> in the engagement, and was appointed after the victory to determine a very dangerous dispute concerning the honour of the day, which he conferred upon the Platæans, giving up the claim of the Athenians, the Lacedemonians following his example. Upon the rebuilding of Athens, he was the first person to promote a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> which divided the administration among the citizens at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and enjoined that the archons, or chief magistrates, should be elected out of the whole body of the people, who had so deservedly merited the favour of the state. Aristides, upon the continuation of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Persians, was sent along with Cimon, the son of Miltiades, to take the command of the Athenian forces in the confederate <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. Their humility and meekness, compared with the haughty domineering temper of Pausanias, so engaged the rest of the allies, that the superiority of rank was conferred upon Athens, with the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> concurrence of the other states. The nomination of Aristides to lay an equal afflament upon all the states for the purpose of defraying the expense of the war, was a signal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the high idea all Greece had of his integrity and justice. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and impartiality with which he performed this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> gave universal satisfaction. He obliged all the confederates, after this affair was terminated, solemnly to swear to all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a>. The advice which he afterwards gave the Athenians to extend their own territories beyond their proper limits must certainly have proceeded from some very pressing <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, when he thus drew <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the consequences of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a> upon his own head. Aristides, on Themistocles's falling under the displeasure of the ruling party, would not concur in a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> prosecution of him; and instead of triumphing over an old enemy, he always spoke of him after his banishment with the highest respect. In that age it was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> for men who had borne Aristides the highest public offices to make no increase to their private fortunes, but no man ever carried this disinterestedness to so high a pitch as Aristides. He was indeed to remarkably <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, that when a prosecution was raised against Callias, a rich relation of his, the orator pleading against him, in order to excite the indignation of his audience, made some remarks upon his ability to assist Aristides, and at the same time upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> indigence in which he permitted him and his family to live. Callias, in his vindication, was forced to call Aristides to testify that he had frequently offered him considerable sums, which he would not accept, saying, "that it better became Aristides to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> in his poverty than Callias in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>," which appear to have been acquired not very honourably. This great man died about 407 years B.C. according to some at Athens, at an advanced age; others say at Pontus, where he was transacting public business. He was buried at the public expense, and his daughters received portions out of the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>; and a pension and an estate in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> was bestowed on his son Lyfimachus, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> for the signal services Aristides had done his country. (Gen. Biog.) Aristides of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILETUS">Miletus</a>, a famous Greek author, often cited by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. Aristides, a very eloquent Athenian orator, who became a convert to the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and about the year 124 presented to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Adrian an apology for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. Aristides, Ælius, a celebrated orator, born in Mytilene, about 129 years before the Christian era. The best edition of his works is that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, printed in Greek and Latin, in two volumes quarto. Aristides, a painter contemporary with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APELLES">Apelles</a>, flourished at Thebes about the 122d Olympiad. He was the first, according to Pliny, who expressed character and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind, and its several emotions; but he was not remarkable for softness of colouring. "His most celebrated picture was of an infant (on the taking of a town) at the mother's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, who is wounded and expiring. The sensations of the mother were clearly marked, and her fear left the child, upon failure of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, should suck her blood." Alexander the Great (continues the same author) took this picture with him to Pella. Junius (in his Treatise de Pictura Veterum) conjectures that the following beautiful epigram of Æmilianus was written on this exquisite picture: Ελεύθερον ἀνάστατον ναῦς κατὰ Φυλίππους, Η δὲ γυνὴ ἐξέρεσται λιπασμένης ἀλλὰ τα μόρια Φιλέτης καὶ ἐν αἰώνιον παιδεύοντας εὐφρονεῖ. Elegantly translated thus: Suck, little wretch, while yet thy mother lives, Suck the last drop her fainting bosom gives! She dies! her tendernels survives her breath, And her fond <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> is provident in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Webb's Inquiry, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAL">Dial</a>. VII. p. 161. Aristippus, the founder of the Cyrenaic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, was the son of Areteas, and born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRENE">Cyrene</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>. He flourished about the 96th Olympiad. The great reputation of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> induced him Aristippus to leave his own country, and remove to Athens, that he might have the satisfaction of hearing his discourses. He was chiefly delighted with those discourses of Socrates that related the most to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; which he affected to be the ultimate end in which all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> consists. His manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was agreeable to his opinion; for he indulged himself extremely in all the luxuries of dress, wine, and women. Though he had a good estate, and three country seats, yet he was the only one of the disciples of Socrates who took <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> for teaching; which being observed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, he asked Aristippus, How he came to have so much? Who in reply asked him, How he came to have so little? Upon his leaving Socrates, he went to Aegina, as Athenaeus informs us, where he lived with more freedom and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> than before. Socrates sent frequent exhortations to him, in order to reclaim him; but all in vain; and with the same view he published that discourse which we find in Xenophon. Here Aristippus became acquainted with Laïs, the famous courtezan of Corinth; for whose sake he took a voyage to that city. He <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> at Aegina till the death of Socrates, as appears from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>'s Phaedo, and the epistle which he wrote upon that occasion. He returned at last into his own country Cyrene, where he professed philosophy, and instituted a sect which, as we observed above, was called the Cyrenaic, from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and by some writers the Hedonic or voluptuous, from its doctrines. During the height of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> of Dionysius the Sicilian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>, a great many philosophers resorted to him; and among the rest Aristippus, who was tempted thither by the magnificence of that court. Dionysius asking him the reason of his coming, he replied, "That it was in order to give what he had, and to receive what he had not;" or, as others represent it, "That when he wanted wisdom, he went to Socrates; but now as he wanted money, he was come to him." He very soon infatuated himself into the favour of Dionysius; for being a man of a soft easy temper, he conformed himself exactly to every place, time, and person, and was a complete <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of the most refined complaisance. We have several remarkable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> concerning him during his residence at that court mentioned by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> Laërtius. Dionysius, at a feast, commanded that all should put on women's purple habits, and dance in them. But Plato refused, repeating these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>: I cannot in this gay effeminate dress Disgrace my manhood or my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a> betray. But Aristippus readily submitted to the command, and made this reply immediately: — At feasts, where mirth is free, A sober mind can never be corrupted. At another time, interceding with Dionysius in behalf of a friend, but not prevailing, he <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> himself at his feet: being reproved by one for that excess of humility, he replied, "That it was not he who was the cause of that submission; but Dionysius, whose ears were in his feet." Dionysius showed him three beautiful courtezans, and ordered him to take his choice. Upon which he took them all three away with him, alleging that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> was punished for preferring one to the other two; but when he had brought them to his door, he dismissed them, in order to show that he could either enjoy Aristippus or reject with the same indifference. Having desired money of Dionysius, the latter observed to him, that he had assured him a wife man wanted nothing. "Give me (says he) what I ask, and we will talk of that afterwards." When Dionysius had given it him, "Now (says he), you see I do not want." By his complacence he gained so much upon Dionysius, that he had a greater regard for him than for all the rest of the philosophers, though he sometimes spoke with such freedom to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, that he incurred his displeasure. When Dionysius asked, Why philosophers haunted the gates of rich men, but not rich men those of philosophers; he replied, "Because the latter know what they want, and the others not." Another time, Dionysius repeating (out of Sophocles, as Plutarch affirms, who ascribes this to Zeno) these verses, He that with tyrants seeks for bare support, Enslaves himself, though free he came to court; he immediately answered, He is no slave, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he be free to come. Diogenes, as Laërtius informs us, related this in his Lives of the Philosophers; though others ascribe this saying to Plato. Aristippus had a contest with Antitheus the Cynic philosopher; notwithstanding which, he was very ready to employ his interest at court for some friends of Antitheus, to preserve them from death, as we find by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of his to that philosopher. Diogenes followed the example of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> Antitheus in ridiculing Aristippus, and called him the courtesan. We have many apophthegms of his preferred. To one who asked him what his son would be the better for being a scholar? "If for nothing else (said he), yet for this alone, that when he comes into the theatre, one <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> will not fit upon another." When a certain person recommended his son to him, he demanded 300 drachmas; and upon the father's replying, that he could buy a slave for that sum, "Do so (said he), and then you will be master of a couple." Being reproached, because, having a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of law depending, he fee'd a lawyer to plead for him, "Just so (said he), when I have a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a> to make, I always hire a cook." Being asked what was the difference between a wise man and a fool, he replied, "Send both of them together naked to those who are acquainted with neither of them, and then you will know." Being reproved by a certain person (who, according to Mr Stanley, was Plato) for his costly and voluptuous feasts, "I warrant you (said he), that you would not have bestowed three farthings upon such a dinner;" which the other confessing, "Why, then (said he), I find myself less indulgent to my palate than you are to your covetous humour;" or, as it is otherwise represented, "I find, that I love my belly, and you love your money." When Simus, treasurer to Dionysius, showed him his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> magnificently furnished, and paved with costly marble, (for he was a Phrygian, and consequently profuse;) Aristippus spit in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>: upon which the other growing angry, "Why, truly (said he), I could not find a fitter place." His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> carrying after him a great <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of money, and being ready to sink upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> under his burden, Aristippus burden, he bid him throw away all that was too much for him to carry. Horace mentions this fact in his third satire of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> book: Quid simile illi? Gracius Arilippus & qui servos proiecer aurum In media jusit Libyae, quia tardius irent Propter onus fognes. Being asked, what things were most proper for children to be instructed in? he answered, "Those which might prove of the greatest advantage to them when they came to be men." Being reproached for going from Socrates to Dionysius, he replied, "That he went to Socrates when he wanted serious instruction, and to Dionysius for diversion." Having received money of Dionysius at the same time that Plato accepted a book only, and being reproached for it, "The reason is plain (says he), I want money, and Plato wants books." Having lost a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>, he said to one who seemed excessively to compassionate his loss, "You have but one field; I have three left; why should not I rather grieve for you?" Plutarch, who relates this in his book, De Tranquillitate Animi, observes upon it, that it is very absurd to lament for what is lost, and not to rejoice for what is left. When a person told him, "That the land for his sake was lost," he replied "That it was better so, than that he should be lost for the land." Being cast by shipwreck ashore on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, and perceiving mathematical schemes and diagrams drawn upon the ground, he said, "Courage, friends; for I see the footsteps of men." After he had lived a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time with Dionysius, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Arete sent to him, to desire his presence at Cyrene, in order to take care of her affairs, since she was in danger of being oppressed by the magistrates. But he fell sick in his return home, and died at Lipara, an Eolian island. With regard to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> opinions, like Socrates, he rejected the sciences as they were then taught, and pretended that logic alone was sufficient to teach <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and fix its bounds. He asserted, that pleasure and pain were the criterions by which we were to be determined; that these alone made up all our passions; that the first produced all the soft emotions, and the latter all the violent ones. The assemblage of all pleasure, he asserted, made true happiness, and that the best way to attain this was to enjoy the present moments. He wrote a great many books: particularly the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Libya, dedicated to Dionysius; several Dialogues; and four books of the Luxury of the ancients. There are four epistles of his extant in the Socratic collection published by Leo Allatius. Besides Arete his daughter, whom he educated in philosophy, Aristippus had also a son, whom he disinherited for his stupidity. Arete had a son who was named Aristippus from his grandfather, and had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Menodotus, from his mother's instructing him in philosophy. Among his auditors, besides his daughter Arete, we have an account of Aethiops of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMAIS">Ptolemais</a>, and Antipater of Cyrene. Arete communicated the philosophy which she received from her father to her son Aristippus, who transmitted it to Theodorus the Athenian, who instituted the sect called Theodorean. Antipater communicated the philosophy of Aristippus to Epitomedes his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a>; Epitomedes to Parabates; Parabates to Hegesias and Anniceris; Aristocracy and these two last improving it by some additions of their own, obtained the honour each of them of giving a name to the Hegesiae and Annicerian sect.

ARISTO

Pages 262-262

a Stoic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Zeno the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the Stoics, flourished about 290 years before the Christian era. He differed but little from his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> Zeno. He rejected logic as of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> as being above the reach of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> understanding. It is said, that being bald, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> burnt his head; and that this caused his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>.—There is a saying of his recorded, which might render the doctrine of Aristippus less obvious than it ordinarily is; (see Aristippus). He used to say, "That a philosopher might do those of his hearers a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> who put a wrong interpretation upon good meanings; as for example that the school of Aristippus might send out debauchees, and that of Zeno Cynics," which seems to imply, that the doctrine of this philosopher never produced this effect but when it was misunderstood. He should also have added, that every teacher is therefore obliged to forbear laying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> ambiguous maxims, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to prevent false glosses being put upon them.

ARISTOCRACY

Pages 262-262

a form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> where the supreme power is vested in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> persons of the state. The word is derived from αριστος, optimus, and κρατος, impero, "I govern." The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers of politics prefer the aristocratical form of government to all others. The republic of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> is an aristocracy. Aristocracy seems to coincide with oligarchy; which, however, is more ordinarily used to signify a corruption of an aristocratical state, where the administration is in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of too few, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> where some one or two usurp the whole power.

ARISTOGITON

Pages 262-262

a famous Athenian, who, with Harmodius, killed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIPPARCHUS">Hipparchus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, about 513 years before the Christian era. The Athenians erected a statue to him.

ARISTOMENES

Pages 262-262

a general of the Messenians, renowned for his valour and virtue. See Messenia.

ARISTOPHANES

Pages 262-263

a celebrated comic poet of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. He was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a>; and most of his plays were written during the Peloponnesian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. His imagination was warm and lively, and his genius particularly turned to raillery. He had also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> spirit and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>; and was a declared enemy to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>, and to all those who wanted to oppress their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The Athenians suffered themselves in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to be governed by men who had no other views than to make themselves masters of the commonwealth. Aristophanes exposed the designs of these men, with great <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and severity, upon the stage. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEON">Cleon</a> was the first whom he attacked, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> of the Equites; and as there was not one of the comedians who would venture to personate a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of his great authority, Aristophanes played the character himself, and with so much success, that the Athenians obliged Cleon to pay a fine of five talents, which were given to the poet. He described the affairs of the Athenians in so exact a manner, that his comedies are a faithful <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of that people. For this reason, when Dionysius <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a> desired to learn the state and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of Athens, Plato sent him the comedies of Aristophanes, telling him, these were the best representations thereof. He wrote above 50 comedies; but there are only 11 extant which are perfect: these are, Plutus, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">Clouds</a>, the Frogs, Equites, the Acharnenses, the Wasps, Peace, the Birds, the Ecclesiazusae <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">Female</a> Orators, the Themopho- diazusae or Priestesses of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>, and Lystrata.
