The Clouds, which he wrote in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> of Socrates*, is the most celebrated of all his comedies. Madame Dacier tells us, she was so much charmed with this performance, that after she had translated it, and read it over 200 times, it did not become the least tedious to her, which she could not say of any other piece; and that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> which she received from it was so exquisite, that she forgot all the contempt and indignation which Aristophanes deserved for employing his wit to ruin a man, who was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> itself, and the greatest ornament of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Athens. Aristophanes having conceived some aversion to the poet Euripides, satirizes him in several of his plays, particularly in his Frogs and his Themophodiazusae. He wrote his Peace in the 10th year of the Peloponnesian war, when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> for 50 years was concluded between the Athenians and the Lacedemonians, though it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years. The Acharnenses was written after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERICLES">Pericles</a> and the loss of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, in order to dissuade the people from intrusting the safety of the commonwealth to such imprudent generals as Lamachus. Soon after, he represented his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVES">Aves</a> or Birds; by which he admonished the Athenians to justify Decelea, which he calls by a fictitious name Nephelococygia. The Vespas, or Wasps, was written after another loss in Sicily, which the Athenians suffered from the misconduct of Chares. He wrote the Lystrata when all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> was involved in a war; in which comedy the women are introduced debating upon the affairs of the commonwealth; when they come to a resolution, not to go to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> with their husbands till a peace should be concluded. His Plutus, and other comedies of that kind, were written after the magistrates had given orders that no person should be exposed by name upon the stage. He invented a peculiar kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, which was called by his name, and is mentioned by Cicero in his Brutus; and Suidas says, that he also was the inventor of the tetrameter and octameter verse. Aristophanes was greatly admired among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, especially for the true Attic elegance of his style. The time of his death is unknown; but it is certain he was living after the expulsion of the tyrants by Thrasybulus, whom he mentions in his Plutus and other comedies. There have been several editions and translations of this poet. Nicodemus Frischin, a German, famous for his classical knowledge, in the 16th century, translated Plutus, the Clouds, the Frogs, the Equites, and the Acharnenses, into Latin verse. Quintus Septimus Florens, rendered into Latin verse the Wasps, the Peace, and Lystrata; but his translation is full of obsolete words and phrases. Madame Dacier published at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1692, a French version of Plutus and the Clouds, with critical notes, and an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of them according to the rules of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Theobald likewise translated these two comedies into English, and published them with remarks. The most noble edition of this author is that published Aristotelia by Ludolphus Kuter, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, in folio, in 1710, and dedicated to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Montague <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a>.

ARISTOTELIA

Pages 263-263

in Antiquity, annual feasts celebrated by the citizens of Stagyra, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, who was born there; and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> for his having procured from Alexander the rebuilding and repopulation of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, which had been demolished by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>.

ARISTOTELIAN

Pages 263-263

something that relates to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>. ARISTOTELIAN <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, the philosophy taught by Aristotle, and maintained by his followers. The Aristotelian is otherwise called the Peripatetic Philosophy. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIPATETICS">Peripatetics</a>.

ARISTOTELIANS

Pages 263-263

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of philosophers, otherwise called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIPATETICS">Peripatetics</a>. The Aristotelians and their dogmata prevailed for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> while in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>; even in spite of all the efforts of the Cartesians, Newtonians, and other corporealists. But the systems of the latter have at length gained the pre-eminence; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEWTONIAN_PHILOSOPHY">Newtonian <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> in particular is now very generally received. The principles of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARISTOTLE_S_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" href="</a>vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s philosophy, the learned agree, are chiefly laid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in the four books de Caelo; the eight books of Physical Axiomata, φυσικῶν ἀξιωμάτων, belonging rather to logic, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>, than to physics. Instead of the more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> systems, he introduced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, form, and privation, as the principles of all things; but he does not seem to have derived much benefit from them in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> philosophy. His doctrines are, for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, so obscurely expressed, that it has not yet been satisfactorily ascertained what were his sentiments on some of the most important subjects. He attempted to refute the Pythagorean doctrine concerning the twofold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; and pretended to demonstrate, that the matter of the heavens is ungenerated, incorruptible, and subject to no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a>; and he supposed that the stars were carried round the earth in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> orbs. The reader <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> find a distinct account of the logical part of his philosophy, by Dr Reid professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral philosophy</a> in the university of Glasgow, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> volume of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Kames's Sketches of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>. Mr Harris has published a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> on his Categories, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Philosophical Arrangements.

ARISTOTLE

Pages 263-264

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the Peripatetic philosophers, born at Stagyra, a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> in Macedon, in the 99th Olympiad, about 384 years before the birth of Christ. He was the son of Nicomachus, physician to Amyntas the grandfather of Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>. He lost his parents in his infancy; and Proxenus, a friend of his father's, who had the care of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, taking but little notice of him, he quitted his studies, and gave himself up to the follies of youth. After he had spent most of his patrimony, he entered into the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; but not succeeding in this profession, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a> to consult the oracle what course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he should follow; when he was advised to go to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. He accordingly went thither about 18 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and studied under <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> till he was 37. By this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he had spent his whole fortune; and we are told that he got his living by selling powders, and some receipts in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>. He Aristotle followed his studies with most extraordinary diligence, so that he soon surpassed all in Plato's school. He ate little, and slept less; and that he might not overleep himself, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> Laërtius tells us, that he lay always with one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>, having a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> of braids in it, which, by its falling into a basin of the same metal, awakened him. We are told, that Aristotle had several conferences with a learned Jew at Athens, and that by this means he instructed himself in the sciences and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the Egyptians, and thereby saved himself the trouble of travelling into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. When he had studied about 15 years under Plato, he began to form different tenets from those of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, who became highly piqued at his behaviour. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Plato, he quitted Athens; and retired to Aetarnya, a little city of Myttra, where his old friend Hermias reigned. Here he married Pythias, the sister of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, whom he is said to have loved so passionately, that he offered sacrifice to her. Some time after, Hermias having been taken prisoner by Mardon, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>'s general, Aristotle went to Mitylene the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Leibos, where he remained till <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> king of Macedon having heard of his great reputation, sent for him to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> him to his son Alexander, then about 14 years of age: Aristotle accepted the offer; and in eight years taught him <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> philosophy, ethics, politics, and a certain sort of philosophy, according to Plutarch, which he taught nobody else. Philip erected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Aristotle; and for his sake rebuilt Stagyra, which had been almost ruined by the wars. The last fourteen years of his life he spent mostly at Athens, surrounded with every assistance which men and books could afford him for prosecuting his philosophical inquiries. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of Alexander's name, which then filled the world, ensured tranquillity and respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> whom he distinguished as his friend: but after the premature death of that illustrious protector, the invidious jealousy of priests and sophists inflamed the malignant and superstitious fury of the Athenian populace; and the same odious passions which proved fatal to the offensive virtue of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, fiercely assailed the fame and merit of Aristotle. To avoid the cruelty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>, he secretly withdrew himself to Chalcis in Euboea. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> was sufficiently justified by a prudent regard to his personal safety; but his conduct should appear unmanly, when contrasted with the firmness of Socrates in a similar situation, he condescended to apologize for his flight, by saying, that he was unwilling to afford the Athenians a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> opportunity "to sin against philosophy." He seems to have survived his retreat from Athens only a few months; vexation and regret probably ended his days. Besides his treatises on philosophy, he wrote also on <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, rhetoric, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, &c., to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 400 treatises, according to Diogenes Laërtius; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more, according to Francis Patricius of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. An account of such as are extant, and of those said to be lost, may be seen in Fabricius's Bibliotheca Graeca. He left his writings with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a>, his beloved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> and successor in the Lyceum; and forbade that they should ever be published. Theophrastus, at his death, trusted them to Neleus, his good friend and disciple; whose heirs buried them in the ground at Scopis, a town of Troas, to secure them from the king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERGAMUS">Pergamus</a>, who made great search everywhere for books to adorn his library. Here they lay concealed 160 years, until, being almost spoiled, they were sold to one Apollon, a rich citizen of Athens. Sylla found them at this man's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and ordered them to be carried to Rome. They were some time after purchased by Tyrannion a grammarian: and Andronicus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a> having bought them of his heirs, was in a manner the first restorer of the works of this great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>; for he not only repaired what had been decayed by time and ill keeping, but also put them in a better order, and got them copied. There were many who followed the doctrine of Aristotle in the reigns of the 12 Caesars, and their numbers increased much under Adrian and Antoninus: Alexander Aphrodisius was the first professor of the Peripatetic philosophy at Rome, being appointed by the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus; and in succeeding ages the doctrine of Aristotle prevailed among almost all men of letters, and many commentaries were written upon his works. The first doctors of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> disapproved of the doctrine of Aristotle, as allowing too much to reason and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>; but Anatolius bishop of Laodicea, Didymus of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, St Jerome, St Augustin, and several others, at length wrote and spoke in favour of it. In the fifth age, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOETHIUS">Boethius</a> made him known in the west, and translated some of his pieces into Latin. But from the time of Boethius to the eighth age, Joannes Damascenus was the only man who made an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">abridgment</a> of his philosophy, or wrote any thing concerning him. The Grecians, who took great pains to restore learning in the 11th and following ages, applied much to the works of this philosopher, and many learned men wrote commentaries on his writings: amongst these were Alfarabius, Algazel, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AVICENNA">Avicenna</a>, and Averroes. They taught his doctrine in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and afterwards at Cordova in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. The Spaniards introduced his doctrine into France, with the commentaries of Averroes and Avicenna; and it was taught in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, until Amauri having supported some particular tenets on the principles of this philosopher, was condemned of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> held there in 1210, when all the works of Aristotle that could be found were burnt, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> of them forbidden under pain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCOMMUNICATION">excommunication</a>. This prohibition was confirmed, as to the physics and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>, in 1215, by the pope's legate; though at the same time he gave leave for his logic to be read, instead of St Augustin's used at that time in the university. In the year 1265, Simon, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> of St Cecil, and legate from the holy see, prohibited the reading of the physics and metaphysics of Aristotle. All these prohibitions, however, were taken off in 1366; for the cardinals of St Mark and St Martin, who were deputed by Pope Urban V. to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> the university of Paris, permitted the reading of those books which had been prohibited: and in the year 1448, Pope Stephen approved of all his works, and took care to have a new translation of them into Latin.

ARISTOXENUS

Pages 264-266

one of the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> musical writers, was born at Tarentum, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> in Magna Graecia, now <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>. He was the son of a musician, and it appears that he lived about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> and his first successors. His Harmonies <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>. A R I T H M E T I C. Arithmo- nies in three books, all that are come <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to us, together with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s Harmonics, were first published by Gogavimus, but not very correctly, at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, 1562, in 4to, with a Latin version. John Meurisius next translated the three books of Arithmoxenus into Latin, from the MS. of Jof. Scaliger; but according to Meibomius, very negligently. With these he printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, 1616, 4to, Nicomachus and Alpyius, two other Greek writers on music. After this, Meibomius collected these musical writers together; to which he added Euclid, Bacchius senior, Ariftides Quintilianus; and published the whole with a Latin version and notes, from the elegant press of Elzevir, Amt. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">ARITHMETIC</a> Is a science which explains the properties of numbers, and shows the method <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> art of computing by them. History of Arithmetic. At what time this science was first introduced into the world, we can by no means determine. That some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, however, was coeval with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> is absolutely certain. We cannot conceive how any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> endowed with reason can be without some knowledge of numbers. We are indeed, told of nations in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> who have no word in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> to express a greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> than three; and this they call paxarrarvorinouroac: but that such nations should have no idea of a greater number than this, is absolutely incredible. Perhaps they may compute by threes, as we compute by tens; and this may have occasioned the notion that they have no greater number than three. But though we cannot suppose any <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, or indeed any single person, ever to have been without some knowledge of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between, greater and smaller numbers, it is possible that mankind may have subsisted for a considerable time without bringing this science to any perfection, or computing by any regular <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, as 10, 60, &c. That this, however, was very early introduced into the world, even before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, we may gather from the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> in Enoch's prophecy, as mentioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> Jude: "Behold, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> cometh with ten thousands of his saints." This shows, that even at that time men had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of numbers as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as we have at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and computed them also in the same manner, namely by tens. The directions also given to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a> concerning the dimensions of the ark, leave us no room to doubt that he had a knowledge of numbers, and of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> likewise. When Rebekah was sent away to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>'s son, her relations wished she might be the mother of thousands of millions; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were totally unacquainted with the rule of multiplication, it is difficult to see how such a wish could have been formed. It is probable, therefore, that the four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> rules of Arithmetic have always been known to some nation or other. No doubt, as some nations, like the Europeans formerly, and the Africans and Americans now, have been immersed in the most abject and deplorable state of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, they might remain for some time unacquainted with numbers, except such as they had immediate occasion for; and, when they came afterwards to improve, either from their own industry, or hints given by others, might fancy that they themselves, or those from whom they got the hints, had invented what was known <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before. The Greeks were the first European nation among whom arithmetic arrived at any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection. M. Goguet is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that they first used pebbles in their calculations: a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of which he imagines is, that the word ἀριθμός, which comes from ἀριθμέω, a little <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, or flint, among other things, signifies to calculate. The same, he thinks, is probable of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; and derives the word calculation from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of little <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> (calculi) in their first arithmetical operations. If this method, however, was at all made use of, it must have been but for a short time, since we find the Greeks very early made use of the letters of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a> to represent their numbers. The 24 letters of their alphabet taken according to their order, at first denoted the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, and 800; to which they added the three following, r, s, Θ, to represent 6, 90, and 900. The difficulty of performing arithmetical operations by such marks as these may easily be imagined, and is very conspicuous from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHIMEDES">Archimedes</a>'s treatise concerning the dimensions of a circle. The Romans followed a like method; and besides <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> for each <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of classes, they introduced others for five, fifty, and five hundred. Their method is still used for distinguishing the chapters of books, and some other purposes. Their numeral letters and values are the following: I V X L C D M One, five, ten, fifty, one hundred, five hundred, one thousand. Any number, however great, may be represented by repeating and combining these according to the following rules: 1st. When the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> is repeated twice, or oftener, its value is represented as often. Thus II signifies two; XXX thirty, CC two hundred. 2nd. When a numeral letter of lesser value is placed after one of greater, their values are added: thus XI signifies signifies eleven, LXV sixty-five, MDCXXVIII one thousand five hundred and twenty-eight. 3d. When a numeral letter of lesser value is placed before one of greater, the value of the lesser is taken from that of the greater: thus IV signifies four, XL forty, XC ninety, CD four hundred. Sometimes IO is used instead of D for 500, and the value is increased ten times by annexing O to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>.

[1st.] 3592 at L. 3 : 12 : 8 | 72 20 | | --- | --- | | 7184 72 | | 25144 | At 45s. 165735 | 4d. = 1/5 of 1197 4 | | --- | --- | | At 1d. = 1/12 of 307 11 | | 4d. = 1/5 of 1197 4 | 44s. 11d. 165427 | 8d. | 26118 8 | | --- | --- | | L. 13050 18 8 | The learner should at first try every calculation more ways than one; which will not only serve the purpose of proving the operation, but will render him expert at discovering the best method for solving each question, and will lead him to invent other methods; for we have not exhausted the subject. Thus, if the number of articles be 20, each shilling of the rate makes a pound of the amount. If it be 12, each penny of the rate makes a shilling of the amount. If 240, each penny of the rate makes a pound of the amount. If 480, each halfpenny makes a pound. If 960, each farthing makes a pound. If the number of articles be a multiple, or an aliquot part of any of these, the amount is easily calculated. And if it be near to any such number, we may calculate for that number, and add or subtract for the difference. We have hitherto explained the various methods of computation, when the quantity is a whole number, and in one denomination. It remains to give the proper directions when the quantity contains a fraction, or is expressed in several denominations. When the quantity contains a fraction, work for the integers by the preceding rules, and for the fraction take proportional parts. When the quantity is expressed by several denominations, and the rate given for the higher; calculate the higher, consider the lower ones as fractions, and work by the last rule. When the rate is given for the lower denomination, reduce the higher denomination to the lower, and calculate accordingly. Note 1st, 7 lb. 14 lb. and 21 lb. are aliquot parts of 1 qr.; and 16 lb. is 1/4 of 1 cwt.; and are therefore easily calculated. 2d. If the price of a dozen be so many threepence, that of an article is as many pence; and if the price of a groat be so many threepence, that of a dozen is as many pence. 3d. If the price of a ton or score be so many pounds, that of 1 cwt. or a single article, is as many threepence. 4th. Though a fraction less than a farthing is of no consequence, and may be rejected, the learner must be careful lest he lose more than a farthing, by rejecting several remainders in the same calculation. Sect. II. Deductions on Weights, &c. The full weight of any merchandise, together with that of the cask, box, or other package, in which it is contained, is called the gross weight. From this we must make proper deductions, in order to discover the quantity, for which price or duty should be charged, which is called the net weight. Tare is the allowance for the weight of the package; and this should be ascertained by weighing it before the goods are packed. Sometimes, however, particularly in payment of duty, it is customary to allow so much per C. or so much per 100 lb. in place of tare. Tret is an allowance of 4 lb. on 104 granted on currants, and other goods on which there is waste, in order that the weight may answer when the goods are retailed. Cloff, or Draught, is a further allowance granted on some goods in London, of 2 lb. on every 3 C. to turn the scale in favour of the purchaser. The method of calculating these and the like will appear from the following examples. Ex. 1st. It is frequently required to calculate allowances on sums of money, at the rate of so many per 100. Of this kind is Commission, or the allowance due to a factor for buying or selling goods, or transacting any other business; Premium of Insurance, or allowance given for engaging to repay one's losses at sea, or otherwise; Exchange, or the allowance necessary to be added or subtracted for reducing the money of one place to that of another; Premiums on Stock, or the allowance given for any share of a public stock above the original value. All these and others of a like kind are calculated by the following Rule. "Multiply the sum by the rate, and divide the product by 100. If the rate contain a fraction, take proportional parts." Ex. What is the commission on 728l. at 2\(\frac{1}{2}\) per cent? \[ \begin{array}{c} 728 \\ \times 2\text{ per cent.} \\ \hline 1456 \\ \times \frac{1}{2} \\ \hline 364 \\ \times \frac{1}{4} \\ \hline 182 \\ \times 100 \\ \hline 20 \\ \times 20 \\ \hline 40 \\ \times 12 \\ \hline 480 \\ \times 4 \\ \hline 120 \\ \end{array} \] Answ. L. 20 — 4\(\frac{1}{2}\) When the rate is given in guineas, which is common in cases of insurance, you may add a twentieth part to the sum before you calculate. Or you may calculate at an equal number of pounds, and add a twentieth part to the answer. When the given sum is an exact number of 10 pounds, the calculation may be done without setting down any figures. Every 10l. at \(\frac{1}{2}\) per cent, is a shilling; and at other rates in proportion. Thus, 170l. at \(\frac{1}{2}\) per cent, is 17s.; and, at \(\frac{1}{2}\) per cent, 8s. 6d. Sect. IV. Interest. Interest is the allowance given for the use of money by the borrower to the lender. This is computed at so many pounds for each hundred lent for a year, and a like proportion for a greater or a less time. The highest rate is limited by our laws to 5 per cent, which is called the legal interest; and is due on all debts constituted by bond or bill, which are not paid at the proper term, and is always understood when no other rate is mentioned. The interest of any sum for a year, at any rate, is found by the method explained in the last section. The interest of any number of pounds for a year, at 5 per cent, is one twentieth part, or an equal number of shillings. Thus, the interest of 34675l. for a year is 34675 shillings. The interest for a day is obtained by dividing the interest for a year, by the number of days in a year. Thus, the interest of 34675l. for a day is found by dividing 34675 shillings by 365, and comes to 95 shillings. The interest for any number of days is obtained by multiplying the daily interest by the number of days. Thus the interest of 34675l. for 17 days, is 17 times 95 shillings, or 1615 shillings; and this divided by 20, in order to reduce it, comes to 80l. 15s. It would have served the same purpose, and been easier to multiply at first by 17, the number of days; and, instead of dividing separately by 365, and by 20, to divide at once by 7300, the product of 365 multiplied by 20; and this division may be facilitated by the table inserted p. 621, col. 1. The following practical rules may be inferred from the foregoing observations. I. To calculate interest at 5 per cent. Multiply the principal by the number of days, and divide the product by 7300. II. To calculate interest at any other rate. Find what it comes to at 5 per cent, and take a proper portion of the same for the rate required. Ex. 1st. Interest on 34675l. for 17 days, at 5 per cent. \[ \begin{array}{c} 34675 \\ \times 17 \\ \hline 242725 \\ \times 365 \\ \hline 89475(80) \\ \times 584 \\ \hline 5475 \\ \times 20 \\ \hline 109500 \\ \times 73 \\ \hline 365 \\ \times 365 \\ \hline 0 \\ \end{array} \] Ex. 2d. Interest on 304l. 3s. 4d. for 8 days, at 4 per cent. \[ \begin{array}{c} L. 304 \\ \times 3 \\ \times 4 \\ \times 8 \\ \hline 2433 \\ \times 7300 \\ \hline 58400 \\ \times 584 \\ \hline 0 \\ \end{array} \] Here the sums on either side of the account are introduced according to the order of their dates. Those on the Dr. side are added to the former balance, and those on the Cr. side subtracted. Before we calculate the days, we try if the last sum 91L be equal to the balance of the account, which proves the additions and subtractions; and, before multiplying, we try if the sum of the column of days be equal to the number of days, from 15th January to 31st July. In the 5th and 6th multiplications, we begin at the pence column, and take in the carriage. In the 7th, instead of multiplying the 6s. 8d. by 21, we add the third part 21 to the product, because 6s. 8d. is the third of a pound. This is done by marking down the second line 1287, instead of 1280. As the computation on the odd shillings and pence is troublesome, and makes a very small increase of the interest, some neglect them altogether; others add one to the pound, when the shillings exceed 10, and neglect them when below it.
