The Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> now, finding the cold very severe, though it was no later in the year than the autumnal equinox, requested their general to allow them to retire into winter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. This request he rejected with indignation; upon which they mutinied. Lucullus did all he could to persuade them to continue in their duty; and prevailed so far that they consented to lay siege to Nifbis in hopes of booty. This place they took; and Lucullus, to the great satisfaction of his troops, took up his winter quarters there. The next year, however, his forces again mutinied, accusing him of amassing immense wealth for himself; and throwing their empty purses at his feet, told him, that Armenia, as he enriched himself alone, he might carry on the war by himself. He endeavoured to appease them as much as possible; but the sedition being fomented by a party who favoured Pompey the Great, at that time aspiring to the command of Lucullus's army, the latter found himself obliged to fit still and see Mithridates and Tigranes overrun Cappadocia, and recover all Armenia and great part of Pontus. They would have gained much greater advantages, had not a son of Tigranes taken arms against his father, and obliged him to divide his troops. The father and son coming to a pitched battle, the latter was defeated, and forced to leave himself in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTHIA">Parthia</a>, where he persuaded Phraates, king of that country, to assist him with a numerous army against his father. Phraates having laid siege to Artaxata, Tigranes the elder was obliged to hide himself in the mountainous parts of his kingdom; upon which the king of Parthia returned home. Of this Tigranes the father being apprized, he immediately abandoned the fastnesses of the mountains; and falling upon his son at Artaxata, dispersed the rebels with great slaughter; and entered his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> in triumph. Tigranes the son first fled to Mithridates; but finding him reduced to great straits, having been overcome a few days before, with the loss of 40,000 men, by Pompey, he went over to the Romans, and led them into Armenia against his father as an ally of Mithridates. Tigranes, being now quite dispirited, and unable to make head against the Romans, resolved at once to submit. Accordingly he waited on Pompey in his camp, and having delivered his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> to two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LICTORS">lictors</a>, prostrated himself before him, and laid his diadem at his feet. Pompey, however, gave him a gracious reception, restored him the kingdom of Armenia, but fined him of 6000 talents for making war on the Roman people without cause. As the king had appealed to the Roman general for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> against his son, Pompey heard both parties the next day, and made the son governor of Gordyene and Sophene; but the treasures that were kept in the latter he adjudged to his father, because without them he could not pay the fine. The son, being thus disappointed, endeavoured first to make his escape, and afterwards, by private messengers, solicited the inhabitants not to deliver up the treasures to his father. This being taken very much amiss by Pompey, he cauled him to be kept in irons; and even then he found means to stir up Phraates king of Parthia, whose daughter he had married, against the Romans, and to form a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> against his father's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; whereupon Pompey sent him in chains to Rome, where he was kept prisoner in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of L. Flavius a senator, till the tribuneship of P. Clodius, who, being bribed with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, set him at liberty in spite of Pompey and the senate. Tigranes being now thoroughly humbled, willingly yielded to the Romans, Cappadocia, Syria, Cilicia, and that part of Phoenicia which he possessed, contenting himself with his paternal kingdom; and not only paid the fine laid upon him, but made large presents to Pompey, and all the officers of his army, which procured him the title of the friend and ally of the Roman people. He afterwards entered into a war with Phraates king of Parthia, by whom he was overcome, and would have been driven out of his kingdom, had not a peace been brought about by the mediation of Pompey. He ever after cultivated a strict friendship with the Romans; inasmuch that he not only refused to receive Mithridates, who fled to him after he had been routed by Pompey near Mount Stella, but even offered a reward of 150 talents to any one that would put him to death. His second son also, by name Sariafter, took up arms against him; but by the affiance of the Romans, that rebellion was soon quelled. He died in the 85th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and was succeeded by his son Artuadès, called by Josephus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTABAZUS">Artabazus</a>, by Orosius Artabanus, and by others Artanides. From this time to the time of Trajan, Armenia was governed by its own kings; but as they were plainly vassals to the Romans, though they did not take that title till the reign of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Nero, their history falls to be considered under that of the Romans. By Trajan the kingdom of Armenia Major was reduced to the form of a Roman province; but it soon recovered its liberty, and was again governed by its own kings in the reigns of Constantine the Great, and his successor, to whom the kings of Armenia were feudatories. In the reign of Justin II. the Saracens subdued and held it till the irruption of the Turks, who possessed themselves of this kingdom and gave it the name of Turcomania. The Turks, after the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Armenia, invaded <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and other countries subject to the emperors of the east; which gave the Armenians an opportunity of shaking off the Turkish yoke, and setting up kings of their own, by whom they were governed till the country was again subdued by Occadan, or, as some style him Hecata, the son of Cingis, and first chaim of the Tartars. Neither was the conquest of Armenia by the Tartars so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> as to extirpate the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of their kings; seeing we read of Haithon, famished the Armenian, reigning some time after, and going in person to treat with Mungo, the great chaim of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, of the concerns of his kingdom; and in our chronicles we find mention made of Leo king of Armenia, who, in the reign of Richard II., came into England to sue for aid against the Turks, by whom he had been driven from his kingdom. In the year 1472 of the Christian era, Ufian Caflanes king of Armenia succeeding to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Persia, made Armenia a province of that empire; in which state it continued till the year 1522, when it was subdued by Selim II. and made a province of the Turkish empire. Some say that Selim I. reduced it on his return from Persia, where he had gained a complete victory over the great Sophi Imael. But Sanovin affirms us, that in the reign of Selim I. who died in 1520, both the Lesser and Greater Armenia had their own kings; and adds, that Selim caused the head of the king of the Lesser Armenia to be cut off and sent to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> as a mark of his victory. We read nowhere else of any kings of Armenia after it became a province of Persia. Be that as it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, the Turkish annals cited by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALVI">Calvi</a>- fius inform us, that Selim II. conquered Armenia in 1522, since which time it has ever continued subject to the Turks, except the eastern part, which the Persians are masters of to this day. Concerning Armenia Minor, we find very little recorded, except what has been already mentioned, and what falls under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman history</a>. It was made a Roman province by Vespasian, continued to till the division division of the empire, when it was subjected to the emperors of the east; and, on the decline of their power, was subdued first by the Persians, and afterwards by the Turks, who gave it the name of Genech, and have kept it ever since. This country is still divided into the Great and Small. Great Armenia comprehends what is now called Turcomania. It has <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a> on the north, from which it is separated by high mountains; the river Euphrates on the west; Diarbeker, Curdistan, and Aderbijan, on the south; and Shirvan on the east. The chief <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in that part of Armenia belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> are Arzum the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of the Euphrates, a large city and a great thoroughfare for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a> between Turkey and Persia; Kara, a strong city, head of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the same name; Bayazid, a republic of Kurds, near Mount Ararat; Baha, another republic of the same name; and Van or Wan, on the lake Van, the head of a government of the same name; with other towns of less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. That part of Armenia subject to Persia is chiefly contained in the province of Aran, in which are several fine towns; as, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERIVAN">Erivan</a> or Rivan, the capital of the whole; Ganjals, one of the finest cities in Persia, in the north of the province, near the Kur; Kapan, on the south side, near the Aras; besides Nakshvan, Astabad Julia, Ordabad, Baylakan or Pilkan, on the Aras; Berdah and Shilkah on the Kur. The country in general is full of mountains and valleys, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>; particularly the country about the Three Churches, near Erivan, is admirably fine, being full of rivulets, which render it extremely fruitful. Besides great quantities of all sorts of grain, here are fields of a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>: but it is not a native of the place, though supposed by some to be the terrestrial paradise; for it all came originally from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. The rest of the country produces <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, melons, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>: in short, there is nothing wanting but olives; which is by some thought to prove that the ark could not rest on Mount Ararat, because the dove brought an olive branch in her mouth, and this tree never leaves a place where it once grew. It seems, however, to have been otherwise anciently; for Strabo tells us, that the olive grew in Gogarene, a province of Armenia. They get <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> to burn from the ricinus, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> linseed oil in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>. The watermelons are as cool as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a> in the hottest day, and melt in the mouth; the best are produced in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> lands, near the Three Churches and the river Aras. After <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> salt lies in crystals upon the fields, and even crackles under the feet. About ten miles from the Three Churches, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEFLIS">Teflis</a>, there are pits or quarries of fossil salt, which yield enough to supply all Persia, without being exhausted: they cut it into large pieces like <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and each buffalo carries two of them; the mountain from whence it is dug is nothing but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of salt, which appears like a rock of silver when the sun shines on the places not covered with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. This country has been remarkable for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> cold from the remotest antiquity; Sir John Chardin tells us, that he found ice in the rivulets in the mornings even of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>. In many places, also, if they had not the convenience of watering their grounds, they would be almost entirely barren. The Armenians are an honest, civil, polite people, Armenia, scarce troubling themselves about anything else but trade, which they carry on in most parts of the world, by which means they have spread themselves over the east, and also a great part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and wherever they come, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> is carried on with spirit and advantage. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the Armenians is the Christian, of the Eutychian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>: that is, they own but one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ; and when they speak of the hypostatical union, that he is perfect God and perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> without mixture. They have a high esteem for a book they call the Little Gospel, which treats of the infancy of Jesus, and says that the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> being pregnant, her sister Salome accused her of having prostituted herself; to which the Virgin answered, that she needed only to lay her hand on her belly, and she would know how the same came to be with child: this Salome accordingly did, and fire came out of her belly, which consumed the half of her arm; upon which the acknowledged her fault, and drew it back; after which it was healed by putting it to the same place. The Armenian clergy consist of patriarchs, archbishops, doctors, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> priests, and monks. The secular priests are not allowed to marry a second time; and therefore they take care to choose young healthy wives: they maintain themselves and families by following some occupation, inasmuch that they have hardly time to perform their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> functions: they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in the churches on the vigils of those days they are obliged to officiate. The Armenian monks are of the order of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>; and every Wednesday and Friday they eat neither fish, nor eggs, nor oil, nor any thing made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, and during <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">Lent</a> they live upon nothing but roots; they are allowed wine only on the Saturday in the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">Week</a>, and meat on the Easter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>. Besides the great Lent they have four others of eight days each, which are instituted to prepare for the four great festivals of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">Nativity</a>, the Ascension, the Annunciation, and of St George; in which times they must not so much as speak of eggs, fish, oil, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>. The Armenians have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sacraments; <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a>, the eucharist, extreme unction, orders, and matrimony. In baptism, the child is plunged three times into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and the same form of words that is used with us is repeated every time; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> then puts a small <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a> made with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and cotton on the neck of the infant, and anoints his forehead, chin, stomach, arm pits, hands, and feet, making the sign of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> on each part. When the child is baptized, he is carried home by the godfather with the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of drums and trumpets. The women do not go to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> till forty days after their delivery; and they observe many Jewish customs. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>, to which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> of two or three months old are admitted, the priests give a piece of the consecrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOST">host</a> soaked in the consecrated wine. The elements are covered with a great veil, and placed in a cupboard near the altar, on the side of the gospels. When the priest takes the chalice and paten, he is followed by his deacons and subdeacons, with flambeaux and plates of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> furnished with bells: in this manner, with a center before him, he goes in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> round the sanctuary; he then sets them on the altar, pronounces pronounces the words of consecration, and turns himself to the people, who fall down, kis the earth, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> their breasts; then, after taking it himself, he distributes the host soaked in wine to the people. The Armenians seem to place the chief part of their religion in fastings and abstinences; and among the clergy, the higher the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> the lower they must live; inasmuch that it is said the archbishops live on nothing but <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>. They consecrate holy water but once a-year; at which time every one fills a pot and carries it home, which brings in a considerable revenue to the church. ARMENIACA. See Prunus.

ARMENIAN

Pages 316-316

something belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> produced in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>: thus we say, Armenian bone, Armenian <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, &c. See Bone, and Armenian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">Lapis</a>.

ARMENIANS

Pages 316-316

a small handfome town of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, and district of Ypres. It was taken by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> XIV. in 1667, who dismantled it; and it now belongs to the French. It is seated on the river Lis. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 3. N. Lat. 50° 40'. ARMENUS <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">Lapis</a>, Armenian <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a mineral substance, which is but improperly called a stone; being no other than an ochreous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and properly called blue ochre. It is a very valuable substance in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, being a bright and lively blue. It was in so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> esteem as a paint among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, that counterfeits were continually attempted to serve in its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Theophratus has recorded it as a thing judged worthy a place in the Egyptian annals, which of their kings had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of inventing the fictitious kind; and he tells us the genuine native substance was a thing of that value, that presents were made of it to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> persons, and that the Phoenicians paid their tribute in it.—It is a very beautiful earth, of an even and regular texture; and of a fine blue, sometimes deeper, sometimes paler, and frequently mixed with green. It is soft, tender, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; of an even, but somewhat dull surface: it adheres firmly to the tongue, and is dry, but not harsh to the touch. It easily breaks between the fingers, and does not stain the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. It is of a brickish disagreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and does not ferment with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>. It is a very scarce fossil; but is found very pure, though but in small quantities, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> at Goffelaer in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>. It is frequently found spotted with green, and sometimes with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; and very often is mixed among the green ochre, called berggruen by the Germans, which has thence been erroneously called by its name. See further the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BICE">Bice</a>.

ARMERS

Pages 316-316

a town of Hainault, in the French <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, seated on the river Sambre. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 45. N. Lat. 50° 15'.

ARMIGER

Pages 316-316

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, belonging to such gentlemen as bear arms; and these are either by courtesy, as sons of noblemen, eldest sons of knights, &c.; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, such as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s servants, &c. See <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ESQUIRE">Esquire</a>.

ARMILLARY

Pages 316-316

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, something consisting of rings <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> circles. Armillary Sphere, an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> sphere composed of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of circles of the mundane sphere, put together in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order, to ease and assist the imagination in conceiving the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the heavens, Armillarium, and the motions of the celestial bodies. The armillary sphere revolves upon its axis within a silvered horizon, which is divided into degrees, and moveable every way upon a bras supporter. The other parts are the equinoctial, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>, meridian, the two tropics, and the two polar circles. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>.

ARMILOSTRUM

Pages 316-316

in Roman Antiquity, a feast held among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, in which they sacrificed, armed, to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of trumpets.

ARMINIANS

Pages 316-318

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> party, which arose in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, by a separation from the Calvinists. They followed the doctrine of Arminius (see the next article); who, thinking the doctrine of Calvin, with regard to free-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREDESTINATION">predestination</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, too severe, began to expostulate his doubts concerning them in the year 1591; and upon further inquiry adopted sentiments more nearly resembling those of the Lutherans than of the Calvinists. After his appointment to the theological <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, he thought it his duty to avow and vindicate the principles which he had embraced; and the freedom with which he published and defended them exposed him to the resentment of those that adhered to the theological system of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, which then prevailed in Holland; but his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> opponent was Gomar, his colleague. The controversy which was thus begun, became more general after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Arminius, in the year 1609, and threatened to involve the United Provinces in civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a>. The Arminian tenets gained ground under the mild and favourable treatment of the magistrates of Holland, and were adopted by several persons of merit and distinction. The Calvinists, or Gomarists, as they were now called, appealed to a national <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a>: accordingly the synod of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DORT">Dort</a> was convened by order of the States General, in 1618, and was composed of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> deputies from the United Provinces, as well as from the reformed churches of England, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a>, Bremen, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">Palatinate</a>. The principal advocate in favour of the Arminians was Episcopus, who, at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> at Leyden. It was first proposed to discuss the principal subjects in dispute, and that the Arminians should be allowed to state and vindicate the grounds on which their opinions were founded: but some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> arising as to the proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of conducting the debate, the Arminians were excluded from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>; their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> was tried in their absence; and they were pronounced guilty of pestilential errors, and condemned as corrupters of the true <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this decision, they were treated with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> severity; they were deprived of all their posts and employments; their ministers were silenced, and their congregations were suppressed. However, after the death of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Maurice, who had been a violent partisan in favour of the Gomarists, in the year 1625, the Arminian exiles were restored to their former reputation and tranquility; and under the toleration of the state, they erected churches and founded a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, appointing Episcopus to be the first theological professor. The Arminian system has very much prevailed in England since the time of Archbishop Laud, and its votaries in other countries are very numerous. The distinguishing tenets of the Arminians may be comprised Arminians, comprised in the following five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>; relating to predestination, universal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a>, the corruption of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, conversion, and perseverance. 1. With respect to the first, they maintained, "That God, from all eternity, determined to bestow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> on those who he foresaw would persevere unto the end in their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> in Christ <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a>; and to inflict everlasting punishments on those who should continue in their unbelief, and resist until the end his divine succours: so that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> was conditional, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REPROBATION">reprobation</a> in like manner the result of foreseen <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a> and persevering wickedness." 2. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> point the Arminians taught, "That Jesus Christ, by his sufferings and death, made an atonement for the sins of all mankind in general, and of every individual in particular; that, however, none but those who believe in him can be partakers of their divine benefit." 3. On the third article, they held, "That true faith cannot proceed from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> faculties and powers, nor from the force and operation of free will; since man, in consequence of his natural corruption, is incapable either of thinking or doing any good thing; and that therefore it is necessary, in order to his conversion and salvation, that he be regenerated and renewed by the operation of the Holy Ghost, which is the gift of God through Jesus Christ." 4. "That this divine grace, or energy of the Holy Ghost, begins and perfects everything that can be called good in man, and consequently all good works are to be attributed to God alone; that, nevertheless, this grace is offered to all, and does not force men to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> against their inclination, but may be resisted and rendered ineffectual by the perverse will of the impenitent sinner." Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Arminians interpret this and the last article with a greater latitude. 5. "That God gives to the truly faithful, who are regenerated by his grace, the means of preserving themselves in this state;" and though the first Arminians made some doubt with respect to the closing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of this article, their followers uniformly maintain, "that the regenerate may lose true justifying faith, forfeit their state of grace, and die in their sins." The modern system of Arminianism likewise, founded on a comprehensive <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> projected by Arminius himself, as appears from a passage in his last will, extends the limits of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and relaxes the bonds of fraternal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> in such a manner, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of all sects and denominations, whatever their sentiments and opinions may be, Papists excepted, may be formed into one religious body, and live together in brotherly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and concord. But, in order to avoid the reproach of being altogether unconnected by any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> principles, Episcopius drew up a confession of faith, expressed for the most part in words and phrases of Holy Scripture, which the Arminians have generally adopted, though not enjoined upon them by any authoritative obligation. The Arminians are also called <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMONSTRANTS">Remonstrants</a>, from a humble petition, entitled their Remonstrance, which, in the year 1619, they addressed to the States of Holland. Their principal writers are Arminius, Episcopius, Vorstius, Grotius, Curcellius, Limborch, Le Clerc, and Wetstein; not to mention many others of more modern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a>. Arminius, James, whose real name in Low Dutch was James Harmann, a famous Protestant divine, from whom the modern sect of Arminians (see the preceding article) take their name, was born at Oude <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, in Holland, in 1560. He was ordained minister at Amsterdam on the 11th of August 1588; where he soon distinguished himself by his sermons, which were remarkable for their fidelity and learning, and gained him universal applause: but Martin Lydia, professor of divinity at Franeker, judging him a fit person to refute a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> in which Beza's doctrine of predestination had been attacked by some ministers of Delft, Arminius at his entreaties undertook the task; but upon thoroughly examining the reasons on both sides, he came into the opinions he proposed to destroy, and afterwards went still farther than the ministers of Delft had done. In 1600, he opposed those who maintained that ministers should subscribe the confession and catechism every year. In 1602, a pestilential <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> raged at Amsterdam, during which he acted with the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> and courage, in afflicting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and comforting the sick; and Lucas Trelacius and Francis Junius dying of that disease at Leyden, the curators of that university chose Arminius professor of divinity there, and he was afterwards made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of divinity. Difficulties upon grace were soon after kindled in that university; and he was at length engaged in a new contest, occasioned by a disputatious of his concerning the divinity of the Son. These contests, his continual labour, and the concern of seeing his reputation blasted by a multitude of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">flanders</a> in relation to his opinions, impaired his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, and threw him into a fit of sickness, of which he died on the 19th of October 1609. Arminius was esteemed an excellent preacher: his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> was low, but very agreeable; and his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a> admirable: he was easy and affable to persons of all ranks, and facetious in his conversation amongst his friends. His great desire was, that Christians would bear with one another in all controversies which did not affect the fundamentals of their religion; and when they persecuted each other for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of indifference, it gave him the utmost dissatisfaction. The curators of the university of Leyden had so great a regard for him, that they settled a pension upon his wife and children. He left several works, viz. 1. Disputationes de diversis Christianae religionis capitibus. 2. Orationes, itemque tractatus insigniores aliquot. 3. Examen modelli libelli Gulielmi Perkinii de praedestinationis modo et ordine, itemque de amplitude gratiae divinae. 4. Analytis capitis noni <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> Romanos. 5. Diffutatione de vero et genuino fenulo capitis septimi epistolae ad Romanos. 6. Amica collatio cum D. Francisco Junio de praedestinatione per literas habita. 7. Epistola ad Hippolyrum à collibus." Armiro, a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, in European <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>; seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Velo. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 23° 40'. N. Lat. 38° 34'. Armistice, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">Military</a> Affairs, a temporary truce or cessation of arms for a very short space of time. The word is Latin, armistitium; and compounded of arma, arms, and /o "to stand, or stop." Armoisin, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> stuff, or kind of taffety, manufactured in the East Indies, at Lyons, in France, and at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. That of the Indies is <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than those made in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Armoniac. ARMONIAC. See Ammoniac, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. ARMONICA. See Harmonica.

ARMORIAL

Pages 318-318

something relating to arms <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> coats of arms. See Arms and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>.

ARMORIC

Pages 318-318
or Aremeric, something that belongs to the province of Bretagne, or Britanny, in France. The name Armorica was anciently given to all the northern and western coast of Gaul, from the Pyrenees to the Rhine; under which name it was known even in Caesar's time. The word is of Bas Breton origin, and denotes as much as maritime; compounded, according to M. Menage, of ar, "upon," and more, "sea."

ARMORUM CONCUSSIO

Pages 318-318

the clashing of arms practised by the Roman armies previous to an engagement, and intended to strike a panic into their enemies; it always followed the clasticum and the barritus. See Classicum and Barritus.

ARMOUR

Pages 318-318

Coat, is the escutcheon of any person, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> family, with its several charges, and other furniture; as mantling, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRESTS">crests</a>, supporters, motto, &c. Thus we say, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of coat armour; meaning one who bears arms.

ARMOURER

Pages 318-318

a maker of arms, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> armour.—The Roman armourers were disposed in certain places in the empire, it being forbidden either to sell, or buy, or make arms elsewhere. They were exempt from all offices and taxes, and received a salary from the public. When once they had taken the employment on themselves, neither they, nor their children, were allowed to quit it. To prevent this, they had a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, or stigma, impressed on the arm, whereby they might be known. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any of them fled, or secreted their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, the rest were obliged to answer for him; on account of which, the effects of such as died without a legal heir went to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. There were 15 armamentaries, or repositories of arms, in the Eastern empire, placed near the frontiers, and 19 in the Western. ARMOURER OF A SHIP, a person whose office is to take care that the arms be in a condition fit for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>.

ARMOURY

Pages 318-318

a storehouse of arms, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> wherein <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> habiliments are kept, to be ready for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. There are armories in the Tower, and in all arsenals, citadels, castles, &c. ARMOURY is also used for a branch of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>; being the knowledge of coat armours, as to their blazons, and various intemements.

ARMOZA

Pages 318-318
or HARMOZIA, a town in Caramania, at the mouth of the Anamis, which falls into the Persian gulf (Arrian); Armusa, (Ptolemy); and from this the neighbouring island, and a small kingdom, take the modern name of Ormus. E. Long. 56° 17'. N. Lat. 27° 20'.

ARMS

Pages 318-319

ARMA, in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, includes all kinds of weapons, whether for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> offence. Nicod derives the word from the Latin phrase quod operant armor, because they cover the shoulders or sides; but Varro derives arma, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> arcendo, eo quod arcant hostes. It is supposed that the first <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> arms were of wood, and were only employed against beasts; and that Belus, the son of Nimrod, was the first that waged <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; whence, according to some, came the appellation belium. Diodorus Siculus takes Belus to be the same with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, who first trained <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> up to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>.—Arms of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and even of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, appear to have been used before they came to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>. Josephus affirms us, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> first taught the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of iron arms in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, arming the troops of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARAOH">Pharaoh</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASQUE">casque</a> and buckler. What contributed most to render the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> masters of the world, was, that having successively warred against all nations, they constantly renounced their own methods, arms, &c. whenever they met with better. Thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> during his war with the Sabines, a bold and warlike <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, adopted their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> buckler in lieu of the small Argian buckler, which he had used till that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> arms of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Britons were hatchets, scythes, lances, swords, and bucklers: the Saxons, &c. brought in the halbard, bow, arrows, arbalists, &c. By the ancient laws of England, every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was obliged to bear arms, except the judges and clergy. Under Henry VIII. it was expressly enjoined on all persons to be regularly instructed, even from their tender years, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of the arms then in use; viz. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> bow and arrows; and to be provided with a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of them. 33 Hen. VIII. Arms, Arma, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, are extended to anything which a man takes in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in his wrath, to call at, or strike another. By the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, it is an offence for persons to go or ride armed with dangerous weapons; but gentlemen may wear common armour, according to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, &c. 3d Inst. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> may prohibit force of arms, and punish offenders according to law; and herein every subject is bound to be aiding. Stat. 7. Edw. I. None shall come with force and arms before the king's justices, nor ride armed in affray of the peace, on pain to forfeit their armour, and to suffer imprisonment, &c. 2d Edw. III. c. 3. The importation of arms and ammunition are prohibited by 1 Jac. II. c. 8. and by 1 W. and M. stat. 2. c. 2. Protestant subjects may have arms for their defense. Arms. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a>. So likewise arms, &c., shipped after prohibition, are forfeited by Geo. I. c. 16, sec. 2. Arms of offence in use among us present are, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, pike, musket, bayonet, pike, &c. The arms of the Highlanders are, the broadsword, target, poniard, and whinyar or durk, &c. There are several acts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> for disarming the Highlanders; see Geo. I. c. 54; Geo. I. c. 26; Geo. II. c. 39; Geo. II. c. 34; Geo. II. c. 22, and 29. Fire Arms are those <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with powder and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>: such are cannon, mortars, and other ordnance; muskets, carbines, pistols, and even bombs, grenades, carcasses, &c. In the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Academy for the year 1707, we have an account of some experiments made with fire arms, differently loaded, by M. Caffini. Among other things he observes, that by loading the piece with a ball which is somewhat less than the calibre, and only laying a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a> below the ball and a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> above it, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> yield a vehement noise, but have no sensible effect or impulse on the ball. This he takes to have been all the secret of those people who pretended to sell the art of rendering one's self invulnerable, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>. Arms, past of, was a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> in use among the ancient cavaliers. Arms, band of. A stand of arms signifies a musket, a bayonet, a sword, belt, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARTRIDGE">cartridge</a>-box. Arms of parade or courtly, were those used in the ancient jousts and tournaments; which were <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> unhayed lances, swords without edge or point, wooden swords, and even canes. Arms denote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> weapons, or parts of defense, of beasts: as claws, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, tusks of elephants, beaks of birds, &c. Arms, are also used figuratively for the profession of a soldier. Thus we say, He was bred to arms. Arms, or Armories, are also used in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a> for marks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, regularly composed of certain figures and colours, given or authorized by sovereigns, and borne on banners, shields, coats, &c., for the distinction of persons, families, and states; and passing by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> to posterity. They are called arms; in regard they are borne principally on the buckler, curfus, banners, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> of war. They are also called coats of arms, coat armour, &c., because anciently embroidered on surcoats, &c. See Heraldry. Some will have the name to have been first occasioned by the ancient knights, who in their jousts and tournaments bore certain marks (which were frequently their mistresses' favours) in their armour, i.e. their helmets or shields, to distinguish them from each other. Arms at present follow the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of titles, which being made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>, these are also become so, being the several marks for distinguishing of families and kindreds, as names are of persons and individuals. Arms are variously distinguished by the Heralds. Arms of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">Alliance</a>, are those which families or private persons join to their own, to denote the alliances which they have contracted by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. Arms presumptive, are such as a man has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to assume of himself, in virtue of some gallant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. As, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a man who is no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of blood, nor has coat armour, takes a gentleman, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, prisoner in any lawful war; he becomes entitled to bear the shield of such prisoner, and enjoy it to him and his heirs. The foundation hereof is that principle in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> law, that the dominion of things taken in lawful war passes to the conqueror. Arms, canting, are those wherein the figures bear an allusion to the name of the family. Such are those of the family of La Tour in Auvergne, who bear a tower; that of the family of Prado in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, whose field is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a>. Most authors hold these the most noble and regular, as is shown by an infinity of instances produced by Father Varrenne and Monetrier.—They are much debased when they come to partake of the Rebus. Arms, charged, are such as retain their ancient integrity and value, with the addition of some new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a>, in consideration of some noble action. Arms of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>, are those of bishoprics, cities, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, and other bodies corporate. Arms of concession, or augmentation of honour, are either entire arms, or else one or more figures given by princes, as a reward for some extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. Arms of dominion, are those which emperors, kings, and sovereign states bear; being annexed to the territories which they possess. Thus the three lions are the arms of England; the fleurs de lys those of France, &c. Arms of family, or paternal arms, are such as belong to a particular family, and which no other person has a right to assume. Arms, full, or entire, are such as retain their primitive purity, integrity, or value; without any alterations, diminutions, abatements, or the like. It is a rule, that the simpler and less diversified the arms, the more noble and ancient they are. For this reason Garcias Ximenes, first king of Navarre, and his successors for several ages, bore only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULES">gules</a>, without any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> at all. The arms of princes of the blood, of all younger sons, and junior families, are not pure and full; but distinguished and diminished by proper differences, &c. Arms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a>, are those which governors of provinces, lords of manors, &c., add to their family arms, in token of their peculiar superiority and jurisdiction. Arms of pretension, are those of such kingdoms or territories to which a prince or lord has some claim, and which he adds to his own, though the kingdoms or territories be possessed by a foreign prince or other lord. Thus the kings of England have quartered the arms of France with their own, ever since the claim of Edward III. to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, in 1330. Arms of succession, are assumed by those who inherit estates, manors, &c., by will, entail, or donation, and which they either impale or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> with their own arms. Arms are also said to be parted, couped, quartered, &c. Arms are said to be false and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, when there is something in them contrary to the established rules of heraldry. As, when metal is put on metal, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> on colour, &c. The laws, and other affairs of arms, with the cognizance of offences committed therein, belong, among us, to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> marshal and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of arms. Arms, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALCONRY">Falconry</a>, denote the legs of a hawk, from the thigh to the foot. See Falconry.

ARMSTRONG

Pages 319-320

ARMSTRONG, Dr John, an eminent physician, poet, and miscellaneous writer, was born in Caffleton <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROXBURGHSHIRE">Roxburghshire</a>, where his father and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> were ministers; completed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, where he took his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> in physic, Feb. 4, 1732, with much reputation; and published his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESIS">thesis</a>, as the forms of that university require; the subject was De tabe purulenta. In 1735 he published a little humorous fugitive pamphlet in 8vo, entitled, "An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> for abridging the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">Study</a> of Physic;" to which is added a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">Dialogue</a> betwixt Hygeia, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, and Pluto, relating to the practice of physic, as it is managed by a certain illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>. As also an Epistle from Uftek the Persian to Joshua <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">Ward</a>, Esq." This piece contains much fun and drollery; in the dialogue, he has caught the very spirit of Lucian. In 1737 he published a Synopsis of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> and Cure of the Venereal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">Disease</a>, 8vo. This was soon followed by the Economy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a>; a poem which has much merit; but, it must be confessed, is too strongly tinged with the licentiousness of Ovid. It is said, however, that his maturer judgment expunged many of the luxuriances of youthful fancy, in an edition "revised and corrected by the author" in 1768. It appears by one of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> on literary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, that Mr Millar paid 50 guineas for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPYRIGHT">copyright</a> of this poem, which was intended as a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLESQUE">burlesque</a> on some didactic writers. It has been observed by Dr Armstrong, that his works have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> inequalities, some of them being possessed of every requisite to be sought after in the most perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, while others can hardly be considered as superior to the productions of mediocrity. The Art of preserving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">Health</a>, his best performance, which was published in 1744, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> transmit his name to posterity as one of the first English writers, has been honoured with the following testimony of a respectable critic. On this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> we shall also transcribe a beautiful eulogium from an eminent physician: "Of all the poetical performances on this subject that have come to my <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, Dr Armstrong's Art of preserving Health is by far the best. To quote every charming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> and beautiful passage of this poem, one must transcribe the whole. We cannot, however, expect new rules, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> was to raise and warm the heart into a compliance with the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> precepts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, which he has enforced with great strength and elegance. And, upon the whole, he has convinced us, by his own example, that we ought not to blame antiquity for acknowledging One power of physic, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>, and song." In 1746 Dr Armstrong was appointed one of the physicians to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a> for Lame and Sick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">Soldiers</a> behind <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. In 1751 he published his poem on Benevolence, in folio; and in 1753, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">Taste</a>, an Epistle to a young Critic." In 1758 appeared, "Sketches <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Essays on various subjects, by Launcelot Temple, Esq., in two parts." In this production, which possesses much humour and knowledge of the world, and which had a remarkably rapid <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, he is supposed to have been assisted by Mr Wilkes. In 1760 he had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of being appointed physician to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in Germany, where in 1671 he wrote a poem called "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">Day</a>, an Epistle to John Wilkes of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AYLESBURY">Aylesbury</a>, Esq." In this poem, which is not collected in his works, he wantonly hazarded a reflection on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>-Armydene, ill, which drew on him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>-toothed vengeance of that severest of satirists, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBALMING">embalming</a> or corrosive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> could defy or lampoon any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, according as he acquiesced with, or disented from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> principles. In 1770 Dr Armstrong published a collection of "Miscellanies, in 2 vols.; containing, 1. The Art of preserving Health. 2. Of Benevolence, an Epistle to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUMENES">Eumenes</a>. 3. Taste, an Epistle to a young Critic, 1733. 4. Imitations of Shakespeare and Spencer. 5. The Universal <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALMANACK">Almanack</a>, by Noureddin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>. 6. The Forced <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">Marriage</a>, a tragedy. 7. Sketches." In 1771 he published "A short Ramble through some parts of France and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, by Launcelot Temple;" and in 1773, in his own name, a quarto pamphlet, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of "Medical Essays;" towards the conclusion of which, he accounts for his not having such extensive practice as some of his brethren, from his not being qualified to employ the usual means, from a ticklish state of spirits, and a distempered excess of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a>. He complains much of the behaviour of some of his brethren, of the herd of critics, and particularly of the reviewers. He died in Sept. 1779; and to the no small surprise of his friends, left behind him more than 300l. saved out of a very moderate income, arising principally from his half-pay.

ARMY

Pages 320-323

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and foot, completely armed, and provided with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, ammunition, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, &c. under the command of one general, having <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-generals, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>-generals, brigadiers, and other officers under him. An army is composed of squadrons and battalions; and is usually divided into three corps, and formed into three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>: the first line is called the van-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> the main-body, and the third the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REAR_GUARD">rear-guard</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> body of reserve. The middle of each line is posted by the foot; the cavalry form the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and left wing of each line; and sometimes they <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> squadrons of horse in the intervals between the battalions. When the army is drawn up in order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, the horse are placed at five feet distance from each other, and the foot at three. In each line the battalions are distant from each other 180 feet, which is nearly equal to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a>; and the same holds of the squadrons, which are about 300 feet distant, the extent of their own front. These intervals are left for the squadrons and battalions of the second line to range themselves against the intervals of the first, that both may more readily <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> through these spaces to the enemy; the first line is usually 300 feet distant from the second, and the second from the third, that there may be sufficient room to rally when the squadrons and battalions are broken. See the article <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a>. This is to be understood of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> army only. A naval or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> army is a number of ships of war, equipped and manned with sailors and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARINES">marines</a>, under the command of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, with other inferior officers under him. See Naval <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TACTICS">Tactics</a>. It has been observed, that in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> with a million of subjects cannot keep an army of above 10,000 men, without ruining himself. It was otherwise wife in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> republics: the proportion of soldiers to the rest of the people, which is now as about one to 100, might then be as about one to eight. The reason seems owing to that equal partition of lands which the ancient founders of commonwealths made among their subjects; so that every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> had a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> to defend, and means to defend it with: whereas, among us, the lands and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> being shared among a few, the rest have no way of subsisting but by trades, arts, and the like; and have neither any free property to defend, nor means to enable them to go to war in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of it, without starving their families. A large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of our people are either artisans or servants, and so only minister to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> and effeminacy of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. While the equality of lands subsisted, Rome, though only a little state, being refused the succours which the Latins were obliged to furnish after the taking of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the conflagration of Camillus, professed raised ten legions within its own walls; which was more, Livy affirms us, than they were able to do in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, though matters of the greatest part of the world. A full <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, adds the historian, that we are not grown stronger; and that what swells our city is only luxury, and the means and effects of it. Our armies anciently were a sort of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, composed chiefly of the vassals and tenants of the lords. When each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> had served the number of days or months enjoined by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a>, or the customs of the fees they held, they returned home. The armies of the empire consist of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> bodies of troops furnished by the several circles. The gos of the French armies under the Merovingian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, consisted of infantry. Under Pepin and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>, the armies consisted almost equally of cavalry and foot; but since the declension of the Carlovingian line, the fees being become <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>, the national armies, says Le Gendre, are chiefly cavalry. A well regulated standing army is greatly superior to a militia; although a militia, it is to be observed, after serving two or three campaigns, may become equal to a standing army, and in every respect a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a> for veteran troops. See Militia. One of the first standing armies of which we have a distinct account, in any well authenticated <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, is that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> of Macedon. His frequent wars with the Thracians, Illyrians, Thessalians, and some of the Greek cities in the neighbourhood of Macedon, gradually formed his troops, which in the beginning were probably militia, to the exact <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of a standing army. When he was at peace, which was very seldom, and never for any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time together, he was careful not to disband that army. It vanquished and subdued, after a long and violent struggle, indeed, the gallant and well exercised militias of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> republics of ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; and afterwards, with very little struggle, the effeminate and ill exercised militia of the great Persian empire. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the Greek republics and of the Persian empire, was the effect of the irresistible superiority which a standing army has over every sort of militia. It is the first great revolution in the affairs of mankind of which history has preserved any distinct or circumstantial account. The fall of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, and the consequent elevation of Rome, is the second. All the varieties in the fortune of those two famous republics may very well be accounted for from the same cause. From the end of the first to the beginning of the second Carthaginian war, the armies of Carthage were continually in the field, and employed under three great generals, who succeeded one another in the command; Hamilcar, his son-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> Africabul, and his son <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a>; first in chastising their own rebellious slaves, afterwards in subduing the revolted nations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>; and, lastly, in conquering the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. The army which Hannibal led from Spain into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> must necessarily, in those different wars, have been gradually formed to the exact discipline of a standing army. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, though they had not been altogether at peace, yet they had not during this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, been engaged in any war of very great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>; and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> discipline, it is generally said, was a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> relaxed. The Roman armies which Hannibal encountered at Trebia, Thrasyllus, and Cannae, were militia opposed to a standing army. This circumstance, it is probable, contributed more than any other to determine the fate of those battles. The standing army which Hannibal left behind him in Spain, had the like superiority over the militia which the Romans sent to oppose it, and in a few years, under the command of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> the younger Africabul, expelled them almost entirely from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Hannibal was ill supplied from home. The Roman militia, being continually in the field, became in the progress of the war a well disciplined and well exercised standing army; and the superiority of Hannibal grew every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> less and less. Africabul judged it necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> the whole, or almost the whole, of the standing army which he commanded in Spain, to the assistance of his brother in Italy. In this march he is said to have been misled by his guides; and in a country which he did not know, was surprised and attacked by another standing army, in every respect equal or superior to his own, and was entirely defeated. When Africabul had left Spain, the great Scipio found nothing to oppose him but a militia inferior to his own. He conquered and subdued that militia; and in the course of the war, his own militia necessarily became a well disciplined and well exercised standing army. That standing army was afterwards carried to Africa, where it found nothing but a militia to oppose it. In order to defend Carthage, it became necessary to recall the standing army of Hannibal. The disheartened and frequently defeated African militia joined it, and at the battle of Zama composed the greater part of the troops of Hannibal. The event of that day determined the fate of the two rival republics. From the end of the second Carthaginian war till the fall of the Roman republic, the armies of Rome were in every respect standing armies. The standing army of Macedon made some resistance to their arms. In the height of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> it cost them two great wars and three great battles, to subdue that little kingdom; of which the conquest would probably have been still more difficult, had it not been for the cowardice of its last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>. The militias of all the civilized nations of the ancient world, of Greece, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, and of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, made but a feeble resistance to the standing armies of Rome. The militias of some barbarous nations defended themselves much better. The Scythian or Tartar militia, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a> drew from the countries <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the Euxine and Caspian seas, were the most formidable enemies whom the Romans had to encounter after the second Carthaginian war. The Parthian and German militias too were always respectable, and upon several occasions gained very considerable advantages over the Roman armies. In general, however, and when the Roman armies were well commanded, they appear to have been very much superior. Many different causes contributed to relax the discipline of the Roman armies. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> severity was, perhaps, one of those causes. In the days of their grandeur, when no enemy appeared capable of opposing them, their heavy armour was laid aside as unnecessarily burdensome, their laborious exercises were neglected as unnecessarily toilsome. Under the Roman emperors, besides, the standing armies of Rome, those particularly which guarded the German and Pannonian frontiers, became dangerous to their masters, against whom they used frequently to set up their own generals. In order to render them less formidable, according to some authors Diocletian, according to others Constantine, first withdrew them from the frontiers, where they had always before been encamped in great bodies, generally of two or three legions each, and dispersed them in small bodies through the different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, from whence they were scarce ever removed, but when it became necessary to repel an invasion. Small bodies of soldiers quartered in trading and manufacturing towns, and seldom removed from those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, became themselves tradesmen, artificers, and manufacturers. The civil came to predominate over the military character; and the standing armies of Rome gradually degenerated into a corrupt, neglected, and undisciplined militia, incapable of resisting the attack of the German and Scythian militias, which soon afterwards invaded the western empire. It was only by hiring the militia of some of those nations to oppose to that of others, that the emperors were for some time able to defend themselves. The fall of the western empire is the third great revolution in the affairs of mankind, of which ancient history has preserved any distinct or circumstantial account. It was brought about by the irresistible superiority which the militia of a barbarous has over that of a civilized nation; which the militia of a nation of shepherds has over that of a nation of husbandmen, artificers, and manufacturers. The victories which have been gained by militias have generally been not over standing armies, but over other militias in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> and discipline inferior to themselves. Such were the victories which the Greek militia gained over that of the Persian empire; and such too were those which in later times the Swiss militia gained over that of the Austrians and Burgundians. The military force of the German and Scythian nations, who established themselves upon the ruins of the western empire, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for some time to be of the same kind in their new settlements as it had been in their original country. It was a militia of shepherds and husbandmen, which in time of war took the field under the command of the same chieftains whom it was accustomed to obey in peace. It was therefore tolerably well exercised and tolerably well disciplined. As arts and industry advanced, however, the authority of the chieftains gradually decayed, and the great body of the people had less time to spare for military exercises. Both the discipline and the exercise of the feudal militia, therefore, went gradually to ruin, and standing armies were gradually introduced to supply the place of it.
