When the expedient of a standing army, besides, had once been adopted by one civilized nation, it became necessary that all its neighbours should follow the example. They soon found that their safety depended upon their doing so, and that their own militia was altogether incapable of resisting the attack of such an army. The soldiers of a standing army, though they may never have seen an enemy, yet have frequently appeared to possess all the courage of veteran troops, and the very moment that they took the field, to have been fit to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> the hardest and most experienced veterans. In a long peace the generals perhaps sometimes forget their skill; but where a well regulated standing army has been kept up, the soldiers seem never to forget their valor. When a civilized nation depends for its defence upon a militia, it is at all times exposed to be conquered by any barbarous nation which happens to be in its neighbourhood. The frequent conquests of all the civilized countries in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> by the Tartars, sufficiently demonstrates the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> superiority which the militia of a barbarous has over that of a civilized nation. A well regulated standing army is superior to every militia. Such an army, as it can best be maintained by an opulent and civilized nation, so it can alone defend such a nation against the invasion of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and barbarous neighbour. It is only by means of a standing army, therefore, that the civilization of any country can be perpetuated, or even preserved for any considerable time. As it is only by means of a well regulated standing army that a civilized country can be defended, so it is only by means of it that a barbarous country can be suddenly and tolerably civilized. A standing army establishes, with an irresistible force, the law of the sovereign through the remotest provinces of the empire, and maintains some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of regular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> in countries which could not otherwise admit of any. Whoever examines with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> the improvements which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the Great introduced into the Russian empire, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> find that they almost all resolve themselves into the establishment of a well regulated standing army. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> which executes and maintains all his other regulations. That degree of order and internal peace which that empire has ever since enjoyed, is altogether owing to the influence of that army. Men of republican principles have been jealous of a standing army as dangerous to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. It certainly is so, wherever the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the general and that of the principal officers are not necessarily connected with the support of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the state. The standing army of Caesar destroyed the Roman republic; the standing army of Cromwell turned the long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> out of doors. But where the sovereign is himself the general, general, and the principal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and gentry of the country the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> officers of the army; where the military force is placed under the command of those who have the greatest interest in the support of the civil authority, because they have themselves the greatest share of that authority; a standing army can never be dangerous to liberty; on the contrary it may, in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, be favourable to liberty. The security which it gives to the sovereign renders unnecessary that troublesome jealousy which in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> republics seems to watch over the minutest actions, and to be at all times ready to disturb the peace of every citizen. Where the security of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, though supported by the principal people of the country, is endangered by every popular discontent; where a small tumult is capable of bringing about in a few hours a great revolution; the whole authority of government must be employed to suppress and punish every murmur and complaint against it. To a sovereign, on the contrary, who feels himself supported not only by the natural aristocracy of the country, but by a well regulated standing army, the rudest, the most groundless, and the most licentious remonstrances, can give little disturbance. He can safely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> or neglect them, and his consciousness of his own superiority naturally disposes him to do so. That degree of liberty which approaches to licentiousness can be tolerated only in countries where the sovereign is secured by a well regulated standing army. It is in such countries only that the public safety does not require that the sovereign should be trusted with any discretionary power for suppressing even the impertinent wantonness of this licentious liberty.

ARMYDEN

Pages 320-320

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port town of the United Provinces, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALCHEREN">Walcheren</a>, formerly very flourishing; but now inconsiderable, the sea having stopped up the harbour. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> works are its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> resource. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 40'. N. Lat. 51° 30'.

ARNALL

Pages 323-323

William, a noted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> writer in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of Sir Robert Walpole, was originally an attorney's clerk; but being recommended to Walpole, he employed him for a course of years in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the Free Briton and other papers in defence of his administration. By the report of the secret committee, he appears to have received, in the space of four years, no less than £10,997.6s.8d., out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> for his writings! but spending his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> as fast as it came, and his supplies stopping on Sir Robert's resignation, he died broken-hearted and in debt, in the 26th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> was so quick, that his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> employer used to say, no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in England could write a pamphlet in so little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> as Arnall.

ARNAUD

Pages 323-323

Antony, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of the preceding, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of the Sorbonne, was born in 1612. He published, in 1643, A Treatise on frequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">Communion</a>, which highly displeased the Jesuits; and the disputes upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, which broke out about this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and in which he took a zealous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JANSENISTS">Jansenists</a>, helped to increase the animosity between him and the Jesuits. But nothing raised to greater clamour against him as the two letters he wrote on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTION">Absolution</a>; in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> found two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> which they condemned, and M. Arnaud was expelled the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. Upon this he retired; and during a retreat which lasted near 25 years, he composed that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of works which are extant of his, on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, logic, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>. In 1679, he withdrew from France, living in obscurity in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, and died in 1694. His heart, at his own request, was sent to be deposited in the Port <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a>. Arnaud had a remarkable strength of genius, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, and command of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a>; nor did these decay even to the last year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Mr Bayle says, he had been told by persons who had been admitted into his familiar conversation, that he was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> very simple in his manners; and that unless any one proposed some question to him, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> desired some information, he said nothing that was beyond <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> conversation, or that might make one take him for a man of great abilities; but when he set himself to give an answer to such as proposed a point of learning, he seemed as it were transformed into another man: he would then deliver a multitude of fine things with great perspicuity and learning, and had a particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> at making himself intelligible to persons not of the greatest penetration.

ARNAUD D'ANDILLY

Pages 323-323

Robert, the son of a celebrated advocate of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, was born in 1588; and being introduced young at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, was employed in many considerable offices, all which he discharged with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> integrity and reputation. In 1644, he quitted business, and retired into the convent of Port <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> des Champs, where he passed the remainder of his days in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> application to works of piety and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>; and enriched the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> with many excellent translations of different writers, as well as with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> compositions of his own. He died in 1674, and his works are printed in 8 vols. folio.

ARNAUD DE MEYREUIL

Pages 323-323
or MEREUIL, a poet of Provence, who lived at the beginning of the 13th century. He wrote a book entitled Las recogidas de la concha, and a collection of poems and sonnets. He died in the year 1220. Petrarch mentions him in his Triumph of Love.

ARNAUD DE VILLA NOVA

Pages 323-323

a famous physician, who lived about the end of the 13th and beginning of the 14th century. He studied at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTPELLIER">Montpellier</a>, and travelled through <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. He was well acquainted with languages, and particularly with the Greek, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, and Arabic. He was at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pains to gratify his ardent desire after knowledge; but this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> carried him rather too far in his researches: he endeavoured to discover future events by astrology, imagining this science to be infallible; and upon this foundation he published a prediction, that the world would come to an end in the middle of the 14th century. He practised physic at Paris for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but having advanced some new doctrines, he drew upon himself the resentment of the university; and his friends, fearing he might be arrested, persuaded him to retire from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. Upon his leaving France, he retired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, where he was received by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Frederick of Arragon with the greatest marks of kindness and esteem. Some time afterwards, this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> sent him to France, to attend Pope Clement in an illness; and he was shipwrecked on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, about the year 1313. The works of Arnaud, with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> prefixed, were printed in one volume in folio, at Lyons, in 1520; and at Basel in 1585, with the notes of Nicholas Tulerus.

ARNAY-LE-DUC

Pages 323-323

a town of France, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, which carries on a pretty good trade. It is seated on the Auxois, in a valley near the river Aroux. F. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 26'. N. Lat. 47° 7'.

ARNDT

Pages 323-324

ARNDT, John, a famous Protestant divine of Germany, born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BALLENSTEDT">Ballenstedt</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Anhalt, in the year 1555. At first he applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of physic; but falling into a dangerous sickness, he made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOW">vow</a> to change his profession for that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he should be restored to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>; which he accordingly did upon his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>. He was minister first at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEDLINBURG">Quedlinburg</a> and then at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a>. He met with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> opposition in this last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>; his success as a preacher raised the enmity of his brethren, who became his bitter enemies. In order to ruin his character, they ascribed a variety of errors to him; and persecuted him to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that he was obliged to leave Brunswick, and retire to Iisleb, where he was minister for three years. In 1611, George <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUNEBURG">Luneburg</a>, who had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of his integrity and sanctity, gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Zell, and appointed him superintendent of all the churches in the duchy of Lüneburg; which office he discharged for 11 years, and died in 1621. It is reported that he foretold his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, having said to his wife, upon his return home after his last sermon, that now he had preached his funeral sermon. He wrote in High Dutch A Treatise on true Christianity, which has been translated into several languages.

ARNE

Pages 324-324

Dr Thomas Augustine, distinguished by his skill in music, was the son of Mr Arne an upholsterer in Covent Garden, whom Addison supposed to have characterized in No 155 and No 160 of The Tatler; and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Mrs Cibber the player. He was early devoted to music, and soon became eminent in his profession. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 6, 1759, he had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of music conferred on him at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. His compositions are universally applauded, and he was also particularly skilful in instructing vocal performers. He died <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 5, 1778, having written the following pieces: Artaserxes, 1762; The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">Guardian</a> outwitted, 1764; The Rose, 1778; all of them operas.

ARNHEIM

Pages 324-324

a town of the Low Countries, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Guelderland, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Veluwe. It is adorned with several fine churches, particularly that of St Walburg and of St Eusebius; which last has a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> tower. The town has five gates, and several fine ramparts, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of which are washed by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> and the other parts have wide and deep ditches before them. There is a canal made between this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> and Nimeguen, at the expense of both <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, on which boats <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> backwards and forwards to carry on a trade between them. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is very healthful; on which account it is inhabited by persons of distinction. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 55'. N. Lat. 52° 0'.

ARNICA

Pages 324-324

leopards bane. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. ARNISÆUS, Henningus, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and physician of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation, about the beginning of the 17th century. He was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALBERSTADT">Halberstadt</a> in Germany, and was professor of physic in the university of Helmstadt. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> works are much esteemed. The most remarkable of them is his book De authoritate principum in populum semper inviolabili, printed at Frankfort in 1612. In this he maintains that the authority of princes ought not to be violated. He wrote also upon the same doctrine his three books, De jure Majestatis, printed at the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in 1613; and his Reflectiones Politicae, printed at Frankfort in 1615. Having received an invitation to go to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, he went thither, and was made councillor and physician to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>. He travelled into France and England, and died in November 1635. Besides the pieces already mentioned, he wrote several philosophical, medical, and political treatises.

ARNOBIVS

Pages 324-324

professor of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> at Sicca, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMIDIA">Numidia</a>, towards the end of the third century. It was owing to certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a> which he had that he became desirous of embracing Christianity. For this purpose he applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> to be admitted into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. But they, remembering the violence with which he had always opposed the true <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, had some distrust of him; and before they would admit him, insisted on some proofs of his sincerity. In compliance with this demand, he wrote against the Gentiles; wherein he has refuted the absurdities of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and ridiculed their false gods. In this treatise he has employed all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of rhetoric, and displayed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning; but from an impatience to be admitted into the body of the faithful, he is thought to have been in too great a hurry in composing his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and thence it is that there does not appear in this piece such an exact order and disposition as could be wished; and not having a perfect and exact knowledge of the Christian faith, he published some very dangerous errors. Mr Bayle remarks, that his notions about the origin of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, and the cause of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> evil, and several other important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, are highly pernicious. St Jerome, in his epistle to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAULINUS">Paulinus</a>, is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that his style is unequal and too diffuse, and that his book is written without any method; but Dr Cave thinks this judgment too severe, and that Arnobius wants neither elegance nor order in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. Vossius styles him the Varro of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers. Du <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">Pin</a> observes that his work is written in a manner worthy of a professor of rhetoric: the turn of his sentiments is very oratorical; but his style is a little African, his expressions being harsh and inelegant. We have several editions of this work of Arnobius against the Gentiles, one published at Rome in 1542, at Basle in 1546 and 1562, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1570, at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> in 1582, and one at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMBURG">Hamburg</a> in 1610, with notes by Gebhard Elmenhoffer, besides many others. He wrote also a piece entitled De Rhetorica Institutione; but this is not extant.

ARNOLD

Pages 324-326

of Brescia, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, distinguished himself by being the founder of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> which opposed the wealth and power of the Roman clergy. He went into France, where he studied under the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABELARD">Abelard</a>. Upon his return to Italy, he put on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of a monk, and opened his invectives in the streets of Brescia. The people crowded round him. He told them he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> abuses, to pull <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the proud and to exalt the humble. He then pointed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLAMATION">declamation</a> against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, against the clergy, against the monks, and finally against the Roman pontiff himself; to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a> only he was indulgent. Churchmen, said he, who hold benefices, bishops who have domains, and monks that have possessions, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> all be damned. His hearers shouted approbation. These things, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> he, belong to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; he may give them to whom he pleases, but he must give them to the laity. It is on their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a>, and the voluntary contributions Arnold, contributions of the people, that those sons of God must live: they must be frugal, continent, and mortified. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Brescia was soon thrown into the greatest confusion, and the people, already prejudiced against their ministers, threatened to overturn their altars. The sacred writings he urged in support of his reflections, and from them he denounced the vengeance of heaven against the violators of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. Indeed, nothing could be more glaringly offensive than the ostentatious parade of the bishops and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abbots, and the soft and licentious lives of the monks and clergy. In 1139 was celebrated a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> at Rome. Arnold was cited to appear before it. His accusers were the bishop of Brescia, and many others, whom he had ridiculed and insulted. Nor from his judges could he look for much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>. He was found guilty, and sentenced to perpetual silence. Upon this he left Italy, crossed the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, and found a refuge in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZURICH">Zurich</a>. Though Arnold had quitted Italy, yet had his opinions taken deep root, and Rome itself was infected by them. Irritated by the conduct of their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> Innocent II., the Roman people assembled in the capitol. It was proposed that the power of the pontiff, which they called exorbitant, should be restrained; this was carried; then suddenly, inspired as it were by the genius of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, they moved that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> which for years had been abolished, should be restored. The proposition was received with the loudest acclamations. Innocent in vain opposed the bold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>; there was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> in it which spread irresistibly, and for a moment seemed to rouse the fallen spirit of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. The pope viewed with horror the reverse of fortune which threatened the tiara; to be scorned of his mighty power, and to become the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> shepherd of the Christian people, was a thought too afflicting: he fell sick and died. Under his two immediate successors <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CELESTINE">Celestine</a> and Lucius, whose reigns were but of a few months, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> pursued their darling object. They waited on the latter, and, in an imperious tone, demanded the restitution of all the honours and civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> which had been usurped from the people. The prince of the senate, said they, whom we have chosen, will best administer the important trust: the tithes and offerings of the faithful will sufficiently answer all the exigencies of your <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a>: it was thus that our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> bishops lived. Lucius survived this event but a few days. His successor was Eugenius III., the friend and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of the renowned Bernard. The night before his consecration the senators assembled, and it was agreed, that either he should solemnly confirm all their proceedings, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> they would annul his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> was notified to him. He called together his friends; and it was their advice, that he should neither accede to the extravagant demand, nor expose himself, by a refusal, to the fury of the populace. He therefore silently withdrew from Rome, and retired to a neighbouring fortress. Here the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of his consecration was performed. Arnold, who in banishment had contemplated the effect of his admonitions on the minds of the Romans, and the success which seemed to follow their exertions, was now informed that the pope had retired, and that the gates of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> were open to receive him: it was likewise suggested to him, that his presence was more than ever necessary, to give energy to their resolves, form to their plans, and stability to their undertakings. Arnold took fire at the news; an unusual twill of enthusiasm filled his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>; and he fancied that, like Junius Brutus, he was called at once to give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to Rome. At his appearance a new stream of vigour animated the citizens; they called him their friend and deliverer. The Breician walked amongst them; his deportment was humble, his countenance emaciated, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> affable, and he spoke to them of moderation, of submission, of obedience. With the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> and new senators he held another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; though to them also he was mild and diffident, speaking much of virtue and of respect for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and the laws. But no sooner was he sensible of his own real influence, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the lengths to which the revolters had already carried their designs, than he threw aside the mask, and appeared in his own character, daring, impetuous, self-sufficient, vain. He harangued the people; he talked of their forefathers the ancient Romans, who, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of their senate and the valour of their armies, had conquered nations and subdued the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. He dwelt on the names and the achievements of the Bruti, the Gracchi, and the Scipios; and of these men, said he, are you not the children? He advised, that the capitol be instantly repaired; that the equestrian order be restored; that the people have their tribunes; that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> attend the senate; that the laws, which had been silent and neglected, be revived in all their vigour. He spoke of the pope as of a deposed and banished <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>: "But should you again be deposed (continued he) to admit him within these walls; first fix your own rights and determine his. He is but your bishop: let him therefore have his spiritual jurisdiction. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Rome, its civil establishments, and its territories, belong to you. These you will keep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you have the spirit of men and the hearts of Romans." Fired by this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARANGUE">harangue</a>, the people, headed by the most disaffected of the nobles, publicly attacked the few cardinals and churchmen who remained in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>; they set fire to the palaces; and they compelled the citizens to swear obedience to the new government. Moderate men, who saw the folly of the attempt, were shocked at these excesses of popular frenzy; but it was in vain to oppose the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a>: they submitted, looking forward with some curiosity to the termination of an event which had begun in extravagance, and must end in disappointment. Eugenius till now had viewed, with some concern, the wild derangement of his people: but when it seemed that their eyes opened to their own excesses, he could be inactive no longer. He excommunicated the ringleaders of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a>; and at the head of his troops, who were chiefly composed of Tiburtini, a people always hostile to the Romans, he marched against the enemy. His friends within the walls, who were numerous, co-operated with his designs, and in a few days overtures for peace were made to the pontiff. He acceded to them, but on condition that they should annul the arrangements they had made, and if they would have senators, that they should acknowledge all. Arnold all their power was from him. The people were satisfied, and they threw open the gates, through which Eugenius entered, amid the acclamations of a fawning and inconstant multitude. Before this event Arnold had retired; but he left behind him many friends strongly attached to his person and principles. Of himself we hear little more till the reign of Adrian our countryman; when, on account of fresh tumults, he and his adherents were excommunicated, and Rome was threatened with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERDICT">interdict</a> unless they expelled the whole party from their walls. This they did. The Arnoldists retired with their champion into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, where he was received as a prophet and honoured as a saint. His enemies, however, prevailed; he was made prisoner, and conducted under a strong escort to Rome. In vain was great <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> made to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; he was condemned and executed, and his ashes thrown into the Tiber, left the people should collect his remains and venerate them as the relics of a martyred <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a>. *Hist. of the Lives of whole views, we perhaps should be disposed to admire, Abélard and Heloïsa.* Such was Arnold of Brescia; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> (says Mr. Barington*), whose character, whose principles, and the lives of whole views, we perhaps should be disposed to admire, Abélard and Heloïsa, and not brought down to us drawn in the blackest colours which party, bigotted zeal, and enthusiasm, could lay on. He was rash, misjudging, and intemperate, or never would he have engaged in so unequal a contest. The view of such a phenomenon in the 12th century excites a pleasing admiration. To attack the Roman pontiff and his clergy in the very centre of their power, required a more than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> share of fortitude; to adopt a settled scheme of restoring to its pristine <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> the republic of Rome, demanded a stretch of thought comprehensive and enterprising; and to forego the ease and indulgence of a dilapidated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, for the reformation of manners and the suppression of what he thought usurped dominion, argued a character of mind disinterested, generous, and benevolent. But Arnold, like other reformers, went too far; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> soon vitiated undertakings which were begun perhaps with motives the most laudable.—The readiness with which the Roman people embraced this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOWERING">lowering</a> the jurisdiction of the pontiff, and restraining it within those bounds which the true spirit of Christianity had fixed, at once shows that they could reason justly, and that they considered the unbounded sway of the triple <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, to which reluctantly they submitted, as an assumed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>, to which violence or misconstruction, and not Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, had given efficacy."

ARNOLDISTS

Pages 326-326

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> so called from their leader Arnold of Brescia. See the preceding article.

ARNOLDUS

Pages 326-326

Gothofredus, pastor and inspector of the churches of Perleberg, and historiographer to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, was born at Annaburg in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Misnia in 1666. He was a zealous defender of the Pietists, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> among the German <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, and composed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> works; particularly an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, which exposed him to the resentment of the divines; and another giving an account of the doctrines and manners from the first ages, in which he frequently animadverted upon Cave's Primitive Christianity. He died in 1714. Various are the opinions concerning Arnoldus in Germany; some of his own countrymen and profession extolling him to the skies as a saint of the last century, and setting an infallible value upon his works; while others pronounce damnation upon him as an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>-heretic, and condemn his writings as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HETERODOX">heterodox</a>.

ARNON

Pages 326-326

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a brook running between the borders of the Moabites and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMONITES">Ammonites</a> on the other side Jordan (Moles, Joshua): Josephus calls it a river rising on the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, and at length falling into the Dead <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>. It is also called the river of Gad, as appears 2 Sam. xxxv. compared with 2 Kings x. 33. ARNOT. See Bunium, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ARNOTTO

Pages 326-326

the same with Anotta. See Anotta and Bixa, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ARNSTADE

Pages 326-326

a town of Germany, in Thuringia, on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GERA">Gera</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11. 3. N. Lat. 50. 54.

ARNULPH

Pages 326-326
or Ernulph, bishop of Rochester in the reign of Henry I. He was born in France, where he was some time a monk of St Lucian de Beauvais. The monks led most irregular lives in this monastery; for which reason he resolved to quit it, but first took the advice of Lanfranc archbishop of Canterbury, under whom he had studied in the abbey of Bec, when Lanfranc was prior of that monastery. This prelate invited him over to England, and placed him in the monastery of Canterbury, where he lived a private monk till Lanfranc's death. When Anselm came to the archiepiscopal see, Arnulph was made prior of the monastery of Canterbury, and afterwards abbot of Peterborough. In 1115, he was consecrated bishop of Rochester, which see he held nine years, and died in March 1124, aged 84. Arnulph wrote, 1. A piece in Latin concerning the foundation, endowment, charters, laws, and other things relating to the church of Rochester; it is generally known by the title of Textus Roffensis, and is preserved in the archives of the cathedral church of Rochester. 2. An Epistle in Antwerp to some Questions of Lambert abbot of Münster; and, 3. An Epistle on incestuous Marriage.

ARNUS

Pages 326-326

now Arno, a very rapid river of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, which it divides, and in its course washes <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a>; rising in the Apennines, to the east of Florence, near a village called S. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> della Gratia, on the borders of Romagna, 15 miles to the west of the sources of the Tiber; and then <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> southwards towards <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-AREZZO">Arezzo</a>, it is there increased by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> of the Chiana; after which it runs westward, dividing Florence into two parts, and at length washing Pisa, falls eight miles below it into the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>.

ARNWAY

Pages 326-327

John, a clergyman distinguished by his benevolence and loyalty to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. was descended from a very good family in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Salop, from which he inherited a considerable estate. He was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; and, having received holy orders, obtained the rectories of Hodnet and Lighthfield, where he distinguished himself by his piety and exemplary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>: for it was his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> to clothe annually 12 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people, and every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> to entertain as many at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, not only plentifully, but with intimacy and respect. The civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> breaking out, he preached against rebellion, and raised and clothed eight troopers for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of King Charles I., upon which his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was ARP was plundered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. He then went to Oxford to serve the king in person, which subjected him to a new train of misfortunes: for his estate was soon after sequestrated, and himself imprisoned till the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; after which he went to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>, where he published, 1. The Tablet, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Moderation of Charles I. the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">Martyr</a>; and, 2. An Alarm to the Subjects of England. He at last went to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, where he died in 1653. AROBE. See ARROBAS.

AROIS

Pages 351-351

a late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of France, and one of the finest and most fertile in the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Formerly it was one of the 17 provinces of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, but now belongs entirely to France, and is included in the department of the Straits of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALAIS">Calais</a>. The names of Artois, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARRAS">Arras</a> its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, are derived from the Atrebates, a people of Gallia <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a>, mentioned by Julius Caesar. Its greatest length from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south is about 24 leagues, and its breadth about 12, being bounded to the south and west by Picardy, to the east by Hainault, and to the north by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>. A considerable trade is carried on in the province in grain, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, hops, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth. The most considerable places in Artois are, Arras the capital, Bapaume, Bethune, St Venant, and St Omer.

AROMA PHILOSOPHORUM

Pages 327-327

denotes either saffron, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the aroth of Paracelsus; as aroma germanicum, denotes elecampane. See AROPH.

AROMATA

Pages 327-327

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Lydia, famous for its generous wines; and hence the appellation, (Strabo.) Also the name of a trading town, and promontory of Ethiopia, at the termination of the Sinus Avalites of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, (Arrian).

AROMATIC

Pages 327-327

an appellation given to such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> as yield a brisk fragrant smell, and a warm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; as all kinds of spices, &c. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>.

ARONA

Pages 327-327

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, with a strong castle. It stands on the lake Maggiore. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 25. N. Lat. 45. 41.

ARONCHES

Pages 327-327

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALENTEJO">Alentejo</a>, on the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, seated on the river Caro. It is well fortified, and has about 500 inhabitants. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 16. N. Lat. 14. 39.

AROOL

Pages 327-327

a town of the empire of Russia, in the Ukraine, seated on the river Occa. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 38. 15. N. Lat. 51. 48.

AROPH

Pages 327-327

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of aroma philosophorum; a name given to saffron.

AROPH PARACELSI

Pages 327-327

a name given to a kind of chemical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, probably of the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> with the Ens Veneris, elegantly prepared by sublimation from equal quantities of lepis hematitis and sal ammoniac. AROPH is also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used frequently by Paracelsus in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> with lithontriptic.

AROSBAY

Pages 327-327

a town of the East Indies, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADURA">Madura</a>, near <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. 30. N. Lat. 9. 30.

AROURA

Pages 327-327

a Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of 50 feet. It was more frequently used for a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> measure of half the plethron. The Egyptian aroura was the square of 100 feet.

ARPAD

Pages 327-327

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, is thought to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>. It was always placed with Hamath, (2 Kings xviii. 34. xix. 13. Isaiah x. 9. xxxvi. 19. xxxviii. 13. Jerem. xlix. 23.) Sennacherib boasts of having reduced Arpad and Hamath, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of having destroyed the gods of these two places. Hamath is known to be the same with Emesa; and it is thought that Arpad is the same with Arad or Arvad, as it is sometimes called in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>. See ARAD.

ARPAGIUS

Pages 327-327
or Harpagius, among the ancients, a person who died in the cradle, at least in early youth. The word is formed from the Greek ἀγραπή, I snatch. The Romans made no funerals for their arpagii. They neither burnt their bodies, nor made tombs, monuments, or epitaphs for them; which occasioned Juvenal to say, --- Terra clauditur infans Et minor igne rogì. In after times it became the custom to burn such as had lived to the age of 40 days, and had cut any teeth; and these they called ἀγραπτοί, or ἀγραπτοί, q. d. rapti, ravished. The usage seems to have been borrowed from the Greeks; among whom, Eustathius affirms us, it was the custom never to bury their children either by night or full day, but at the first appearance of the morning; and that they did not call their departure by the name of death, but by a softer appellation, ἀγραπτοί ἀγραπτοί, importing that they were ravished by Aurora, or taken away to her embraces.

ARPENT

Pages 327-327

signifies an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURLONG">furlong</a> of ground; and according to the old French account in Doomday-book, 100 perches make an arpent. The most ordinary acre, called l'arpent de France, is 100 perches <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>: but some account it but half an acre.

ARPHAXAD

Pages 327-327

the son of Shem and father of Salah. Arphaxad was born in the year of the world 1658, a year after the deluge, and died in the year of the world 2096, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 438 years, (Gen. xi. 12, &c.) ARPI. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a> Hippium.

ARPINAS

Pages 327-327
or ARPINO, JOSEPH CAESAR, a famous painter, born in the year 1550, at the castle of Arpinas, in the kingdom of Naples. He lived in great intimacy with Pope Clement VIII. who conferred upon him the honour of knighthood, and bestowed on him many other marks of his friendship. In the year 1600, he went to Paris with Cardinal Aldobrandini, who was sent legate to the French court on the marriage of Henry IV. with Mary of Medicis. His Christian majesty gave Arpinas many considerable presents, and created him a knight of St Michael. The colouring of this painter is thought to be cold and inanimate; yet there is spirit in his designs, and his compositions have somewhat of fire and elevation. The touches of his pencil being free and bold, give therefore pleasure to connoisseurs in painting; but they are generally incorrect. What he painted of the Roman s="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history is the most esteemed of all his works. The following pieces of this master were in the late royal collection of France, viz. the Nativity of our Saviour, Diana and Acteon, the Rape of Europa, and a Sufanna. He died at Rome in 1640.

ARPINUM

Pages 327-327

a town of the Volsci, a little to the east of the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Liris and Fibrenus, in the Terra di Lavora; now decayed, and called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARPINO">Arpino</a>. It was the native <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Cicero, and of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> Marius, (Sallust.)

ARQUA

Pages 327-327

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the Paduan, and territory of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, remarkable for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of Petrarch. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11. 43. N. Lat. 45. 43. ARQUEBUS. See HARQUEBUS.

ARQUES

Pages 327-327

a town of Normandy, now the department of the Lower <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, in France, seated on a small river of the same name. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 30. N. Lat. 49. 54.

ARRACHEE

Pages 327-327

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to the representations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> torn up by the roots. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARRACK">ARRACK</a>. See ARACK.

ARRAGON

Pages 327-328

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Pyrenean <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which separate it Arragon from France; on the west by Navarre and the two Castiles; on the south, by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a>; and on the east, by Catalonia. It is in length about 180 miles, and in breadth 149; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> is mountainous, dry, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stony, badly cultivated, and worse peopled. How- ever it does not want <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>; for besides the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EBRO">Ebro</a>, which crosses it in the middle, there are the Xalo, the Cineo, the Galego, and the Arragon. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is pure and wholesome; and there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and some of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. The most fertile parts are about the ri- vers: for there the land produces corn, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, various <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of saffron, besides <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> flocks of sheep, and plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a> in the woods. The Arragonese have the character of being bold, courageous, and well bred; but positive in their opi- <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NIONS">nions</a>, and bigotted in their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. There were the first of the Spaniards that threw off the Moorish yoke. Saragossa is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of this province; and the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are Balbastro, Jaca, Sarazona, Haecla, Calatajud, Albarracin, Trevel, Daroca, and Boria.

ARRAIGNMENT

Pages 328-329

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the arraigning <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fet- ting a thing in order, as a person is said to arrange a writ of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVEL">novel</a> disseisin, who prepares and fits it for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>. ARRAIGNMENT is most properly used to call a person to answer in form of law upon an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a>, &c. When brought to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, the criminal is called up- on by name to hold up his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; which though it may seem a trifling circumstance, yet is of this im- portance, that by the holding up of his hand confit de persona, and he owns himself to be of that name by which he is called. However it is not an indispensible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>; for being calculated merely for the pur- pose of identifying the person, any other acknowledg- ment <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> answer the purpose as well: therefore, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the prisoner obstinately and contemptuously refuses to hold up his hand, but confesses he is the person named, it is fully sufficient. Then the indictment is to be read to him distinctly in the English tongue (which was law, even while all other proceedings were in Latin), that he may fully understand his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. After which it is to be demand- ed of him, whether he be guilty of the crime whereof he stands indicted, or not guilty? When a criminal is arraigned he either stands <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUTE">mute</a>, or confesses the fact, or else he pleads to the indict- ment. 1. If he says nothing, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> ought ex officio to impanel a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a> to inquire whether he stands obstinately mute, or whether he be dumb ex violatione Dei. If the latter appears to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the judges of the court (who are to be of counsel for the prisoner, and to see that he hath law and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>) shall proceed to the trial, and examine all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> as if he had pleaded not guilty. But whether judgment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> can be given against such a prisoner, who hath never pleaded, and can say nothing in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> of judgment, is a point yet undetermined. If he be found to be obstinately mute (which a pri- soner hath been held to be that hath cut his own tongue), then, if it be on an indictment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> trea- son, it hath <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> been clearly settled, that standing mute is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to a conviction, and he shall receive the same judgment and execution. The English judgment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a> for standing mute was as follows: That the prisoner be remanded to the prison from whence he came, and put into a low dark chamber; and there be laid on his back, on the bare <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, naked, unless where decency forbids; that there be placed upon his body as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> as he could bear, and more; that he have no sustenance, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> only, on the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, three morsels of the worst <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>; and, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> day, three draughts of standing wa- ter that should be nearest to the prison door; and in this situation this should be alternately his daily diet, till he died, or, as anciently the judgment ran, till be answered. It hath been doubted whether this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> sub- stituted at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, or was introduced in conse- quence of the statute Westm. I, 3 Edw. I, c. 12, which seems to be the better <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. For not a word of it is mentioned in Glanvil or Bracton, or in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> author, case, or record (that hath yet been produced), previous to the reign of Edward I.: but there are in- stances on record in the reign of Henry III., where per- sons accused of felony, and standing mute, were tried in a particular manner, by two successive juries, and convicted; and it is asserted by the judges in 8 Henry IV. that, by the common law before the sta- tute, standing mute on an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> amounted to a con- viction of the felony. This statute of Edward I. di- rects such persons, "as will not put themselves upon inquests of felonies before the judges at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, to be put into hard and strong prison (soient mys en la prisone fort et dure) as those which refuse to be at the common law of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>." And, immedi- ately after this statute, the form of the judgment ap- pears in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLETA">Fleta</a> and Britton to have been only a very strict confinement in prison, with hardly any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of sustenance; but no weight is directed to be laid up- on the body, so as to hasten the death of the miserable sufferer: and indeed any surcharge of punishment on persons adjudged to penance, so as to shorten their lives, is reckoned by Horne in the Mirror as a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of criminal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMICIDE">homicide</a>. It also clearly appears, by a re- <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a> of 31 Edw. III. that the prisoner might then possibly subsist for 40 days under this lingering punish- ment. It is therefore imagined that the practice of loading him with weights, or, as it is usually called, preying him to death, was gradually introduced between 31 Edward III. and 8 Henry IV. at which last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> it first appears upon the books; being intended as a species of mercy to the delinquent, by delivering him the sooner from his torment: and hence it is also pro- bable, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of the penance was then first altered; and instead of continuing till be answered, it was directly to continue till be died, which must very soon happen under an enormous prelude. The uncertainty of its original, the doubts that were conceived of its legality, and the repugnance of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> (for it rarely was carried into practice) to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> of the laws of England, all concurred to re- quire a legislative abolition of this cruel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, and a restitution of the ancient common law; whereby the standing mute in felony, as well as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> and in trespass, amounted to a confession of the charge. 2. If the prisoner made a simple and plain confession, the court hath nothing to do but to award judgment: but it is usually very backward in receiving and re- cording According such confession, out of tenderness to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of the subject; and will generally advise the prisoner to retract it, and, 3. Plead to the indictment; as to which, see the article <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">Plea</a> of Indictment.

ARRAN

Pages 329-330

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Scotland, in the frith of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a>, between Kintyre and Cunningham. Of this island the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> we have is that given by Mr Pennant in his Tour through Scotland, vol. ii. 172—184. "Arran, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> properly Arr-unn, or, 'the island of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>,' seems not to have been noticed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, notwithstanding it must have been known to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, whose <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Agricola, had its station in the Glottae Fluvium, or the Frith of Clyde. Camden, indeed, makes this island the Glotta of Antonine, but no such name occurs in his Itinerary: it therefore was bestowed on Arran by some of his commentators. By the immense cairns, the vast monumental <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and many relics of Druidism, this island must have been considerable in very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times. Here are still traditions of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> Fingal, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIN">Fin</a> Mac Coul, who is supposed here to have enjoyed the pleasures of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>; and many places retain his name: but I can discover nothing but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORAL">oral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> that relates to the island till the time of Magnus the Barefooted, the Norwegian victor, who probably included Arran in his conquests of Kintyre. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> he did not conquer that island, it was certainly included among those that Donald Bane was to cede; for it appears that Acho, one of the successors of Magnus, in 1263, laid claim to Arran, Bute, and the Cumbres, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>: the two first he subdued, but the defeat he met with at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGS">Largs</a> soon obliged him to give up his conquests. Arran was the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. Robert Bruce retired thither during his distresses, and met with protection from his faithful vassals. Numbers of them followed his fortunes; and after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BANNOCKBURN">Bannockburn</a> he rewarded several, such as the Maccocks, Mackimons, Macbrides, and Maclois, or Fullertons, with different charters of lands in their native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. All these are now absorbed by this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> family, except the Fullertons, and a Stewart, descended from a son of Robert III., who gave him a settlement here. In the time of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a> of the Isles, his descendant possessed Cattle Douan; and he and his blood, says the Dean, are the best men in that country. About the year 1334, this island appears to have formed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the estate of Robert Stewart, great <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> of Scotland, afterwards Robert II. At that time they took arms to support the cause of their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>; who afterwards, in reward, not only granted at their request an immunity from their annual tribute of corn, but added several new privileges, and a donative to all the inhabitants that were present. In 1456, the whole island was ravaged by Donald <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Ross and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the Isles. At that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, it was still the property of James II.; but in the reign of his successor James III., when that monarch matched his sister to Thomas lord Boyd, he created him earl of Arran, and gave him the island as a portion. Soon after, on the disgrace of that family, he caused the countess to be divorced from her unfortunate husband; and bestowed both the lady and island on Sir James <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a>, in whose family it continues to this time, a very few farms excepted. "Arran is of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, being 23 miles from Sgreadan Point <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to Beinn-an-south; and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants are about 7000, who chiefly inhabit the coasts; the far greater part of the country being uninhabited by reason of the vast and barren mountains. Here are only two parishes, Kilbride and Kilmore; with a fort of chapel of ease to each, founded in the last century, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of this island, when it was blessed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> duchess of Hamilton, whose amiable disposition and humane <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the welfare of Arran render at this distant time her <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> dear to every inhabitant. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> mountains of Arran are, Goatfield, or Gaoilbeinn, or "the mountain of the winds," of a height equal to most of the Scottish <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, composed of immense piles of moorstone, in form of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> packs, clothed only with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LICHENS">lichens</a> and mosses, inhabited by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a> and ptarmigans; Beinn-bharrain, or "the sharp-pointed;" Ceum-na-caillich, "the step of the carline or old hag;" and Grianan-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHOL">Athol</a>, that yields to none in ruggedness. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> are, Loch-jorsa, where salmon come to spawn; Loch-tana; Loch-nah-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURA">jura</a>, on the top of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> hill; Loch-mhachrai; and Loch-knoc-a-charbel, full of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> eels. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are, Abhan-mhor, Moima-mhor, Slon-drai-machrei, and Jorsa; the two last remarkable for the abundance of salmon. "The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> are very few; only otters, wild cats, shrew mice, rabbits, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATS">bats</a>: the flags, which used to abound, are now reduced to about a dozen. The birds are, eagles, hooded crows, wild pigeons, stags, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, grouse, ptarmigans, daws, green plovers, and curlews. It may be remarked, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTRIDGE">partridge</a> at present inhabits this island, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the advancement of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>. "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is very severe: for besides the violence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> is very rigorous; and snow lay here in the valleys for 13 weeks of the last winter. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is remarkably salubrious; and many invalids <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> here on that account, and to drink the whey of goats <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>. "The principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> here is the pleurisy: smallpox, measles, and chincough, visit the island once in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight years. The practice of bleeding twice every year seems to have been intended as a preventive against the pleurisy: but it is now performed with the utmost regularity at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Hamilton keeps a surgeon in pay; who at those seasons makes a tour of the island. On notice of his approach, the inhabitants of each <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a> assemble in the open air; extend their arms; and are bled into a hole made in the ground, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> receptacle of the vital fluid. In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> fevers, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a> of wood forrel is used with success, to allay the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. An infusion of ramsons, or allium urfaeum, in brandy, is esteemed here a good remedy for the gravel. "The men are strong, tall, and well made; all speak the Erse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, but the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> is entirely laid aside. Their diet is chiefly potatoes and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>; and during winter, some dried mutton or goat is added to their hard fare. A deep dejection appears in general through the countenances of all; no time can be spared for amusement of any kind; the whole being given for procuring the means of paying their rent, of laying in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, or getting a scanty pittance of meat and clothing." "The leafes of farms are 19 years. The succeeding tenants generally find the ground little better than a caput mortuum; and for this reason: Should they at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of the lease leave the lands in a good state, some avaricious neighbours would have the preference in the next setting, by offering a price more than the person who had expended part of his substance in enriching the farm could possibly do. This induces them to leave it in the original state. The method of setting a farm is very singular; each is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> possessed by a number of small tenants; thus a farm of 40l. a year is occupied by 18 different people, who by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEASES">leases</a> are bound, conjunctly and severally, for the payment of the rent to the proprietor. These live in the farm in houses cluttered together, so that each farm appears like a little village. The tenants annually divide the arable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>; each has his ridge of land, to which he puts his mark, such as he would do to any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>; and this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of farm is called run-rig, (i.e.) ridge. They join in ploughing; every one keeps a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> or more; and the number of those animals consumes so much corn, as often to occasion a scarcity; the corn and peas raised being (much of it) designed for their subsistence, and that of the cattle, during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> winter. The pasture and moor land annexed to the farm is common to all the possessors. All the farms are open. Enclosures of any form, except in two or three places, are quite unknown: so that there must be a great loss of time in preserving their corn, &c., from trespassers. The usual manure is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, coral and shells. The run-rig farms are now discouraged; but since the tenements are let by roup or auction, and advanced by an unnatural force to above <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the old rent, without any allowance for enclosing, any example set in agriculture, any security of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> by lengthening the leases, affairs <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> turn retrograde, and the farms relapse into their old state of rudeness; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIGRATION">migration</a> will increase (for it has begun), and the rents be reduced even below their former value: the late rents were scarce 1200l. a-year; the expected rents 3000l.
