Father Daniel might well be mistaken in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> which he made between the effects of ancient and modern artillery, and in his conclusion that the latter was of little use: the situation of this good father removed him from the scenes of war and the opportunities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. But it is astonishing, that one so learned in the military art as the commentator of Polybius, who had ocular demonstration of the success of modern artillery, should have declared so violently against it. Whatever be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with these authors and their maxims, it may be affirmed, that cannon is one of the most singular discoveries which have been made amongst men; and by little and little it has changed the whole art of war, and of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> influenced the whole system of policy in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The era of artillery is dated from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Crecy in 1346, because it is only from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> that cannons were mentioned in battle. Edward III. of England successfully employed some pieces of artillery placed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of artillery was then known in France as well as in England; but probably <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> VI. marched with so much hurry and precipitation to attack his enemy, that he left his cannon as useless encumbrances behind him. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> arts considerably retarded the progress of artillery; and that of which they were then possessed was so unwieldy and imperfect, that they could not possibly discern its importance and efficiency in practice. After the invention of gunpowder, the Spaniards were the first who armed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of their foot with muskets and harquebusses, and mixed them with the pikes. In this they were soon imitated by most other nations; though the English had not entirely laid aside their favourite weapon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> bow, and generally taken to The first muskets were very heavy, and could not be fired without a rest; they had matchlocks, and barrels of a wide bore, that carried a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of powder, and did execution at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance. The musketeers on a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> carried only their rests and ammunition; and had boys to bear their muskets after them, for which they were allowed great additional pay. They were very slow in loading, not only by reason of the unwieldiness of the pieces, and because they carried the powder and balls separate, but from the time it took to prepare and adjust the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a>; so that their fire was not near so brisk as ours is now. Afterwards a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> kind of matchlock musket came into use; and they carried their ammunition in bandoliers, which were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> belts that came over the shoulder, to which were hung several little <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of wood covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, each containing a charge of powder; the balls they carried loose in a pouch, and they had also a priming <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a> hanging by their side. Matchlocks were, about the beginning of this century, universally diffused in Europe, and the troops were armed with firelocks; to which, much about the same time, the bayonet being added, pikes also were laid aside; which latter change, whether it was for the better or not, is a point that still admits of dispute among the best military writers, who are divided in their opinions about it, though most of them disapprove of it. The old English writers call those large muskets calivers; the harquebus was a lighter piece, that could be fired without a rest. The matchlock was fired by a match, fixed by a kind of tongs in the fermente or cock, which by pulling the trigger was brought down with great quickness upon the priming in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">pan</a>, over which there was a sliding cover, which was drawn back by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> at the time of firing. There was a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of nicety and care required to fit the match properly to the cock, so as to come down exactly true on the priming, to blow the ashes from the coal, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the pan from the sparks that fell from it: a great deal of time was also lost in taking it out of the cock, and returning it between the fingers of the left hand, every time that the piece was fired; and wet <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> often rendered the matches useless. However, most writers allow that they were very sure, and less apt to miss fire than the firelock. The firelock is so called, from producing fire of itself, by the action of the flint and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>. The most ancient invention of this sort is the wheel lock, which we find mentioned in Luigi Collado's Treatise of Artillery, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, 1586, as then lately invented in Germany. This sort of lock was used till within these hundred years, especially for pistols and carbines. It was composed of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> steel wheel, with an axis, to which was fastened a chain, which, by being wound round it drew up a very strong <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; on pulling the trigger, the spring acting, whirled the wheel about with great velocity, and the friction of the edge of it (which was a little notched) against the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> produced the fire; the cock was made so as to bring the stone upon the edge of the wheel, part of which was in the pan, and touched the priming; they used any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> hard pebble for that purpose, which served as well as flint. These locks were inconvenient, took time to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> up (or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAN">span</a>, as they termed it), and sometimes would not go off; an instance of which may be seen in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUDLOW">Ludlow</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a>. When the firelock, such as we now use, was invented, we cannot ascertain; it is called by writers of about the middle of the last century, a snapflame or snapbance, which being the Dutch word for a firelock, seems to indicate that it is a Dutch invention, and that we took it from them. But <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">Ward</a>, in his Animadversions of War, printed in 1639, p. 502, after describing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of the firelock, pistol, and carbine (by which he means the wheel-lock), says, that as most of our pieces go with English locks, which differ from firelocks, he shall add the method of handling them; and then gives the exercise of the snapfire carbine; by which it appears, that there was little or no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between that and the pieces now in use. The more modern writers call it a fusée, from the French word fusil; whence the name of fusiliers is still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to several of our regiments, which were the first that were armed with them on the diffuse of matchlocks. They used the musket and rest in England so late as the beginning of the civil wars, as may be seen in Col. Bariffe's Young Artillery <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, 1643. Figueria, in his embassy in 1518, relates, that the Persians would neither make use of infantry nor of artillery, because by them the impetuosity of attack and the facility of retreat were equally encumbered and retarded: in these expedients alone their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> and their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> consisted. This method of advancing and retreating is widely different from the present conduct of war, as the artillery in armies is now prodigiously multiplied, and must be transported to every place where any body of troops whatever is destined to operate. The length and diameter of cannon has been much diminished, which must likewise proportionably diminish their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. It is by long practice and experience that they have discovered how much might be deduced from their magnitude in both these respects with propriety, without hurting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> effects which, on some occasions, it is necessary they should produce, by rendering them more easy to be wielded, which was the advantage pursued by lessening their size. See further the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Cannon, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNNERY">Gunnery</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROJECTILES">Projectiles</a>. Improvements, however, are still making, and will probably long continue to be made, in these ignominious machines that mock the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>, which, though they seem to be invented for the destruction of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> and the subversion of empires, have yet by their effects rendered war less <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> and less sanguine; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> alliances have been more successfully conciliated among all nations, conquests are become less frequent and less rapid, and successes in war have been more easily reduced to calculation. The change introduced in the military art by the modern artillery, Dr Smith observes, has enhanced greatly both the expense of exercising and disciplining any particular <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> in time of peace, and that of employing them in time of war. Both their arms and their ammunition are become more expensive. A musket is a more expensive machine than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JAVELIN">javelin</a>. Artillery, or a bow and arrows; a cannon or a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, than a ballista or a catapulta. The powder which is spent in a modern review is lost irrecoverably, and occasions a very considerable expense. The javelins and arrows which were thrown or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> in an ancient one, could easily be picked up again, and were besides of very little value. The cannon and the mortar are not only much dearer, but much heavier machines than the ballista or catapulta, and require a greater expense, not only to prepare them for the field, but to carry them to it. As the superiority of the modern artillery too over that of the ancients is very great, it has become much more difficult, and consequently much more expensive, to fortify a town so as to resist even for a few weeks the attack of that superior artillery. In modern war the great expense of fire arms gives an evident advantage to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> which can best afford that expense; and consequently, to an opulent and civilized, over a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and barbarous nation. In ancient times, the opulent and civilized found it difficult to defend themselves against the poor and barbarous nations. In modern times the poor and barbarous find it difficult to defend themselves against the opulent and civilized. The invention of fire arms, an invention which at first sight appears to be so pernicious, is certainly favourable both to the permanency and to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of civilization. It has to many appeared <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of surprise, that the battles of the ancients should be described with an order, perspicuity, and circumstantial minuteness, which are not to be found in the military writers of modern times. Scholars have endeavoured to explain this difference by observing the immense disproportion, in point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and abilities, between the military historians of modern Europe and those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> and Rome. But the difficulty will be better solved, Dr Gillies thinks, by reflecting on the changes introduced into the art of war by the change of artillery; which in military operations, form the pivot on which the whole turns. 1. From the nature of fire arms, modern battles are involved in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> and confusion. 2. From the same cause, modern armies occupy a much greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of ground, and begin to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> at much greater distances: which renders it more difficult to observe and ascertain their manoeuvres. 3. The immense train of artillery, ammunition, &c., required in the practice of modern war, gives a certain immobility to our armies, which renders it impossible to perform, without great danger, those rapid evolutions in sight of an enemy, which so often decided the battles of the ancients. With us, almost everything depends on the judicious choice of ground, a matter requiring great military genius, but not admitting the embellishments of hiforical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. In the battles of the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, the extraordinary disproportion between the numbers slain on the side of the victors and the vanquished has been observed as another remarkable circumstance. But this necessarily resulted from the nature of their arms. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> weapons being not missile, but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a>, armies could not begin to act till they had approached so near to each other, that the conquered found themselves cut off from all possibility of retreat. In modern times, such consequences seldom take place. The use of fire arms (which often renders the action itself more bloody, furnishes the defeated party with various means of retreating with considerable safety. The sphere of military action is so widely extended in modern times, that before the victors can run over the space which separates them from the vanquished, the latter may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> back, and proceed with little loss beyond their reach; and should any village, hedge, ravine, &c., be found in their way, may often check the ardour of the pursuers. Upon these considerations, the invention of gunpowder and modern artillery may be said to have saved the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a> of human blood. Equestrian engagements (since the principles on which cavalry act remain nearly the same in every age) are still distinguished by similar circumstances to those which appear so extraordinary in the battles of antiquity. Artillery <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">Park</a>, the place in the rear of both lines in an army, for encamping the artillery, which is drawn up in lines, of which one is formed by the guns; the ammunition waggons make two or three lines, 60 paces behind the guns, and 30 distant from one another; the pontoons and tumbrels make the last line. The whole is surrounded with a rope which forms the park; the gunners and matroes encamp on the flanks; and the bombardiers, pontoon men, and artificers, in the rear. Artillery Train, a certain number of pieces of ordnance, mounted on carriages, with all their furniture fit for marching. Artillery <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>, a band of infantry, consisting of 600 men, making part of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> guard of London. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">Artist</a>, in a general sense, a person skilled in some art. Mr Harris defines an artist to be, "A person possessing an habitual power of becoming the cause of some effect, according to a system of various and well approved precepts." See Art. We are told * of a privilege granted at Vicenza to artists, like that of clergy in England: in virtue thereof, criminals adjudged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> their lives if they can prove themselves the most excellent and consummate workmen in any useful art. This benefit is allowed them in favorem artis, for the first offence, except in some particular crimes, of which coining is one; for here the greater the art, the more dangerous the person. Artist (Artista), in an academical sense, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> or proficient in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of arts. In the early ages of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> liberal arts completed the whole course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, as it is called: whence the masters of this faculty were denominated Artists. What they understood by the liberal arts used to be summed up in the following Latin <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>: Lingua, Tropus, Ratio, Numerus, Tonus, Angulus, Affra. Artist is more peculiarly used, by Paracelsus and other adepts, for a chemist or alchemist. We find frequent mention, in authors of this class, of Elias Artist, or Elias the artist, who is to come some time before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the world, and restore and make perfect all arts and sciences, but especially the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>-making art; and usher in a truly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> age, or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MILLENNIUM">millennium</a>. The lower and meaner things in this sublime art, Paracelsus observes, God has permitted to be already discovered; but for the greater and more important

a town of Vindelicia (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>): Now Altzberg, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, on the Danube, below Ingolstadt (Aventinus): but Cluverius supposes it to be Leibecan, on the Salzach, below Laufen, in the archbishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALZBURG">Salzburg</a>.

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Salalii in Gallia Cispadana, at the foot of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>: now called la Tuile by the inhabitants, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMLET">hamlet</a> of Savoy, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Auflot, at the foot of Mount St Bernard the Lefs.

ARTOTYRITES

Pages 351-351

a Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, in the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, who celebrated the eucharist with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and cheese, saying, that the first oblations of men, were not only of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, but of their flocks. The word is derived from \(\alpha\eta\gamma\sigma\tau\sigma\), bread, and \(\tau\eta\gamma\sigma\tau\sigma\), cheese. The Artotyrites admitted women to the priesthood and episcopacy; and Epiphanius tells us, it was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> thing to see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> girls at once enter into their church, robed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and holding a torch in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; where they wept, and bewailed the wretchedness of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and the miseries of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>.

ARUBA

Pages 351-352

a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Terra Fir- Vol. II. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> II. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, which had been given to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Edward by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and sold by the latter to Bishop <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARUNDEL">Arundel</a>. In 1386, he was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of England; two years after, he was translated to the see of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>; and, in 1396, was advanced to the archiepiscopal see of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, when he resigned the chancellorship. This was the first instance of the translation of an archbishop of York to the see of Canterbury. Scarcely was he fixed in this see, when he had a contest with the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of visitation. The affair was referred to King Richard, who determined it in favour of the archbishop. At his visitation in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, he revived an old <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, by which the inhabitants of the respective parishes were obliged to pay to their rector one halfpenny in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> out of the rent of their houses. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> year of his translation, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> being held at London, the commons with the king's leave impeached the archbishop, together with his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Arundel, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>. The archbishop was sentenced to be banished, and within forty days to depart the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> on pain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. He retired first to France; and then to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Rome, where Pope Boniface IX. gave him a kind reception. About this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a> (afterwards Henry IV.) was in France, having been banished by King Richard. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and others, tired with the oppressions of Richard, solicited the duke to take the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. This their request they drew up in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, and sent it over by faithful messengers to Archbishop Arundel, desiring him to be their advocate on this occasion with the duke. The archbishop, being a fellow sufferer, gladly accepted the office; and went with the messengers to the duke at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where they delivered the letters from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> and commons of England, and the archbishop seconded them with the best arguments he could invent. The inviting offer, after some objections which were easily obviated, the duke accepted; and upon his accession to the throne, Arundel, who had returned with him to England, was restored to his see. In the first year of this prince's reign, Arundel summoned a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> which sat at St Paul's. The next year the commons moved that the revenues of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> might be applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the public; but Arundel opposed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> with such vigour, that it was thrown aside. In the year 1408, Arundel began to exert himself against the Lollards, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Wickliffites; and his zeal for suppressing that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> carried him to several unjustifiable severities against the heads of it, particularly against Sir John Oldcastle and Lord Cobham. He also procured a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNODICAL">synodical</a> constitution, which forbade the translation of the Scriptures into the vulgar tongue. This prelate died at Canterbury, Feb. 20, 1413, of an inflammation in his throat, with which he was seized (as it is pretended) whilst he was pronouncing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> upon Lord Cobham. The Lollards asserted this to be a judgment from God; and indeed Bishop Goodwin speaks in the same manner, saying, "He who had withheld from the people the word of God, the food of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> judgment of God had his throat so closed, that he could not speak a single word, nor swallow meat or drink, and was so starved to death." He was buried in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> church of Canterbury, near the west end, under a monument erected by himself in his lifetime. To this church he was a considerable benefactor; for Arundel built the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANTERN">lantern</a>-tower and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of the nave: Arundel gave a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> of five bells, called from him Arundel's ring; several rich vestments, a mitre enchased with jewels, a silver gilt crosier, and two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> chalices. Arundel, a borough and market town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west side of the river Arun, over which there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. It had a harbour, wherein a ship of 150 tons burden might ride; but the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> had ruined it so far, that, in 1733, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> passed for repairing it, and for erecting new piers, locks, &c. The castle, which gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of earl to its possessors, is seated on the east of the Tame, and is reputed to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in compass. It sends two members to parliament; and is 55 miles south-west-by-south of London, and 10 miles east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHICHESTER">Chichester</a>. Arundel is the premier earldom in England, belonging to the illustrious family of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>; and is the only title in England that goes along with the lands. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 25. N. Lat. 50. 45. ARUNDEL <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">Oil</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>. At <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a>, Gombroon, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURAT">Surat</a>, in the East Indies, there grows a tree which bears a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> enclosed in a rough husk, which resembles much the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-chestnut; and the kernel of the nut yields an oil by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, which is of a purgative <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a>-spoonful of it is reckoned a dose. The tree goes by the name of the arundel tree at Bombay, and its oil by that of the arundel oil. Mr Sinclair, one of the surgeons belonging to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> regiment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, who was formerly surgeon to an East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> ship, gave Dr Monro of London a small bottle full of this oil, which he said was much used for the cure of the dysentery in India, and that he had given it in four recent <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of dysentery with success. Dr Monro thinks it probable that this is the oil of the purging nuts mentioned in Dale's Pharmacologia, which are got from the tree called lignum moluccense, pavonia diutium, fructu avellanae, J. B. i. 342; and pinus Indica, nucleo purgante, C. B. 402; and the palma Chrissi Indica, Tournefort Mat. Med.

ARUNDELIAN MARBLES

Pages 352-356
OXFORD MARBLES, or PARIAN CHRONICLE, are ancient stones (as has been supposed), whereon is inscribed a chronicle of the city of Athens, engraven in capital letters in the island of Paros, one of the Cyclades, 261 years before Jesus Christ. They take their first name from Thomas earl of Arundel, who procured them out of the East, or from Henry his grandson, who presented them to the university of Oxford. The Arundelian marbles, in their perfect state, contained a chronological detail of the principal events of Greece during a period of 1318 years, beginning with Cecrops, before Christ 1582 years, and ending with the archonship of Diognetus, before Christ 264. But the chronicle of the last 90 years is lost; so that the part now remaining ends at the archonship of Diotimus, 354 years before the birth of Christ; and in this fragment the inscription is at present so much corroded and effaced, that the sense can only be discovered by very learned and industrious antiquaries; or, more properly speaking, supplied by their conjectures. This chronicle, and many other relics of antiquity, real or pretended, were purchased in Asia Minor, in Greece, or in the islands of the Archipelago, by Mr William Petty, who in the year 1624 was sent by Thomas Thomas earl of Arundel for the purpose of making such collections for him in the east. They were brought into England about the beginning of the year 1619, and placed in the gardens belonging to Arundel house in London. Soon after their arrival they excited a general curiosity, and were viewed by many inquisitive and learned men; among others by Sir Robert Cotton, who prevailed upon Selden to employ his abilities in explaining the Greek inscriptions. Selden and two of his friends, Patrick Young, or, as he styled himself in Latin, Patricius Junius, and Richard James, immediately commenced their operations, by cleaning and examining the marble containing the Smyrnean and Magnesian league, and afterwards proceeded to the Parian chronicle. The following year Selden published a small volume in quarto, including about 39 inscriptions copied from the marbles. In the turbulent reign of Charles I. and the subsequent usurpation, Arundel house was often deserted by the illustrious owners; and, in their absence, some of the marbles were defaced and broken, and others either stolen or used for the ordinary purposes of architecture. The chronological marble in particular, was unfortunately broken and defaced. The upper part, containing 31 epochs, is said to have been worked up in repairing a chimney in Arundel house. In the year 1667, the Hon. Henry Howard, afterwards duke of Norfolk, the grandson of the first collector, presented these supposed remains of antiquity to the university of Oxford. Selden's work becoming very scarce, Bishop Fell engaged Mr Prideaux to publish a new edition of the inscriptions, which was printed at Oxford in 1676. In 1732 Mr Maittaire obliged the public with a more comprehensive view of the marbles than either of his predecessors. Lastly, Dr Chandler published a new and improved copy of the marbles in 1763, in which he corrected the mistakes of the former editors; and in some of the inscriptions, particularly that of the Parian chronicle, supplied the lacunae by many ingenious conjectures. The Arundelian marbles have generally been regarded as a curious monument of antiquity. They were, however, discovered in some instances to be inconsistent with the most authentic historical accounts; Sir Isaac Newton and several other modern philosophers paid little or no regard to them; and of late their absolute authenticity has been severely questioned in an express dissertation upon the subject, entitled The Parian Chronicle. In this dissertation much ingenuity as well as judgment and a great extent of ancient learning are displayed. His doubts, the author observes, arise from the following considerations. I. "The characters have no certain or unequivocal marks of antiquity." The Π and Ζ, which frequently occur in the form supposed to be the most ancient (viz. the perpendicular line of the Π on the right hand only half as long as that on the left, and the Ζ in the form of a prostrate Π), are so well known, that any modern fabricator of a Greek inscription, which he intends to impose upon the world as a relic of antiquity, would most probably use them in preference to the more common and ordinary forms. But the letters in the Parian chronicle have no appearance of antiquity except this very equivocal one. They do not in the least resemble the Sigean, the Nemean, or the Delian inscriptions, which are supposed to be of a more ancient date. They differ in many respects from the letters on the Marmor Sandvicense, which, according to the learned editor of that inscription, was engraved in the year before Christ 374. They bear no sort of resemblance to the characters on the Farnese pillars, to those of the Alexandrian manuscript, or others of a later date. They seem, continues our author, to resemble perhaps more than any other the letters of the alphabet taken by Montfaucon from the Marmor Cyzicenum at Venice. They are plain and simple in their form, and such as an ordinary stonecutter of the present age would probably make, if he were employed to engrave a Greek inscription according to the alphabet now in use. The small letters intermixed among the larger have, in the opinion of our author, an air of affectation and artifice, rather than genuine antiquity; and he is persuaded, that the antiquity of an inscription can never be proved by the mere form of the letters, because the most ancient characters may be as easily counterfeited as those which compose our present alphabets. That the learned reader may form a competent idea of the characters in the Parian chronicle, the author has compared them with those of other inscriptions, and given what is usually termed a facsimile. In regard to several archaisms, as they are called, in this chronicle, and which our author specifies, he contends, that no conclusion can be drawn from them in favour of its antiquity. What reason could there be, he asks, for introducing these into the Parian chronicle? We do not usually find them in Greek writers of the same age, or even in those of the most early date. The reign of Ptolemy Philadelphus, with the 21st year of which the date of the chronicle coincides, was not an age of rude antiquity with respect to the Greek language; being only 130 years after the time of Xenophon and Plato, when the Greek was spoken and written in its utmost purity and elegance; and we can scarcely suppose, that even a stonecutter, in that refined age, would have been permitted to disgrace a superb and learned monument with such barbarisms as occur in the chronicle. The archaisms, however, he remarks, are not uniformly observed in this inscription. He adduces five instances of deviation; and adds, he is almost tempted to suspect, that ἡμεῖς ἐπέστην, ἡμεῖς ἐπέστην, and other pretended archaisms, are owing to a mere affectation of antiquity, or to a corrupted dialect and pronunciation in later ages. Those archaisms, our author acknowledges, appear on other marbles; but he thinks, that, for that very reason, they would naturally be adopted by the fabricator of a supposititious inscription; and the authenticity of those inscriptions in which they appear must be established before they can be urged in opposition to the present argument. II. "It is not probable that the chronicle was engraved for private use?"—Our author thinks it an impossible supposition that such an expensive and burdensome work could have been executed by a private citizen, either for his own amusement, or for the benefit of his fellow citizens. In the first place, a long inscription could not be engraved in marble without such an expense as few learned Greeks were able to afford. Or, if its author, by an uncommon felicity, was able to erect such a literary monument, the scheme would have been useless and imprudent; as all the contents of the inscription might have been published more commodiously and effectually by the common mode of writing in use at that time. A variety of arguments is adduced, illustrating the superiority of a manuscript to such an inscription as the chronicle, in a number of respects; and enforcing the improbability of its having ever been executed, either for public or private use. Much evidence from ancient history is likewise produced in support of the assertion, that the common mode of writing, in the reign of Ptolemy Philadelphus, was not on stones. It is not, however, necessary to prove, by the testimony of ancient authors, that books were written on parchment, or paper made of the Egyptian papyrus, or any such materials, before the date of the Parian chronicle. This is sufficiently evinced by the very existence of the writings of Moses, David, Solomon, and the Jewish prophets; the works of Homer, Hesiod, Anacreon, Pindar, Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides, Herodotus, Hippocrates, Aristophanes, Thucydides, Xenophon, Plato, Demosthenes, Aristotle, &c.; and it is still more incontrovertibly proved by the libraries which were collected in preceding ages, or about that time; such as those of Polycrates in Samos, Pifilatus and Euclides at Athens, Nicocrates in Cyprus, Euripides the poet, Aristotle the philosopher, Clearchus at Heraclea Pontica, and the most extensive and magnificent library of Ptolemy Philadelphus in Egypt, founded in or before the year 284, which in his time is said to have contained 100,000 volumes, and to have been enlarged by his successors to the amount of almost 600,000. Not long afterwards a library was founded at Pergamus by Attalus and Eumenes, which, according to Plutarch, contained 200,000. There are clear and decisive proofs that the common mode of writing in the time of Ptolemy Philadelphus was not on stones. III. "The chronicle does not appear to have been engraved by public authority." 1. The first argument in support of this opinion is, that inscriptions of that kind usually being with a particular form; as, Ἡ ΒΟΥΛΗ ΚΑΙ Ο ΔΗΜΟΣ, 'The senate and the people;' or thus, ΕΛΩΣΕΝ ΤΗΝ ΒΟΥΛΗΝ ΚΑΙ ΤΟΙ ΔΗΜΩΙ, 'It pleased the senate and the people, &c.' But the Parian chronicle begins in the manner of a private man, speaking of his own performance in the first person singular. This argument, our author remarks, cannot be much affected by observing, that the beginning of the inscription is obliterated; for it is necessarily implied by the words now remaining. 2. The facts and dates, which are mentioned in this chronicle, do not appear to have been extracted from any public records, or calculated to answer the purpose of authentic documents; as many eminent princes and magistrates are passed over without notice; in several instances, the transactions of whole centuries are omitted; and the facts, chiefly specified, are not matters of general or national importance. 3. The Parian inscription is such a one as we can hardly suppose the magistrates or the people of Paros would have ordered to be engraved. Stately sepulchres, pillars, triumphal arches, and the like, were erected to perpetuate the glory of eminent men. The remembrance of events in which nations were interested, the succession of princes, &c., were preserved in the same manner. Leagues, decrees, and laws, were likewise engraved on marble or brass, and fixed to a pillar, the walls of a temple, or other public buildings; because such inscriptions were designed for the inspection of the people, as they essentially concerned their conduct, their property, their liberty, or their lives. But, our author asks, for whom could the chronicle of Paros be intended? It contains no encomiums of any of the patriots, the heroes, or the demigods of the country, no decrees of the magistrates, no public records, no laws of state. On the contrary, it is a work of mere speculation and learning, in which the inhabitants of that island, especially the common people, had not the least interest or concern. These words at the beginning, αὐχον τος ῥη Παρω, would naturally lead us to suppose, that the inscription related to Paros. And, if so, it would have been natural for the author to have mentioned some of the most important occurrences in the history of that island. But, says this acute and learned critic, what scheme does our chronologer pursue on this occasion? Does he record the events and revolutions of his own country? Does he mention any of the battles, sieges, and treaties of the Parians? any of their public institutions? any of their poets, patriots, or warriors? Does he mention Archilochus, who was honoured by his countrymen, and distinguished as a poet in a general assembly of the Greeks? Not a syllable on any of these subjects! On the contrary, he rambles from place to place, and records the transactions of Athens, Corinth, Macedon, Lydia, Crete, Cyprus, Sicily, Persia, and other foreign countries with which Paros had no connection. In this view the inscription seems to have been as impertinent in the island of Paros, as a marble monument would be in this country, recording the antiquities of France or Spain; or one in Jamaica recording the revolutions of England. But upon supposition that the inscription is a forgery, it is easy to account for this extraordinary circumstance. A few chronological occurrences in the ancient history of Paros would not have been so interesting to the generality of readers, or so valuable in the estimation of every lover of antiquities, or, in short, so profitable to the compiler, as a general system of Grecian chronology. VI. "The Greek and Roman writers, for a long time after the date of this work, complain that they had no chronological account of the affairs of ancient Greece." This position is confirmed by the testimony of Julius Africanus, Justin ss="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">Martyr, Plutarch, Josephus, Varro, Diodorus Siculus, and others; and the following series of interrogatories is subjoined: "Thucydides, I know, lived 140 years before the chronicle is said to have been written; but if Thucydides, as well as other writers, complained that there was nothing but uncertainty in the earlier period of Grecian history, from whence can we suppose the author of this inscription collected such a clear, determinate, and comprehensive system of chronology? If he had any sources of information, which were unknown to succeeding writers, how happens it, that they should all of them overlook this most considerable, most exact, most creditable author?" Why did they omit this ancient account of their early ages? Why did they not copy his most memorable epochs? Why did they not produce his authority? or at least, why did they not mention his opinion? Surely nothing, to all appearance, could be more elaborate, more important, or of higher authority, than a chronological table, which was thought worthy of being engraved on marble. V. "The chronicle is not once mentioned by any writer of antiquity. This indeed appears a strong argument against its authenticity. Apollodorus, an Athenian, the disciple of Aristaarchus the grammarian, and Panætius the philosopher, wrote a genealogical and historical work on the early ages of Greece; but, though composed 120 years after the date of the Parian chronicle, it does not contain the smallest traces of a systematical chronology. It is remarkable too that the chronicle of Apollodorus is quoted by Diodorus Siculus, Strabo, Plutarch, A. Gellius, Lucian, and many other writers of antiquity; while the Parian chronicle, which comprehends a more extensive period, is entirely unnoticed. It contains, however, such wonderful discoveries in ancient history, that if it had existed 264 years before the Christian era, it must have excited a general attention, and been referred to as an authority by writers of succeeding times. But we do not find, in any author of antiquity, either poet or historian, geographer or chronologer, mythologist or scholiast, the most distant allusion to the Parian chronicle; though it was such a common practice among the ancients to mention the works of their predecessors, that in many books we find references and allusions to three, four, five, six, or seven hundred different authors of every denomination. VI. "Some of the facts mentioned in the chronicle seem to have been taken from writers of a later date." Our inquirer collates several passages in the Parian chronicle with parallel passages in Greek authors, to evince that there is, in the former, an appearance of imitation, or a stronger resemblance than such as may be supposed to arise from accident; that there are likewise some improbabilities attending the account of Deucalion, as related in the Parian chronicle; and that the names of six, and, if the lacunæ are properly supplied, the names of 12 cities appear to have been engraved on the marble, exactly as we find them in Ælian's Various History. But there is not, our author observes, any imaginable reason for this particular arrangement. It does not correspond with the time of their foundation, with their situation in Ionia, with their relative importance, or with the order in which they are placed by other eminent historians. The argument by which our author endeavours to prove that the Parian chronicle has, in this instance, copied Ælian's Various History, seems decisive of the fact. He observes, that six names may be transposed 720 different ways; and that 12 names admit of 479,001,600 different transpositions. Supposing then, that there is no particular reason for one arrangement rather than another, it will follow, that the chance of two authors, placing them in the same order, is, in the former case, as 1 to 720; and in the latter as 1 to 479,001,600. It is therefore, says he, utterly improbable, that these names should have been placed in this order on the marble, if the author of the inscription had not transcribed them from the historian." It may indeed be urged, with regard to this similarity of arrangement in the Parian chronicle and Ælian's Various History, that the inference might be the very inverse of that which is specified by our author. But that Ælian should have seen the Parian chronicle, without once mentioning it; or that he should have exactly copied a list of towns, arranged neither according to chronological nor topographical order; is indeed a supposition equally improbable with the other. VII. "Parachronisms appear in some of the epochs, which we can scarcely suppose a Greek chronologer in the 12th Olympiad would be liable to commit." After specifying these, our inquirer asks, Would a writer of reputation and learning, in one of the most polished and enlightened eras of ancient Greece, commit such mistakes in opposition to the positive attestations of the most accurate historians, in events of public notoriety? Would a private citizen, or a magistrate of Paros, order a crude and inaccurate series of epochs to be engraved, at a great expense, and transmitted to posterity on a marble monument? It is hardly probable. VIII. "The history of the discovery of the Parian chronicle is obscure and unsatisfactory." Our author observes, that it is attended with some suspicious circumstances, and without any of those clear and unequivocal evidences which always discriminate truth from falsehood. There are no data in the inscription by which to discover the place where the marble was erected. The place likewise where it was found is not ascertained; though the generality of writers who have had occasion to mention it have supposed that it was found in the island of Paros. If it was erected at Smyrna, as some imagine, our author asks for what purpose does the writer mention Aftyranax the archon of Paros, and not one circumstance relative to Smyrna? If, adds he, it was erected at Paros, why does he not mention more archons of that city than one? Or how shall we account for his profound silence with respect to all the events and revolutions which must have happened in that island, and have been infinitely more interesting to the natives than the transactions of any foreign country? The train of circumstances by which the Parian chronicle came into the possession of Mr Petty, whom Lord Arundel had sent into the east for the purpose of collecting antiquities, as well as the subsequent conduct of Peirene its former owner, affords our author a strong presumption, that "the inscription was actually fabricated, with the view of obtaining for it a high price, upon the pretence that it was a relic of great antiquity. It is certain, that there is something mysterious in the conduct of the first ostensible proprietors. These marbles had been totally unknown, or unnoticed, for almost 1900 years, and at last they are dug out of the ground—nobody can tell us when or where!" IX. "The literary world has been frequently imposed upon by spurious books and inscriptions, and therefore we should be extremely cautious with regard to what we receive under the venerable name of antiquity." This proposition is illustrated by a great variety variety of examples, and very properly exposes the forgeries which have disgraced the republic of letters in different ages; and although one of the more recent ones cited, namely Offian's poems, be a point very far indeed from being established, yet that deceptions of this kind have been practised is an unquestionable fact. In endeavouring towards the end of his dissertation, to investigate the time of the supposed forgery, he observes, that the 16th century, and the prior part of the 17th, produced a multitude of grammarians, critics, and commentators, deeply versed in Grecian literature, and amply qualified for the compilation of such a chronological system as that of the Arundelian marbles. Above all, the science of chronology was particularly studied and investigated about that time: "Nunc fert verum chronologia," says Scaliger in the year 1605, "omnes hoc terrum excalcatum." Caiusbon treats those persons with contempt who were unacquainted with the improvements which had been made in that department of learning after the revival of letters. Innumerable systems of chronology had been published before the year 1625: from which it was easy to extract a series of memorable events, and give the compilation a Grecian dress. "The avidity," says our author, "with which all relics of antiquity were then collected, and the high price at which they were purchased, were sufficient inducements to any one, whose avarice or whose necessity was stronger than his integrity, to engrave his labours on marble, and transmit them to Smyrna, as a commodious emporium for such rarities." The precise period of the fabrication, however, must still be reckoned apocryphal and uncertain. The sum of fifty guineas, which Peirese gave to the supposed fabricator, was inadequate to such a laborious and expensive work. Upon the whole, perhaps, it would be too hasty to pronounce decisively that this famous chronicle, so long respected, is an imposition upon the public. It may, however, be safely affirmed, that the suspicions against it are extremely strong, and the objections already cited of a nature very difficult to be removed. No attempts have yet been made with this view: But under some future article, as Chronology, Marbles, or Parian Chronicle, we may possibly have an opportunity of resuming the subject with additional information.

ARUSINI CAMPI

Pages 356-356

plains in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCANIA">Lucania</a>, famous for the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> and Pyrrhus. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> being at Tarentum, and hearing that the two new consuls Curius Dentatus and Cornelius Lentulus had divided their forces, the one including Lucania and the other Samnium; he likewise divided a chosen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> into two bodies, marching with his Epirots against Dentatus, in hopes of surprising him in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> near Beneventum. But the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> having notice of his approach, marched out of his intrenchments with a strong detachment of legionaries to meet him, repulsed his vanguard, put many of the Epirots to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and took some of their elephants. Curius, encouraged by this success, marched into the Arufian fields, and drew up his army in a plain, which was wide enough for his troops, but too narrow for the Epirot phalanx to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> with its full effect. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s eagerness to try his strength and skill with so renowned a commander, stimulated him to engage at that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> disadvantage. Upon the first signal the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> began; and one of the king's wings giving way, victory seemed to incline to the Romans. But that wing where the king fought in person repulsed the enemy and drove them to their intrenchments. This advantage was in great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> owing to the elephants; a circumstance which Curius perceiving, commanded a body of reserve, which he had posted near the camp, to advance and attack those animals with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> torches; which frightened and annoyed them to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that they wheeled about, broke into the phalanx, and put that body into the utmost disorder. The Romans taking advantage of this confusion, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with such fury that the enemy were entirely broken and defeated. Pyrrhus retired to Tarentum, attended only by a small body of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, leaving the Romans in full possession of his camp; which they so much admired, that they made it a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> which they followed ever after.

ARUSPICES

Pages 356-356
or HARUSPICES, in Roman Antiquity, an order of priests who pretended to foretell future events by inspecting the entrails of victims killed in sacrifice; they were also consulted on occasion of portents and prodigies. The haruspices were always chosen from the best families; and as their employment was of the same nature as that of the augurs, they were as much honoured. Their college, as well as those of the other religious orders, had its particular registers and records.

ARVALES FRATRES

Pages 351-351

in Roman Antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of 12 priests, instituted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>, and chosen out of the most noble families, himself being one of that body: they assisted in the sacrifices of the ambervalia annually offered to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, for the prosperity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; when they wore on their heads crowns made of ears of corn. The original of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> was as follows: Acca Laurentia, Romulus's nurse, was accustomed once a-year to make a solemn sacrifice for a blessing on the fields, her 12 sons always assiting her in the solemnity; but at last losing one of her sons, Romulus offered himself to supply his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and gave this small <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> the name of Arvalis fratres. This order was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> repute at Rome: they held the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and never lost it upon account of imprisonment, banishment, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any other accident.

ARX

Pages 356-356

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">Military</a> Art, a town, fort, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> castle, for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The arx in ancient Rome was a distinct edifice from the capitol, though some have confounded the two. According to Ryckius, the arx, properly speaking, was a place on the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Capitoline mount, stronger and better fortified than the rest, with towers and pinnated walls; in which was also the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Capitolinus. Arx also denoted a consecrated place on the Palatine mount, where the augurs publicly performed their office. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have the arx to have been the augural temple; but Varro expressly distinguishes between the two. Arx was particularly used for a public place in Rome, set apart for the operations of the augurs. In which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> arx amounts to the same with what is otherwise called auguraculum and auguratorium, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> augurale. Out of this arx it was that the faciales, or heralds, gathered the graft used in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of making leagues and treaties. Arx Britannica, a citadel of Batavia, whose foundation is seen at low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, near the old mouth of the middle <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>: some imagine it the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHAROS">pharos</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> tower of Caligula, as Suetonius calls it; a monument of Caligula's Roman conquest of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. Others, that it was built by Drusus, with an altar afterwards by Claudius, on his expedition into Britain. But the usual passage was from Gefforiacum; and Suetonius expressly says, Claudius passed over thence. The ancient name of this citadel, now covered by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, is nowhere expressed: Now <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called 't Huis Britten, or Brittenburg; that is, Arx Britannica; but from what authority does not appear.

ARYTENOIDES

Pages 356-357

ARYTENOIDES, in Anatomy, the name of two cartilages which, together with others, constitute the head of the larynx. It is also applied to some muscles of the larynx.

ARYTHMUS

Pages 357-357

in Medicine, the want of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODULATION">modulation</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>. It is opposed to eurythmus, a pulse modulated agreeably to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>.

ARZILLA

Pages 357-357

a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a>, about five leagues from Tangiers. It is built at the mouth of a river, and inhabited by Moors and Jews, who carry on no trade. It was formerly a Roman colony; afterwards fell under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>; and was next taken by the Mahometans. Alphonso of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, named the African, took it by assault in 1471, and brought away the presumptive heir of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. After that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> came to the throne, he besieged it, in 1508, with 100,000 men; but was obliged to abandon the undertaking. However, at length the Portuguese forsook it of their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. s. c. N. Lat. 35° 30'.

AS

Pages 357-357

in Antiquity, a particular <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, consisting of 12 ounces; being the same with libra, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>. The word is derived from the Greek ασις, which in the Doric dialect is used for ὁ, one, q. d. an entire thing; though others <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it named as quasi ασις, because made of bas. As was also the name of a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, which was of different weights and different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in different ages of the commonwealth. Under Numa Pompilius, according to Eusebius, the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> was either of wood, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, or shells. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Tullus Hostilius, it was of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>; and called as, libra, libella, or pondus, because actually weighing a pound or 12 ounces. Four hundred and twenty years after, the first Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> having exhausted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, they reduced the as to two ounces. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Punic war, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a> pressing very hard upon them, they reduced the as to half its weight, viz. to one ounce. And, lastly, by the Papirian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, they took away half an ounce more, and consequently reduced the as to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> weight of half an ounce: and it is generally thought that it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the same during the commonwealth, and even till the reign of Vespasian. The as therefore was of four different weights in the commonwealth. Its original stamp was that of a sheep, ox, or sow; but from the time of the emperors, it had on one side a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANUS">Janus</a> with two faces, and on the reverse the rostrum or prow of a ship. As was also used to denote any integer or whole. Whence the English word ace. Thus as signified the whole inheritance; whence heres ex ase, the heir to the whole estate.

ASA

Pages 357-357

among Naturalists. The writers of the later ages have formed this word afa from the lasar of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and attributed it to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> very different from that anciently known by the name they have thus corrupted. The afa of the ancients was an odoriferous and fragrant gum; and the afa of the after ages had so little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to this epithet, that they distinguished it by one, expressing its being of an offensive <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stinking smell. The Arabian writers, according to this distinction, describe two kinds of afa, the one stinking, the other aromatic; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Greeks preferred the name afa, or lasar, to the stinking gum the Latins called by that name, but added a distinctive epithet to express its smell, and called it foardolafarmum. ASA or Assa, in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, a name given to two very different substances, called afa-dulcis and afa-sweetida. ASA Dulcis is the same with Benzoin. ASA-Sweetida is the concrete juice of an umbelliferous plant growing in several parts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERULA">Ferula</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> and Materia Medica <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ASAMEA

Pages 358-358

a fountain of Cappadocia, near Tyana, sacred to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, and to an oath. Though this fountain bubbled up, as in a state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>, yet its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>; and never ran over, but fell back again: (Philolitrus, Ammian).

ASAPH

Pages 357-357

St., a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLINTSHIRE">Flintshire</a>, with a bishop's see; on which account principally it deserves notice, being in itself but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. As a bishopric, it is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity, and was founded about the year 560, by Kentigern, a Scotman, bishop of Glaigow. He began the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> on the banks of the river Elwy, whence it is called by the Welsh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">Land</a> Elwy, and in Latin Elwenfis. Kentigern returning into Scotland, left a holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> his successor, St Asaph. Who was his successor is uncertain, as there are no records that mention it; and it seems rather probable that the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> settled here had been necessitated to remove to some more peaceable abode, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was frequently the seat of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> between the English and the Welsh. This see was formerly a very wealthy one; but its revenues were greatly lessened by the profusion of Bishop Parlew, who alienated much of the lands belonging to this bishopric. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> doth not contain any one whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>; but consists of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Denbigh, Flint (where its church is), <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTGOMERY">Montgomery</a>, and Merioneth threes, and a small part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a>; wherein are 121 parishes, and 131 churches and chapels, most of which are in the immediate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of the bishop. This see hath but one archdeaconry, viz. that of St Asaph, which is united to the bishopric, for the better maintenance thereof. This see is valued in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s books at 187l. 11s. 6d. but computed to be worth annually 1500l. The tenth of the clergy comes to 186l. 19s. 6½d. To this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> belongs a bishop, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, archdeacon, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, &c.

ASAPPES

Pages 357-357
or Azapes, an order of soldiers in the Turkish army, whom they always expose to the first shock of the enemy: to the end that the enemy being thus fatigued, and their swords blunted, the fahis and janizaries may fall on and find an easy conquest. The word is derived from the Turkish apab, which signifies rank, from whence they have formed apabap, "to range in battle." The azappes are said to be held of so little value, that they frequently serve as bridges for the cavalry to pass over in bad roads, and as fascines to fill up the ditches of places besieged. They travel on foot, and have no pay but the plunder they can get from the enemy.

ASAR-ADDON

Pages 357-358
or Esar-Haddon, the son of Senacherib, succeeded his father about 712 years before the Christian era, and united the kingdoms of Nineveh and Babylon. He rendered himself master of Syria; sent a colony to Samaria; and his generals took King King Manesse, and carried him loaded with chains to Babylon. Asar-Addon died after a reign of 12 years. ASARINA. See Chelone.

ASAROTA

Pages 358-358

aragora, from a and egea, I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEEP">sweep</a>, a kind of painted pavement in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> before the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of mosaic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. The most celebrated was that at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERGAMUS">Pergamus</a>, painted by Selus, and exhibiting the appearance of crumbs, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> had not been swept after dinner; whence, according to Pliny, the denomination. Perrault supposes them to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> kind of pavements of a spongy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>.

ASBESTOS

Pages 358-358

a native <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which may be split into threads and filaments, from one inch to ten inches in length, very fine, brittle, yet somewhat <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>, silky, and of a grayish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, not unlike tallow of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. It is almost insipid to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, insoluble in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and possesses the wonderful <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of remaining unconfumed in the fire, which only whitens it. The industry of mankind has found a method of working this mineral, and employing it in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, chiefly cloth and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>. The manufacture is undoubtedly difficult enough. Pliny calls the asbestos inventum rarum, textu difficillimum. Wormius assures us, that the method of making cloth of asbestos is now entirely unknown. And indeed one would scarcely imagine the thing practicable, without the mixture of some other plant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, along with the asbestos, the filaments of this latter appearing too coarse and brittle to make any tolerable fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. However this be, Bap. Porta assures us, that in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> of asbestos was a thing known to everybody at Venice. Sig. Caftagnatta, superintendent of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, is said to have carried the manufacture to such perfection, that his asbestos was soft and tractable, much resembling lamb skin dressed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>: he could thicken and thin it at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and thus either make it into a very white skin or a very white paper. This kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth was chiefly esteemed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; though then better known and more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> than among us, being held equally precious with the richest pearls: nor is it now of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> value, even in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> where it is most generally made, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> cover (i.e. a piece of 23 inches and three-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>) being worth 80 tale, i.e. 36l. 13s. 4d. Pliny says, he himself had seen napkins thereof, which, being taken foul from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> after a feast, were thrown into the fire, and by that means were better scoured than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had been washed in water, &c. But its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, according to Pliny, was for the making of shrouds, for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> funerals, to wrap up the corpse, so that the ashes might be preserved distinct from those of the wood, &c. whereof the funeral pile was composed: and the princes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, according to the accounts in the Philosophical Transactions, still use it at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> their dead. Some of the ancients are said to have made themselves clothes of it, particularly the Brachmans among the Indians. The wicks for their perpetual lamps, according to Dr. Lif- ter, were also made of it: some to this day use it for asbestos the wicks of such lamps as they would not have any trouble with; because the asbestos never withering, there is no occasion for shifting the wick. Septalla, canon of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, had thread, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, nets, and paper, made of the asbestos. A handkerchief or pattern of the linen was long since presented to the Royal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, a foot long and half a foot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. This gave two proofs of its resisting fire; though, in both experiments, it lost above three drachms of its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. When taken out <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hot, it did not burn a piece of white paper on which it was laid. Mr Villette pretends that his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> burning concave usually vitrifies the asbestos. The method of preparing the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INCOMBUSTIBLE">incombustible</a> paper and cloth is thus described by Ciampini: The stone is laid to soak in warm water; then opened and divided by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, that the earthy matter may be washed out.
