The ablution being several times repeated, the flaxlike filaments are collected and dried; and they are most conveniently spun with an addition of flax. Two or three filaments of the asbestos are easily twisted along with the flaxen thread, if the operator's fingers are kept oiled. The cloth also, when woven, is best preserved by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> from breaking or wasting. On exposure to the fire, the flax and the oil burn out, and the cloth remains pure and white. Probably from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> of some extraneous matter of this kind proceeded the diminution of weight in the handkerchief <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> recited; for pure asbestos leaves nothing. The shorter filaments which separate in washing the stone may be made into paper in the common manner. The asbestos is found in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a> and Cyprus; in Tartary; at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAMUR">Namur</a> in the Low Countries; in Thuringia among the mines; in the old Noricum; in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>; at Puteoli; in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Corfu; in the island of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLESEY">Anglesey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABERDEENSHIRE">Aberdeenshire</a> in Scotland; at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTAUBAN">Montauban</a> in France; and in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>.

ASCALON

Pages 358-358

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and one of the five satrapies <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> principalities of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILISTINES">Philistines</a>; situated on the Mediterranean, 43 miles to the south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> (Antonine), between <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AZOTUS">Azotus</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and Gaza to the south. The birthplace of Herod the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, hence named Acalonita (Stephanus). Famous for its scallops, which take name from this town (Strabo, Pliny). Now Scalon. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 34° 30'. Lat. 31° 30'.

ASCANIUS

Pages 358-358

the son of Æneas and Creusa, succeeded his father in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the Latins, and defeated Mezentius <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Tuscans, who had refused to conclude a peace with him. At length he founded <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBA">Alba</a> Longa; and died about 1139 years before the Christian era, after a reign of 38 years. ASCARIS. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ASCENDANT

Pages 358-358

in Astrology, denotes the horoscope, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of the ecliptic which rises upon the horizon at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the birth of any one. This is supposed to have an influence on the person's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and fortune, by giving him a bent and propensity to one thing more than another. In the celestial theme, this is also called the first <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of the East or Oriental angle, and the significator of life. Such a planet ruled in his ascendant: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> was in his ascendant, &c. Hence the word is also used in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MORAL_SENSE">moral <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, for a certain superiority which

ASCENDANTS

Pages 358-359

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, are opposed to descendants in succession; i.e., when a father succeeded his son, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> an uncle his nephew, &c., heritage is said to ascend, or go to ascendants.

ASCENDING

Pages 359-359

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, is said of such stars as are rising above the horizon in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> of the equator. ASCENDING Latitude, is the latitude of a planet when going towards the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> pole. ASCENDING Node, is that point of a planet's orbit, wherein it passes the ecliptic, to proceed northward. This is otherwise called the northern node, and represented by this character Ω. ASCENDING Veins, in Anatomy, those which carry the blood upwards; as the aorta ascends. See ANATOMY.

ASCENSION

Pages 359-360

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, is either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> oblique. Right ascension of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, or a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a>, is that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of the equinoctial, counted from the beginning of Aries, which rises with the sun or star in a right sphere. Oblique ascension is an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of the equator intercepted between the first point of Aries and that point of the equator which rises together with a star in an oblique sphere. ASCENSION <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">Day</a>, a festival of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, held ten days before Whitunday, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of our Saviour's ascension into heaven after his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a>. ASCENSION <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARREN_ISLAND">barren island</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, lying in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17° 20'. S. Lat 7° 5'. The following account is given of it by Mr Forster. "This island was first discovered in 1501, by João de Nova Gallego, a Portuguese navigator, who named it Ilha de Nossa Senhora de Conceição." The same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> on his return to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> in 1502, discovered the island of St Helena, which obtained that name from the day of the discovery. Ascension was seen a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> by Alfonso d'<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBUQUERQUE">Albuquerque</a> on his voyage to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> in 1503, and then received the name it now bears; but was already at that time in the same desolate condition as at present. We sent several parties on shore, who passed the night on the watch for turtles, which came to lay their eggs on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> shores. The dreariness of this island surpassed all the horrors of Easter island and Tierra del <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEGO">Fuego</a>, even without the affluence of snow. It was a ruinous heap of rocks, many of which, as far as we could discern from the ship, seemed to be totally changed by the fire of a volcano. Nearly in the centre of the island rises a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> mountain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> height, on which we discerned some verdure by the help of our glasses, from whence it has obtained the name of Green Mountain. "We landed early in the morning among some rocks, the turf being always immensely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> on the great beach; which consists of minute shell-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, chiefly of a snowy white, very deep, dry, and intolerable to the eyes when the sun shines. We ascended among heaps of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cavernous <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which perfectly resembles the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> lavas of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a>, and of which the broken pieces looked as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had been accumulated by art. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAVA">lava</a> currents cooling very suddenly, may easily be imagined to produce such an effect. Having ascended about 12 or 15 yards perpendicular, we found ourselves on a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> plain of six or eight miles in circuit; in the different corners of which we observed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> hill of an exact conical shape, and of a reddish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, standing perfectly insulated. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> of the plain between these conic hills was covered with great numbers of smaller hillocks, consisting of the same wild and ragged lava as that near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and ringing like glass when two pieces are knocked together. The ground between the heaps of lava was covered with a black <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, on which we walked very firmly; but when these heaps did not appear, the whole was a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> earth, which was so loose, and in such dry minute particles, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> raised <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> of dust upon it. The conic hills consisted of a very different sort of lava, which was red, soft, and crumbling into earth. One of these hills stands directly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, and has a wooden <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> on its summit, from whence the bay is said to take its name. Its sides are very steep, but a path near three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> long winds round it to the summit. After examining this remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> a little longer, we concluded, with a great degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> on our side, that the plain on which we stood was once the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRATER">crater</a> or seat of a volcano, by the accumulation of whose cinders and pumice <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> the conic hills had been gradually formed; that the currents of lava which we now <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> divided into many heaps, had perhaps been gradually buried in fresh cinders and ashes; and the waters coming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the interior mountain in the rainy season had smoothed everything in their way, and filled up by degrees the cavity of the crater. The rocky black lava was the residence of numberless men-of-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> birds and boobies, which sat on their eggs, and suffered us to come <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to them. "About eight in the evening, it being then quite dark, a small vessel came into the bay, and anchored directly within us. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook having hailed her repeatedly, received in answer that she was the Luceria, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_YORK">New <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a> sloop, which had been at Sierra Leon, and was now come to catch turtles, in order to sell them at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDWARD">windward</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of the West Indies. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> was sent on board, who learned from the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, that he had taken our ship to be a French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a>, and was very desirous of trading with English India ships, in which he was disappointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>'s regulations. He dined with our officers the next day, but on the 31st at day-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> left the island. On the 30th in the morning, we landed a second time; and, crossing the plain, arrived at a prodigious lava current, intersected by many channels from six to eight yards deep, which bore strong marks of being worn by vast torrents of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, but were at present perfectly dry, the sun being in the northern hemisphere. In these gullies we found a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> consisting of a black volcanic earth, mixed with some whitish particles gritty to the touch. Here we saw some small bunches of purple, and a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of grass (panicum fanguineum) which found sufficient nutriment in the dry soil. Having at last, with great fatigue, climbed over this extensive and tremendous current of lava, which was much more <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> than the heaps nearer to the sea, we came to the foot of the Green Mountain, which even from the ship's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the bay we had plainly distinguished to be of a different <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> from all the rest of the country. Those parts of the lava which surrounded it were covered with a prodigious quantity of Ascension Island, and a new kind of fern, *Lonicera* (Adscensionis), where several flocks of wild goats were feeding. The great mountain is divided in its extremities, by various cliffs, into several bodies; but in the centre they all run together, and form one broad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of great height. The whole appears to consist of a gritty topaceous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>, which has never been attacked by the volcano, but probably existed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to its eruption; its sides are covered with a kind of grass, peculiar to the island, which Linnaeus has named *Arifida* (Adscensionis). We likewise observed several flocks of goats feeding on it; but they were all excessively shy, and ran with surprising velocity along tremendous precipices, where it was impossible to follow them. The master of the New York <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIGHTHOUSE">lighthouse</a> acquainted us, that there is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of water on one part of this mountain, which falls down a great precipice, and is afterwards absorbed in the sand. I am almost persuaded, that, with a little trouble, Ascension might shortly be made fit for the residence of men. The introduction of furze (*Ulex europaeus*), and of a few other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which thrive best in a parched soil, and are not likely to be attacked by rats or goats, would soon have the same effect as at St Helena. The moisture attracted from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> by the high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in the centre of the island, would then no longer be evaporated by the violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the sun, but collect into rivulets, and gradually supply the whole island. A sod of grass would everywhere cover the surface of the ground, and annually increase the stratum of mould, till it could be planted with more useful vegetables. We returned gradually to Crofs Bay, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of noon, over the plain; having a space of more than five miles to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a>, where the sun burnt and blistered our faces and necks, and heated the soil to such a degree, that our feet were likewise extremely sore. About three o'clock we arrived at the water's side; and after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a> in a small cove among a few rocks, we made the signal for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>, and were taken on board. The next forenoon we made another small excursion, in company with Captain Cook, towards the Green Mountain; but we were all of us so much fatigued, that we could not reach it. We made no new observations in the course of this day, the nature of the island being dreary beyond <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> in its outskirts."

ASCENSIONAL DIFFERENCE

Pages 360-360

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and oblique ascension of the same point to the surface of the sphere.

ASCENT

Pages 360-360

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, implies the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of a body upwards, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the continual rise of a body from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIPATETICS">Peripatetics</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> the spontaneous ascent of bodies to a principle of levity inherent in them. The moderns deny any such thing as spontaneous levity; and show, that whatever ascends, does it in virtue of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> impulse or extrusion. Thus it is that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> and other rare bodies ascend in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> woods, &c., in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; not by any external principle of levity, but by the superior gravity or tendency downwards of the parts of the medium wherein they are. The ascent of light bodies in heavy mediums is produced after the same manner as the ascent of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a>. It is not that such scale has an internal principle whereby it immediately tends upwards; but it is impelled upwards by the preponderancy of the other scale; the excess of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the one having the same effect, by augmenting its impetus downwards, as so much real levity in the other; by reason the tendencies mutually oppose each other, and that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REACTION">reaction</a> are always equal.

ASCENT OF BODIES ON INCLINED PLANES

Pages 360-360

the reader <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> find explained under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>; **ASCENT OF <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">FLUIDS</a>**, under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYDROSTATICS">Hydrostatics</a>; and **ASCENT OF VAPOURS**, under the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVAPORATION">Evaporation</a>.

ASCESIS

Pages 360-360

properly denotes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of the body. It is formed from the verb *exercere*, used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> in speaking of the sports and combats of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATHLETE">athlete</a>. **ASCESIS** is also used by philosophers, to denote an exercise conducive to virtue, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to the acquiring a greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of virtue. This is particularly denominated the *philosophical ascetic*, because practised chiefly by philosophers, who make a more peculiar profession of improving themselves in virtue; on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> whereof the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> introduced a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> Ascetic.

ASCETERIUM

Pages 360-360

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> Writers, is frequently used for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> set apart for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of virtue and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. The word is formed from *aescetos*, "exercise;" or *aescetra*, "one who performs exercise." Originally it signified a place where the athletes or gladiators performed their exercises.

ASCETIC

Pages 360-360

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> appellation given to such persons as, in the primitive times, devoted themselves more immediately to the exercises of piety and virtue, in a retired <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and particularly to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a>, and mortification. The word is derived from *exercere*, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>," "I exercise." Afterwards, when the monks came in fashion, this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> was bestowed upon them; especially upon such of them as lived in solitude. **ASCETIC** is also a title of several books of spiritual exercises.—As, the *Asceticon*, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> devout exercises of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. We also say the *aesthetic* life, meaning the exercise of prayer, meditation, and mortification.

ASCHAFENBURG

Pages 360-360

a town of Germany, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, in the circle of the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and territory of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>, who has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> there. It is memorable for being the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> took up his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> the night before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Dettingen. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 35' N. Lat. 50° 14'.

ASCHEM

Pages 360-361

ROGER**, an Englishman of considerable learning in the 16th century, was born at Kirby Wiske, a village in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, near Northallerton. John Ascham, his father, was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> in the family of Scroop, and by his wife, Margaret, was connected with several respectable families. A short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, Sir Anthony Winfield, having conceived a predilection for his third son Roger, took him into his family, and extended his bounty so far as to give him the advantage of a private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> along with his own sons. Under a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>, he made a rapid progress in classical learning, and early discovered a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> partiality for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>. The superiority of genius and docility of temper which he constantly displayed, displayed, induced his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> to send him to St John's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, in the year 1530. The revival of Grecian and Roman literature at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> Alcham entered upon his studies, was peculiarly favourable to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> bent of his inclination. A desire of excelling uniformly influenced his conduct, and adopting the maxim, *Qui docet, dicit*, he began to teach boys the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, as soon as he was acquainted with the elementary parts himself. His <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> was approved by Pember; and under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of this valuable friend, he soon became acquainted with the best Greek and Latin authors. But he took particular delight in reading Cicero and Caesar; and upon them he formed the elegance of his Latin style, which proved so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> and so advantageous in the after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Alcham took his first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of bachelor of arts in the 18th year of his life, and was chosen fellow of the college about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> afterwards. The favourable disposition, however, which he manifested towards the reformed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, was no small obstacle in the way of his preferment. He was elected <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts in the year 1537, the 21st of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and about this period he began to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> in the capacity of a tutor. His reputation for Greek learning soon brought him many pupils; and these were so well instructed, that several of them afterwards rose to considerable eminence. Of these, William Grindall was one of the most distinguished, who obtained the station of master of languages to the lady <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, upon the recommendation of Sir John Cheke. It appears uncertain why Alcham himself was not appointed to that honourable station; but his partiality for the university, seems, from a hint in one of his letters, to have been the cause. At that period there was no particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> appropriated to the Greek language; but Alcham was appointed by the university, to read lectures upon that language in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. A dispute arose in the university at that time about the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a> of the Greek language, in which Alcham first opposed the method observed by Sir John Cheke and Sir Thomas Smith; but upon more mature deliberation, he adopted that method, which has ever since been practised in the English schools. Both on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of his handwriting, and the purity and elegance of his Latin, he was employed to write the public letters of the university. By the advice of his friend Pember, he turned his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of instrumental music, and thereby enlivened his leisure hours, and prepared his mind for renewed exertion. In his study he also amused himself with embellishing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> with beautiful draughts; and in the field, he joined in the diversion of the bow and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a>. The learned Alcham did not deem his labour improperly bestowed in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> a book entitled *Toxophilus*, in that age when the practice of firearms was in its infancy, and the proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the bow was of more importance than for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> amusement. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was useful at that time for introducing into the English language, a more natural, easy, and truly English diction, than was formerly in use; and it also abounds with many beautiful allusions and curious fragments of English <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. Alcham candidly acknowledges, that being anxious to make the tour of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, which was then the great republic of letters, and particularly of Grecian Alcham literature, he wished, by dedicating his book to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, to obtain a pension, to enable him to make that tour. It reflects some lustre on the benevolence of Henry VIII. that in the year 1544, he settled upon him an annual pension of £10, which Dr Johnson, considering the circumstance of the times, estimates at the value of £100. Upon the death of Henry, this pension was for some time discontinued, but was again renewed by Edward VI. and doubled by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>. In the same year also, Alcham obtained the appointment of orator to the university, an office which he retained with great reputation, during the period he was connected with the university. For some years he received an annual gratuity from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEE">Lee</a>, archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, but to what amount is not recorded; and, in 1548, upon the death of his pupil Grindall, preceptor to the lady Elizabeth, his pupils and writings had acquired him such celebrity, that he was appointed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the studies of that princess. He successfully acquitted himself in that honourable <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>; but two years after, from some unknown cause of dissatisfaction, he returned to the university, having taken an abrupt leave of the princess. This part of his conduct did not lessen him in the esteem of Elizabeth; for in the same year, she recalled him to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and appointed him secretary to Sir Richard Morifine, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. In his way to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, he paid a visit to Lady Jane Gray, whom he found in her chamber, reading <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>'s Phaedo in Greek, "and that," says he, "with as much delight, as some gentlemen would read a merry tale in Boccaccio;" while the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> and duchess, and the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, were hunting in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">park</a>. In the character of secretary to Sir Richard, besides aiding him in the management of his public affairs, he also conducted his private studies. During the mornings of four days in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, he read with him a portion of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEMOSTHENES">Demosthenes</a>; and, in the evenings, some pages of Sophocles or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a>; and, on the other mornings, he wrote the letters of public business; and, on the evenings, he either wrote his own private letters, or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his diary and remarks. While Alcham was on his travels, he made a short excursion to Italy; but was much delighted with the manners of that people, especially of the Venetians. After his return from that tour, he favoured the world with a curious tract, entitled "A Report, and Discourse of the Affairs and State of Germany," &c. Upon the death of Edward VI. Morifine was recalled, and Alcham returned to the university. But through the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Bishop Gardiner, the fortune of Alcham soon took a favourable turn, who although he knew him to be a Protestant, obtained him the office of Latin secretary to the queen, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to retain his university emoluments; and the additional salary of £10 a-year. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> of Alcham enabled him to act a respectable part, both under the intolerant reign of Mary, and also in the most perilous situations during the reign of Elizabeth; and the readiness and elegance of his Latin style, rendered him a useful member at court. He is reported, to have written during the course of three days 47 letters, to persons in the highest ranks of life. When the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> passed to a Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, it

ASCLEPIA

Pages 361-362

a festival of Æsculapius the god of physic, observed particularly at Epidaurus, where it was attended with a contest between the poets and musicians, whence it was likewise called Ἱερὸς Αγών, Apulum.

ASCLEPIAD

Pages 362-362

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> composed of four feet, the first of which is a spondee, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> a choriambus, and the two last dactyls; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of four feet and a caesura, the first a spondee, the second a dactyl, after which comes the caesura, then the two dactyls; as, Meceenas avatis edita regibus.

ASCLEPIADES

Pages 362-362

a famous physician under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HADRIAN">Hadrian</a>, of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> with the former. He wrote several books concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of medicines; both internal and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a>.

ASCLEPIAS

Pages 362-362

SWALLOW-WORT. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. ASCODUTÆ, in Antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of heretics, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century, who rejected all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of symbols and sacraments, on this principle, That incorporeal things cannot be communicated by things corporeal, nor divine <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> by anything visible.

ASCOLI

Pages 362-362

formerly Asculum Apulum, a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and populous town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the marquisate of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a>, and territory of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. It is a bishop's see, and seated on a mountain, at the bottom of which runs the river Fronto. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15. 20. N. Lat. 42. 47.

ASCOLIA

Pages 362-362

in Grecian Antiquity, a festival celebrated by the Athenian husbandmen in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, to whom they sacrifice a he-goat, because it destroys the vines (Ovid. Fast. i. 357); and, to show the greater indignity to an animal hated by Bacchus, the peasants, after having killed him, made a foot-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> of his skin. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> has beautifully described the occasion of the sacrifice and manner of celebrating the festival, Georg. ii. 380.

ASCRIPITII

Pages 362-362
or ASCRIPITII, were a kind of villains, who, coming from abroad, settle in the lands of some new lord, whose subjects or servants they commence; being so annexed to the lands, that they may be transferred and sold with the same. Ascripitii is sometimes also used in speaking of aliens or foreigners newly admitted to the freedom of a city or country. ASCRIPITII was also used in the military laws for the recruits appointed to supply the losses of the legions, called also Accensi.

ASCRIVIUM

Pages 362-362

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, on the Sinus Rhizicus (Pliny, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>): Now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATTARO">Cattaro</a> (Harduin); the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the territory of Cattaro, in Venetian Dalmatia. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19. 20. N. Lat. 45. 25.

ASCULUM APULUM

Pages 362-363

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Apulia, much mentioned in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with Pyrrhus. ASH Pyrrhus (Florus, Plutarch): Now called Acoli; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPITANATA">Capitanata</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. Asculum Picenum, in Ancient Geography, a town of the Piceni (Cæsar); and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> (Florus): Now Acoli, in the marquisate of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a>, on the river Fronto. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15. 5. Lat. 42. 50.

ASEKI

Pages 363-363
or ASEKAI, the name which the Turks give to the favourite sultanas who have brought forth sons. These are greatly distinguished above others in their apartments, attendants, pensions, and honours. They have sometimes shared the government. The sultana who first presents the emperor with a male child, is reckoned the chief favourite, is called bayuk aseki, and ranks as a legitimate wife: though, from the time of Bajazet I. the sultans are forbidden to marry by a public law, which Soliman II. violated in favour of Roxalana.

ASELLUS

Pages 363-363

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of oniscus. See Oniscus, Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ASGILL

Pages 363-363

JOHN, a late humorous writer, was bred to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and practised in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success. He was there elected a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons, but was expelled for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> a treatise on the possibility of avoiding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; and being afterwards chosen a member for the borough of Bromber in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, he was also on the same account expelled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of England. After this, he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> 30 years a prisoner in the Mint, Fleet, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a>'s-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>; during which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he published a multitude of small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> pamphlets, several of which were in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the succession of the house of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>, and against the pretender. He died in the rules of the King's-bench, in the year 1738, when he was upwards of four score.

ASHBORN

Pages 363-363

a town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>, seated between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Dore and Compton, over which there is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, in a rich foil. It is a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town, though not so flourishing as formerly. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 35. N. Lat. 53. 0.

ASHBURTON

Pages 363-363

a town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>. It sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and is one of the four stannery <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. It is seated among the hills, which are remarkable for tin and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>; and has a very handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; as also a chapel, which is turned into a school. It gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Baron to the family of Dunning. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 10. N. Lat. 50. 30.

ASHBY DE LA ZOUCH

Pages 363-363

a market-town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 20. N. Lat. 52. 40. It had a castle which was long in the possession of the family of de la Zouch. It afterwards fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Edward IV. who granted it to Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HASTINGS">Hastings</a>, created Baron Hastings, with license to make a castle of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, to which he adjoined a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> tower. It was demolished in 1648; but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the tower is still standing. It now belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Huntingdon.

ASHES

Pages 363-363

the earthy particles of combustible substances after they have been burnt. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the ashes are produced from vegetable bodies, they contain a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fixed <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, blended with earthy particles; and from these ashes the fixed alkaline salts called pot-a/b, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a>-a/b, &c., are extracted. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The ashes of all vegetables are vitrifiable, and found to contain <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>.—They are also an excellent manure for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and wet grounds. Several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ceremonies depend upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of ashes. St Jerome relates, that the Jews in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> rolled themselves in ashes, as a sign of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a>. To repent in sackcloth and ashes, is a frequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> in Scripture for mourning and being afflicted for our sins. There was a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> and lustral <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> made with the ashes of a heifer sacrificed upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIATION">expiation</a>; the ashes whereof were distributed to the people, and this water was used in purifications, as often as any touched a dead body, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> was present at funerals, (Num. xix. 17.) Tamar after the injury received from her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Amnon, covered her head with ashes, (2 Sam. xiii. 19.) The Psalmist in great sorrow says, that he had eaten ashes as if it were <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, (Ps. cii. 9.) which, however, is to be considered as an hyperbole. He sat on ashes, he threw ashes on his head; his food, his bread, was spoiled with the ashes wherewith he was covered. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Persians had a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for some great criminals, which consisted in executing them in ashes. The criminal was thrown headlong from a tower 50 cubits <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, which was filled with ashes to a particular height, (2 Mac. xiii. 5, 6.) The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> which the criminal used to disengage himself from this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, plunged him still deeper into it, and this agitation was further increased by a wheel which stirred the ashes continually about him till at last he was stifled.

ASHFORD

Pages 363-363

a market town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, situated about 12 miles south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 45. and N. Lat. 51. 15.

ASHLAR

Pages 363-363

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used among builders; by which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> free <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, as they come out of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a>, of different lengths and thicknesses.

ASHLERING

Pages 363-363

among Builders, signifies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERING">quartering</a>, to lath to, in garrets, about two and a half <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, perpendicular to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, up to the under side of the rafters.

ASHMOLE

Pages 363-364

ELIAS, an industrious English antiquarian, and an eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> of the 17th century, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LITCHFIELD">Litchfield</a> in 1617. Having enjoyed the advantages of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 16, and resided in the family of James Paget, Esq., one of the barons of the exchequer, and then turned his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> and other branches of literature. In the year 1638, he married, and commenced the business of attorney in London. When the civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> began, he then being a widower, entered entered into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in the ordinance department. When residing in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> in that capacity, he entered Brazen Nose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, and began the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. Naturally inclined to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> and scientific trifles, he wandered too far into the wilds of astrological imposture, not a little encouraged by several eminent men of that age. From the same cause, he entered keenly into the secrets of masonry, and made considerable additions to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. When <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a> was surrendered to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> in 1646, Ashmole retired to London, where he became acquainted with the famous astrologers, Moore, Lilly, and Booker. Having retired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a> in the year following, he added the knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a> to his other acquirements. There he became acquainted with Lady Mainwaring, a well-jointed widow, whom he married in 1649; and although her estate was sequestrated on account of his loyalty, yet through the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Lilly and others, he again recovered his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, and afterwards settled in London, where his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> became the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of all the curious literati of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALCHEMY">alchemy</a>, was produced, by his conversation with William Backhouse; and Ashmole, under a feigned name, published a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> upon that subject. The next effort of his industry, was a collection of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> of English chemists, which he published under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of *Theatrum Chymicum Britannicum*, in 4to. This work was the effect of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> labour and much expense; and although it procured him much fame among the learned, yet it was only a collection of *Alchemy*; and he appears to have been ignorant of real chemical knowledge. About this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, he began to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> among his acquaintances Selden, Oughtred, and Dr Wharton. The wealth he acquired by his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> engaged him in several disputes, and the lady herself at last made an attack upon him in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, but he was honourably acquitted, and the lady restored to her affectionate husband. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> industry never wavered out, and he next attended to the study of antiquity and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of records. Along with Sir W. Dugdale, he about this period traced a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to Litchfield. Abandoning all other pursuits, he began to make preparations for his "History of the order of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">Garter</a>," a production which procured him lasting fame. Upon a visit to Oxford, he gave a full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the coins bequeathed to that university by Laud; and about this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, John Tradescant, the famous gardener of Lambeth, presented him with the collection of curiosities, which both he and his father had procured. Upon the restoration, Ashmole was greatly respected by the king, who made him <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERALD">herald</a>, and employed him to give a description of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> medals. The offices of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> and comptroller of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a> were conferred upon him; and being called to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> in the Middle Temple, he was afterwards admitted a fellow of the Royal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>. The university of Oxford conferred upon him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of physic, and several other employments and emoluments were given him, until he rose to the highest eminence in the literary world. About this time his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> wife died, and he married the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of his friend Sir W. Dugdale. In May 1672, he addressed his great work on the order of the Garter, to the king, entitled "The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, laws, and ceremonies of the most noble order of the Garter; collected and digested into one body, by Elias Ashmole of the Middle Temple, Esq. Windsor herald at arms," folio, London, 1672. In favour of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>-in-law, Mr Dugdale, he resigned his office of herald of Windsor; and when offered the office of garter king-at-arms, he declined it in favour of Sir W. Dugdale. About this time a fire broke out in one of the chambers of the temple adjacent to his, and consumed a library which he had been collecting during the course of thirty-three years, together with 9000 coins, and many valuable antiquities; but his manuscripts and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> medals fortunately were saved. In 1683, he sent his manuscripts and curiosities to the university of Oxford, which laid the foundation of the *Musaeum Ashmoleanum*, still in Oxford. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Sir W. Dugdale, he refused a second time the office which he held. At the advanced age of 76, he died, and was interred in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Great Lambeth. Industry, perseverance, curiosity, and accuracy, appear to have been the leading features in his character. (Gen. Biog.)

ASIA

Pages 364-378

according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, was one of the three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> divisions of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and is considered by the moderns as one of the four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the habitable globe. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> is immense; and its importance, both in a historical and in a philosophical point of view, is very great. It contains every variety of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, and is inhabited by nations which possess undoubted claims to the highest antiquity. When <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> was yet covered by deep forests, thinly inhabited by a few wild animals, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by a barbarous <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of men, destitute of science, and even of the meanest of those accommodations which the progress of art now enables all classes of people to enjoy, Asia abounded with flourishing cities and populous nations, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> had reached a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of improvement. The revolutions which have occurred in different regions of the great Asiatic continent, occupy a great space in the general <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> race. These revolutions have possessed this peculiar character, that connected when they commenced in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of Asia, we most frequently find that they extended themselves, in a few years, to the remotest regions, and even sometimes into the centre of Europe. As the human mind usually derives its character from the situation in which it is placed, we shall be enabled by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the soil and climate, and geographical position of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> parts of Asia, to form some general principles from which to deduce the causes that have influenced the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a> of the nations by which it is inhabited. Without enlightened notions of general <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, history degenerates into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> detail of romantic adventures, and no valuable progress can be made in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> or in commercial science. We shall here therefore give a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of this vast continent, considering it, as far as possible, as one great whole, the various parts of which have at times possessed an influence over each other; leaving its particular districts and countries, to be separately discussed as they occur in the arrangement of our <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, unless in such instances... Beginning with its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west corner adjoining to Europe, the boundary of Asia commences at Waigats straits, opposite to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol16.html#article-NOVA_ZEMBLA">Nova Zembla</a>, in what is called the Northern ocean or Icy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. From thence the boundary extends southward along the Uralian chain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which are thus accounted half European and half Asiatic. After leaving these mountains, Asia is understood by geographers to proceed in a south-western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, through the provinces of the Russian empire, till it meets the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a>, where it approaches nearest to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOLGA">Volga</a>. Proceeding along the river Don, it enters into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> sea, which it crosses diagonally, proceeding to the south-west through the straits of the Bosphorus, at Constantinople, and through the Propontis and Hellespont; from whence <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> south it proceeds through the Archipelago, and the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Mediterranean sea called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, to the isthmus of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUEZ">Suez</a>, a narrow neck of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of 60 miles over, which divides Asia from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. The remaining part of the western boundary of Asia, is formed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> sea or Arabian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>, which is connected with the Arabian sea, by the strait of Bab-el-mandeb. The southern boundary of Asia, is formed by the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean, under a variety of names derived from the different parts of the Asiatic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, which are washed by its waters. Along the whole of this southern boundary, the ocean and the land <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> encroach upon each other, thereby forming immense bays and gulfs of the ocean, and peninsulated tracts of land. Thus to the eastward of the straits of Bab-el-mandeb, the Indian ocean advances northward under the appellation of the Arabian sea, having the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> on the west, and the western peninsula of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> on the east. Penetrating still farther north, it receives the name of the gulf of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORMUS">Ormus</a>, and afterwards of the Persian gulf, which advances very far in a north-western direction, having Arabia on the north-west, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> on the north-east. The same Arabian sea in its northern extremity, making a slighter inroad upon the land, receives the river <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDUS">Indus</a> on the east of Persia, and is called the gulf of Scinde. To the eastward of the nearest peninsula of India, the same Indian ocean forms a most extensive gulf, called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, bounded on the east and west by the two Indian peninsulas. The farther peninsula stretches to a great distance southward under the name of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALACCA">Malacca</a>, beyond which the boundaries of the continent assume in general an easterly direction, more especially after passing the gulf of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a>, immediately beyond Malacca and the gulf of Tonkin, on the boundaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> and of the farther India. The Chinese empire encroaches eastward upon the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific ocean</a>, which is here the boundary of Asia. Its coasts are sufficiently regular. Its bays and gulfs are trifling when compared with those of the Indian ocean, although towards its northern extremity, the Pacific ocean, under the name of the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol21.html#article-YELLOW_SEA"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">Yellow</a> sea, advances into the continent, forming to the eastward the peninsula of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COREA">Corea</a>, of moderate extent. After which this eastern ocean affords the isles of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, at a great distance to the north, again encroaches on the land, forming the sea or great bay of Ochotik, which has the peninsula of Kamchatka on its eastern side, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a> or the mainland of Asia on the west. Beyond Kamchatka one more gulf is formed in that direction, called the sea of Anadyr, terminating in the gulf of Notcher, to which succeeds the peninsula of Tschuktschi, stretching to the eastward, till it approaches the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> at the bay of St. Lawrence. After which turning to the westward, the Asiatic continent is entirely bounded on its northern side by the Icy sea, forming obscure gulfs and promontories, of which little knowledge has yet been obtained, and which can never be of much importance to the human race. The great continent whose general outline we have thus slightly traced, must necessarily vary considerably in breadth and length, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> continent from which an estimate of its menuration is formed. Some idea, however, may be obtained of the territory included in it, from observing that the continent of Asia, from the Hellespont at 26° E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>., extends to nearly 190° E. Long., at East <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a>, or to the 170° W. Long., being a line of 164° or 6,500 geographic miles, allowing 60 miles to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> breadth of this continent, from the south cape of Malacca, in the 2° N. Lat., to Cape Severo Volfotechnoi, in 7° N. Lat., amounts to about 4500 geographic miles. Hence the length of the continent of Asia is not less than 7,583 British miles, and its breadth from south to north is about 5,250. That the relative situation of the nations inhabiting this continent may be rightly understood, it is necessary to remark that the centre of Asia consists of an immense and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> plain, which is elevated to a vast height above the surrounding countries, and extends some thousand miles in every direction. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> elevated region or high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of land, stands aloft like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and is supported by a crest or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of lofty and precipitous rocks, which overlook in every direction the surrounding regions. The high level or elevated territory, which these rocks surround and seem to uphold on all sides, constitutes the proper country of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>. The climate, even in latitude 27°, which elsewhere is extremely hot, is here very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and the soil is barren. In some directions, to the extent of 1,000 miles, nothing is to be found but frightful deserts, covered with moving sands, which at times are carried aloft, as in Arabia and Africa, by the winds. They are rendered passable by ridges of mountains which divide them; and the summits of these mountains are covered with perpetual snow. Even where the soil seems more favourable, only the hardiest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and trees can flourish in this barren region, whose inhabitants have in all ages remained in the pastoral state, subsisting by the produce of their flocks and herds, without engaging in the labours of agriculture. This vast upland tract, which is probably the highest region of the old hemisphere, and which forms the largest extent of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> elevated land upon the countries of the globe, contains in general the tract or countries of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KALMUCKS">Kalmucks</a>, of the Mongols, Thibet, and Eastern Turkestan, or the original country of the Turks. From the borders of this tract in the centre of Asia, the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of that continent descend towards the ocean in every direction, such as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OXUS">Oxus</a> and Jaxartes. on the west, the Amur on the east, the Ganges and Burrampoeter on the south, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBY">Oby</a> and Jenisea on the north. The countries that surround this tract are, therefore, justly considered by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> Rennell and others, as a kind of inclined planes or hanging levels, or defecents along the skirts of it, seeing the waters flow so regularly and uninterruptedly from it, as from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> center to all the surrounding seas. On the south of this elevated region, are the vast countries of India, descending gradually to the great southern or Indian ocean. They receive from their exposure, the fiercest rays of a tropical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and are sheltered by the rocky front of the high country behind them from every northern blast. On the west of the elevated tract, are the countries which formed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Persian empire, and which in like manner descend gradually, though more irregularly, towards the setting sun, and the territory of Europe. On the east of the high table, or elevated central region, is the immense empire of China, descending with its rivers towards the great Pacific or Eastern ocean. On the north of the same region is Siberia, descending gradually to the Icy sea. The high country to the south intercepts from Siberia the heated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> which might otherwise advance towards it from a more fervid climate, while its gradual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> towards the north exposes it unprotected to every blast that may ascend from the icy regions of the pole, and thus the climate is rendered as much too cold in proportion to its latitude, as India is too hot. The soil, however, of Siberia, is in many places equal in fertility to that of almost any other country of the globe, and it has only been prevented from rising into importance, by the intolerable severity of a long winter, which has always operated as a tax upon the industry of its inhabitants, to prevent any great increase of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>. Its rivers are bound up during half the year, under a covering of almost impenetrable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>; and the ocean into which they flow, can at no season be navigated with safety, a circumstance which banishes those resources which an extensive commerce might afford, to compensate the evils of the climate. It may here be remarked, that the rivers which descend towards the south, from the high centre of Asia, through countries subject to periodical rainy seasons, have by their alluvions, or by carrying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> immense quantities of mud and earth, formed vast fertile plains near the sea coasts, similar in their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> to the Delta, or rich valley of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. Accordingly, in the south of Asia, from Persia to China; near the mouths of the Indus, the Ganges, and other rivers, immense tracts of level country are found, which are periodically overflowed, and which, aided by the warmth of the climate, exhibit a degree of fertility in all the productions of the vegetable world, of which in our temperate and colder regions we have little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>. The high level of which we have now spoken, which is of so much importance both to the geography and to the history of Asia, is bounded, as already mentioned, on all sides by a crest or ridge of mountains adjoining to which are lesser chains of hills, which gradually subside in the neighbouring low countries. The great ridge called Imau by the ancients, or the Indian Lavefus, is properly the crest or front of the western declivity towards Persia. The part of this crest or the front of the high level towards the south was anciently called Emodus, and sometimes also Imau, of which it is a continuation. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> name is Hindoo-Kho.—The northern front of the high territory which overlooks the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAIKAL">Baikal</a> lake, and the whole length of Siberia, is of immense extent, and is usually called by historians the Altai ridge or chain. The appellation of the front of the same high country towards China is little known to European geographers, but it forms in itself nothing more than a continuation of the ridges of Imau and Altai surrounding the high country of Tartary. This high country or elevated level, which may with chains of propriety be called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Tartary, sends forth in different directions various ramifications of itself, or chains of mountains, to the utmost extremities of Asia. Thus it sends forth eastward a chain of mountains to the gulf of Corea to the northward of Pekin. This chain appears like a continuation of the Altai mountains, which may thus be considered as proceeding from the 70° to the 140° of east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, or about 5000 miles. Another mountainous chain proceeds north-eastward to the gulf or sea of Ochotik opposite Kamchatka. A similar ridge called the Uralian chain, proceeds to the north-west, and terminating in the vicinity of Nova Zembla, within the polar circle, has already been mentioned as one of the boundaries which divide Asia from Europe. Another chain, better known to both ancient and modern writers, proceeds from Imau, or the front of the great high level, westward under the celebrated name of Mount Taurus, and terminates in the Mediterranean sea at the peninsula of Lesser Asia. This important ridge has on the one side, or to the south, a great part of the ancient Persian empire, and on the north the great <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> lake called the Caspian sea, and also the Black sea, with the high country of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a> between them, which anciently received the appellation of the Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a>. A great tract of low country which lies to the east and to the north of the Caspian, and proceeds westward along the shores of the Black sea, also receives from modern geographers the appellation of Tartary, and was anciently denominated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCYTHIA">Scythia</a>. Hence what is called Tartary must be regarded as consisting of two very distinct tracts of country situated upon very different levels. Eastern Tartary, lying beyond the mountains of Imau and southward of the mountains of Altai, constitutes the high level or elevated central region of Asia; whereas the country called Tartary situated upon the Caspian and the Black seas, now sometimes called Russian Tartary, is not only situated upon a lower level, but instead of consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> plain, it lies upon a south exposure, and its rivers, such as the Wolga and the Don, descend southward into the Caspian and the Black seas, which are placed along the northern basis of the ridge of mountains anciently denominated Taurus. Beyond the sources of the Don and the Wolga, however, the country begins to descend towards the polar circle and the Icy sea, like the rest of Siberia, of which it partakes the name. In all ages Asia might be divided into two regions; Asia divided into the civilized, containing men who cultivated the soil and lived in cities; and the barbarous, whose inhabitants subsisted by hunting or by the pastoral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>.
