His officers have instantly conspired against him, because by robbing the Banians, or bankers in whose hands their money was deposited, he ultimately plundered the very persons who supported his power, and had the readiest access to his person. About 150 miles above Moultan, is Lahore, the capital of the Seiks, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of religionists who venerate the ox like the Hindoos, but who are pure Monotheists and Predestinarians, worshipping God without the use of images. They form a sort of aristocratical republic. They can raise 100,000 cavalry, and they have of late become very formidable. They are a kind of Indian reformers, hostile both to the government and the religion of the country. They admit of profylaxes, and have no castes or division into distinct hereditary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a>. In their territory a vast mountain of rock salt is found, which is cut into dishes, plates, and stands for lamps. Between Lahore and Moultan, the Chunaub is joined by the Behut or the fabulous Hydaphes, which flows, as already mentioned, from the romantic Calmire. A little above the mouth of the Chunaub, the Indus receives an obscure river, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a>, from the territory on the north-west, called the Kingdom of Candahar. The city of Candahar, situated in N. Lat. 33° E. Long. 67° 15', was anciently a place of much importance, being the gate of India, with respect to Persia, and the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> of Indian and Persian goods. goods. Somewhat higher, that is, more northerly, two tributary streams enter the Indus, called the Coss or Cophenet, and the Kameb or Gurdus. On the former stands the city of Ghizni, and on the latter is Kabul. This last city is in N. Lat. 34° 36' and E. Long. 68° 58', near the foot of the Indian Caucasus, or Imaus. It stands in so happy a climate, that it produces the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> both of the temperate and torrid zones, though it is in the near neighbourhood of mountains, whose summits are covered with perpetual snow. The Indian historians speak of it with raptures. Kabul is the residence of the kings of Candahar. It has at all times been of much importance, as the frontier of India towards the river Oxus, which flows into the Caspian sea and towards Tartary. In ancient times, it always was a great commercial magazine, as well as an important fortress. To this day, it is on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> road by which the commerce of the southern parts of the Russian empire is carried on with India. It is at present noted for its vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> of horses and cattle, the first of which are brought hither by the Uzbek Tartars; and merchants resort to these markets from Persia, China, and Tartary. Near the mouth of the river Kameb, the city of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTOCK">Attock</a> stands upon the Indus. Attock signifies forbidden; this being the original boundary of Hindoostan, towards the north-west, which the Hindoos were prohibited to pass. Here the river is three quarters of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> broad, and the water is cold, and the stream rapid and turbulent, having much black sand suspended in it. To this place the Indus descends from the lofty mountains of Imaus, and the high region of Tartary. The remainder of its course, therefore, lies through a country little known, and so rude in its soil and climate, as scarcely to admit even of the most slender population. Returning to the ocean, it is to be observed, that the most eastern of the branches into which the Indus is divided towards its mouth, flows into the bay or gulf of Cutch, which advances far into the country, receiving the river Puddar. This river, and the bay into which it flows, form one side of the fertile peninsula of Guzerat, the other side of the same peninsula being contiguous to the gulf of Cambay. The western parts of the peninsula of Guzerat are mountainous and woody. The rest is extremely rich, and once famed for a very considerable commerce of its productions. Here stood in former times, on the promontory of Guzerat in the neighbourhood of Diu, one of the last remaining possessions of the Portuguese in India, the great temple or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGODA">pagoda</a> of Sumnat. It was destroyed in the eleventh century by Mahmud, the greatest of the princes of that race of Tartars called Turks. He was the sovereign of Ghizni, which we have already noticed as a town in the kingdom of Candahar, upon one of the streams that fall into the Indus from the north-west. Being a most fanatical Mahometan, he undertook 12 holy wars as they were called, against the unbelieving nations of India. Lahore, Multan, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a>, were compelled to open their gates to him, and he at last reached and conquered the rich peninsula or kingdom of Guzerat. On the payment of a tribute, the rajahs preserved their dominions, and the people their lives and fortunes; but to the religion of the country Mahmud was inexorable. Many hundred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> or pagodas were levelled with the ground. Many thousand idols were demolished, and the servants of the Arabian prophet were stimulated, and rewarded, by the precious materials of which they were composed. The pagoda of Sumnat was at this time conspicuous beyond all the retreats of Indian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>. Its magnificence and its destruction deserve well to be noticed, as indicating the character of two Asiatic nations: the riches and devout superstition of the one, and the furious fanaticism which the other had been able to diffuse over a great part of the world. This pagoda or temple, was endowed with the revenue of 2000 villages; 2000 Brahmans were consecrated to the service of the deity, whom they washed each morning and evening with water from the distant Ganges. The subordinate-ministers consisted of 300 musicians, 300 barbers, and 500 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> girls, conspicuous for their birth or beauty. Three sides of the temple were protected by the ocean; the narrow isthmus was fortified by a natural or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> precipice, and the city and adjacent country were peopled by a nation of fanatics. They confessed the sins and the punishment of Kinnoe and Delhi; but they boasted, that if the impious stranger should presume to approach their holy precincts, he would surely be overwhelmed by a blast of the divine vengeance. By this challenge the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of Mahmud was animated to a personal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of the strength of this Indian deity. Fifty thousand of his worshippers were pierced by the spears of the Molems; the walls were scaled; the sanctuary was profaned; and the conqueror aimed a blow of his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> mace at the head of the idol. The trembling Brahmans are said to have offered ten millions <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> for his ransom; and it was urged by the wisest counsellors, that the destruction of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> image would not change the hearts of the Gentooes, and that such a sum might be dedicated to the relief of the true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEVERS">believers</a>: "Your reasons," replied the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a>, "are specious and strong; but never in the eyes of posterity, shall Mahmud appear as a merchant of idols." He repeated his blows, and a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> of pearls and rubies, concealed in the belly of the statue, explained in some degree the devout prodigality of the Brahmans. The fragments of the idol were distributed to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAZNA">Gazna</a>, Mecca, and Medina. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a> listened, says the historian, Gibbon, to the edifying tale; and Mahmud was saluted by the caliph, with the title of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">Guardian</a> of the fortune and faith of Mahomet. Adjoining to the peninsula of Guzerat, and at the city of bottom of the gulf of Cambay, stands the city of that name, which once was the capital of a considerable kingdom. It is situated in a great manufacturing country, which furnishes large quantities of coarse unbleached cotton cloth, for Persia, Arabia, Egypt, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>; also blue cloths for the same countries, and for the English and Dutch trade on the western coast of Africa; likewise blue and white checks to be used as mantles in Arabia and Turkey, some coarse, and others enriched with gold; muslins for turbans, gauzes, mixed stuffs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and cotton, and shawls made of the Cashmerean wool. This country also sends annually to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURAT">Surat</a>, Bengal, China, Persia, and Arabia, immense quantities of raw cotton, as well as rich embroideries of various kinds. From the bottom of the gulf of Cambay, the peninsula of the fafa of western India may be laid to begin in the strict Hindoostan. Asi. eft <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a>; as a line of coast here commences, which proceeds without interruption, or any considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDING">bending</a>, to Cape Comorin, the southern part of the peninsula, after which the coast suddenly turns to the north-east; and the bay of Bengal bounds the peninsula on the east. From Cambay to Cape Comorin, the western coast of the peninsula may be divided into three unequal parts. The first extends from the most advanced part of the gulf southward, a little beyond the city of Surat. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> tract of coast, which is more extensive than this, in a fourfold proportion, is called the coast of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONCAN">Concan</a>, or the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIRATE">pirate</a> coast. To the southward of this, the coast of the peninsula, all the way to Cape Comorin, receives the appellation of the Malabar coast. The first of these divisions, lying upon the eastern shore of the gulf of Cambay, consists of a low country, into which the rivers descend from the upper part of the peninsula of Hindoofan. After passing Surat, however, the physical structure of the peninsula assumes a peculiar character well worthy of attention. The Concan and Malabar coasts which form almost the whole of the western shores of the peninsula are extremely low, and a narrow stripe of level land, of from 40 to 70 miles in breadth, runs along the coast from Surat to Cape Comorin. At the back of this stripe of low land, a chain of mountains runs parallel to the sea shore. They are called the Ghauts, and rise to a surprising height, opposing to the west a lofty wall of rugged and precipitous rocks. The whole chain seems one connected crest or wall, inaccessible to the summit, unless by paths which have been worked by the hand of man, and which cannot be ascended even by a single traveller, without the fatiguing labour of many hours. From the root of these rocks, the plain towards the sea is variegated with small hills, which gradually descend into a level and fertile country, blest with a cool and healthy air. The small hills near the foot of the Ghauts are clothed with forests of the most valuable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>; and from the sides of the mountains magnificent cataracts descend, forming torrents which facilitate the conveyance of the timber to the sea coast.

ASIDE

Pages 437-437

in the Drama, something said by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a>, which some, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even all the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> present are supposed not to hear; a circumstance justly condemned as being unnatural and improbable.

ASIENTO

Pages 446-446

a Spanish word signifying a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, is used for a bargain between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> and other powers, for importing <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> into the Spanish dominions in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and particularly to Buenos Ayres. The first affiento was made with the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; and, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, transferred to the English, who were to furnish 4800 negroes annually.

ASINARA

Pages 437-437

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, on the western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 30. N. Lat. 41. 0.

ASINIUS POLLIO

Pages 437-437

a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> and orator, distinguishing himself under Augustus by his exploits and his literary works. He is frequently mentioned with praises by Horace and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, and is said to have collected the first library at Rome. He died at Frecati, at 80 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>.

ASIONGABER

Pages 437-437

ESIONGEBER, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> EZIONGEBER, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Petraea, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Elath, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Arabian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCK">dock</a> or station for the ships of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a> and Jehoshaphat; an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town, mentioned also by Moses. It was afterwards called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERENICE">Berenice</a> (Josephus).

ASISIA

Pages 437-438
or ASSISIA, a town of Liburnia (Ptolemy, Antonine), now in ruins, but exhibiting many monuments of antiquity. It is the Afferia or Afferia of Pliny. This author, after having specified the Liburnian cities that were obliged to attend the congress or diet of Scardona, adds to the catalogue the free Affarians, immuniaque Affarites; and this people, who created their own magistrates, and were governed by their own municipal laws, were no doubt more rich and powerful than their neighbours. The vestiges of the walls of Afferia that still remain, are a sufficient proof of this; for their circumference is clearly distinguishable above ground, and measures 3600 Roman feet. The space enclosed by them forms an oblong polygon, and they are built with common Dalmatian marble; but not taken from the hill on which they stand; for that furnishes only soft stone. The walls are invested, both inside and out, with this marble: some of the stones are ten feet long; and they are all of considerable dimensions. The thickness of these fortifications is commonly about eight feet: but at the narrowest extremity, which falls towards the foot of the hill, they are eleven feet thick; and, in some parts, their height still above ground reaches to near 30 feet. An antiquary, or even a simple lover of the fine arts, or of erudition, the Abbé Fortis observes, cannot help wishing at Podgorje (the modern name of Afferia); ASN Afrin), that some powerful hand quæcund sub terra est in apricum profert: and such a work becomes stronger when he reflects, that since the destruction of that city no search has ever been made under ground, with a view to discover any thing curious; and yet these walls without doubt enclose a valuable deposit of antiquities, thrown down in heaps, who knows by what cause; perhaps naturally, by an earthquake, or perhaps by a sudden inundation of barbarians, which is still worse. The gate now demolished, the considerable height of the walls to be seen in several places from without, some pieces of thick walls that still appear levelled to the ground among the bushes, are circumstances which give ground to hope that many costly monuments might be recovered out of these ruins. The magnificence of the remaining wall, and the many pieces of well-cut stone and fine marble scattered over the contiguous fields, afford sufficient proof that both good taste and grandeur once flourished in that country. In the midst of the rubbish which covers the remains of Afrin, the parish church of the little village stands insulated; it is built of broken pieces of ancient ruins, taken as they happened to be nearest, mixed with mutilated inscriptions and fragments of noble cornices.

ASISIO

Pages 438-438
or ASITIO, a city of the pope's territories in Italy, situated about 16 miles east of Perugia. E. Long. 13. 35. N. Lat. 43. ASKELON. See ASCALON.

ASITTO

Pages 437-437

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERUGIA">Perugia</a>, and in the Pope's territories. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 23. 40. N. Lat. 43. 0.

ASKERON

Pages 438-438

a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> five miles from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DONCASTER">Doncaster</a>, noted for a medicinal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. It is a strong sulphurous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and is slightly impregnated with a purging <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. It is recommended internally and externally in strumous and other ulcers, scabs, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEPROSY">leprosy</a>, and similar complaints. It is good in chronic obstructions, and in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> and foulness of the bowels.

ASKRIG

Pages 438-438

a town in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> riding of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 5. N. Lat. 53. 50.

ASLANI

Pages 438-438

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, a silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, worth from 115 to 120 alpers. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASPER">ASPER</a>.

ASMONEUS

Pages 438-438
or ASSAMONEUS, the father of Simon, and chief of the Asmonæans, a family that reigned over the Jews during 126 years.

ASNA

Pages 438-438
or ESNA, a town in Upper Egypt, seated upon the Nile, believed by some authors to be the ancient Syene, though others say the ruins of it are still to be seen near Assuan. It is so near the cataracts of the Nile, that they may be heard from thence. It contains several monuments of antiquity; and among the rest an ancient Egyptian temple, pretty entire, all painted throughout, except in some places that are effaced by time. The columns are full of hieroglyphic figures. This superb structure is now made use of for a stable, wherein they put oxen, camels, and goats. A little way from thence are the ruins of an ancient nunnery, said to be built by St. Helena, surrounded with tombs.—Asna is the principal town in these parts, and the inhabitants are rich in corn and cattle. They drive a considerable trade into Lower Egypt and Nubia, by means of the Nile, and also by the caravans that pass over the desert. The inhabitants are all Arabs, except about 200 Copts, the ancient inhabitants, and a fort of Christians. They are under the government of the Turks, who have a cadi, and the Arabs have two sheriffs of their own nation. E. Long. 31. 40. N. Lat. 33. 15.

ASOLA

Pages 438-438

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRESLAU">Breslau</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, belonging to the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. 18. N. Lat. 4. 15.

ASOLO

Pages 438-438

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the Trevilian, seated on a mountain 17 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Trevilian, and 10 north-east of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BASSANO">Bassano</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12. 2. N. Lat. 45. 49.

ASOPH

Pages 438-438

a town of Cuban <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a>, near its mouth, a little to the east of the Palus Maeotis, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of Alop. It has been several times taken and retaken of late years; but in 1730, the contending powers agreed that the fortifications should be demolished; and the town remains under the dominion of Russia. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 41. 30. N. Lat. 47. 18.

ASOPUS

Pages 438-438

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACONIA">Laconia</a>, (Pausanias;) on the Sinus Laconicus, with a port in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, between Boe to the east, and the mouth of the Eurotas to the west. The citadel only remains standing, now called by the sailors Cañel Rampano.

ASOR

Pages 438-438
or HAZOR, in Ancient Geography, a town of the tribe of Judah, to the south-west, on the borders of Ashcalon, (Joshua;) as also Hazor-Hadatha, translated by the seventy Aramaic Kama (id.). Another Asor, Aforus, or Hazor, a town of Galilee; called the capital of all the kingdoms to the north of Palestine. It was taken by Joshua; the inhabitants were put to the sword, and their houses burnt. It was afterwards rebuilt (Judges, 1 Sam.) but remained till in the hands of the Canaanites, though in the lot of the tribe of Naphtali, (Joshua.) It lay to the north of the Lacus Samachonites, called in Scripture the Waters of Merom, (Jospehus.)

ASOW

Pages 438-439

a celebrated and important fortress of Russia, once a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of considerable trade, but now demolished. It was situated in the district of Bachmut, near the place where the Greeks many centuries ago built the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Tanais, which was very famous for its trade, and underwent many vicissitudes. The Genoese, who settled a trade with Russia soon after the discovery of Archangel by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">Chancellor</a>, became masters of this place, and gave it the name of Tana, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Catana: but the Tartars, who were very powerful in these parts, seem to have been in possession of it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before; for, as Butting informs us, there are Alov coins yet extant, on which is the name of Zactamysa Kama. From the Genoese it fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Turks, lost its its trade, and became an inconsiderable town. In 1637, it was taken by the Cossacks, who defended it against the Turks in 1641, and next year let fire to it, and blew it up. The Turks rebuilt it with strong fortifications. The Russians laid claim to it in 1672, and took it in 1696; but, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of Pruth in 1711, it was restored to the Turks. In 1736, the Russians became masters of Aofow; but by the treaty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELGRADE">Belgrade</a> they were obliged to relinquish it, and entirely destroy the place.

ASP

Pages 439-439

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a small poisonous kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>, whose bite gives a speedy but easy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. It is said to be thus denominated from the Greek ἀσπίς, field, in regard to the manner of its lying convolved in a circle, in the centre of which is the head, which it exerts, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> raises, like the umbo or umbilicus of a buckler. This <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of serpent is very frequently mentioned by authors; but so carelessly described, that it is not easy to determine which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any of the species known at present, may properly be called by this name. It is said to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and about the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>; and Bellonius mentions a small species of serpent which he had met with in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and which had a sort of callous excrescence on the forehead, which he takes to have been the apsis of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. It is with the asp that Cleopatra is said to have despatched herself, and prevented the designs of Augustus, who intended to have carried her captive to adorn his triumphal entry into Rome. But the fact is contested: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">Brown</a> places it among his vulgar errors. The indications of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s having used the ministry of the asp, were only two almost invisible pricks found in her arm; and Plutarch says it is unknown what she died of. At the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, it must be observed that the lightness of the pricks found in her arm furnishes no presumption against the fact; for no more than the prick of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> point dipped in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a> was necessary for the purpose. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a> makes the asp the least painful of all the instruments of death. He supposes it to have an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> to opium, but to be less disagreeable in its operation; and his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> seems to correspond with the accounts of most writers, as well as with the effects described to have been produced upon Cleopatra. The ancients had a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> called Ἀσπιδία, made of this terrible animal, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> efficacy as a diuretic of strumae and other indurations, and used likewise against pains of the gout. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, and skin or exuviae, of the creature, had also their share in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a>.

ASPASIA OF MILETUS

Pages 439-439

a courtezan who settled at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> under the administration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERICLES">Pericles</a>, and one of the most noted ladies of antiquity. She was of admirable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>: yet her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and eloquence, still more than her beauty, gained her extraordinary reputation among all ranks in the republic. In eloquence she surpassed all her contemporaries; and her conversation was so entertaining and instructive, that notwithstanding the dishonourable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> she carried on in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ASPASIA">Aspasia</a>'s virtue, persons of the first distinction, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> and female, referred to her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> as to an academy: the even numbered <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> among her hearers and admirers. She captivated Pericles in such a manner, that he dismissed his own wife, in order to espouse her; and, by her universal knowledge, irresistible eloquence, and intriguing genius, she in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> influenced the administration of Athens. She was accused of having excited, from motives of personal resentment, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>; yet, calamitous as that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and obstinate conflict proved to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, and particularly to Athens, it may be suspected that Aspasia occasioned still more incurable evils to both. Her example, and still more her instructions, formed a school at Athens, by which her dangerous profession was reduced into system. The companions of Aspasia served as models for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> and statuary, and themes for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a>. Nor were they merely the objects, but the authors of many literary works, in which they established rules for the behaviour of their lovers, particularly at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>; and explained the art of gaining the heart and captivating the affections. The dress, behaviour, and artifices of this class of women, became continually more seductive and dangerous; and Athens thenceforth remained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> school of vice and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, as well as of literature and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>.

ASPASTICUM

Pages 439-439

(from ἀσπάστωμα, "I salute,") in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> apartment, adjoining to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> churches, wherein the bishop and presbyters sat, to receive the salutations of the persons who came to visit them, before their blessing, or consult them on business.—This is also called alpasticum diaconicum, receptorium, metatorium, or metatorium, and salutorium: in English, "greeting-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>."

ASPECT

Pages 439-439

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, denotes the situation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> and stars with respect to each other. There are five different aspects. 1. Sextile aspect is when the planets <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stars are 60° distant and marked thus ♌. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTILE">quartile</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRATURE">quadrature</a>, when they are 90° distant, marked □. 3. Trine, when 120° distant, marked Δ. 4. Opposition, when 180° distant, marked ⊙. And, 5. Conjunction, when both in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, marked &. Kepler, who added eight new ones, defines aspect to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> formed by the rays of two stars meeting on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, whereby their good or bad influence is measured: for it is to be observed, that these aspects being first introduced by astrologers, were distinguished into benign, malignant, and indifferent; the quartile and opposition being accounted malign; the trine and sextile, benign or friendly; and the conjunction, indifferent. ASPEN TREE. See Populus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ASPER

Pages 439-439

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCENT">accent</a> peculiar to the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, marked thus (') and importing, that the letters over which it is placed ought to be strongly aspirated, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pronounced as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> an b were joined with them. Asper, or Aspre, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, a Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, three of which make a Medike.

ASPERA ARTERIA

Pages 439-439

in Anatomy, the same with the windpipe <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> trachaea. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ASPERIFOLIATE

Pages 439-442
or Asperifolious, among Botanists, such plants as are rough-leaved, having their leaves... Asperifoliæ leaves placed alternately on their stalks, and a monopetalous flower divided into five parts.—They constitute an order of plants in the *Fragmenta methodi naturalis* of Linnaeus, in which are these genera, viz. tournefortia, cerinthe, lymphytum, pulmonaria, anchusa, lithospermum, myotis heliotropium, cynoglossum, alpeugo, lycopsis, echium, borrago: *magis minusve oleraceae, mucilaginose, et glutinosae sunt.* Lin. In the present system, these are among the pentandrae monogynia. **ASPERIFOLIÆ PLANTAE,** rough-leaved plants; the name of a class in Hermannus, Boerhaave, and Ray's methods, consisting of plants which have four naked seeds, and whose leaves are rough to the touch. In Tournefort's System, these plants constitute the third section or order of the second class; and in Linnaeus's Sexual Method, they make a part of the pentandrae monogynia. **ASPERITY,** the inequality of the surface of any body, which hinders the hand from passing over it freely.—From the testimony of some blind persons, it has been supposed that every colour hath its particular degree of asperity: though this has been denied by others. See the article **BLIND.** **ASPEROSA,** a town of Turkey in Europe; it is a bishop's see, situated on the coast of the Archipelago. E. Long. 25. 20. N. Lat. 40. 58. **ASPERUGO,** small wild bugloss. See Botany Index. **ASPERULA,** woodroot. See Botany Index. **ASPHALTITES,** so called from the great quantity of bitumen it produces; called also the Dead Sea; and from its situation, the East Sea; the Salt Sea, the Sea of Sodom, the Sea of the Desert, and the Sea of the Plain, in the sacred writings: A lake of Judea. Many things have been said and written of this famed, or, if they were indeed true, rather infamous lake; such as that it arose from the submersion of the vale of Siddim, where once stood, as is commonly reported, the three cities which perished in the miraculous conflagration, with those of Sodom and Gomorrah, for their unnatural and detestable wickedness: on which account this lake has been looked upon as a lasting monument of the just judgment of God, to deter mankind from such abominations. Hence it is added, that the waters of the lake are so impregnated with salt, sulphur, and other bituminous stuff, that nothing will sink or live in it; and that it casts such stench and smoke, that the very birds die in attempting to fly over it. The description likewise of the apples that grew about it, fair without, and only ashes and bitternes within, were looked upon as a farther monument of God's anger. So likewise the description which many travellers give not only of the lake, but of all the country round about, of the whole appearing dreadful to behold, all sulphurous, bituminous, stinking, and suffocating: and lastly, what hath been farther affirmed of the ruins of the five cities being still to be seen in clear weather, and having been actually seen in these latter times; all these surprising things, and ill-grounded notions, though commonly, and so long, received among Christians, have been of late so much exploded, not only by the testimony of very credible witnesses, but even by arguments drawn from Scripture, that we must give them up as inventions, unless we will suppose the face and nature of all these things, to have been entirely changed. Thoese, in particular, of bodies not sinking in the water, and of birds being stifled by the exhalations of it; appear now false in fact. It is true, the quantity of salt, alum, and sulphur, with which it is impregnated, render it so much specifically heavier (Dr Pococke says one-fifth) than fresh water, that bodies will not so easily float; yet that author, and others, assure us, they have swam and dived in it; and, as to the birds, we are told likewise, that they will fly over it without any harm. To reconcile these things with the experiments which Pliny tells us had been made by Vespa, Nat. Hist., is impossible, without supposing that those ingredients have been since much exhausted, which is not at all improbable; such quantities of them, that is, of the bitumen and salt, having been all along, and being still taken off, and such streams of fresh water continually pouring into it, as may reasonably be supposed to have considerably diminished its gravity and density. For, with respect to its salt, we are told, the Arabs make quantities of it from that lake, in large pits about the shore, which they fill with that water, and leave to be crystallized by the sun. This salt is in some cases much commended by Galen, as very wholesome, and a strengthener of the stomach, &c. on account of its unpleasing bitterness. What likewise relates to the constant smoke ascending from the lake, its changing the colour of its water three times a-day, so confidently affirmed by Josephus and other ancients, and confirmed by Prince Radziwill ib. v. cap. 5, and other moderns, who pretend to have been eyewitnesses of it, is all now in the same manner exploded by others of more modern date, and of at least equal candour. The unhealthiness of the air about the lake was affirmed by Josephus and Pliny, especially on the west: the monks that live in the neighbourhood confirm the same, and would have diffused Dr Pococke from going to it on that account; and, as he ventured to go and bathe in it, and was two days after, seized with a dizziness, and violent pain in the stomach, which lasted near three weeks, they made no doubt but it was occasioned by it; and he doth not seem to contradict them. As to the water, it is, though clear, so impregnated with salt, that those who dive into it come out covered with a kind of saline matter. There is one remarkable thing relating to this lake, generally agreed on by all travellers and geographers, viz. that it receives the waters of Jordan, a considerable river, the brooks of Jabbok, Kishon, Arnon, and other springs, which flow into it from the adjacent mountains, and yet never overflows, though there is no visible way to be found by which it discharges that great influx. Some naturalists have been greatly embarrassed to find a discharge for these waters; and have therefore been inclined to suspect the lake had a communication with the Mediterranean. But, besides that we know of no gulf to corroborate this supposition, it has been demonstrated, by accurate calculation, that evaporation is more than sufficient to carry off the waters brought by the river. It is, in fact, very considerable; and frequently becomes sensible to the eye, by the fogs with which the lake is covered at the rising of the sun, and which are afterwards dispersed by the heat. It is enclosed on the east and west with exceeding high mountains, many of them craggy and dreadful to behold. On the north it has the plain of Jericho; or, if we take in both sides of the Jordan, it has the Great Plain, properly so called, on the south; which is open, and extends beyond the reach of the eye. Josephus gives this lake 580 furlongs in length, from the mouth of the Jordan to the town of Segor, on the opposite end, that is about 22 leagues; and about 150 furlongs or 5 leagues, in its greatest breadth; but our modern accounts commonly give it 24 leagues in length, and 6 or 7 in breadth. On the west side of it is a kind of promontory, where they pretend to throw the remains of Lot's metamorphosed wife. Josephus says, it was still standing in his time; but when Prince Radziwill inquired after it, they told him there was no such tall pillar or statue to be found in all that part. However, they have found means, about a century after him, to recover, as they pretended to assure Mr Maundrell, a block or stump of it, which may in time grow up, with a little art, into its ancient bulk. It is to be observed here, that the name of Dead Sea is not to be found in the sacred writings; but hath been given to this lake because no creature will live in it, on account of its excessive saltness, or rather bituminous quality; for the Hebrews rank sulphur, nitre, and bitumen, under the general name of salt. However, some late travellers have found cause to suspect the common report of its breeding no living creature; one of them having observed, on the shore, two or three shells of fish like those of an oyster, and which he supposes to have been thrown up by the waves, at two miles distance from the mouth of the Jordan, which he there takes notice of, lest they should be suspected to have been brought into the lake by that way. And Dr Pococke, though he neither saw fish nor shells, tells us, on the authority of a monk, that some sort of fish had been caught in it; and gives us his opinion, that as so many sorts live in salt water, some kind may be so formed as to live in a bituminous one. Mr Volney, however, affirms that it contains neither animal nor vegetable life. We see no verdure on its banks, nor are fish to be found within its waters. But he adds, that it is not true that its exhalations are pestiferous, so as to destroy birds flying over it. "It is very common (says he) to see swallows skimming its surface, and dipping for the water necessary to build their nests. The real cause which deprives it of vegetables and animals is the extreme saltness of the water, which is infinitely stronger than that of the sea. The foil around it, equally impregnated with this salt, produces no plants; and the air itself, which becomes loaded with it from evaporation, and which receives also the sulphurous and bituminous vapours, cannot be favourable to vegetation; hence the deadly aspect which reigns around this lake. In other respects, the ground about it, however, is not marlily; and its waters are limpid and incorruptible, as must be the case with a dilution of salt. The origin of this mineral is easy to be discovered; for on the south-west shore are mines of fossil salt, of which I have brought away several specimens. They are situated in the side of the mountains which extend along that border; and, from time immemorial, have supplied the neighboring Arabs, and even the city of Jerusalem. We find also on this shore fragments of sulphur and bitumen, which the Arabs convert into a trifling article of commerce; as also hot fountains, and deep crevices, which are discovered at a distance by little pyramids built on the brink of them. We likewise find a fort of stone, which, on rubbing, emits a noxious smell, burns like bitumen, receives a polish like white alabaster, and is used for the paving of court-yards. At intervals, we also meet with unhewn blocks, which prejudiced eyes mistake for mutilated statues, and which pass with ignorant and superstitious pilgrims for monuments of the adventure of Lot's wife; though it is nowhere said she was metamorphosed into stone like Niobe, but into salt, which must have melted the ensuing winter." It is on account of this bitumen that it hath had the name of Asphaltite lake; it being reported to have thrown up great quantities of that drug, which was much in use among the Egyptians, and other nations, for embalming of dead bodies. Josephus affirms us, that in his days it rose in lumps as big as an ox without its head, and some even larger. But whatever it may have formerly done, we are assured by Mr Maundrell and others, that it is now to be found but in small quantities along the shore, though in much greater near the mountains on both sides the lake. But the contrary is since affirmed by two or more late * travellers; one * Pococke's whom tells us, that it is observed to float on the surface of the water, and to come on the shore after windy p. 56 weather, where the Arabians gather it, and put it to all the uses that common pitch is used for, even in the composition of some medicines; and another † tells ‡ Shew's us, he was there informed, that it was raised at certain times from the bottom, in large hemispheres, which, as soon as they touch the surface, and are acted upon by the external air, burst at once, with great noise and smoke, like the fulminans of the chemists, dispersing themselves about in a thousand pieces. From both these judicious authors we may conclude the reason of Mr Maundrell's mistake, both as to the lake's throwing it up only on certain feasts (that reverend gentleman might chance to be there at the wrong time); and likewise as to his not observing it about the shores, seeing the Arabs are there ready to gather it as soon as thrown up: all of them describe it as resembling our black pitch, so as not to be distinguished from it by its fuliginous smoke and stench when set on fire; and it hath been commonly thought to be the same with that which our druggists sell under the name of bitumen judaicum, or Jewish pitch, though we have reason to think that this last is fictitious, and that there is now none of the right asphaltum brought from Judea. It hath, moreover, been confounded with a sort of blackish combustible stone thrown on the shore, and called by some Moses's stone, which being held in the flame of a candle, will soon burn, and cast a smoke and intolerable stench; but with this extraordinary property, that though it loses much of its weight and colour, it becoming in a manner white, yet it diminishes nothing of its bulk. But these, Dr Pococke tells us, are found about two or three leagues from the shore. He concludes, however, from it, that a stratum of that stone under the lake is probably one part of the matter that feeds the subterraneous fire, and causes the bitumen to boil up out of it. **Asphaltum**, **Bitumen Judaicum**, or **Jews Pitch**, is a light solid bitumen, of a dusky colour on the outside, and a deep shining black within; of very little Asphodelus little taste; and having scarcely any smell, unless heat, when it emits a strong pitchy one. It is found in a soft or liquid state on the surface of the Dead Sea, and by age grows dry and hard. The same kind of bitumen is met with likewise in the earth, in other places of the world, in China, America, and in some places of Europe, as the Carpathian hills, France, Neufchatel, &c. There are several kinds of Jews pitch in the shops; but none of them are the genuine sort, and have little other title to their name than their being artificially compounded by Jews; and as they are a medley of what we know not what ingredients, their medicinal use begins to be deservedly laid aside, notwithstanding the diluent, solvent, pedatorial, and other virtues attributed to this bitumen by the ancients. The true asphaltum was formerly used in embalming the bodies of the dead. The thick and solid asphaltum is at present employed in Egypt, Arabia, and Persia, as pitch for ships; as the fluid ones, for burning in lamps, and for varnishes. Some writers relate, that the wall of Babylon, and the temple of Jerusalem, were cemented with bitumen instead of mortar. This much is certain, that a true natural bitumen, that for instance which is found in the district of Neufchatel, proves an excellent cement for walls, pavements, and other purposes, uncommonly firm, very durable in the air, and not penetrable by water. The watch and clock makers use a composition of asphaltum, fine lamp black, and oil of spike or turpentine, for drawing the black figures on dial plates: this composition is prepared chiefly by certain persons at Augsburg and Nuremberg. See the preceding article.

ASPHODELUS ASPHODEL

Pages 442-442
OR KING'S SPEAR:** See Botany Index. **ASPHERELATA,** in * href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural History,* are semi-metallic foils, fusible by fire, and not malleable in their purest state, being in their native state intimately mixed with sulphur and other adventitious matter, and reduced to what are called ores. Of this series of foils there are only five bodies, each of which makes a distinct genus; viz. antimony, bismuth, cobalt, zinc, and quicksilver.

ASPICUETA

Pages 442-442

MARTIN DE,** <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> of Navarre, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> *Doctor Navarrus,* was descended from a noble family, and born the 13th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1491, at Varasain, a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Navarre, not far from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PAMPLONA">Pamplona</a>. He entered very young into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of regular canons at Roncevaux, where he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, which he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to wear after he left the convent. He studied scholastic learning, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, at Alcala, in New Castile, adopting chiefly the system of Petrus Lombardus, commonly called the *<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> of the Sentences.* He applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a>, and taught it with applause at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAHORS">Cahors</a>. After being first professor of canon law at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMANCA">Salamanca</a> for 14 years, he quitted that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to be professor of law at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIMBRA">Coimbra</a>, with a larger salary. The duties of this office he discharged for the space of 20 years, and then resigned it to retire into his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, where he took care of his nieces, the daughters of his deceased brothers. Having made a journey to Rome to plead the cause of Bartholomeo de Caranza archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>, who had been accused of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> before the tribunal of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">Inquisition</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and whose cause was by the Pope's order, to be tried in that city, Aspicueta's writings, which were well known, procured him a most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> reception. Pope Pius V. made him afflant to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Francis Aciat, his vice <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENITENTIARY">penitentiary</a>; and Gregory XIII. never passed by his door without calling for him, and stopping sometimes a whole <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> to talk with him in the street. His name became so famous, that even in his lifetime the highest encomium on a learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was to call him a *Navarrus.* He was consulted as an oracle. By <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> he prolonged his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> length. His economy enabled him to give substantial proofs of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>. Being very old, he used to ride on a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULE">mule</a> through the city, and relieved all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> he met; to which his mule was so well accustomed, that it stopped of its own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a> at the sight of every poor man till its master had relieved him. He refused several honourable posts in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and state, that he might have leisure to correct and improve the works he had already written, and compose others. He died at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 94, on the 21st of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1586. He wrote a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of treatises, all which are either on morality or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law. **ASPIRATE,** in *<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>,* denotes words marked with the spiritus <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASPER">asper</a>. See *Asper.* **ASPIRATION,** among *Grammarians,* is used to denote the pronouncing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a> with some vehemence.

ASPLENIUM

Pages 442-444

CETERACH.** See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **ASS,** in *<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>,* is ranged as a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of equus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> Index. Coronation of the *Ass,* in *Antiquity,* was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of the feast of Vesta, wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAKERS">bakers</a> put <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> crowns on the heads of these <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>; *Ecce coronatis panis dependet asellis.* Hence, in an *Ovid Fasti,* <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a>, the idea of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> are thus denoted: vi. 311. *Februm est Vesae, Assus coronatur!*—This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, it seems, was done the beast, because, by its braying, it had saved Vesta from being ravished by the Lampascan god. Hence the formula, *Vesae deliciam est assinas.* **ASSAI,** in *Music,* signifies quick; and, according to others, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the piece be kept in a middle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of quickness or slowness. *As, affai allegro, affai presto.* See Allegro and Presto. **ASSANCALA,** a strong town in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>, near the river Aras, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERZERUM">Erzerum</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERIVAN">Erivan</a>, and noted for its hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. It stands on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> hill; the walls are built in a spiral line all round the rock, and strengthened with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> towers. The ditches are about two fathoms over, cut out of hard rock. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 41° 30'. N. Lat. 39° 46'. **ASSANCHIF,** a town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIARBEKIR">Diarbekir</a>, seated on the river Tigris. E. Long. 42° 30'. N. Lat. 37° 20'. **ASSANS.** See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSENS">Assens</a>. **ASSARIUM,** in *Antiquity,* denotes a small <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, being a part or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of the *as.* The word *assarion* is used by Suidas indifferently with *epaxos* and *epaxia,* to denote a small piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; in which he is followed by Cujacius, who defines *assarion* by *Minimus eritis nummus.* We find mention of the assarion in the gospel of St Matthew, chap. x. ver. 29. **ASSARON,** or *omer,* a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of capacity, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the Hebrews, containing five pints. It was the measure of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANNA">manna</a> which God appointed for every Israelite. **ASSASIN,** or *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSASSIN">assassin</a>,* a person who kills another Assassins, therewith the advantage either of an inequality in the weapons, or by means of the situation of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, or by attacking him at unawares. The word assassins is said by some to have been brought from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, where it took its rise from a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the family of the Assassins; popularly called Assassins, living in a castle between Antioch and Damascus, and bringing up a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of young men, ready to pay a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> obedience to his commands; whom he employed in murdering the princes with whom he was at enmity. But according to Mr Volney, the word Hafifassin (from the root hafif, "to kill, to assassinate, to hiten, to surprife,") in the vulgar Arabic signifies "Robbers of the night," persons who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in ambush to kill; and is very universally understood in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a> and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>. Hence it was applied to the Batenians, who flew by surprife. See the next article. There was a certain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW_OF_NATIONS"><a class="xref</a>" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of nations, an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, received in all the republics of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, whereby he that assassinated an usurper of the supreme power was declared a virtuous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. At Rome especially, after the expulsion of the kings, the law was formal and solemn, and instances of it admitted. The commonwealth armed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of any citizen, and created him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> for that moment. Assassins, a tribe or clan in Syria, called also Izmelians and Bataniens or Batenians. These people probably owed their origin to the Karmatians, a famous heretical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> among the Mahometans, who settled in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> about the year 1000; whence, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, they sent a colony into Syria, where they became possessed of a considerable tract of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Lebanon, extending itself from the neighbourhood of Antioch to Damascus. The first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> of this remarkable tribe appears to have been Hafif Sabah, a futile impostor, who by his artifices made fanatical and implicit slaves of his subjects. Their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> was compounded of that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGI">Magi</a>, the Jews, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, and the Mahometans; but the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> article of their creed was to believe that the Holy Ghost resided in their chief; that his orders proceeded from God himself, and were real declarations of his divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. To this monarch the orientals gave the name of Scheik; but he is better known in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> by the name of the Old Man of the Mountain. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, instead of being <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>, was conferred by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>; where merit, that is, a superior multiplicity and enormity of crimes, was the most effectual recommendation to a majority of suffrages. This chief, from his exalted residence on the summit of Mount Lebanon, like a vindictive deity, with the thunderbolt in his hand, sent inevitable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> to all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the world; so that from one end of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> to the other, caliphs, emperors, sultans, kings, princes, Christians, Mahometans, and Jews, every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> and people, execrated and dreaded his sanguinary power, from the stroke of which there was no security. At the least suggestion or whisper that he had threatened the death of any potentate, all immediately doubled their guards, and took every other precaution in their power. It is known that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Augustus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of France, on a premature advice that the Scheik intended to have him assassinated, instituted a new body-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> of men distinguished for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> and courage, called sergeants d'armerie, with bras clubs, bows and arrows; and he himself never appeared without a club, fortified either with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. Most sovereigns paid secretly a pension to the Scheik, however scandalous and derogatory it might be to the luster of majesty, for the safety of their persons. The Knights <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEMPLARS">Templars</a> alone dared to defy his secret machinations and open force. Indeed they were a permanent disfigured body, not to be cut off by massacres or assassinations. This barbarous prince was furnished with resources unknown to all other monarchs, even to the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> despotic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>. His subjects would prostrate themselves at the foot of his throne, requesting to die by his hand or order, as a favour by which they were sure of passing into paradise. On them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> danger made any <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>, it was an emulation to press forward; and if taken in any enterprise, they went to the place of execution with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a> unknown to others. Henry <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Champagne, who married Isabella <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Amaury king of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, passing over part of the territory of the Assassins in his way to Syria, and talking highly of his power, their chief came to meet him, "Are your subjects (said the old man of the mountain) as ready in their submission as mine?" and without flaying for an answer, made a sign with his hand, when ten young men in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, who were standing on an adjacent tower, instantly threw themselves <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. On another occasion, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a> Malek-Shah summoning the Scheik to submit himself to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and threatening him with the power of his arms, should he hesitate to comply; the latter, very composedly <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> himself towards his guards, said to one of them, "Draw your dagger, and plunge it into your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>;" and to another, "Throw yourself headlong from yonder rock." His orders were no sooner uttered than they were joyfully obeyed; and all the answer he deigned to give the sultan's envoy was, "Away to thy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, and let him know I have many thousand subjects of the same disposition." Men so ready to destroy themselves were equally alert and resolute in being the ministers of death to others. At the command of their sovereign, they made no difficulty of stabbing any prince, even on his throne; and being well versed in the different dialects, they conformed to the dress and even the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> religion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, that they might with less difficulty strike the fatal blow required by their chief. With the Saracens they were Mahometans; with the Franks, Christians; in one place they joined with the Mamelukes; in another, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>; and under this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> seized the first opportunity of executing their sanguinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>. Of this we meet with an instance in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Saladin, while he was besieging Manbedge, the celebrated Hieropolis of antiquity. Being one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, with a few attendants, and they at some distance, reconnoitring the place for the better disposition of the attack, a man rushed on him with a dagger in his hand, and wounded him on the head; but the sultan, as he was endeavouring to repeat his stroke, wrestled the dagger from him, and, after receiving several wounds, laid him dead at his feet. Before the sultan had well recovered himself, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> encountered him to finish the treachery of the former. but he met with the same fate: he was succeeded with equal fury by a third, who also fell by the hand of that magnanimous prince whom he was sent to affliliate. And it was observed, that these wretches dealt about their fruitless blows as they lay in the agonies of death. With such rapidity was this tranacted, that it was over before Saladin's guards could come to his afflantage. He retired to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENT">tent</a>, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> perturbation throwing himself on his sopha, ordered his servants to take a strict view of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, and to call all suspected persons; at the same time asking with great earnestness, "Of whom have I deserved such treacherous usage?" But it afterwards appeared, that these villains had been sent by the old man of the mountain; of whom the vizir Kamchelchin had purchased the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of Saladin, to free himself from so great a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a>, whom he could not meet in the field. To animate them in their frantic obedience, the Scheik, before their departure on such attempts, used to give them a small foretaste of some of the delights which he assured them would be their recompense in paradise. Delicious soporific drinks were given them; and while they lay asleep, they were carried into beautiful gardens, where every allurement invited their senses to the most exquisite gratifications. From these seats of voluptuousness, inflamed with liquor and enthusiastic views of perpetual enjoyments, they falled forth to perform afflications of the blackest dye. This people once had, or at least they feigned to have, an intention of embracing the Christian religion. They reigned a long time in Persia and on Mount Lebanon. Hulaku, a khan of the Mogul Tartars, in the year 655 of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEGIRA">Hegira</a>, or 1254 of the Christian era, entered their country and dispossessed them of several places; but it was not till the year 1272 that they were totally conquered. This achievement was owing to the conduct and intrepidity of the Egyptian forces sent against them by the sultan Bibaris. It has, however, been thought, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRUSES">Druses</a>, who still reside among the eminences of Mount Lebanon, and whose religion and customs are so little known, are a remnant of those barbarians.

ASSAULT

Pages 444-444

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">Military</a> Art, a furious effort made to carry a fortified <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fortress, wherein the assailants do not screen themselves by any works: while the assault continues, the batteries cease, for fear of killing their own men. The **enfans perdus** <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> first to the assault. See **Enfans Perdus**.

ASSAY

Pages 444-446

**<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a>**, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> **Say**, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METALLURGY">Metallurgy</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of the goodness, purity, value, &c. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> and metallic substances. See **Essay**. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> statutes this is called **touch**; and those who had the care of it, **keepers of the touch**.—Under Henry VI, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> cities were appointed to have touch for wrought silver-plate, 2 Hen. VI. c. i.5.—By this, one might imagine they had no better method of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSAYING">assaying</a> than the simple one by the touch-flone; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is far otherwise. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry II., the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>, then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, considering that though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> paid into the king's exchequer for his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>-rents did not answer **numero et pondera**, it might nevertheless be mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>: wherefore a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> was made, called the **trial by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBUSTION">combustion</a>**; which differs little or nothing from the present method of assaying silver. See a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of it in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Book in the Exchequer, written by Gervase of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TILBURY">Tilbury</a>, c. xxi. This trial is also called **efluum**, and the officer who made it is named **floris**. The method still in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of assaying <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver was first established by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> 1354. **Assaying**, **ars docimastica**, in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, comprehends particular manners of examining every ore, or mixed metal, according to its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, with the best-adapted fluxes; so as to discover, not only what metals, and what proportions of metal, are contained in ores; but likewise how much sulphur, vitriol, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, arsenic, finely, &c. may be obtained from every one respectively. See **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>**. Assaying is more particularly used by moneyers and goldsmiths, for the making a proof or trial by the cuppel, or teit, of the fineness or purity of the gold and silver to be used in the coining of money, and manufacture of plate, &c. or that have been already used therein. There are two kinds of assaying; the one before metals are melted, in order to bring them to their proper fineness; the other after they are struck, to see that the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> be standard. For the first assay, the assayer is used to take 14 or 15 grains of gold, and half a drachm of silver, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be for money; and 18 grains of the one, and a drachm of the other, if for other occasions. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> assay, it is made of one of the pieces of money already coined, which they cut in four parts. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of gold for an assay among us is six grains; in France nearly the same; and in Germany, about three times as much. The proper <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPELLING">spelling</a> of that word, however, is **es-say**; under which article, therefore, the reader <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> find the subject more particularly treated. **Assay-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">Balance</a>**, or **Effay-Balance**. The flat pieces of glass often placed under the scales of an assay-balance, seem, by their power of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a>, capable of attracting, and thereby making the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> preponderate, where the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> weighed is so very small. See **Effay-Balance**. The electricity of a flat surface of about three inches <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> has been known to hold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> one scale, when there were about 200 grains <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> in the other. See **Balance**. **Assay-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a>**, or **Effay-Master**, an officer under certain corporations, intrusted with the care of making true touch, or assay, of the gold and silver brought to him; and giving a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> report of the goodness or badness thereof. Such is the assay-master of the mint in the Tower, called also **effayer of the king**. The assay-master of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDSMITH">goldsmith</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> is a sort of assistant-warden, called also a **touch-warden**, appointed to survey, assay, and mark all the silver <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, &c. committed committed to him.
